video:video.video:title: 1942 – Did Capcom’s Arcade Shooter Survive on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Capcom and brought to the Commodore 64 in 1986 by Elite Systems, 1942 is a vertically scrolling shoot ’em up set against the backdrop of World War II. Players step into the role of “Super Ace,” piloting a P-38 Lightning through 32 enemy-packed stages filled with hostile aircraft, naval threats, and intense aerial combat. Gameplay is fast and demanding, centred on precision flying and pattern recognition. Players blast through waves of enemies, deploy screen-clearing bombs, and make use of the game’s signature loop-the-loop manoeuvre to evade incoming fire. Power-ups increase survivability, but careful timing and positioning are essential as the difficulty steadily ramps up. The Commodore 64 version does an admirable job of capturing the arcade original’s feel, with smooth vertical scrolling, responsive controls, and an atmospheric soundtrack by Mark Cooksey that drives the action forward.

video:video.video:title: 20 Tons – A Forgotten Boulder Dash-Style C64 Challenge
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Chris Newcombe and published by Argus Press Software for the Commodore 64, 20 Tons is a single-player puzzle-action game inspired by the maze-based mechanics popularised in the mid-1980s. Players are tasked with navigating compact underground levels while collecting all the rings needed to progress. Gameplay revolves around careful movement and planning. Falling boulders can be pushed to clear paths, trigger chain reactions, or eliminate threats, but a single misstep can result in being crushed. Timing is crucial, as each level demands observation, patience, and an understanding of how the environment reacts to player actions. The C64 version features bright, colourful graphics and a lively soundtrack that keeps the pace engaging while you work through increasingly demanding layouts. Although often compared to Boulder Dash, 20 Tons has its own identity, with tighter spaces and a greater emphasis on controlled movement and risk management.

video:video.video:title: 720 Degrees – Could the C64 Handle Atari’s Skateboarding Arcade Hit?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64 by Tiertex Design Studios and published by U. S. Gold, 720° is a faithful home conversion of Atari Games’ iconic arcade skateboarding hit. Players skate through the vibrant Skate City hub, earning tickets by scoring points in order to unlock access to four challenge parks: Ramp, Downhill, Slalom, and Jump. Each park features timed stunt events that test balance, speed, and precision, with trick spins, slalom gates, and hazardous obstacles standing between you and high scores. Fail to complete events quickly enough and Skate City becomes even more dangerous, introducing hazards such as water traps and swarms of bees. Between events, players can visit in-game shops to spend prize money on upgraded boards, pads, and helmets that improve performance and survivability. The UK and European C64 version is especially praised for its smoother scrolling, weightier controls, and strong SID soundtrack by Ben Daglish.

video:video.video:title: A Nightmare on Elm Street – Could You Survive Freddy Krueger on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 and developed by Westwood Associates, A Nightmare on Elm Street brings the iconic horror film series to the Commodore 64 in an unusual top-down action-adventure format. Loosely inspired by the Dream Warriors era of the films, the game blends exploration, combat, and light RPG mechanics into a tense and atmospheric experience. Players choose from six characters, each equipped with a unique dream power that influences how the game unfolds. The main objective is to explore Elm Street, locate Freddy Krueger’s house, and navigate its maze-like interior while rescuing trapped friends and surviving a range of nightmarish enemies. Progress relies on careful exploration, item use, and learning how each character’s abilities affect combat and puzzle-solving. The gameplay runs in real time, with Freddy able to appear suddenly and attack without warning, keeping tension high throughout.

video:video.video:title: A Question of Sport – Could You Beat the BBC Quiz on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Elite Systems for the Commodore 64, A Question of Sport brings the long-running BBC television quiz show to home computers. You assemble teams of sporting experts and compete across a full studio-style quiz format, testing knowledge rather than reflexes. The game follows the structure of the TV show closely, featuring rounds such as Picture Board, Mystery Personality, Home or Away, What Happened Next? , Quickfire, and a final Picture Board. Each team is made up of three personalities, chosen from a wider pool, with each member specialising in a different sport. Picking the right balance becomes part of the strategy. Gameplay uses a point-and-click interface to select answers and interact with the quiz rounds. While the Commodore 64 version lacks some of the digitised presentation found on later 16-bit systems, it keeps the core mechanics intact and supports both single-player and competitive two-player matches.

video:video.video:title: Accolade’s Comics – The C64 Game That Played Like an Interactive Comic
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Accolade’s Comics is an experimental adventure-action title developed by Distinctive Software and published by Accolade. Designed by Don Mattrick and Jeff Sember, the game stars wisecracking secret agent Steve Keene in a globe-trotting spy caper told through an interactive comic book format. The experience alternates between story and action. In the comic panel sections, players make decisions that influence the direction of the narrative, echoing the structure of Choose Your Own Adventure books and giving the story a branching feel. Between story beats, the game switches to arcade-style sequences that test reflexes and timing. These include swimming through hazardous waters, climbing obstacles, and surviving combat encounters, adding tension and variety to the unfolding plot. Visually, Accolade’s Comics stands out for its animated comic panels and bold presentation, which helped it feel fresh and different from traditional adventures of the time.

video:video.video:title: Ace of Aces – The C64 Bomber Sim That Threw You Into Enemy Skies
video:video.video:description: Ace of Aces is a classic World War II combat flight simulator developed by Artech Digital Entertainment and released in 1986 for the Commodore 64. Published by Accolade in North America and U. S. Gold in Europe, the game puts you in the cockpit of a British RAF Mosquito twin-engine fighter-bomber on a wide range of dangerous combat missions. Players take part in aerial operations including intercepting enemy bombers, destroying V-1 flying bombs, attacking trains, and hunting U-boats — all viewed from multiple immersive perspectives such as cockpit, wing, bomb bay, and navigation map. The game stands out for its ambitious design, featuring mission planning, adjustable fuel and weapon loadouts, and environmental effects such as clouds and thunderstorms that impact visibility and atmosphere. Although reviews were mixed at release, Ace of Aces became one of Accolade’s best-selling Commodore 64 titles and is now remembered as one of the most ambitious flight simulators on 8-bit hardware.

video:video.video:title: Action Biker – Clumsy Colin’s Strange C64 Motorbike Adventure
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Mastertronic, Action Biker is a distinctive isometric motorcycle game for the Commodore 64 that puts players in control of Clumsy Colin, the mascot from KP Skips. Rather than traditional racing, the game focuses on free-roaming exploration across a sprawling town as you prepare for a climactic drag race. Gameplay revolves around navigating the city to locate vital bike upgrades, including a turbocharger, improved gearbox, and larger fuel tank. These items are essential for overcoming obstacles such as lakes, fairgrounds, construction sites, and other environmental challenges scattered throughout the map. Fuel management and careful riding are key, as collisions can quickly halt progress. The open-ended structure encourages exploration and planning, with optional routes and surprises along the way, including a memorable rollercoaster section that adds variety to the experience. Action Biker is further elevated by Rob Hubbard’s instantly recognisable soundtrack, which brings energy and momentum to the ride.

video:video.video:title: Action Service – The C64 Military Game That Let You Build Your Own Combat Course
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by CobraSoft for the Commodore 64, Action Service is an ambitious military training simulation, also known in North America as Combat Course. Players step into the boots of a trainee soldier, facing a series of demanding exercises designed to test endurance, reflexes, and tactical awareness. The game uses a split-screen interface, with the upper display showing vital status information and the lower section presenting the action. Gameplay centres on completing structured training modules, including obstacle courses, combat drills, and manoeuvre challenges that require precise timing and coordination. Players must master a wide range of actions such as running, crawling, jumping, and weapon handling in order to progress. Each course demands careful control and planning, rewarding patience and disciplined execution over fast reflexes alone. A notable feature is the built-in level editor, which allows players to design and share their own custom training courses.

video:video.video:title: After Burner – Could the C64 Keep Up with Sega’s Supersonic Arcade Hit?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Activision, After Burner brings Sega’s high-speed arcade jet combat to the Commodore 64. You take control of an F-14 Tomcat, diving straight into intense dogfights viewed from a behind-the-plane perspective that aims to recreate the thrill of supersonic flight. Gameplay focuses on fast reactions and positioning as you blast enemy aircraft with machine guns and homing missiles while weaving through incoming fire. Stages escalate quickly, throwing waves of enemies at you to test your reflexes and endurance as you chase high scores. On the C64, the game captures the core feel of the arcade experience, though hardware limits mean simpler visuals and no in-game music. Even so, the sense of speed and constant pressure remains intact, making it a solid example of ambitious arcade conversion design. Later released as a budget title by The Hit Squad in the UK, After Burner remains a nostalgic reminder of how developers pushed 8-bit hardware to deliver blockbuster arcade action at home.

video:video.video:title: Agony – The Amiga Shooter Where an Owl Took on a Nightmare World
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992, Agony is a horizontally scrolling shooter for the Commodore Amiga developed by Art & Magic and published by Psygnosis. Players take control of Alestes, a magician’s apprentice transformed into an owl, journeying through a dark, surreal fantasy world filled with twisted creatures and nightmarish landscapes. Unlike many shooters of the era, Agony places less emphasis on relentless speed and more on exploration, positioning, and deliberate combat. Levels are densely detailed and encourage careful movement, with enemies and hazards woven into the environment rather than simply streamed in waves. Boss encounters are visually striking and contribute heavily to the game’s oppressive atmosphere. One of Agony’s defining features is its audiovisual presentation. The richly illustrated backgrounds, fluid animations, and distinctive art style showcase the Amiga’s strengths, while the atmospheric soundtrack enhances the sense of unease and immersion throughout the journey.

video:video.video:title: Airborne Ranger – The C64 Game That Dropped You Behind Enemy Lines
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Airborne Ranger is a distinctive action-simulation title developed by MicroProse that places players in the role of an elite U. S. Army Airborne Ranger operating deep behind enemy lines. The game blends fast-paced action with careful planning, setting it apart from more straightforward shooters of the era. Each mission begins with a detailed briefing and loadout phase, where players choose weapons, explosives, and medical supplies to be delivered via supply pods. This is followed by a parachute insertion sequence, requiring careful decisions about drop locations before landing in hostile territory. On the ground, gameplay shifts to tense tactical action as players navigate varied environments, avoid patrols, engage enemies, and complete objectives such as rescues, sabotage, or high-value captures. Time pressure adds urgency, as successful extraction is just as important as mission completion.

video:video.video:title: Airwolf – Why Was This C64 TV Licence So Brutally Difficult?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Elite Systems for the Commodore 64, Airwolf is a licensed action-shooter based on the popular television series, placing players in control of Stringfellow Hawke’s advanced military helicopter. The mission centres on rescuing five trapped scientists from a vast underground complex, requiring careful navigation through narrow caverns filled with hazards and enemy defences. Gameplay focuses on precise flying, with players managing momentum, gravity, missiles, shields, and fuel while blasting through walls and activating switches to open new routes. Progress demands accurate positioning and timing, as falling debris, tight corridors, and hostile fire punish even minor mistakes. Visually, the game delivers colourful 8-bit sprites and smooth side-scrolling environments that maintain a strong sense of speed and tension. The experience is enhanced by a looping rendition of the iconic Airwolf television theme by Sylvester Levay, adapted effectively for the SID chip.

video:video.video:title: Aladdin – Better Than You Remember? | Commodore Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released for the Commodore Amiga in 1994 by Virgin Interactive, Aladdin is a colourful platform game based on Disney’s hugely successful animated film. Developed from the same design as the Mega Drive version, the Amiga port brought the adventure of Agrabah to home computer players with detailed sprites, lively animation, and fast arcade-style gameplay. Players take control of Aladdin as he runs, jumps, and fights his way through stages inspired by the movie. From the busy rooftops of Agrabah to the treacherous Cave of Wonders and the Sultan’s palace, each level mixes precise platforming with combat using Aladdin’s scimitar or thrown apples to defeat enemies. The game also includes collectible gems, bonus tokens, and special mini-games featuring Genie and Abu. These extra challenges provide opportunities to earn additional lives and rewards, encouraging players to explore levels carefully rather than simply rushing to the exit.

video:video.video:title: Alcatraz – Was This Amiga Commando Mission Worth Revisiting?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Infogrames for the Commodore Amiga, Alcatraz is a fast-paced action-shooter developed by 221B Software Developments that blends side-scrolling combat with first-person stealth gameplay. Players take on the role of a U. S. Navy SEAL sent to storm Alcatraz prison, destroy hidden weapons caches, and capture the criminal mastermind controlling the operation. The game is divided into multiple levels that alternate between outdoor run-and-gun sections and indoor infiltration missions. Outdoor stages feature heavy firepower such as flamethrowers, machine guns, and grenades, while indoor sections focus on radar-guided navigation and precision shooting. This dual-perspective design creates constant variety, requiring players to adapt their tactics between fast reflex-based combat and careful stealth-based movement. Alcatraz supports both single-player and two-player split-screen cooperative play, allowing friends to tackle missions together and coordinate their strategies. Visually, the game delivers smooth animations, detailed environments, and strong visual effects that were widely praised in contemporary Amiga magazines.

video:video.video:title: Alcazar: The Forgotten Fortress – 22 Castles Between You and the Crown | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Activision for the Commodore 64, Alcazar: The Forgotten Fortress is an ambitious action-adventure game designed and programmed by Tom Loughry. Players set out on a quest to recover a stolen crown by navigating a dynamically generated world map filled with twenty-two castles, each containing unique layouts, hazards, and hidden treasures. Gameplay is presented from a top-down perspective, with every castle forming a maze of interconnected rooms. Players must overcome traps, enemies, and environmental puzzles in order to progress. A variety of tools and items aid exploration and combat, including pistols, grappling hooks, magic carpets, and secret passages. Limited ammunition and careful resource management add a strong strategic element. The game features multiple difficulty levels and a built-in demonstration mode, both of which were advanced features for home computer games of the mid-1980s.

video:video.video:title: Alien – Why Didn’t the Nostromo Crew Always Obey Your Orders? | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Concept Software and published by Argus Press Software for the Commodore 64, ALIEN is a tense hybrid of strategy and adventure inspired by Ridley Scott’s 1979 science-fiction classic. Set aboard the doomed spaceship Nostromo, the game challenges players to manage a vulnerable crew while a deadly alien stalks the corridors. Gameplay unfolds in real time from a top-down perspective, with players controlling all seven crew members simultaneously. Each character has an individual emotional state, ranging from calm and confident to panicked and broken, directly affecting their performance and chances of survival. Balancing morale, positioning, and resources is essential to keeping the team alive. Progression depends on careful exploration and intelligent decision-making. Players must search the ship for weapons, oxygen tanks, and vital equipment while tracking the alien’s movements and planning ambushes.

video:video.video:title: Alien Breed – Why Team17’s Amiga Shooter Still Feels So Tense
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Team17, Alien Breed is a tense top-down run-and-gun shooter for the Commodore Amiga, heavily inspired by the atmosphere and themes of the Alien film series. Set aboard a sprawling, maze-like space station, players must survive relentless alien infestations while uncovering keys, unlocking doors, and racing against time to trigger self-destruct systems. Gameplay blends fast-paced action with strategic resource management. Ammunition, health packs, and credits are limited, forcing players to carefully plan each encounter and explore thoroughly. A wide range of weapons adds variety to combat, each delivering distinct firepower and visual impact as alien hordes close in from all directions. The experience is elevated by strong visual design and moody lighting that enhances tension throughout the station. Allister Brimble’s atmospheric soundtrack and sound effects amplify the sense of isolation and danger, making every corridor feel threatening and unpredictable.

video:video.video:title: Aliens: The Computer Game – Why Did the C64 Get Two Completely Different Versions
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 for the Commodore 64, Aliens: The Computer Game arrived in two distinct versions. The US release was developed by Activision, while the European version was handled by Software Studios and published by Electric Dreams. Both were based on James Cameron’s Aliens, but each took a very different approach to translating the film onto 8-bit hardware. The Activision version is built around six mini-missions that mirror key moments from the movie. These range from piloting the Sulaco dropship and navigating air-duct mazes to managing a squad of marines and confronting the Alien Queen. Gameplay switches between fast joystick-driven action and tactical decision-making inside the Mobile Tactical Operations Bay, where players monitor stamina, ammunition, and marine status. Exploration plays a major role, with a sprawling maze of up to 255 rooms filled with aliens, acid pools, and limited resources.

video:video.video:title: Alleykat – Andrew Braybrook’s Overlooked C64 Racing Shooter
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Hewson Consultants and developed by Andrew Braybrook, Alleykat is a technically ambitious hybrid that blends vertical scrolling shooter action with high-speed futuristic racing. Set within a competitive racing league, players pilot a multi-mode speeder across hostile tracks packed with obstacles and enemy threats. Gameplay revolves around completing laps while managing speed, firepower, and energy reserves. The speeder can switch between different flight modes, each affecting handling and weapon strength, forcing players to adapt on the fly. Tracks are filled with destructible scenery and aggressive enemies, including the infamous Katerkiller, a relentless caterpillar-like menace that demands quick reactions and precise control. A variety of race types keep the structure varied, ranging from time-based challenges to endurance events with shifting priorities. Energy management is critical, as collisions and sustained damage can quickly end a run if resources aren’t carefully balanced.

video:video.video:title: Alter Ego – The C64 Game That Let You Live an Entire Life
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Activision and designed by Peter J. Favaro for the Commodore 64, Alter Ego is a pioneering life simulation RPG that broke away from traditional game design. Instead of focusing on combat or high scores, it invites players to shape the life of an imaginary character and experience the long-term consequences of their decisions. The game begins with a detailed personality test that determines core attributes such as confidence, intelligence, and physical health. From there, players guide their alter ego through seven stages of life, from infancy to old age, facing moral, social, and practical choices that influence relationships, careers, and personal development. Progression is entirely choice-driven, with each decision subtly altering future opportunities and risks. Some paths lead to success and fulfilment, while others can result in failure, regret, or even premature death, giving the game remarkable emotional depth and replay value.

video:video.video:title: American 3D Pool – Did the Commodore 64 Need a 3D Pool Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 for the Commodore 64, American 3D Pool is an ambitious cue sports game developed by Zeppelin Games that attempted something rarely seen on 8-bit hardware: a first-person, pseudo-3D pool simulation. Instead of the usual overhead view, the game places players right at table level, emphasising depth, angles, and shot precision. Gameplay revolves around realistic aiming, power control, and judging perspective. The 3D-style camera changes how shots are lined up, forcing players to think carefully about spin, force, and positioning rather than relying on simple top-down geometry. This approach added a surprising amount of strategy and skill to each frame of play. Technically, American 3D Pool pushes the Commodore 64 hard, using clever shading and perspective tricks to create the illusion of depth on an 8-bit system. While performance is naturally limited by the hardware, the table, balls, and collision physics feel convincing for the era, with simple but effective sound effects reinforcing each shot.

video:video.video:title: Android 2 – Five Millitoids, One Maze and a Ticking Clock on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 for the Commodore 64, Android 2 (also known as Android Two) is a top-down sci-fi maze shooter developed by Costa Panayi and published by Vortex Software. You control a lone android dropped into a hostile, futuristic maze with one objective: eliminate five deadly Millitoids before time runs out. Gameplay blends fast maze navigation with careful combat. The wrap-around arena design keeps enemies constantly in play, while hazards like landmines, indestructible robots, and hostile aliens force you to think several moves ahead. Ammunition is limited, so success depends on positioning, timing, and knowing when to engage or evade. What truly sets Android 2 apart is its technical ambition. The scrolling, pseudo-3D maze was highly unusual for early 1980s home computers, giving the game a strong arcade feel and a real sense of depth and motion.

video:video.video:title: Android Nim – Can This 1985 C64 Game Outsmart You?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1982 by Courbois Software for the Commodore 64, Android Nim is a clever one-player adaptation of the classic Nim strategy game, later redeveloped in 1985 by Don Dennis and Pete Gerrard for Argus Press Software and 64 Tape Computing. Players face off against an android opponent, taking turns to remove figures from multiple stacks, with the goal of forcing the computer to take the final piece. Each turn is enhanced by animated android characters that move, aim, and react before making their choice, adding personality and tension to an otherwise minimalist puzzle format. The game supports both keyboard and joystick control, allowing players to carefully calculate winning positions and engage in a pure battle of logic and foresight. Its intelligent AI and clear presentation make every match feel like a genuine mental duel, rewarding players who learn optimal strategies.

video:video.video:title: Andy Capp – Who Turned a Missing Dole Cheque into a Commodore 64 Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Mirrorsoft and developed by Blitter Animations, Andy Capp brings the iconic British comic strip to the Commodore 64 in a surprisingly ambitious life-simulation adventure. Players step into the shoes of Andy himself, attempting to survive a chaotic week of everyday life without running out of money—or patience. Gameplay unfolds across fixed-screen locations as time rapidly ticks through the days of the week. Players must juggle Andy’s priorities, including securing unemployment benefits, managing cash, visiting the pub, dodging the police, and dealing with his long-suffering wife, Flo. Choices and timing are crucial, as certain locations and characters are only available at specific times. The presentation leans heavily into the comic’s roots, with monochrome visuals that closely resemble the original artwork. The soundtrack famously features a rendition of Dvořák’s New World Symphony, an unusual but memorable choice that gives the game a distinctive identity.

video:video.video:title: Another World – The Amiga Game That Looked Like Nothing Else in 1991
video:video.video:description: Released in November 1991 by Delphine Software for the Commodore Amiga, Another World is a groundbreaking cinematic platform adventure created by Éric Chahi. The game follows physicist Lester Knight Chaykin, who is thrown into a hostile alien world after a failed experiment, with its story told entirely through visuals and atmosphere rather than text or dialogue. Gameplay blends precise platforming, environmental puzzles, and tense combat as players guide Lester through dangerous landscapes filled with alien creatures and deadly traps. Survival depends on observation, timing, and learning from mistakes, creating a challenging but deeply immersive experience. A key gameplay feature is Lester’s energy gun, which can fire standard shots, generate protective shields, and unleash powerful charged blasts. Mastering these abilities is essential for overcoming enemies and solving environmental obstacles throughout the journey. Visually, Another World stands out for its use of vector-style graphics and fluid animation, delivering expressive characters and cinematic scenes that were years ahead of their time.

video:video.video:title: Ant Attack – Why Did This C64 Game Feel So Unsettling?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64 by Quicksilva, following its original 1983 Spectrum debut by Sandy White, Ant Attack is a pioneering isometric adventure that introduced true three-dimensional movement to home computer gaming. Set in the surreal walled city of Antescher, inspired by the artwork of M. C. Escher, players choose to control either a boy or a girl on a dangerous rescue mission. The objective is to navigate the maze-like city, avoid towering hostile ants, and locate your captured partner before time runs out. Movement allows players to travel forward, backward, sideways, and vertically, creating a genuine sense of height and depth rarely seen at the time. Ants can be temporarily stunned by jumping on them or by using limited grenades, though careless use can put both characters at risk. Once the captive is found, players must carefully guide them to safety, with the rescued character following at a slight delay that demands precise navigation.

video:video.video:title: Antheads – Did the Amiga Giant Ant Sequel Deserve More Attention?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Cinemaware, Antheads: It Came from the Desert II is a direct sequel to the cult classic It Came from the Desert, pushing the story five years into a darker, more unsettling future. The once-quiet town of Lizard Breath is again under threat—this time from townsfolk mutating into terrifying ant-headed creatures. Players step into the role of Brick Nash, now a war veteran turned truck driver, drawn back into the mystery as the town unravels. The game retains Cinemaware’s signature blend of real-time exploration, dialogue-driven encounters, and action sequences, all unfolding under a strict 15-day countdown that keeps the pressure firmly on. While it reuses much of the original game’s structure and assets, Antheads introduces new story beats, locations, and a heavier emphasis on investigation. The tone is noticeably darker, with paranoia and body-horror elements replacing some of the B-movie camp of its predecessor.

video:video.video:title: Apocalypse – Five Missions, No Saves… Was This Amiga Shooter Too Harsh?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1994 by Miracle Games for the Commodore Amiga, Apocalypse is a helicopter-based shoot ’em up inspired by classics like Choplifter. You take control of a combat chopper flying deep into hostile jungle territory, tasked with rescuing prisoners of war while dismantling enemy defences. Gameplay unfolds across fast-moving, multi-scrolling missions featuring parallax jungle backdrops and constant pressure from tanks, enemy helicopters, watchtowers, and heavy artillery. Success depends on precise control, careful positioning, and knowing when to press the attack or pull back to stay alive. Each mission challenges you to balance rescue objectives with aggressive combat, all while navigating tight terrain and deadly hazards that punish even small mistakes. Instant-death threats demand sharp reflexes and disciplined flying rather than reckless firepower. Short but intense, Apocalypse delivers a focused burst of Amiga-era action. It’s remembered as a tough, no-nonsense shooter that rewards skill and concentration, offering a satisfying challenge for fans of helicopter combat games.

video:video.video:title: Apollo 18 – Could the C64 Really Simulate a Mission to the Moon?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Accolade and developed by Artech, Apollo 18: Mission to the Moon is an ambitious space simulation for the Commodore 64 that imagines an alternate-history Apollo mission. Players take full control of a lunar expedition, managing every phase from launch and orbital docking to moon landing, EVA missions, and the perilous return to Earth. Gameplay is divided into distinct, skill-based mission segments that demand precision and concentration. Tasks such as orbital rendezvous and lunar descent require careful monitoring of instruments, fuel levels, and timing, capturing the tension and complexity of real-world spaceflight. One of the game’s most striking features is its use of digitized speech for mission control, a rare and immersive touch on 8-bit hardware. Combined with realistic telemetry readouts and functional interfaces, the game delivers an experience that feels both educational and dramatic.

video:video.video:title: Arachnophobia – Did This Spider-Filled Film Licence Work on C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by BlueSky Software and published by Disney Software for the Commodore 64, Arachnophobia is an action-packed adaptation of the horror-comedy film that casts players as fearless exterminator Delbert McClintock. The mission takes you across eight spider-infested towns in the USA and deep into the Amazon, battling a growing infestation that threatens every location. Gameplay blends top-down van exploration with tense side-view platform stages set inside houses, farms, schools, and graveyards. Players wield the versatile Toxi-Max pesticide in spray or flame mode, alongside powerful bombs, to destroy spiders and their constantly regenerating egg sacs. An onboard arachno-detector warns of nearby threats, while rescuing trapped civilians adds extra scoring and risk-reward strategy. Enemy behaviour varies, with spiders crawling on ceilings, leaping from hiding places, and ambushing from multiple angles. Boss encounters against giant queen spiders and South American creatures provide climactic tests of skill and resource management.

video:video.video:title: Arcade Classics – Asteroids, Invaders, Snakes AND Space Wars on One C64 Release
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, Arcade Classics is a nostalgic compilation that brings together four reimagined arcade favourites in one polished package. Developed by David Korn with music by Rob Hubbard, the collection celebrates the golden age of coin-op gaming while showcasing the C64’s home arcade potential. The compilation features updated versions of Asteroids, Snakes, Space Invaders, and Space Wars, each adapted to suit the strengths of the Commodore 64. Familiar mechanics are enhanced with smoother controls, improved visuals, and refined sound, delivering experiences that feel both authentic and refreshed. Asteroids challenges players to navigate dense asteroid fields while blasting debris and enemy craft with precise timing. Snakes offers a fast-paced twist on the classic growing-line formula, demanding sharp reflexes and careful movement. Space Invaders recreates the iconic alien assault with upgraded presentation, while Space Wars delivers intense two-player duels influenced by gravity-based physics.

video:video.video:title: Arcade Flight Simulator – WWI, WWII AND WWIII in One C64 Shooter
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989, Arcade Flight Simulator is a top-down, horizontally scrolling shoot ’em up for the Commodore 64 developed by Amazing Games and published by Codemasters. Despite its misleading title, the game focuses firmly on fast-paced arcade action rather than realistic flight simulation. The game is split across three distinct eras of aerial warfare. Players dogfight in fragile biplanes during World War I, take on classic prop-driven combat in World War II over the Pacific, and finish with futuristic jet battles set in a fictional World War III scenario. Each stage brings different enemies, aircraft, and visual styles. Gameplay centres on shooting down enemy planes, destroying ground targets, and managing fuel by landing safely to refuel mid-mission. The constantly scrolling landscapes keep the action moving, while a two-player mode allows head-to-head aerial battles, adding a competitive edge.

video:video.video:title: Arcade Pool – Was This Team17’s Most Addictive Amiga Sports Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1994 by Team17 for the Commodore Amiga, Arcade Pool is a polished top-down cue sports game that blends accessible arcade-style play with surprisingly deep and realistic simulation mechanics. It quickly became a favourite among Amiga owners looking for both competitive and casual multiplayer fun. The game includes several popular pool variants, such as UK 8-ball, US 9-ball, and Killer, with options to compete against computer opponents or up to eight players in hot-seat multiplayer. Its intuitive aiming system and responsive controls make it easy to learn, while still rewarding precision and tactical thinking. Arcade Pool stands out for its convincing ball physics, clean visual presentation, and smooth animation. Subtle touches such as custom player names, humorous in-game messages, and Team17’s trademark personality give the game added charm and replay value. Rather than aiming for strict realism, the game strikes a careful balance between authenticity and fun.

video:video.video:title: Archon – The C64 Chess Game Where the Pieces Fought Back
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Free Fall Associates and published by Electronic Arts, Archon: The Light and the Dark is a pioneering hybrid that blends turn-based strategy with fast-paced real-time combat. Designed by Jon Freeman and Paul Reiche III, with programming by Anne Westfall, the game challenges players to command either the forces of Light or Dark in a battle for control of a magical board. The board resembles a chess layout, but instead of static captures, opposing pieces trigger one-on-one real-time battles when they meet. Each creature has unique movement patterns, strengths, and special abilities, making positioning and timing just as important as combat skill. Control is achieved by occupying five power points or eliminating the opposing army entirely. Light and Dark units offer distinct play styles, from agile and precise to powerful and aggressive, ensuring that no two matches play out the same.

video:video.video:title: Arctic Shipwreck – Can You Survive Stranded in the Frozen North? | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Commodore International for the Commodore 64, Arctic Shipwreck is an early adventure game built around survival, strategy, and isolation. You take on the role of a ship’s captain left stranded in the Arctic following a devastating shipwreck, with nothing but your wits to keep you alive. Gameplay focuses on careful decision-making and resource management. Every move matters as you navigate icy terrain, avoid environmental dangers, and search for supplies that may mean the difference between survival and failure. Progress depends on planning ahead, managing limited resources, and learning how to use the harsh environment to your advantage. The presentation is deliberately minimal, using simple graphics and sparse sound to reinforce the bleak, hostile setting. This stripped-back approach helps build tension and atmosphere, making each choice feel weighty and consequential. Arctic Shipwreck stands out as one of the Commodore 64’s early survival-focused experiences, offering a slower, more thoughtful challenge compared to arcade-heavy titles of the era.

video:video.video:title: Arkanoid – Did the C64 Get One of the Best Arcade Conversions of 1987?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Taito and ported to the Commodore 64 by Imagine Software, Arkanoid is one of the most iconic block-breaking games of the 1980s. Players control the paddle-shaped spaceship Vaus, bouncing an energy ball to smash through colourful brick formations and clear each stage without letting the ball fall. Gameplay is built around precision, timing, and fast reactions, with increasingly complex layouts and enemy hazards appearing as the game progresses. The introduction of power-ups such as multi-ball, laser paddles, extended bats, and speed modifiers adds strategic depth and keeps every stage feeling fresh and unpredictable. Progression depends on mastering ball control, anticipating rebounds, and making smart use of collected upgrades. Later levels demand near-perfect positioning and concentration, rewarding skilled players with high scores and extended survival. The Commodore 64 version closely follows the original arcade release, delivering vibrant visuals and smooth animation that capture the feel of the coin-op experience.

video:video.video:title: Army Moves – Was This C64 Action Game Difficult for the Wrong Reasons?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Army Moves is a tough scrolling action shooter developed by Dinamic Software and published by Imagine Software. As the first entry in the famous Moves trilogy, it tasks players with a dangerous military mission to recover stolen secret documents from heavily guarded enemy territory. The game is split into two distinct gameplay phases across seven levels. The opening stages place you in control of a jeep and later a helicopter, navigating hostile landscapes packed with enemy vehicles, gun emplacements, and relentless fire. These sections demand sharp reflexes, precise positioning, and constant awareness as threats attack from all directions. The final stages switch perspective to on-foot action, transforming the game into a tense platform shooter. Players must infiltrate enemy bases, dodge grenades, avoid traps, and carefully time jumps while pushing deeper into fortified areas.

video:video.video:title: Arnie – Zeppelin’s £3.99 C64 Shooter Dropped You Behind Enemy Lines
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Zeppelin Games for the Commodore 64, Arnie is a fast-paced action shooter that arrived late in the system’s lifespan and leaned hard into pure arcade intensity. Players control Arnie, a lone futuristic soldier fighting through hostile environments packed with relentless enemy forces. The gameplay is presented from a top-down perspective, demanding precise movement and constant firing as waves of enemies flood the screen. Progression relies on sharp reflexes, careful positioning, and learning enemy patterns, with very little margin for error as the difficulty ramps up quickly. Combat is the game’s sole focus, with each stage throwing increasingly aggressive opposition at the player. Survival depends on mastering the controls, reacting instantly to threats, and pushing forward under sustained pressure rather than exploration or puzzle-solving. On the Commodore 64, Arnie delivers a strong sci-fi atmosphere through bold visuals and an energetic soundtrack that keeps the pace high.

video:video.video:title: Asterix and the Magic Cauldron – You Get ONE Magic Potion for the Entire C64 Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Melbourne House and developed by Beam Software, Asterix and the Magic Cauldron brings the famous Gaulish heroes to the Commodore 64 in a light adventure inspired by the beloved comic series. The story begins when Getafix’s magic cauldron explodes, scattering seven vital pieces across the land and leaving the village defenceless. Players control Asterix and Obelix as they explore a network of interconnected screens representing the Gaulish village, forests, and Roman camps. Progress depends on careful exploration, collecting keys to unlock new areas, and engaging in one-on-one combat with Roman soldiers and wild boars. Resource management plays a central role, with food needed to maintain strength and a single vial of magic potion providing temporary invincibility when used wisely. Choosing when to fight, explore, or retreat adds a strategic layer beneath the game’s cartoon charm.

video:video.video:title: Attack of the Mutant Camels – Jeff Minter’s Strangest C64 Shooter?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Jeff Minter’s Llamasoft, Attack of the Mutant Camels is a horizontally scrolling shooter that perfectly sums up Minter’s distinctive style. You pilot a small jet fighter defending Earth from waves of giant mutant camels, grotesquely transformed by hostile aliens and marching relentlessly toward your base. The action is fast and unforgiving. Each camel takes multiple hits to bring down and fires back with streams of deadly projectiles, forcing you to balance aggression with precise movement. Clear a wave and you’re thrown into a hyperspace sequence, dodging high-speed missiles before the next assault begins. What sets the game apart is its unmistakable presentation. Psychedelic visuals, intense pacing, and an absurd premise combine to create an experience that feels chaotic, funny, and surprisingly tense all at once. It’s instantly recognisable as a Llamasoft production.

video:video.video:title: Auf Wiedersehen Monty – Did Monty’s European Tour Improve the Series?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Gremlin Graphics, Auf Wiedersehen Monty is the fourth entry in the Monty Mole series and one of the most ambitious platform adventures on the Commodore 64. Designed by Peter Harrap and Shaun Hollingworth, the game follows Monty Mole as he travels across Europe with a bold goal: earning enough money to buy his own Greek island, Montos. The game uses a flick-screen platform design spread across 80 interconnected screens laid out to resemble a map of Europe. Players explore countries such as France, Germany, Italy, and Spain, collecting Eurocheques and key items while avoiding traps, enemies, and environmental hazards. Navigation becomes a strategic challenge as players learn routes and screen connections across the continent. Each region introduces themed gameplay twists, including bullfighting hazards in Spain and alcohol effects in Germany that temporarily disrupt Monty’s controls.

video:video.video:title: Aussie Games – Beer Bottles, Belly Flops and Boomerangs on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Beam Software for the Commodore 64, Aussie Games is a lighthearted sports compilation inspired by the success of Epyx’s California Games. It brings a distinctly Australian flavour to the multi-event formula, blending competitive gameplay with humour and cultural references. Players compete across a variety of quirky events set in iconic Australian locations, including boomerang throwing, bellywack diving, Aussie Rules football punting, dry boat racing, and beer can skeet shooting. Each mini-game offers different control schemes and timing challenges, keeping the experience varied and engaging. The presentation is enhanced by traditional Australian tunes such as “Waltzing Matilda” and “Botany Bay,” which help create a strong sense of atmosphere. Combined with colourful graphics and playful animations, the game delivers a fun and approachable arcade-style experience. Aussie Games supports both single-player and multiplayer modes, making it ideal for friendly competition.

video:video.video:title: Automania – Build Six Car Parts Before the Factory Beats You | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Mikro-Gen for the Commodore 64, Automania (also known as Manic Mechanic) is a fast-paced arcade platformer starring the unlucky Wally Week. You’re dropped onto a chaotic car assembly line with one job: build cars piece by piece before time runs out. Each level tasks you with collecting six scattered car parts and placing them in the correct positions on the production line. The challenge comes from the factory itself, packed with lethal hazards including rogue robots, bouncing tyres, and spinning air blades that demand sharp timing and precise movement. As the game progresses, layouts become more complex and the pressure ramps up, turning every run into a test of memory, reflexes, and nerve. There’s no combat here—survival is all about learning the patterns and keeping one step ahead of the machinery.

video:video.video:title: Aztec Challenge – Could You Survive the C64’s Infamous Spear Gauntlet?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Cosmi and developed by Paul Norman, Aztec Challenge throws you into a relentless series of seven deadly trials inspired by ancient temple myths. Each challenge demands sharp reflexes, precise timing, and sheer endurance as you fight to survive rather than explore. The opening trial, The Gauntlet, sets the tone immediately as you sprint toward a distant temple while dodging and leaping over spears hurled by Aztec warriors. From there, the game constantly shifts perspective and mechanics, forcing you to adapt as you climb collapsing stairs, avoid falling stones, navigate trap-filled corridors, swim through piranha-infested waters, and cross a crumbling bridge with missing planks. Every stage feels deliberately unforgiving, turning simple actions into high-pressure tests of nerve. There’s no margin for error, and success comes only through memorisation, rhythm, and persistence. Paul Norman’s tense soundtrack reinforces the pressure, heightening the sense that each mistake could be your last.

video:video.video:title: Back to Reality – Why Must You Become Immortal to Escape This C64 Alien Artefact?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Back to Reality is a tense action-adventure that drops players into a hostile alien maze with little guidance and even less time. You play as an astronaut trapped deep within an unfamiliar environment, where survival depends on memory, precision, and calm decision-making under pressure. Gameplay centres on navigating a complex maze, learning safe routes, and avoiding hazards while racing against the clock. With no hand-holding and a deliberately stripped-back presentation, progress comes from careful observation and mastering the layout through repetition. The minimalist design heightens the sense of isolation and urgency, turning each run into a test of focus and spatial awareness. Difficulty is unforgiving, but success feels earned as players slowly build knowledge of the maze and push closer to escape. Back to Reality stands as a solid example of Mastertronic’s no-frills approach, delivering a challenging and distinctive experience that rewards persistence.

video:video.video:title: Back to the Future – Can Marty Stop the Family Photo Fading on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Electric Dreams Software, Back to the Future brings the hit movie to home computers, casting players as Marty McFly in a race against time to secure his own future. Set across familiar locations from the film, the game challenges players to make sure George and Lorraine meet and fall in love before time runs out. Gameplay is split into several distinct sequences inspired by key movie moments. These include navigating town areas, a hoverboard-style chase, the Enchantment Under the Sea dance, and the dramatic clock tower finale. Each section must be completed within strict time limits, adding pressure to every decision and movement. Presentation leans heavily into the film licence, featuring digitised speech samples and a soundtrack that incorporates the instantly recognisable “The Power of Love” theme. These elements help capture the feel of the movie, even within the technical limits of the Commodore 64.

video:video.video:title: Bad Dudes vs DragonNinja – Are You Bad Enough to Rescue President Ronnie on C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Data East, Bad Dudes vs. DragonNinja brings classic arcade brawling to the Commodore 64 with its tongue-in-cheek premise and tough street action. You take control of Blade or Striker, two hard-hitting vigilantes on a mission to rescue “President Ronnie” from the ruthless Dragon Ninja clan. The action unfolds across six side-scrolling stages packed with gangs, ambushes, and end-of-level bosses, including a memorable crossover appearance from Data East’s Karnov. Combat focuses on punches, kicks, and timing, with weapons such as nunchaku and knives adding extra punch when picked up. The C64 conversion, developed by David Collier with graphics by Stephen Wahid and John Palmer, does a solid job of translating the arcade experience. Large character sprites and recognisable environments give the game real presence, while Jonathan Dunn’s music helps drive the action forward.

video:video.video:title: Badlands – Could the C64 Handle Atari’s Post-Apocalyptic Arcade Racer?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Teque Software and published by Domark under the Tengen label for the Commodore 64, Badlands is an overhead racing game that blends high-speed competition with vehicular combat. Inspired by Atari’s Super Sprint series, it adds a distinctive post-apocalyptic twist to the arcade racing formula. Gameplay features three armed vehicles battling for position over four-lap races across eight hazardous tracks. Viewed from a top-down perspective, each race demands sharp steering, careful braking, and constant awareness of rivals and environmental dangers. During races, players can collect wrenches that are exchanged between events for upgrades such as improved speed, acceleration, and enhanced weapon systems. These progression mechanics add a strategic layer, rewarding consistent performance and smart investment. Tracks are packed with hazards including mines, retractable barriers, and tight corners, forcing players to balance aggression with precision.

video:video.video:title: Bangkok Knights – Was This the C64’s Most Ambitious Kickboxing Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by System 3 and programmed by Mark Cale and Tim Best, Bangkok Knights is a distinctive one-on-one fighting game that brought the intensity of Muay Thai boxing to the Commodore 64. Rather than a generic brawler, it grounds its action in a specific martial art and cultural setting. Players begin their journey in rural Thailand and fight their way toward the legendary Lumpini Stadium in Bangkok, facing eight opponents along the way. Each fighter has their own style and behaviour, forcing players to adapt rather than rely on a single tactic throughout the game. Combat offers a broad move set, including punches, kicks, knees, and elbow strikes, executed through precise directional inputs. The arenas use a 2.5D perspective with movement in all eight directions, and their larger-than-screen layouts add space, positioning, and footwork into the mix.

video:video.video:title: Barbarian II – Why Did the C64 Sequel Abandon One-on-One Combat?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Palace Software for the Commodore 64, Barbarian II: The Dungeon of Drax takes the series in a new direction, shifting away from one-on-one duels and into a single-player action-adventure packed with combat and exploration. You can choose to play as the barbarian or Princess Mariana, each fighting their way through three hostile environments: a volcanic wasteland, a twisting cave network, and the infamous Dungeon of Drax itself. Progress is built around flip-screen exploration, with a sword-shaped compass guiding you toward your objective while still leaving plenty of room to get lost. Combat remains the core focus, featuring brutal encounters with multiple enemy types and the return of the series’ signature decapitations when strikes are perfectly timed. Environmental hazards such as lava pits and deadly drops add constant pressure, forcing careful movement as well as sharp reactions.

video:video.video:title: Barbarian – The C64 Fighting Game Famous for One Brutal Move
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Palace Software, Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior brought raw, one-on-one sword combat to the Commodore 64 and left a lasting mark on the fighting game genre. Inspired by sword-and-sorcery cinema, it throws you into savage duels where timing, spacing, and nerve matter as much as button presses. Combat revolves around a tight set of slashes, thrusts, and defensive moves, with victory coming either by draining your opponent’s energy or landing the infamous decapitation strike. That single move became legendary, instantly setting Barbarian apart from anything else on the system. Battles take place across a variety of arenas, each subtly influencing how aggressively you can fight. The single-player mode pushes you through increasingly dangerous opponents, while the two-player mode delivers tense, skill-based showdowns that made Barbarian a party favourite. On the Commodore 64, the game makes strong use of character animation and colour to sell the weight of combat.

video:video.video:title: Barry McGuigan Boxing – Still the C64’s Best Boxing Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Activision for the Commodore 64, Barry McGuigan World Championship Boxing is a deep and realistic sports simulation that combines career management with fast-paced ring action. Also known as Star Rank Boxing in North America, the game places players in control of a rising boxer aiming for world title glory. Players begin by creating their own fighter, choosing attributes such as name, appearance, and fighting style. Training plays a vital role, with time allocated to roadwork, sparring, and weight sessions that directly affect stamina, strength, and endurance in future bouts. Careful preparation is essential for long-term success. Career mode challenges players to climb the rankings by selecting opponents wisely. Tougher fighters offer greater rewards but pose serious risks. Each match is a full 12-round contest featuring jabs, hooks, uppercuts, blocking, and tactical movement.

video:video.video:title: Batman: The Caped Crusader – The C64 Batman Game Built Like a Comic Book
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 for the Commodore 64, Batman: The Caped Crusader is an inventive action-adventure developed by Special FX Software and published by Ocean Software. Rather than following a conventional layout, the game presents its world like a living comic book, with each new area revealed as a fresh panel complete with captions and dramatic transitions. The game is split into two self-contained episodes. “A Bird in the Hand” pits Batman against the Penguin, while “A Fete Worse Than Death” focuses on the Joker. Both episodes mix side-scrolling combat with exploration and environmental interaction, requiring you to think as much as you fight. Batman’s moveset includes punches, kicks, and his iconic Batarang, but progress often depends on using the surroundings to your advantage. Solving light puzzles, timing actions correctly, and understanding each location’s layout are just as important as defeating enemies.

video:video.video:title: Batman: The Movie – Did Ocean Deliver the Best Batman Game on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Batman: The Movie is a multi-genre action game based on Tim Burton’s hugely influential film. You guide Batman through a series of levels inspired directly by key moments from the movie, blending platforming, puzzles, and vehicle-based action into one varied experience. The game shifts style between stages, starting with side-scrolling platform sections where precise movement and gadget use are essential. You’ll also take control of the Batmobile through Gotham’s streets, tackle a deduction-based puzzle involving Joker-tainted products, and pilot the Batwing in a tense shooting sequence high above the city. Strong atmosphere runs throughout, helped by moody visuals and a standout soundtrack by Matthew Cannon. Despite minor technical quirks, the Commodore 64 version delivers a confident, ambitious adaptation that captures the tone of the film while offering constantly changing gameplay.

video:video.video:title: Battle Chess – The Amiga Chess Game Where Every Capture Became a Fight
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Interplay Productions, Battle Chess takes the ancient game of chess and gives it a dramatic Amiga makeover, turning every capture into a fully animated battle between the pieces. Knights duel, bishops cast spells, and pawns meet surprisingly brutal ends, adding personality and humour to every move. Underneath the spectacle sits a complete and authentic chess engine, letting you play strong matches against the computer or a human opponent. You can switch between a fast, traditional 2D board or the animated 2.5D mode, where each capture triggers one of 35 unique battle sequences, many packed with visual gags and pop culture nods. The Amiga hardware allows Battle Chess to shine, with smooth animations, detailed sprites, and a presentation that makes even casual games feel theatrical. The balance between strategy and spectacle keeps matches engaging without getting in the way of thoughtful play.

video:video.video:title: B.C. Bill – The C64 Game Voted “Most Sexist” of 1984
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Creative Technology Group and published by Imagine Software for the Commodore 64, B. C. Bill is a quirky prehistoric action game that blends arcade gameplay with light survival management. Players take on the role of Bill, a caveman determined to build and protect his growing family in a dangerous stone-age world. Gameplay revolves around hunting animals for food, stunning cavewomen to bring back to your cave, and defending your home from roaming dinosaurs. Armed with only a club, Bill must carefully balance exploration, combat, and resource gathering to keep his family alive. A distinctive feature is the changing seasonal cycle, which affects food supplies and family survival. Poor planning can lead to starvation, while successful hunts and rescues help expand your tribe. This adds a surprising strategic layer beneath the game’s humorous exterior.

video:video.video:title: B.C. II: Grog’s Revenge – A C64 Quest for Clams and the Meaning of Life
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64, B. C. II: Grog’s Revenge is an action-adventure sequel developed by Sydney Development and published by Sierra On-Line. Continuing the comic-inspired world of B. C. ’s Quest for Tires, the game once again follows Thor, the stone-age caveman on his stone unicycle, as he sets off in search of the “Meaning of Life.” Gameplay alternates between two distinct styles. Mountain sections require careful balance and timing as Thor navigates narrow paths, avoids rocks and holes, and collects clams used as currency to pay tolls. Cave sections shift the pace, limiting visibility to a narrow beam of light and demanding precise movement to avoid hazards while gathering more clams. Adding constant tension is the ever-present threat of Grog. His thunderous roar can knock Thor from his unicycle at any moment, abruptly ending the journey and reinforcing the game’s risk-reward balance.

video:video.video:title: B.C.’s Quest for Tires – Why Was Thor Riding a Stone Unicycle on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Sydney Development and published by Sierra On-Line, B. C. ’s Quest for Tires brings Johnny Hart’s famous comic strip to life on the Commodore 64. Players take control of Thor, the Stone Age inventor of the unicycle, as he sets off to rescue his girlfriend Cute Chick from a hungry dinosaur. Gameplay is presented as a side-scrolling platformer, with Thor riding across prehistoric landscapes including meadows, forests, and caves. Players must time jumps and ducking carefully to avoid rocks, logs, branches, and other hazards, while tackling memorable challenges such as crossing rivers on turtles and steering clear of bubbling lava pits. The game’s humour and simplicity are key to its appeal. Its presentation mirrors the comic strip’s playful tone, delivering a lighthearted experience that focuses on rhythm, timing, and obstacle navigation rather than complex mechanics.

video:video.video:title: Beach-Head – Minefields, Tanks and a Final Fortress in One C64 Invasion
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Access Software for the Commodore 64, Beach-Head is a landmark World War II action game that tasks players with launching a full-scale assault on a heavily fortified enemy island. Rather than focusing on a single gameplay style, the game unfolds across multiple distinct stages, each representing a different phase of the invasion. The opening sequence sees players navigating a fleet of ships through dangerous waters, choosing between a direct route under enemy fire or a hidden passage filled with mines and torpedoes. This is followed by a shift to anti-aircraft defence, where quick reflexes are required to protect the fleet from waves of enemy planes. Later stages introduce artillery combat against enemy battleships and a side-scrolling beach assault, where tanks must survive long enough to reach the enemy fortress. The number of tanks that make it ashore directly affects the difficulty of the final confrontation, adding strategic weight to earlier performance.

video:video.video:title: Beach-Head II – The C64 Sequel That Made the Dictator Talk
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by U. S. Gold and developed by Access Software, Beach-Head II expands on the original with bigger ideas, tighter action, and one of the most memorable audio features of the 8-bit era. This time, the conflict escalates as you take the fight directly to the Dictator across a series of varied combat scenarios. The game is split into four distinct stages that constantly change the pace. You begin by advancing soldiers under fire, using cover to destroy the Dictator’s gun. This is followed by a rescue mission where precision shooting is required to save prisoners from deadly traps. Next comes a helicopter escape, dodging enemy fire while evacuating survivors, before everything culminates in a tense knife-throwing duel across a chasm. What truly set Beach-Head II apart was its use of speech synthesis.

video:video.video:title: Below the Root – The Remarkable C64 Adventure That Let You Live in Its Fantasy World
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Windham Classics and developed by Dale Disharoon, Below the Root is a distinctive adventure game based on Zilpha Keatley Snyder’s Green-Sky Trilogy. Set in the tranquil, tree-dwelling world of Green-Sky, the game offers a thoughtful alternative to the combat-heavy adventures common at the time. Players choose from five different characters, each with their own strengths and abilities, and set out to investigate mysterious visions that threaten the harmony of their society. Exploration takes place across a large, interconnected world of platforms, villages, and natural environments, encouraging curiosity and careful observation. Rather than relying on violence, Below the Root introduces unique mechanics such as pens (telepathy), kiniporting (telekinesis), and grunspreking (plant manipulation). Progress depends on communication, puzzle-solving, and understanding the world and its inhabitants, making every interaction meaningful. The game was praised for its atmospheric visuals and depth, as well as its open-ended structure that allows players to approach challenges in different ways.

video:video.video:title: Beneath a Steel Sky – Why This Amiga Cyberpunk Adventure Still Stands Out
video:video.video:description: Released in 1994 by Revolution Software, Beneath a Steel Sky is a landmark cyberpunk adventure set in a dystopian future Australia. You follow Robert Foster, a man raised outside the city who is abruptly dragged into an oppressive urban world ruled by corporate power and a controlling artificial intelligence. The game uses Revolution’s Virtual Theatre engine to create a living city where characters move, work, and interact independently of your actions. Progress comes through exploration, sharp dialogue, and puzzle-solving, all woven into a story that balances dark themes with moments of dry humour. Gameplay focuses on classic point-and-click mechanics, encouraging observation and logical thinking rather than reflexes. The Amiga version stands out for its detailed pixel art, strong atmosphere, and immersive sound design, with the CD32 release also adding voice acting to key scenes. Widely regarded as one of the finest adventure games of its era, Beneath a Steel Sky is praised for its storytelling, world-building, and lasting influence on narrative-driven games.

video:video.video:title: Benefactor – The Overlooked Amiga Puzzle Platformer from Psygnosis
video:video.video:description: Released in 1994 by Digital Illusions CE (DICE) and published by Psygnosis for the Commodore Amiga and Amiga CD32, Benefactor is a distinctive puzzle-platformer that blends thoughtful problem-solving with precise character control. Players take on the role of Ben E. Factor, a former soldier turned hero, tasked with rescuing the kidnapped Merry Men across six moons of the planet Minniat. The game spans 60 carefully designed levels that combine traditional platforming with strategic planning. Players must avoid enemies, activate switches, manipulate the environment, and escort vulnerable characters to safety, creating gameplay reminiscent of Lemmings but with direct, hands-on control. Each Merry Man has unique behaviours and abilities that influence how puzzles are solved. Some require protection and guidance, while others must be “reformed” using special colouring machines before they can be rescued. These mechanics add variety and depth to every stage.

video:video.video:title: Beyond the Forbidden Forest – The C64 Horror Game That Made Archery Terrifying
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Paul Norman and published by Cosmi for the Commodore 64, Beyond the Forbidden Forest is an atmospheric sequel to the cult classic Forbidden Forest. Expanding on the original’s formula, the game introduces a pseudo-3D movement system known as “OmniDimension 4D,” allowing players to move their archer both horizontally and into the depth of the screen. Gameplay centres on surviving relentless waves of monstrous creatures using unlimited standard arrows. Every defeated enemy drops a valuable golden arrow, which must be collected in order to progress. These special arrows become essential later in the game, particularly during the dangerous cave sequences. Progression shifts in the second phase as players enter the caverns beneath the forest, where precision and resource management become critical. Here, powerful enemies such as the multi-headed hydra and the final boss, the Demogorgon, demand careful use of stored golden arrows and perfect timing.

video:video.video:title: Big Trouble in Little China – Why Does the C64 Game Scroll the Wrong Way?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Electric Dreams Software for the Commodore 64, Big Trouble in Little China is a side-scrolling beat ’em up developed by Software Studios and based on John Carpenter’s cult action-fantasy film. Players switch between three heroes — Jack Burton, Wang Chi, and Egg Shen — as they battle through Chinatown’s criminal underworld to rescue two kidnapped girls. Each character brings unique abilities, from Jack’s firearm to Wang’s fragile swords and Shen’s growing magic attacks. Combat takes place against waves of enemies attacking from both directions, requiring careful positioning and weapon management. Picking the right character and knowing when to use special abilities is key to surviving the later stages. Visually, the game features large character sprites and atmospheric urban backdrops that push the limits of 1987 C64 hardware. The presentation is supported by sparse but effective sound effects, including digitised punches and minimal musical stabs.

video:video.video:title: Bionic Commando – Did Capcom’s Arcade Platformer Survive the Move to C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 for the Commodore 64, Bionic Commando is a side-scrolling action-platformer developed by Software Creations for the UK release and Pacific Dataworks International for the US version, published by U. S. Gold, GO! , and Capcom. Unlike most platform games of the era, the hero cannot jump. Instead, movement is based entirely around a powerful bionic arm that functions as a grappling hook for swinging, climbing, attacking enemies, and collecting items. The C64 version closely follows the arcade structure across five demanding levels, requiring careful planning and precise execution to survive hostile terrain. Players must shoot supply crates dropped by parachutes to upgrade weapons, then skillfully use the bionic arm to traverse gaps, scale platforms, and avoid deadly hazards. Gameplay focuses on timing, positioning, and momentum, rewarding players who master the unique swinging mechanics.

video:video.video:title: Bionic Granny – One of the Strangest C64 Games Ever Released?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by David and Richard Darling and published by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Bionic Granny is one of the most unconventional arcade-style titles of the early home computer era. Players take control of an elderly woman with bionic enhancements, tasked with chasing down schoolchildren after class and tapping them with her walking stick. The game is presented from a top-down perspective, with the screen divided into three lanes where children walk steadily across the playfield. Players move left and right along the bottom of the screen, positioning Granny to intercept each child at the right moment. Timing and positioning are essential, as players must also avoid lollipops thrown by the crossing guard, which can cost lives and interrupt progress. The simple control scheme keeps the focus on reflexes and rhythm rather than complex mechanics.

video:video.video:title: Bismark – Could You Hunt Down the Battleship on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Argus Press Software Ltd and developed by P. Rawling, Bismark is a strategic naval warfare game that challenges players to outthink rather than outgun their enemy. Also known as Strategy II, it places careful planning and intelligence gathering at the heart of the experience. You command a fleet of twelve Allied ships tasked with locating and sinking the German battleship Bismarck before time runs out. The action unfolds on a 20×15 grid representing the North Atlantic, where every movement must be considered as you patrol sea lanes, avoid threats, and close in on your target. Rather than fast-paced action, Bismark focuses on tactical decision-making and resource management. Players must interpret limited information, position ships effectively, and anticipate the Bismarck’s movements, creating constant tension as the clock ticks down. The game formed part of Argus Press’s Strategy 1 series, designed to bring accessible but demanding strategy titles to home computers.

video:video.video:title: Black Hawk – The C64 Shooter That Switched from Bombing to Dogfighting
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64, Black Hawk is a vertical-scrolling shoot-’em-up developed by Dean M. Lock and published by Creative Sparks. Players take control of the Black Hawk aircraft, flying missions over heavily defended island bases packed with tanks, missile launchers, radar installations, and anti-aircraft fire. The gameplay is split into two distinct phases that give the game its unique structure. In Missile Camera Mode, players guide a targeting camera from an overhead view, locking onto enemy installations by holding the fire button before releasing a missile at the chosen target. Precision and timing are essential to maximise damage and reduce enemy strength. Any surviving threats then trigger a shift into Cockpit Combat Mode. Here, the view moves inside the aircraft, and players must directly engage enemy planes and remaining ground units in fast-paced combat.

video:video.video:title: Black Knight – Could Anyone Survive This Brutal C64 Platformer?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Interdisc for the Commodore 64, Black Knight is a tough-as-nails arcade-style platformer that embodies the unforgiving spirit of early home computer gaming. Players take control of the armoured Black Knight, battling through dangerous medieval environments packed with enemies and deadly traps. Gameplay focuses on precise movement, careful timing, and fast reactions. Each screen presents new hazards, from hostile creatures to narrow platforms and sudden drops, forcing players to learn patterns and master positioning in order to survive. Progress depends heavily on skill and persistence. The game’s level design encourages strategic play, rewarding patience and memorisation. Mistakes are costly, and success comes from learning enemy behaviour, judging jumps accurately, and choosing when to advance or retreat. Visually, Black Knight makes strong use of the C64’s capabilities, featuring detailed character sprites and smoothly animated medieval settings.

video:video.video:title: Black Tiger – Did Capcom’s Arcade Adventure Survive the Amiga?
video:video.video:description: Originally released in arcades by Capcom in 1987 and later ported to the Amiga in 1990 by U. S. Gold, Black Tiger delivers a fast-paced blend of action, exploration, and light RPG mechanics. Players step into the role of a barbarian warrior battling through a hostile fantasy world filled with monsters, traps, and hidden secrets. Armed with a morning star and throwing daggers, the hero must fight through eight sprawling stages packed with enemies and powerful end-of-level bosses. Along the way, players collect the in-game currency Zenny, which can be spent on upgrades such as stronger weapons, armour, keys, and vital items purchased from mysterious wise men found throughout the levels. The Amiga version features both horizontal and vertical scrolling, secret dungeons, and hidden treasure chests that reward careful exploration.

video:video.video:title: Blackwyche – Trapped Aboard a Haunted Galleon on the Commodore 64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Ultimate Play the Game and developed by Dave and Bob Thomas, Blackwyche is the third chapter in the Sir Arthur Pendragon series. This time, the adventure shifts to the haunted decks of the ghost ship Blackwyche, where Sir Arthur must free the trapped soul of Captain Richard Cavendish. Exploration unfolds in an isometric 3D view across five interconnected decks, each filled with hostile skeletons, environmental puzzles, and hidden routes. Progress depends on careful navigation, combat timing, and gradually uncovering the ship’s secrets. Sir Arthur can arm himself with knives, daggers, and a powerful magic sword, while managing a constantly draining energy supply. Survival hinges on knowing when to fight, when to retreat, and when to ring the ship’s mysterious bell to restore strength. Collecting scattered map pieces is essential to locating the captain’s imprisoned soul.

video:video.video:title: Blade Runner – The C64 Game Licensed from the Music, Not the Film
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Blade Runner was developed by Ian Foster and Andy Stodart and published by CRL Group. This early cyberpunk shooter casts you as a bounty hunter tracking down dangerous “Replidroids” across a dystopian future city inspired by Ridley Scott’s iconic film.
