The game opens with an ambitious two-minute rendition of Vangelis’s Blade Runner soundtrack, immediately setting a brooding sci-fi mood that was striking on the C64. From there, gameplay alternates between top-down city navigation in a hover-skimmer and side-scrolling street chases where targets must be eliminated while avoiding traffic and pedestrians. As the game progresses, the pace increases and the Replidroids become faster and more elusive, demanding sharper reactions and better route planning. The mix of overworld scanning and street-level action aims to recreate the feel of a futuristic manhunt rather than straightforward arcade shooting.

video:video.video:title: Blades of Steel – Ice Hockey and Fist Fights on the Commodore 64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Konami for the Commodore 64, Blades of Steel delivers fast-paced, arcade-style ice hockey action that captures the intensity and excitement of the rink. Known for its responsive controls and distinctive features, it stands out as one of the most memorable sports titles on the C64. Players can choose from eight teams representing major hockey cities such as New York, Chicago, Toronto, and Montreal, and compete in exhibition matches or tournament play. The side-scrolling presentation keeps the action flowing at high speed, rewarding quick reflexes, sharp passing, and tactical positioning. Progression relies on mastering puck control, defensive awareness, and well-timed shots on goal. Strategic line changes and smart player movement become increasingly important as matches grow more competitive, especially in two-player showdowns. One of the game’s most iconic features is its fight system.

video:video.video:title: Blagger – Why This C64 Platformer Became a Favourite
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983, Blagger is a classic single-screen platform game for the Commodore 64 developed by Antony Crowther and published by Alligata Software. Players step into the role of Roger the Dodger, tasked with collecting keys scattered around each screen in order to unlock the safe before time runs out. The game spans 30 increasingly challenging levels, each packed with hazards such as collapsing platforms, conveyor belts, and an assortment of bizarre enemies including giant mouths and alien creatures. Movement is tightly controlled, with fixed jump arcs that demand precise timing and careful positioning. Rather than fast reflexes alone, Blagger rewards planning and pattern recognition. Knowing when and where to jump is critical, as a single mistake can quickly end a run. This balance of risk, timing, and spatial awareness gives the game its enduring appeal.

video:video.video:title: Blagger Goes to Hollywood – The C64 Sequel About Stealing a Blockbuster Film
video:video.video:description: Blagger Goes To Hollywood is a 1985 action-arcade game developed and published by Alligata Software for the Commodore 64. A follow-up to the original Blagger trilogy, this quirky title sends the infamous burglar on a chaotic adventure through a Hollywood studio packed with famous movie characters and recognisable theme tunes. In this C64 classic, you guide Blagger through an isometric, side-view world, collecting and using the correct props to defeat characters inspired by Batman, Superman, Jaws, Tarzan, The Incredible Hulk, and more. Each opponent requires a specific item to be launched at the right moment, blending fast arcade action with puzzle-solving and pattern recognition — a fairly unusual concept for mid-80s Commodore 64 games. The game is especially remembered for its catchy chiptune adaptations of film and TV themes, cleverly recreated within the limits of the SID chip, and for its playful pop-culture mash-ups.

video:video.video:title: Blockbusters – Can I Have a P Please, Bob… on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Macsen Software, Blockbusters is a video game adaptation of the hugely popular British television quiz show. Later re-released in 1988 by TV Games, it brings the familiar hexagon board and general knowledge challenges to the Commodore 64, capturing the competitive spirit of the original programme. Gameplay closely follows the TV format, with players selecting letters from a hexagonal grid, each hiding a trivia question. Correct answers allow players to claim hexagons, with the goal of forming a continuous path across the board before the opponent does. The game supports solo play against the computer as well as a two-player mode for head-to-head quiz battles. Presentation on the C64 is simple and functional, keeping the focus firmly on the questions rather than flashy visuals. The stripped-back graphics and sound help maintain clarity during play, making it easy to concentrate on strategy and general knowledge.

video:video.video:title: Blood ’N Guts – The C64 Viking Sports Day with Axe Throwing and Beer
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Greve Graphics and published by American Action for the Commodore 64, Blood ’n Guts is a multi-event sports game set in a ridiculous barbarian fantasy world where brute strength, timing, and sheer nonsense rule the day. Players choose from four grizzled competitors—Knorr, Hawk, Nop, and Dog—and compete across ten wildly varied events that parody traditional athletics. These include tug-of-war, tower jumping, rock rolling, beer drinking, axe throwing, pole fighting, arm wrestling, tightrope walking, and other tongue-in-cheek challenges that mix skill with slapstick humour. Each event relies on precise joystick movement and timing, keeping the action fast and competitive while constantly switching gameplay styles. The constant variety helps maintain momentum and makes the game particularly well suited to multiplayer sessions and score-chasing. With graphics by Nils Hård and music by Lars Hård, Blood ’n Guts delivers a bold, characterful presentation that leans fully into its barbaric theme.

video:video.video:title: Bloodwych – The C64 Dungeon Crawler Built for Two Players
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Image Works for the Commodore 64, Bloodwych is a dark fantasy dungeon-crawling RPG developed by Philip M. Taglione, with assistance from Anthony Taglione. Inspired by the atmospheric style of Dungeon Master, it delivers deep role-playing systems on 8-bit hardware. Players control a party of four champions, choosing from Warrior, Mage, Adventurer, or Thief classes, each aligned to one of four magical colours that influence spellcasting, equipment, and combat abilities. The game features vast multi-level dungeons filled with monsters, traps, elemental crystals, and interactive NPCs accessed through simple dialogue menus. A major innovation is its simultaneous two-player split-screen mode, allowing cooperative dungeon exploration, spellcasting, and combat in real time on a single machine. Progress depends on careful party management, learning powerful spell combinations, gathering resources, and mastering tactical positioning during battles. Visually, Bloodwych is remarkably detailed for the Commodore 64, with richly textured dungeon walls, clear item icons, and smooth animation effects, including the iconic page-turning spellbook.

video:video.video:title: Blue Max – The C64 Fighter-Pilot Game That Set the Standard in 1983
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Synapse Software and developed by Bob Polin, Blue Max is a diagonally scrolling shooter that drops you into the cockpit of a Sopwith Camel during the First World War. Rather than pure arcade blasting, the game blends action with light simulation elements, demanding careful flying and tactical decision-making. Viewed from an isometric perspective, you can move in multiple directions and adjust altitude, giving the battlefield a convincing sense of depth. Missions involve strafing enemy aircraft, bombing ground targets, and navigating anti-air defences while pushing deeper into hostile territory. Fuel and ammunition are limited, forcing you to locate friendly airstrips to land, refuel, and repair damage. These landings add tension and risk, turning survival into more than just shooting skill. The SID soundtrack, featuring a rendition of “Rule, Britannia!” , reinforces the period atmosphere and sense of daring aerial combat.

video:video.video:title: BMX Kidz – Firebird’s C64 Racer Was Tougher Than It Looked
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Gigglywurx and published by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, BMX Kidz is a fast-paced side-scrolling racing game inspired by the BMX craze of the 1980s. Players race against five computer-controlled opponents across a series of challenging tracks, performing wheelies, jumps, and stunts in order to maintain speed and gain an advantage. A key gameplay element is energy and bike management. Crashes and failed tricks drain stamina and damage the bike, while collecting soda cans restores energy and replacement spokes keep performance at its peak. The game uses a distinctive 2.5D perspective that creates a strong sense of depth and motion, helping it stand out among other racing titles of the era. Progression depends on mastering the game’s slippery physics, timing jumps accurately, and choosing when to risk stunts for extra speed.

video:video.video:title: BMX Simulator – The £1.99 C64 Racer That Launched a Codemasters Series
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Codemasters and developed by Richard Darling, BMX Simulator brings fast, competitive BMX racing to the Commodore 64 from a distinctive top-down perspective. As part of Codemasters’ budget “Simulator” series, it delivers tight, demanding gameplay built around speed, precision, and time pressure. You race across seven increasingly challenging tracks packed with ramps, bumps, and tight corners, aiming to complete three laps before the timer runs out. Clean racing is essential, as crashes cost valuable seconds, while faster finishes earn higher scores. The inclusion of a two-player mode adds a strong competitive edge, making head-to-head races a real test of skill. The presentation captures the energy of BMX racing with bright, readable visuals and smooth track layouts. David Whittaker’s soundtrack complements the action perfectly, adding drive and momentum to every race without getting in the way of gameplay.

video:video.video:title: Bocce – Indoor, Outdoor and Beach Bowls… All on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Bocce is a digital adaptation of the traditional Italian lawn bowling game, developed and published by Simulmondo. As the company’s debut title, it holds an important place in European gaming history and helped introduce Italian-developed games to the wider home computer scene. Gameplay faithfully recreates the real-world sport of bocce, tasking players with rolling large balls as close as possible to the smaller target ball, known as the jack. Players can fine-tune each throw by adjusting direction, power, and spin, with success relying more on precision and strategy than speed. Matches can be played across different environments, including outdoor courts with uneven terrain and indoor bocciodromes that offer more controlled conditions. A distinctive split-screen interface enhances the experience, combining a top-down tactical view of the court with a 3D-style perspective of each throw.

video:video.video:title: Bomb Jack – Did Elite Get the Arcade Favourite Right on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Bomb Jack (1986), developed by Elite and based on Tehkan’s 1984 arcade hit, is one of the most successful arcade conversions ever released on the Commodore 64. Players control the agile hero Jack as he leaps between platforms collecting red bombs while avoiding birds, mummies, flying saucers, and other roaming enemies. The game’s precise jumping, mid-air “flutter” ability, and strategic bomb-collection order create fast-paced, skill-based gameplay. Building bonus meters rewards careful play, while special power-ups can temporarily turn enemies into collectible coins. Each set of stages features distinctive themed backdrops, including pyramids in Cairo, the Greek Acropolis, Neuschwanstein Castle, and city nightscapes, giving the game strong visual variety. Mark Cooksey’s energetic soundtrack, including a rendition of Jean-Michel Jarre’s *Magnetic Fields Part II*, adds to the game’s memorable presentation. Bomb Jack is widely regarded as one of the finest arcade ports on the C64, praised for its addictive design, smooth controls, and lasting appeal.

video:video.video:title: Booty – 20 Pirate Holds, Exploding Treasure and One Vicious Parrot on C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Firebird and developed by Kevin A. Moughtin, Booty is a classic platform adventure that casts players as Jim the Cabin Boy, sneaking around a pirate ship to steal treasure from his ruthless masters. Set entirely aboard the ship, the game challenges players to outwit pirates and hazards across a network of interconnected rooms. Gameplay takes place on fixed-screen platform layouts linked by ladders and doors. Each of the 20 rooms is packed with treasure to collect, alongside roaming pirates, parrots, and dangerous booby-trapped items that must be avoided at all costs. Contact with enemies is unforgiving, costing one of Jim’s limited lives. Once all treasure in a room has been collected, the pressure ramps up with a strict 45-second countdown to locate a final key and escape to the next area.

video:video.video:title: Boulder Dash – Why This C64 Puzzle Game Became an All-Time Favourite
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by First Star Software and created by Peter Liepa and Chris Gray, Boulder Dash is a landmark puzzle-platformer that helped define an entire genre. Players guide Rockford, a determined miner, through dangerous underground caves in search of precious diamonds. Each level challenges players to dig through dirt, manipulate the environment, and outthink falling boulders, roaming enemies, and deadly traps. Success depends on careful planning as much as quick reactions, with every movement potentially triggering chain reactions that can either clear a path or seal Rockford’s fate. The Commodore 64 version is especially celebrated for its colourful presentation and distinctive sound effects, which bring the caves to life and heighten the tension as boulders tumble and enemies close in. Level design steadily increases in complexity, encouraging experimentation, memorisation, and mastery of the game’s physics-driven systems.

video:video.video:title: Bounces – The C64 Sports Game Where You Could Beat Up Your Opponent
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Denton Designs and published by Beyond Software for the Commodore 64, Bounces is a distinctive hybrid of competitive sport and arcade-style combat set in a futuristic arena. Players compete in one-on-one matches where the goal is to score points by throwing a bouncing ball into the opponent’s goal or by knocking them out using well-timed attacks. Victory depends on both accuracy and aggression. A unique feature is the elastic tether that connects each player to their side of the screen. This limits movement, adds tactical depth, and forces careful positioning throughout each match. Games are played over two fast-paced 90-second halves, creating intense, high-pressure encounters where momentum can shift quickly. Mastering the elastic physics is key to gaining an advantage. Visually, the game features clean character sprites and colourful arenas that suit its futuristic theme.

video:video.video:title: Bounder – The C64 Arcade Game That Turned a Tennis Ball into a Hero
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Gremlin Graphics for the Commodore 64, Bounder is an inventive action-puzzle game that puts players in control of a constantly bouncing tennis ball navigating a series of suspended platforms high above dangerous voids. The game spans 174 screens across 10 increasingly demanding levels, each built from hexagonal tiles filled with hazards, enemies, and obstacles. Players must carefully time their movements and landings while guiding the ball towards the exit on every screen. Precision and forward planning are essential for survival. Scattered throughout the stages are special tiles that introduce strategic variety, including arrows that propel the ball forward, teleporters that remove sections of the level, and mystery tiles that can either reward or punish the player. Completing each stage unlocks a bonus screen, offering extra points and risk-based scoring opportunities. Visually, Bounder stands out with its clever use of parallax scrolling and pseudo-3D perspective, creating a strong sense of depth on the C64.

video:video.video:title: Bozo’s Night Out – The C64 Game About Getting Home Completely Drunk
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Taskset for the Commodore 64, Bozo’s Night Out is an offbeat action-platformer built around a simple but memorable premise: getting home safely after one too many drinks at the pub. Players control Bozo as he staggers through the streets, trying to reach his front door without meeting an unfortunate end. Gameplay focuses on managing Bozo’s increasingly unpredictable movement. Hazards include trapdoors, hostile pedestrians, police officers, and environmental obstacles that punish poor timing. As Bozo consumes more alcohol, control becomes less reliable, turning basic navigation into a balancing act between risk and restraint. Multiple routes to Bozo’s home offer different challenges, encouraging experimentation and replay. The presentation leans into its comedic tone, with expressive animations and sound effects that reinforce the game’s light-hearted approach. Rather than precision platforming, success depends on anticipation and learning how Bozo’s drunken behaviour affects movement.

video:video.video:title: Breakdance – Epyx Packed Over 100 Dance Moves into a 1984 C64 Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984, Breakdance is a rhythm-based game developed by Beck-Tech and published by Epyx for the Commodore 64, drawing inspiration from the early 1980s breakdancing explosion and films such as Flashdance and Beat Street. Rather than traditional arcade action, the game focuses on timing, memory, and performance, placing dance culture front and centre. The gameplay is split across several distinct modes. Hot Feet is a memory-based dance contest where players must repeat increasingly complex move sequences, while Battle the Rocket Crew pits players against rival dancers in competitive copycat showdowns. Perfection’s Dance Puzzle adds a timed challenge element, requiring players to assemble and perform routines in the correct order. A standout feature is Choreograph Mode, which allows players to create custom dance routines using a set of 14 moves, then perform and replay them.

video:video.video:title: Breakthru – Why Did This C64 Combat Car Need a Jump Button?
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Data East and released in arcades in 1986, BreakThru arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1987 via U. S. Gold, bringing fast-paced military action to home computers. Players take control of a heavily armed combat vehicle on a high-risk mission to recover a stolen fighter jet from enemy forces. The game unfolds across five distinct side-scrolling stages, including mountains, plains, bridges, cities, and an airfield, each packed with enemy troops, vehicles, mines, and environmental hazards. Gameplay revolves around precise movement, timed jumps, and constant firing, with players needing to react quickly to threats coming from all directions. Strategic depth is added through weapon upgrades, most notably the powerful three-way shot that dramatically boosts offensive capability. Mastering jump timing and positioning is essential, especially as enemy density and speed increase with each level.

video:video.video:title: Brian Bloodaxe – The C64 Viking Platformer with a Very British Sense of Humour
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by The Edge for the Commodore 64, Brian Bloodaxe is a Viking-themed action adventure developed by Charles Bystram, blending exploration, puzzles, and humour-inspired gameplay. Players take control of Brian, a helmet-wearing Viking hero, as he explores a large multi-screen world filled with castles, forests, and underground passages. Progress depends on collecting and using items, overcoming hazards, and navigating interconnected areas. Unlike traditional linear platformers, the game focuses on exploration and memory-based navigation. Players are encouraged to learn the map layout, revisit locations, and plan routes carefully. Visually, the Commodore 64 version features colourful character sprites, smoothly scrolling screens, and atmospheric SID music that enhances the medieval setting. Its humorous presentation and unusual fake loading screen help set it apart from similar titles. While sometimes criticised for its difficulty and unconventional mechanics, Brian Bloodaxe remains a distinctive entry in the C64 library.

video:video.video:title: Brian Jacks Superstar Challenge – The C64 Joystick Wrecker
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Martech for the Commodore 64, Brian Jacks Superstar Challenge is a licensed multi-event sports simulation based on British judo champion and TV “Superstars” legend Brian Jacks. Players compete across a series of athletic challenges designed to test speed, strength, timing, and coordination, aiming to achieve the highest possible overall score. The game features eight varied events, including running, weightlifting, and gym-based tests, each requiring different control techniques and reactions. A major highlight is the one-load format, which allows players to move smoothly between events without lengthy loading times, keeping the pace fast and competitive. Gameplay focuses on mastering individual disciplines while maintaining consistency across the full competition, rewarding practice and precision. Visually, the game delivers simple but clear graphics typical of mid-1980s C64 titles, while sound effects provide basic feedback during each event.

video:video.video:title: Bruce Lee – The C64 Platform Fighter Everybody Wanted to Master
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Datasoft, Bruce Lee is a highly regarded action-platformer for the Commodore 64 that blends precise platforming with beat ’em up combat. Designed by Ron J. Fortier, with graphics by Kelly Day and music by John A. Fitzpatrick, the game draws inspiration from martial arts cinema while delivering tight, skill-based gameplay. Players guide Bruce Lee through a series of 20 single-screen rooms, collecting lanterns to unlock new areas on the path to confronting an evil wizard. Each room is carefully designed, combining vertical movement, environmental hazards, and enemy encounters that demand timing and control rather than brute force. Bruce is constantly pursued by two iconic foes: the agile Ninja and the powerful Green Yamo, a sumo wrestler. Combat revolves around punches and flying kicks, while players must also contend with electrified walls, collapsing floors, and explosive traps that punish careless movement.

video:video.video:title: Brutal Sports Football – The Amiga Game Where Every Match Became a Brawl
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Teque London and published by Millennium Interactive for the Commodore Amiga, Brutal Sports Series Football is a chaotic and ultra-violent sports title that blends American football and rugby with explosive arcade-style action. Set in a dystopian arena, the game combines traditional scoring objectives with brutal combat mechanics, allowing players to punch, kick, and even decapitate opponents to gain control of the match. Power-ups such as bombs, weapons, and speed boosts are scattered across the pitch, encouraging aggressive play alongside tactical positioning. Matches are fast, unpredictable, and packed with confrontations. The Amiga version is especially remembered for its frenetic multiplayer mode, distinctive sprite designs, and unusual hybrid of sports and beat-’em-up gameplay. It is often compared to Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe, even though opinions on pacing and scrolling were mixed. Visually, the game embraces a bold, exaggerated style that matches its violent tone, supported by energetic sound effects and a hard-hitting soundtrack that keeps the action intense.

video:video.video:title: Bubble Bobble – Was This the C64’s Greatest Two-Player Arcade Conversion?
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Taito in 1986 and expertly brought to the Commodore 64 in 1987 by Software Creations and Firebird, Bubble Bobble stars Bub and Bob—two bubble-blowing dragons on a quest to rescue their girlfriends from the Cave of Monsters. The adventure unfolds across 100 single-screen stages, each packed with enemies, hazards, and clever routes to master. Core gameplay revolves around trapping foes in bubbles and popping them to clear each level. Those same bubbles can also be used as platforms, opening up vertical movement and encouraging creative solutions as stages become more demanding. Timing, positioning, and planning are key as enemy patterns grow trickier. The C64 port is widely praised for capturing the arcade’s charm and feel, delivering smooth controls, bright visuals, and the series’ unmistakable personality. Single-player fun is complemented by a hugely enjoyable two-player co-op mode, where teamwork and coordination add a whole new layer of strategy.

video:video.video:title: Buggy Boy – Was This the C64’s Best Arcade Racing Conversion?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Elite Systems for the Commodore 64, Buggy Boy is a fast-paced arcade-style racing game originally developed by Tatsumi. Known as Speed Buggy in North America, the game was a major arcade hit, and its C64 conversion successfully captures the colour, speed, and spirit of the original coin-op experience. Players race a dune buggy across five distinct courses—Offroad, North, East, South, and West—each split into multiple legs packed with obstacles, ramps, and tight corners. Scoring is just as important as speed, with points awarded for passing through gates, collecting flags, and pulling off risky stunts such as jumps and two-wheel driving. Fuel management and crash avoidance add an extra layer of pressure to every run. On the Commodore 64, Buggy Boy stands out for its vibrant presentation and impressively smooth scrolling. The controls feel responsive and the action remains quick and demanding, delivering an addictive blend of arcade challenge and score-chasing competition.

video:video.video:title: Bully’s Sporting Darts – Bully Came to the C64… But Was It Anything Like Bullseye?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Alternative Software for the Commodore 64, Bully’s Sporting Darts is a light-hearted darts simulation inspired by the hugely popular UK television game show Bullseye. It blends pub-style darts action with quiz elements and the unmistakable tone of early ’90s British TV entertainment. Gameplay offers several modes, including traditional 501 darts, a sports quiz section based directly on the show’s format, and the famous Bully’s Prize Board. Players take turns throwing darts with simple, accessible controls, making it easy to pick up whether playing solo or against friends. Presentation leans heavily into cartoon-style visuals and digitised speech samples that echo the personality and humour of the TV show. This faithful recreation of Bullseye’s atmosphere is what gives the game its charm, capturing the spirit of the programme rather than aiming for strict darts realism.

video:video.video:title: By Fair Means or Foul – The C64 Boxing Game That Rewarded Cheating
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Superior Software and developed by Jason Benham, By Fair Means or Foul is a boxing game that stands apart by encouraging players to fight smart—or fight dirty. Alongside standard punches like jabs and uppercuts, players can sneak in illegal moves such as headbutts and low blows when the referee isn’t paying attention. A key feature is the referee awareness system, shown via an on-screen indicator that lets players know when fouls can be committed without being caught. This adds a layer of strategy rarely seen in sports games of the era, forcing players to balance risk and reward inside the ring. Single-player mode tasks players with defeating six increasingly tough opponents on the road to becoming World Champion, while two-player mode offers competitive bouts against a friend. The Commodore 64 version also includes a dedicated training mode, allowing players to practise moves on a punching bag before stepping into real matches.

video:video.video:title: Cabal – Ocean’s Explosive C64 Shooting Gallery
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by TAD Corporation and released to arcades in 1988, CABAL arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1989 via Special FX and Ocean Software. This home conversion brings the explosive third-person shooting action to 8-bit hardware while preserving the core intensity of the arcade original. Players control a lone commando assaulting heavily fortified enemy bases, using a distinctive crosshair aiming system that separates movement from shooting. While dodging incoming fire, players must accurately target gun emplacements, buildings, and vehicles, creating a constant push-and-pull between survival and precision. The Commodore 64 version captures the feel of the arcade experience with solid level design and satisfying destruction, even if the action runs at a slightly reduced pace and with simplified visuals due to hardware constraints. These compromises do little to diminish the thrill of clearing screens under heavy fire.

video:video.video:title: Cadaver – The Bitmap Brothers’ Isometric Amiga Adventure
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by The Bitmap Brothers and published by Image Works for the Commodore Amiga, Cadaver is an isometric action-adventure that places you in the boots of Karadoc, a dwarf thief exploring the deadly halls of Castle Wulf in search of treasure. The game focuses on exploration and puzzle-solving rather than direct combat. Each of the five large levels is packed with traps, locked doors, pressure plates, monsters, and environmental hazards that require careful observation and planning to overcome. Progress depends on understanding the castle’s layout and using items intelligently rather than relying on brute force. Gameplay revolves around object manipulation and logical thinking. Players push barrels, collect keys, trigger mechanisms, and cast spells to navigate rooms safely. With no traditional fighting system, timing, positioning, and clever use of the environment are essential for survival.

video:video.video:title: California Games – Six C64 Sports Events, One Bruised Ego, and That Surfing Bit
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Epyx, California Games takes the multi-event formula of Summer Games and Winter Games and reworks it with a laid-back, beach-side vibe. You’re dropped into a colourful celebration of Californian sports culture, where style, timing, and flow matter just as much as raw skill. The game features six distinct events, each with its own controls and rhythm. Half-pipe skateboarding focuses on tricks and balance, footbag is all about keeping the hacky sack airborne, surfing challenges you to read the waves, roller skating demands quick reactions on the boardwalk, BMX mixes racing with jumps, and flying disc tests accuracy and timing. Visually, California Games bursts with colour and personality, capturing the atmosphere of each sport with expressive sprites and smooth animation. The soundtrack adds to the mood, with instantly recognisable tunes like Louie Louie and Wipe Out giving the game a strong identity.

video:video.video:title: Cannon Fodder – The Amiga War Game That Smiled While Everyone Died
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Sensible Software, Cannon Fodder is a top-down, squad-based action game that blends fast-paced shooting with tactical decision-making. You command a small unit of soldiers across jungles, deserts, and frozen landscapes, guiding them through missions that demand careful movement, positioning, and awareness of the terrain. While the controls are immediate and accessible, survival depends on strategy. You need to manage limited ammunition, avoid mines and traps, and keep your squad alive as casualties permanently remove soldiers from your roster. Each loss is marked, reinforcing the game’s underlying message beneath the playful presentation. The bright visuals and catchy theme tune, famously declaring “War Has Never Been So Much Fun,” contrast sharply with the reality of what’s happening on screen. This satirical tone gives Cannon Fodder its identity, using humour to highlight the human cost of conflict rather than glorifying it.

video:video.video:title: Cannon Fodder 2 – Did the Amiga Sequel Go Too Far?
video:video.video:description: Released in November 1994 by Sensible Software and published by Virgin Interactive for the Commodore Amiga, Cannon Fodder 2 builds on the explosive foundations of the original with a bold time-travel twist. This sequel sends your tiny four-soldier squad across wildly different eras, from deserts and medieval battlefields to alien worlds, each with its own tactical challenges. Gameplay retains the tight overhead run-and-gun mechanics that made the series famous. Players command troops armed with machine guns, grenades, rockets, and vehicles such as jeeps, tanks, and helicopters. Success depends on positioning, timing, and knowing when to sacrifice firepower for survival as enemy numbers and hazards escalate. Level design was handled by journalist-turned-designer Stuart Campbell, introducing more complex, puzzle-like layouts packed with hidden routes and pop-culture references. While some critics noted a sharp increase in difficulty and lighter narrative framing, the moment-to-moment action remains fast, precise, and punishing.

video:video.video:title: Card Sharks – Could You Beat the C64’s Money Cards Round?
video:video.video:description: Card Sharks (1988), developed and published by Accolade and designed by Mike Lorenzen, is a multi-game card simulation for the Commodore 64 featuring several popular casino classics. Players can choose between poker (including five-card draw, seven-card stud, and Texas Hold ’Em), hearts, and blackjack, competing against up to three computer-controlled opponents. Opponents are drawn from a cast of quirky characters, including political figures and comic personalities, each adding humour and personality to the matches. Success depends on skill, bluffing, and risk management in poker, careful trick-avoidance in hearts, and disciplined play against the dealer in blackjack. The game features well-drawn character graphics and expressive animations, giving opponents visual reactions to wins and losses, while simple sound effects keep the focus on gameplay. By offering multiple card games in one package with solid presentation and entertaining rivals, Card Sharks remains a fondly remembered title for fans of relaxed, strategic C64 gaming.

video:video.video:title: Castle Master – Exploring Freescape’s Haunted 3D Castle on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Incentive Software and published by Domark, Castle Master is a first-person 3D adventure built using the Freescape engine for the Commodore 64. Set inside a mysterious and dangerous castle, the game focuses on exploration, atmosphere, and puzzle-solving rather than fast-paced action. Players can choose to play as either a prince or a princess, both tasked with rescuing their sibling from the evil Magister. Progress requires carefully navigating interconnected rooms, interpreting cryptic clues, and manipulating objects to unlock new areas, all while surviving encounters with hostile spirits. Combat is limited and deliberate, with a simple slingshot used to defend against supernatural threats. The emphasis remains firmly on observation and problem-solving, encouraging players to study the environment and think logically about each challenge rather than relying on reflexes. Although constrained by the Commodore 64’s hardware, Castle Master delivers a strong sense of immersion through its moody design and ambitious 3D structure.

video:video.video:title: Cauldron – The C64 Witch Game That Looked Magical and Played Nasty
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Palace Software, Cauldron is a distinctive Commodore 64 title that blends platforming and shoot-’em-up action within a spooky, Halloween-inspired fantasy setting. Players take on the role of a young witch determined to overthrow the Pumpkin King and claim the title of Witch Queen. The game is split into two contrasting gameplay styles. One section has you flying on a broomstick, collecting keys and magical ingredients while fending off enemies. The other shifts to underground platform-based caves, where precise jumping and careful movement are required to retrieve potion components needed to progress. Cauldron stands out for its strong atmosphere, with detailed sprites and smooth scrolling that bring its eerie world to life. The experience is reinforced by Keith Miller’s haunting soundtrack, which adds tension and mood throughout both gameplay sections. Known for its demanding difficulty, Cauldron requires careful management of magic points and sharp platforming skills.

video:video.video:title: Cauldron II on the C64 – Why Did They Make You Play as the Pumpkin?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Palace Software, Cauldron II: The Pumpkin Strikes Back turns the tables on its predecessor by putting you in control of Bouncey the Pumpkin, out for revenge against the Witch Queen who destroyed the pumpkin kingdom. The action takes place inside a vast, side-scrolling castle made up of more than 120 interconnected rooms. Progress is driven by exploration as you hunt down six magical items, each unlocking new abilities needed to reach deeper areas and ultimately face the Witch Queen herself. Movement is the game’s defining twist. Bouncey is always bouncing, and you can only influence direction mid-bounce, turning every jump into a test of timing and precision. Combined with traps, enemies, and environmental hazards, this creates a demanding but highly distinctive platforming challenge. Known for its moody visuals and unusual control system, Cauldron II has earned cult status among Commodore 64 fans.

video:video.video:title: Cave of the Word Wizard – The C64 Quiz Game Hiding in a Fantasy Cave
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Timeworks Inc. for the Commodore 64 and developed by Patrick Quinn, Cave of the Word Wizard is an inventive educational action game that blends platforming with spelling challenges. Designed as an early example of “edutainment,” it combines learning and gameplay using pioneering speech synthesis technology. Players choose between two characters, Mark or Becky, and explore a multi-level cave in search of four hidden crystals. The underground environment is filled with hazards such as pits, falling rocks, snakes, and scorpions, requiring careful movement and accurate jumping to survive. Each mistake costs one of the player’s limited bandages. At regular intervals, the mysterious Word Wizard appears to test the player’s spelling skills. Using the keyboard, players must correctly type displayed words to earn rewards. Successful answers restore bandages and trigger encouraging voice feedback, while mistakes result in scolding responses and reduced visibility from a weakening flashlight.

video:video.video:title: Cavelon – The C64 Castle Maze That Wanted You Dead in Armour
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Jetsoft and published by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Cavelon is a medieval-themed action adventure that challenges players to rescue a princess imprisoned deep within the sinister Castle Cavelon. You take the role of a lone knight battling through dangerous dungeons in a race against time. Gameplay spans six horizontally scrolling, maze-like levels filled with enemy knights, archers, and deadly traps. Progression depends on locating and collecting all the scattered pieces of a magical door within each level, which then allows access to the next dungeon on the climb toward the castle’s summit. Combat requires careful positioning and timing, as different enemy types demand different approaches. Along the way, power-ups such as Excalibur grant temporary invincibility and help turn the tide during particularly intense encounters. Each level is also governed by a strict time limit, keeping the pressure high throughout.

video:video.video:title: Caveman Ugh-Lympics – Dino Racing, Clubbing, and C64 Sports Gone Primitive
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Dynamix and published by Electronic Arts for the Commodore 64, Caveman Ugh-Lympics is a tongue-in-cheek sports game that reimagines the Olympic Games through a prehistoric lens. Packed with slapstick humour and over-the-top animation, it turns athletic competition into pure caveman mayhem. The game features six distinct events, each with its own mechanics and timing challenges. From outrunning a rival while a saber-toothed tiger gives chase, to spinning and launching your partner in the absurd Matetoss, every event puts reflexes and precision to the test. Other contests include frantic fire-starting, brutal clubbing duels, dinosaur racing, and pole-vaulting over a very unimpressed Tyrannosaurus rex. Large, expressive sprites and exaggerated animations give the game its unmistakable personality, while simple sound effects reinforce the lighthearted tone. Each event feels different, keeping the action fresh whether you’re playing solo or rotating through challenges with friends.

video:video.video:title: Celtic Legends – The Amiga Strategy Game That Vanished into Myth
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Ubi Soft for the Commodore Amiga, Celtic Legends is a richly detailed turn-based strategy game set in the mystical world of Celtica. Players take on the role of the sorcerer-general Eskel, waging a magical war against his rival Sogrom across a chain of 23 unique islands, each offering distinct terrain and tactical challenges. Gameplay is built around hexagonal battlefields where careful positioning, resource management, and spellcasting are essential for success. Players summon mythical creatures, deploy armies, and unleash powerful magic in order to weaken enemy forces and secure control of each island. Progression relies on long-term planning and adaptive tactics, as every decision affects future encounters. Choosing when to attack, defend, or invest in magical abilities can determine the outcome of extended campaigns, rewarding thoughtful and patient play. Visually, Celtic Legends delivers detailed fantasy environments and well-animated units that bring its myth-inspired setting to life.

video:video.video:title: Championship Wrestling – Did Epyx Give the C64 a Decent Grapple?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Epyx for the Commodore 64, Championship Wrestling is an arcade-style professional wrestling game developed by Free Radical Software. It delivers fast, energetic bouts that capture the spectacle of mid-80s wrestling while offering surprising depth for an 8-bit sports title. Players can choose from eight fictional wrestlers, including The Berserker, Purple Hays, H. Manslayer, Zeke Weasel, Prince Vicious, Colonel Rooski, K. C. Colossus, and Zanto Klaw. Each character has unique strengths, weaknesses, and signature moves, encouraging different strategies depending on who you pick. Matches are viewed from an isometric perspective inside the ring, providing a clear view of the action. Players perform punches, kicks, grapples, and special moves using joystick combinations, all governed by a stamina system that drains with each action. Managing energy is crucial, as reckless attacks can quickly leave a wrestler exhausted and vulnerable.

video:video.video:title: Chase H.Q. – What Went Wrong with the Commodore 64 Conversion?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Ocean Software, Chase H. Q. brings Taito’s famous arcade police chases to the Commodore 64. You step into the role of a highway patrol officer, racing against the clock to hunt down criminals before they escape. Gameplay centres on high-speed pursuits across side-scrolling roads, weaving through traffic and using a limited turbo boost to close the gap on fleeing suspects. Each stage is time-limited, pushing you to balance speed, control, and risk as the pressure mounts. On the C64, the ambition of the arcade conversion is clear, but technical limits take their toll. Performance issues, sluggish controls, and choppy animation impact the flow of the chases, while the audio lacks the punch and excitement of the original coin-op. Often remembered as a missed opportunity, Chase H. Q. on the Commodore 64 stands as a reminder of how difficult it was to translate fast, flashy arcade experiences to 8-bit home computers.

video:video.video:title: Chiller – The C64 Horror Game That Felt Wrong in All the Right Ways
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Mastertronic and developed by David Darling and Richard Darling, Chiller is an early horror-themed platform game for the Commodore 64 that tasks you with rescuing your kidnapped girlfriend from a world inspired by 1980s horror tropes. The game spans five distinct locations — The Forest, The Cinema, The Ghetto, The Graveyard, and The Haunted House — each presented from a top-down perspective. Your goal is to collect magic crosses while avoiding zombies and other unsettling enemies, all while navigating collapsing platforms and hazardous toadstools that steadily drain your energy. Chiller blends fast arcade reactions with light exploration, demanding careful movement and route planning as enemy patterns tighten and room layouts become more punishing. The controls are simple, but the pressure steadily builds as mistakes quickly stack against you. Visually, the game uses bold colours and clear tile design to sell its horror setting, while David Dunn’s atmospheric soundtrack reinforces the eerie tone.

video:video.video:title: Chimera – The C64 Adventure with a Meltdown Timer Breathing Down Your Neck
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Firebird Software and developed by Shahid Ahmad, CHIMERA is an atmospheric isometric action-adventure that places survival and problem-solving at its core. Set aboard a mysterious alien spacecraft orbiting Earth, the stakes are immediate: disable the ship’s weapons and trigger its self-destruct before the planet is destroyed. Players control a lone robot navigating a maze of 64 interconnected rooms, each presented in a classic isometric view. Progress depends on careful exploration, avoiding environmental hazards such as electrical barriers, and solving puzzles that gradually reveal how the ship functions. A key twist is survival management. Food and water steadily deplete, forcing players to plan routes efficiently and prioritise resources alongside puzzle objectives. Items must be gathered and combined to assemble warheads, which are then placed in specific blue rooms to initiate the self-destruct sequence, before racing to the green escape room.

video:video.video:title: China Miner – The C64 Platformer That Punished Every Tiny Mistake
video:video.video:description: China Miner (1984), developed by Ian Gray and published by Interceptor Software, is a notoriously tough single-screen platform game for the Commodore 64. Players control Wally, the sole keeper of the secret location of the Jade Mines of the Pong Dynasty, as he navigates 30 dangerous screens in search of vital objects and an exit key. Each level requires you to collect essential items such as lanterns, pickaxes, and jade artefacts before unlocking the route forward, all while avoiding enemies, lasers, collapsing platforms, and deadly falls. Touching an enemy costs a life and resets all collected objects, making precision, memory, and patience essential to progress. The game’s unforgiving difficulty, flick-screen level design, and tightly timed jumps earned it a reputation as one of the C64’s most challenging platformers. With atmospheric music by Chris Cox and classic early-80s Commodore visuals, China Miner remains a favourite among players who enjoy mastering tough, pattern-based gameplay.

video:video.video:title: Chomp! – Pac-Man Energy, Bigger Teeth, and a Very C64 Appetite
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Cosmi for the Commodore 64, CHOMP! is a quirky side-scrolling action game developed by Robert T. Bonifacio that casts you as a determined goldfish desperate to escape captivity. What begins in a humble fishbowl soon becomes an unusual journey toward freedom. Gameplay revolves around movement, survival, and growth. By eating brine shrimp and other food, your fish grows in size and strength, allowing it to leap into larger tanks and eventually out of the house entirely. Fail to eat enough, and your fish shrinks, becoming weaker and closer to death. Hazards are constant and varied, including aggressive piranhas, swooping fishnets, and even cats’ paws reaching in from above. Players must keep the fish moving at all times to avoid suffocation, adding an extra layer of pressure to every moment. The mechanics are simple but surprisingly tense, with size, health, and momentum all closely linked.

video:video.video:title: Choplifter – The C64 Rescue Mission Where Every Landing Felt Risky
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Dan Gorlin and published by Brøderbund in 1982, Choplifter! is a landmark side-scrolling action game that combines fast reflexes with tactical decision-making. Players take control of a combat helicopter on a dangerous rescue mission deep inside enemy territory. Gameplay unfolds across a horizontally scrolling battlefield where the objective is to rescue hostages from four enemy buildings and safely transport them back to base. The helicopter can carry up to sixteen hostages at a time, requiring multiple risky trips to evacuate all sixty-four prisoners while managing fuel and ammunition. Enemy resistance escalates quickly, with tanks, jet fighters, and ground troops attacking from all directions. Players must carefully land to pick up survivors, avoid accidental friendly fire, and decide when to fight and when to retreat, as fuel shortages can be just as deadly as enemy weapons.

video:video.video:title: Chopper – The Forgotten C64 Shooter That Came Back as Aircop 2000
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Severn Software for the Commodore 64, Chopper is a fast-paced military shoot ’em up that puts players in control of a combat helicopter on a mission to destroy enemy bases and installations across hostile territory. The game features vertically scrolling environments where players must carefully pilot their helicopter through varied landscapes filled with obstacles, ground targets, and airborne threats. Success depends on precise manoeuvring, accurate shooting, and smart positioning under constant pressure. Gameplay places equal emphasis on reflexes and strategy. Players must eliminate enemy defences while conserving ammunition and avoiding damage, making every encounter a balance between aggression and survival. As levels progress, enemy patterns and hazards become increasingly demanding. Visually, Chopper makes strong use of detailed sprites and smooth scrolling to create a convincing sense of speed and altitude. Its presentation highlights the technical strengths of the Commodore 64 and keeps the action clear even during intense sequences.

video:video.video:title: Chuckie Egg – Did the 8-Bit Platform Classic Work on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by A&F Software for the Commodore 64, Chuckie Egg is a fast-paced platform game based on Nigel Alderton’s hugely popular 1983 ZX Spectrum original. The C64 conversion was handled by Sean Townsend and Martin Webb, with music composed by Townsend to suit the SID chip. You play as Hen-House Harry, leaping across single-screen levels packed with platforms, ladders, lifts, and precision jumps. Your goal is simple but relentless: collect every egg on the screen while avoiding patrolling hens and, in later stages, a menacing giant duck that turns each level into a frantic race for survival. A constant countdown timer keeps the pressure high, but grabbing piles of grain will briefly pause it, giving you just enough breathing room to plan your next move. Tight controls and clever level layouts demand accuracy, rhythm, and quick reactions as the difficulty steadily ramps up.

video:video.video:title: Civilization – Building an Empire from 4000 BC on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by MicroProse for the Commodore Amiga, Civilization is the legendary turn-based strategy simulation designed by Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley, following its original PC debut in 1991. Players guide a chosen civilisation from the Stone Age to the modern era, shaping history through city building, exploration, diplomacy, warfare, and technological progress. Each turn involves managing production, trade routes, population growth, scientific research, and government systems while responding to threats from rival nations and roaming barbarians. Victory can be achieved in multiple ways, most famously by constructing and launching a spaceship to Alpha Centauri, rewarding long-term planning and efficient empire management. Strategic depth is enhanced through the construction of iconic Wonders such as the Pyramids, Hoover Dam, and Colossus, each offering powerful bonuses across different eras. The Amiga version includes distinctive audio features, with adapted Civilization themes and tracker-based music suited to the platform’s sound hardware.

video:video.video:title: Cliff Hanger – The C64 Game Inspired by Road Runner-Style Cartoon Traps
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by New Generation Software, Cliff Hanger is a comedic action-adventure for the Commodore 64 inspired by classic cartoon slapstick, particularly the antics of Wile E. Coyote and the Road Runner. Players take control of the cowboy hero Cliff Hanger as he attempts to outwit the villainous El Bandito across a series of carefully staged encounters. Each level is presented like a film set, with success depending on precise timing and positioning rather than reflex-heavy action. Players must move Cliff into the correct spot and trigger traps such as anvils, boulders, cannons, and other contraptions at exactly the right moment to stop El Bandito in his tracks. The gameplay relies heavily on experimentation and learning through failure, as mistimed actions often lead to humorous consequences. Its comic-strip visual style, simple animations, and fitting sound effects reinforce the lighthearted tone, making each scene feel like a playable cartoon gag.

video:video.video:title: Cobra – Stallone’s 1986 Action Film Became a Commodore 64 Platformer
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, COBRA adapts the hard-edged action of the Sylvester Stallone film into a side-scrolling arcade platformer. You step into the boots of Marion “Cobra” Cobretti, taking on the role of a relentless cop racing against time to rescue a kidnapped fashion model. The game unfolds across three distinct stages, moving from city streets to rural areas and finally an industrial factory complex. Progress depends on pushing forward through enemy-packed environments while dealing with hazards and tight jumps along the way. Combat centres around a mix of close-range and ranged weapons, including knives, firearms, and grenades, which must be collected and used carefully. Enemies are persistent, and success often comes down to learning patterns and managing limited space rather than brute force alone. While the presentation and controls were criticised at the time for feeling stiff and slow, COBRA still captures the raw attitude of its source material.

video:video.video:title: Combat School – Ocean Sent the C64 to Basic Training, But Did It Survive?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Combat School is Ocean Software’s home computer adaptation of Konami’s popular arcade title. Programmed by David Collier and Allan Shortt, with graphics by Simon Butler and Sean Ridings and music by Martin Galway, the game delivers a demanding test of skill and endurance wrapped in a military training theme. Players take on the role of a new recruit pushed through a series of gruelling training exercises designed to weed out the weak. These include the obstacle course, firing ranges, the Iron Man race, arm wrestling contests, and hand-to-hand combat against the drill instructor, before putting everything together in a hostage rescue mission. Each event tests different abilities, from precise timing to raw stamina. The gameplay is infamous for its intense joystick-waggling mechanics, requiring fast reactions and physical endurance from the player.

video:video.video:title: Commando – The C64 Arcade Conversion with an Unforgettable SID Tune
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Elite Systems for the Commodore 64, Commando is a vertical-scrolling run-and-gun shooter that adapts Capcom’s arcade hit for home computers. Players take on the role of Super Joe, a lone soldier battling through enemy territory with the mission to survive, push forward, and rescue captured hostages. The gameplay is fast, direct, and relentless. Armed with a machine gun and limited grenades, players must clear waves of enemy soldiers, avoid ambushes from bunkers, and keep moving upward through hostile environments. With only three stages, the focus is firmly on reflexes, positioning, and efficient use of firepower rather than exploration or progression systems. On the Commodore 64, Commando delivers solid sprite work and confident vertical scrolling that keeps the action flowing smoothly. The real highlight is Rob Hubbard’s iconic soundtrack, which injects urgency and atmosphere into every firefight and remains one of the most celebrated pieces of C64 game music.

video:video.video:title: Congo Bongo – Sega’s Isometric Jungle Arcade Game Comes to the C64
video:video.video:description: Originally released in arcades in 1983 by Sega, Congo Bongo is an isometric platform game that puts you in the role of a wronged safari explorer seeking revenge on the mischievous ape Bongo. After your camp is destroyed, the chase takes you through a series of hazard-filled environments viewed from a distinctive angled perspective. Gameplay revolves around timing and positioning as you climb cliffs while dodging coconuts, cross swamps by hopping between hippos and lily pads, and avoid aggressive wildlife along the way. The isometric viewpoint adds depth and challenge, requiring careful judgement of jumps and movement. The Commodore 64 saw two notable versions. The early 1983 release included only the first two stages, trimmed back to suit hardware limits. A later 1985 European release by U. S. Gold restored all four arcade levels with improved visuals and sound, delivering a more complete home conversion.

video:video.video:title: Cops ’N’ Robbers – Jailbreaks, Getaway Vans and C64 Crime Spree
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Atlantis Software and developed by Mike Davis, Cops ’n’ Robbers is a top-down maze action game for the Commodore 64 that casts players as diamond thief Fingers Lonegan. Set across multi-screen maze locations including the Acme Diamond Company and an old mine, the objective is to steal jewels and escape while staying one step ahead of the law. Gameplay focuses on navigating interconnected mazes, collecting diamonds, and returning them safely to the getaway vehicle. Enemies range from police officers and helicopters to more unexpected threats, and players must manage a limited supply of bullets, making every confrontation a tactical decision rather than pure run-and-gun action. The game introduces additional layers through exploration and light puzzle elements. Darkened areas require the use of a torch to see plainly, while keys, TNT, and building interiors add variety and challenge as players progress through the environments.

video:video.video:title: Cosmic Convoy – The C64 Shooter Where Losing the Convoy Meant Everything
video:video.video:description: Cosmic Convoy (1983), developed by Andy Walker and published by Taskset, is a horizontal shoot-’em-up for the Commodore 64 with a unique escort-based gameplay twist. In the game, you pilot a squadron of three fighter ships tasked with protecting a convoy of relief freighters as they travel through the solar system “System Coman.” Unlike many traditional shooters, Cosmic Convoy focuses on defence rather than pure attack. You must intercept incoming alien waves before they crash into the vulnerable convoy ships. Movement is fully four-directional, with the screen scrolling only as your fighters move. A long-range radar display beneath the main play area shows convoy routes and approaching enemies, adding a strategic layer to the action. You are given two squadrons in total, and the game ends if either all freighters are destroyed or your fighters are wiped out.

video:video.video:title: Cosmic Tunnels – Lost in a C64 Space Shooter Nobody Mentions
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Tim Ferris and published by Datamost for the Commodore 64, Cosmic Tunnels is a distinctive space-themed action game that blends several gameplay styles into one ambitious sci-fi adventure. Players take on the role of a pilot tasked with travelling from the planet Sirref and recovering vital energy resources from hostile asteroids. The journey begins with a launch sequence where players dodge falling meteors before entering one of four cosmic tunnels. This leads into a fast-paced 3D tunnel section, requiring quick reflexes to avoid or destroy incoming mines within strict time limits. After exiting the tunnel, players must carefully land on an asteroid platform while battling enemy defences. The final stage switches perspective again, placing players in control of an astronaut who must collect energy bars while avoiding hostile creatures and making use of speed boosts and jetcopters.

video:video.video:title: Countdown to Meltdown – Stop the C64 Reactor Before It Blows
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Creative Sparks and published by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Countdown to Meltdown is an ambitious first-person action-adventure set inside the futuristic Brands Point nuclear facility. Players command a team of androids racing against time to prevent a catastrophic reactor meltdown. The game is presented from a 3D first-person perspective, placing players inside a vast maze of corridors, lifts, and control rooms. With over 2,000 interconnected locations, exploration, memory, and careful navigation are essential to survival and progress. Gameplay focuses on strategic planning and resource management. Players must repair broken elevators, disable security systems, and overcome automated defences while switching between multiple androids, each with unique strengths and limitations. Every decision impacts the race against the clock. Limited energy supplies, hostile environments, and malfunctioning machinery add constant pressure. Success depends on balancing speed with caution, learning the facility’s layout, and using each android effectively to reach the reactor core in time.

video:video.video:title: Crazy Comets – A C64 Shooter That Came at You from Every Angle
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Martech for the Commodore 64, Crazy Comets is a fast-paced multidirectional shooter inspired by Gottlieb’s arcade hit Mad Planets. Players are tasked with defending a vulnerable planet from waves of unpredictable comets and space debris. You control a rotating spaceship positioned at the centre of the screen, firing in all directions to intercept incoming threats. Each stage increases in speed and intensity, demanding sharper reflexes and tighter control as the screen fills with hostile objects. The minimalist design keeps the focus firmly on pure arcade action. With no distractions, success depends entirely on positioning, timing, and managing multiple attack angles at once. The steadily rising difficulty ensures constant pressure throughout every session. One of the game’s defining features is its iconic soundtrack by Rob Hubbard. The energetic SID composition drives the pace of play and adds excitement to every encounter, helping elevate Crazy Comets beyond a simple shooter.

video:video.video:title: Creatures – Cute C64 Sprites, Horrible Little Torture Screens
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Apex Computer Productions and published by Thalamus Ltd, Creatures is one of the most technically impressive platform games on the Commodore 64. The title is an acronym for Clyde Radcliffe Exterminates All The Unfriendly Repulsive Earth-ridden Slime, hinting at the game’s playful tone beneath its demanding gameplay. Players take control of Clyde Radcliffe, a member of the Fuzzy Wuzzies, as he explores a hostile island to rescue his captured friends from sinister demons. Traditional side-scrolling platforming is blended with puzzle-solving, most notably in the infamous “torture screens,” where careful planning and precise execution are required to save trapped creatures from elaborate mechanisms. Creatures is widely praised for its technical achievements, including smooth parallax scrolling, richly detailed environments, and expressive character animation. Steve Rowlands’ energetic soundtrack drives the action and complements the game’s shifting moods, balancing cute visuals with a darker edge.

video:video.video:title: Creatures 2 – The C64 Sequel That Went Full Torture Chamber
video:video.video:description: Creatures 2: Torture Trouble (1992), developed by Apex Computer Productions and published by Thalamus, is one of the most technically impressive late-era releases on the Commodore 64. You play as Clyde Radcliffe, whose children have been kidnapped by demons and hidden across three dangerous islands. To rescue them, you must survive a series of intricate “torture screens,” trampoline bonus stages, boss encounters, and hazardous island-hopping sections. Rather than focusing on traditional platforming, Creatures 2 emphasises puzzle-solving and experimentation. Each torture chamber is filled with elaborate mechanisms that must be activated in the correct order to progress. The game is famous for its detailed cartoon-style graphics, featuring advanced multicolour sprites and smooth animation that pushed the C64 hardware to its limits. Steve Rowlands’ energetic soundtrack and sound effects further enhance the experience. Critically acclaimed on release — including a famous 97% score from Zzap!

video:video.video:title: Crossfire – The C64 Shooter Where Enemies Came from Every Direction
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Sierra On-Line for the Commodore 64, Crossfire is a fast-paced arcade shooter originally developed by Jay Sullivan and Charles Benton. First appearing on the Apple II in 1981, the game made a strong transition to the C64 with its sharp, reflex-driven gameplay intact. You pilot a ship through a grid-based maze, facing relentless waves of alien enemies attacking from all directions. Movement and firing are possible in four directions, forcing you to think quickly at intersections while staying one step ahead of incoming threats. A key twist comes from limited ammunition, meaning survival depends as much on positioning and timing as it does on fast reactions. Charging blindly into danger is rarely rewarded, making Crossfire a tense and strategic experience despite its simple presentation. One of the Commodore 64 version’s standout features is its SID soundtrack, delivering a catchy rendition of the “Peter Gunn” theme that adds extra intensity to the action.

video:video.video:title: Crystal Castles – Bentley Bear’s Arcade Maze on the Commodore 64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984, Crystal Castles is an arcade-style collect-’em-up developed by Atari and brought to the Commodore 64 by US Gold. Players take control of Bentley Bear, navigating a series of colourful, multi-level castles viewed from an isometric perspective that was still relatively uncommon at the time. Each level challenges players to collect every gem scattered across maze-like platforms while avoiding enemies that patrol the castles. Berthilda the Witch and her minions create constant pressure, forcing careful movement and route planning. Occasionally, a magic hat appears, granting temporary invincibility and a brief chance to clear sections without fear. As the castles progress, layouts become more complex and enemy patterns more demanding, pushing reflexes and spatial awareness. The isometric viewpoint adds depth but also increases difficulty, especially when judging movement and avoiding hazards on narrow paths.

video:video.video:title: Crystal Dragon – The Amiga RPG Where the Dungeon Fights Back
video:video.video:description: Released in 1994 by Magnetic Fields for the Commodore Amiga, Crystal Dragon is a classic first-person dungeon crawler inspired by genre-defining titles such as Dungeon Master. Designed for RPG fans who enjoy deep exploration and strategic combat, the game places players in a dangerous fantasy world filled with traps, monsters, and mystery. Players control two adventurers on a quest to recover a powerful artefact from an evil wizard. Exploration takes place across maze-like dungeon levels, where progress depends on solving puzzles, locating hidden passages, and surviving real-time battles against hostile creatures. Combat unfolds in real time, requiring quick reactions and careful positioning. Players must manage weapons, spells, and defensive tactics while monitoring health and stamina. The detailed inventory system allows equipment, food, and key items to be organised and used strategically throughout the journey. Resource management plays a major role in survival.

video:video.video:title: Curse of Ra – Ancient Egypt Meets C64 Puzzle Pain
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Rainbow Arts for the Commodore 64, Curse of Ra is a distinctive top-down puzzle game set deep within an ancient Egyptian pyramid. Players control a scarab beetle navigating fixed-screen chambers, tasked with clearing every stone from the board by matching pairs of identical symbols aligned horizontally or vertically. The puzzle design gradually increases in complexity, introducing immovable blocks, teleporters, slippery tiles, and other hazards that require careful planning rather than quick reflexes. Each room becomes a test of logic and foresight, rewarding players who think several moves ahead. The game offers two plainly defined modes. Logic Mode features over 100 untimed levels focused purely on problem-solving, while Arcade Mode introduces time limits across 75 stages, alongside collectible coins that can be spent on power-ups between rounds. This dual structure caters to both relaxed puzzle fans and players seeking a faster-paced challenge.

video:video.video:title: Curse of the Azure Bonds – Branded, Broke and Trapped in a C64 RPG
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Strategic Simulations Inc. for the Commodore 64, Curse of the Azure Bonds is a classic role-playing game and the acclaimed follow-up to Pool of Radiance in the legendary Gold Box AD&D series. Players build and command a party of adventurers as they journey through the Forgotten Realms, uncovering the mystery of the magical “azure bonds” marked on their arms. The game blends exploration, questing, and tactical turn-based combat. Gameplay alternates between first-person dungeon crawling and overhead battlefield encounters, delivering the deep strategic feel that defined the Gold Box engine. Careful party management, spell selection, and positioning are essential for survival. The game expands on its predecessor with richer quests, more character classes, and improved balance, including options such as paladins and rangers. Its design closely mirrors tabletop AD&D, offering strong replay value and long-term depth.

video:video.video:title: Cybernoid – The Hewson C64 Shooter That Gave You No Breathing Room
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Hewson Consultants and programmed for the Commodore 64 by Nick Jones (based on Raffaele Cecco’s original design), Cybernoid: The Fighting Machine is a futuristic shoot ’em up in which players pilot a highly armed combat craft to reclaim stolen Federation cargo from deadly pirate strongholds. Divided into three flip-screen levels rather than smooth scrolling, the game demands tactical navigation and weapons selection as you confront gun turrets, homing missiles and hostile pirate vessels. Power-ups and built-in ship weapons — including shields, impact mines, bounce bombs and homing seekers — must be used thoughtfully to survive each screen and collect treasure before time runs out. The Commodore 64 version is especially revered for its colourful graphics that pushed the 8-bit system’s palette, and its atmospheric SID soundtrack composed by Jeroen Tel, giving it a distinctive audio-visual identity among classic C64 shooters.

video:video.video:title: D/Generation – The Amiga Office Block Where Everything Wants You Dead
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Mindscape for the Commodore Amiga, D/Generation is a cyberpunk isometric action-adventure set inside a futuristic biolab tower in Singapore. You play as a lone courier caught in the middle of a catastrophic experiment, forced to navigate floors overrun by hostile bioweapon creatures while uncovering what went wrong. Gameplay blends fast, precise combat with methodical puzzle-solving. Armed with an unlimited-ammo laser that can ricochet off walls, alongside grenades, bombs, switches, and teleporters, you must carefully clear rooms, disable security systems, and manage space in tight environments. Every floor is a self-contained maze that rewards planning and sharp reactions. Beyond combat, rescuing trapped survivors and guiding them safely to exits adds another strategic layer, granting extra lives and encouraging exploration. The isometric perspective, smooth animations, and restrained audio design create a tense, focused atmosphere that keeps you constantly alert.

video:video.video:title: Daley Thompson’s Decathlon – The C64 Game That Punished Joysticks
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Ocean Software, Daley Thompson’s Decathlon brought the intensity of Olympic athletics to the Commodore 64 in a way few games had managed before. Officially licensed by double Olympic gold medallist Daley Thompson, it challenges you to survive all ten events of the modern decathlon across two gruelling in-game days. Day one tests raw speed and power with the 100 metres, long jump, shot put, high jump, and 400 metres. Day two raises the stakes with the 110 metre hurdles, pole vault, discus, javelin, and the exhausting 1500 metres. Each event demands qualifying standards, and failure costs one of your limited lives. Complete the full decathlon and the challenge resets with even tougher requirements. The gameplay is infamous for its joystick-waggling controls, where running speed is generated by rapidly moving the stick left and right.

video:video.video:title: Dan Dare II – Why Did the C64 Sequel Let You Play as the Mekon?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988, Dan Dare II: Mekon’s Revenge is a side-scrolling action-adventure for the Commodore 64 developed by Gang of Five and published by Virgin Games. As the second entry in the Dan Dare series, it shifts away from traditional platforming and embraces a more action-driven design inspired by the classic Eagle comic universe. Players can take control of either Dan Dare or his nemesis, the Mekon, exploring the interior of a vast Treen spaceship using a flying motorcycle. Objectives differ depending on the chosen character, with Dan attempting to destroy SuperTreen incubation capsules while the Mekon works to activate and launch them. Combat, exploration, and navigation are tightly interwoven throughout the ship’s maze-like corridors. The game unfolds across four distinct areas, each packed with hazards such as force fields, gravity traps, and moving platforms.

video:video.video:title: Dan Dare III – Did the Eagle Comic Hero Get a Good C64 Send-Off?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Probe Software and published by Virgin Mastertronic, Dan Dare III: The Escape is a sci-fi platform shoot-’em-up based on the classic British comic book hero. In the final chapter of the Dan Dare trilogy, players take control of the legendary space adventurer after he is captured by the evil Treens and imprisoned aboard their orbiting experimental station. His only goal is to escape. Gameplay revolves around exploring five large, maze-like levels, collecting fuel canisters, navigating teleporters, and battling alien enemies using a plasma rifle and jet pack. Progress requires careful navigation and smart resource management. The game blends fast-paced platforming with side-view shooting and multi-directional scrolling. The Commodore 64 version stands out for its responsive joystick controls and atmospheric soundtrack by Maniacs of Noise. Visually, the game features colourful sprites and detailed sci-fi environments that help bring the space station setting to life.

video:video.video:title: Dan Dare – Did the Eagle Hero Get the C64 Game He Deserved?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Gang of Five and published by Virgin Games for the Commodore 64, Dan Dare: Pilot of the Future brings the legendary British comic book hero to home computers in a cinematic sci-fi adventure. Captain Dan Dare must stop his arch-enemy, the Mekon, from destroying Earth by diverting a deadly asteroid on a collision course with the planet. The game unfolds across a series of multi-screen environments, combining platforming, exploration, and light puzzle-solving. Players guide Dan through alien bases and hostile locations, battling enemies in hand-to-hand combat while navigating hazards and searching for the correct route forward. Progress relies on observation and timing as much as reflexes. A standout feature is the comic-inspired presentation, which helps capture the tone and identity of the original Eagle comic strip. The Commodore 64 version delivers a strong sense of atmosphere through detailed environments and moody sci-fi styling, giving the adventure a distinct identity among licensed games of the era.

video:video.video:title: Dancing Monster – Commodore’s Strangest Early C64 Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Commodore Business Machines (UK) Ltd. , Dancing Monster is an unusual first-person action game developed by Peter Dekany and Denes Baan for the Commodore 64. Blending fantasy themes with shooter-style mechanics, it stands out as one of the system’s more experimental early titles.
