Players are tasked with rescuing a princess who has been transformed into a grotesque dancing monster by an evil wizard. Using a crosshair, the goal is to destroy specific parts of the creature in a strict sequence, with each required body part displayed on screen. Speed and accuracy are essential, as mistakes cause previously destroyed parts to regenerate. The challenge ramps up as players must complete the entire sequence within a limited time while managing an action gauge that steadily drains. Missed shots, hesitation, or targeting the wrong area can quickly undo progress and lead to failure.

video:video.video:title: Indy Heat – The Amiga Racing Game Built for Screaming at Your Mates
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992, Danny Sullivan’s Indy Heat is a fast-paced top-down racing game developed by Sales Curve and based on Leland Corporation’s 1991 arcade hit starring IndyCar champion Danny Sullivan. The Amiga version delivers a high-energy racing experience that closely mirrors the speed, intensity, and presentation of the original arcade machine. Players race across nine international circuits, each packed with sharp corners, aggressive rivals, and demanding layouts, culminating in the dramatic Tradewest Speed Bowl finale. Every race is a balance of raw speed and strategy, with fuel levels, vehicle damage, and limited turbo boosts all playing a critical role in success. Pit stops are central to gameplay, allowing drivers to refuel, repair damage, and restock turbos at the cost of valuable race time. The AI is famously unforgiving, particularly Danny Sullivan’s yellow car, which uses heavy rubber-banding to keep the pressure on until the final lap.

video:video.video:title: Darkseed – The Amiga Horror Adventure Built Around H.R. Giger’s Art
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Cyberdreams for the Commodore Amiga, Darkseed is a psychological point-and-click adventure that blends science fiction horror with deeply unsettling themes. You play as Mike Dawson, a successful advertising executive who moves into a quiet mansion, only to discover he has been implanted with an alien embryo while unconscious. Gameplay revolves around exploration, puzzle-solving, and navigating between the real world and a nightmarish parallel dimension known as the Dark World. Every action is governed by a strict in-game time limit, forcing careful planning as the alien embryo slowly matures. Missed clues or wasted time can permanently lock you out of progress, making tension a constant companion. One of Darkseed’s defining features is its striking visual presentation. The game uses high-resolution 640×350 graphics on the Amiga to showcase the biomechanical artwork of H.

video:video.video:title: Davy Crockett – Could This Frontier Legend Survive a C64 Platformer?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Cascade Games Ltd. , Davy: King of the Wild Frontier is a side-scrolling action platformer inspired by the exploits of legendary frontiersman Davy Crockett. Set against the backdrop of the American wilderness, the game challenges players to survive hostile terrain while pushing steadily toward a daring rescue mission. Players guide Davy through forests, rivers, and enemy camps, jumping pits, dodging traps, and taking on adversaries that block the route forward. Progress relies on sharp reflexes and careful timing, with hazards demanding precise movement and awareness as the difficulty ramps up. On the Commodore 64, the game delivers colourful backdrops and plainly defined environments, supported by a light-hearted soundtrack that adds personality to the action. A notable technical feature is its use of speech synthesis, a memorable touch that helped the game stand out among mid-1980s C64 releases.

video:video.video:title: Deactivators – Bomb Disposal, Robots and C64 Panic Under Pressure
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Tigress Marketing and published by Ariolasoft under their Reaktör label, Deactivators is a highly original action-puzzle game built around bomb disposal and spatial problem-solving. In the game, you control a squad of robotic “deactivators” sent into five dangerous research complexes to locate and neutralise bombs planted by terrorists. Gameplay revolves around navigating interconnected rooms, picking up and throwing bombs, activating force-field switches, and using teleporters linked to hidden circuit boards. Each room features shifting gravity orientations, where walls can become floors and ceilings can become walls, forcing players to constantly rethink movement and timing. Security droids patrol many areas, adding a tactical layer as you evade or manipulate them. Visually, the Commodore 64 version uses a restrained colour palette, but impresses with clean layouts and clever spatial design. The standout feature is the atmospheric SID soundtrack by Simon PC Frost, which gives the game a distinctive identity.

video:video.video:title: How Good Was Defender on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Williams Electronics and released on the Commodore 64 by Atarisoft in 1983, Defender brings the relentless arcade action of the 1981 classic into the home. Known for its speed, difficulty, and layered mechanics, it set a new benchmark for shoot ’em ups in the early 1980s. Players pilot a high-speed spacecraft across a horizontally scrolling alien landscape, tasked with protecting stranded astronauts from waves of invading enemies. A key feature is the on-screen radar scanner, which tracks alien positions and human abductions, forcing players to constantly balance situational awareness with fast reactions. Combat is intense and demanding, with smart bombs available to clear the screen in emergencies and hyperspace jumps offering a risky escape option. Mastery comes from learning enemy behaviour, rescuing humans before they mutate, and maintaining control while navigating the terrain at speed.

video:video.video:title: Defender of the Crown – Did the C64 Capture Cinemaware’s Ambition?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Cinemaware for the Commodore 64, Defender of the Crown casts players into 12th-century England following the death of King Richard. Taking the role of a Saxon lord, the objective is to reclaim the throne by driving back Norman invaders and uniting the country under one ruler. The game blends turn-based strategy with action-led sequences. Players manage territories, raise armies, and choose how to advance their campaign through jousting tournaments, castle sieges, and sword fights. Strategic decisions on the map directly affect these encounters, creating a distinctive mix of planning and hands-on gameplay. On the Commodore 64, Defender of the Crown stood out for its cinematic presentation, featuring detailed illustrations and animated scenes rarely seen on the platform at the time. Jim Cuomo’s atmospheric music reinforces the medieval setting and helps sell the sense of scale and drama.

video:video.video:title: Defenders of the Earth – Flash Gordon’s C64 Team-Up Revisited
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990, Defenders of the Earth is a side-scrolling action platformer for the Commodore 64, developed by Enigma Variations and published by Hi-Tec Software. Based on the animated television series, the game brings together legendary heroes Flash Gordon, Mandrake the Magician, Lothar, and the Phantom as they attempt to rescue their kidnapped children from the clutches of Ming the Merciless. Players mainly take control of Flash Gordon, fighting through Ming’s fortress across enemy-filled screens packed with traps and demanding platforming sections. Progress isn’t just about combat, as players must regularly call upon the other Defenders to overcome obstacles and solve environmental challenges. Each hero has a specific ability that is essential for advancement. Mandrake can conjure bridges to cross gaps, Lothar can smash through solid barriers, and the Phantom can unlock sealed doors. Switching between these powers adds a puzzle-like layer to the action and encourages careful planning rather than constant forward momentum.

video:video.video:title: Deflektor – The C64 Laser Puzzle That Made Mirrors Seriously Addictive
video:video.video:description: Deflektor (1987), developed by Vortex Software and published by Gremlin Graphics, is a top-down puzzle-action game that challenges players to guide a laser beam through complex mazes using movable mirrors. Each level requires you to destroy all energy “cells” on screen before directing the beam to its receiver. Along the way, you must contend with mines, polarisation filters, fibre-optic connectors, and other hazards that constantly alter the beam’s behaviour. The laser has limited energy, and careless reflections can cause it to overheat, forcing players to balance precision, speed, and planning in real time. With 60 increasingly demanding levels, Deflektor combines logical problem-solving with fast-paced arcade pressure, creating a uniquely tense gameplay experience. Its inventive mechanics and elegant design have influenced many later puzzle games, securing Deflektor’s reputation as one of the finest cerebral action titles on the Commodore 64.

video:video.video:title: Delta – C64 Shooting with a Soundtrack People Still Talk About
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Thalamus Ltd and developed by Stavros Fasoulas, Delta is a horizontally scrolling shoot-’em-up set deep within the Delta Sector of space. Players take on the role of an elite Delta Patrol pilot, battling alien forces while rescuing stranded ships across a long and demanding campaign. The game spans 32 levels filled with tightly choreographed enemy waves and environmental hazards. Destroying specific formations releases power-ups that boost speed, firepower, and shields, but not all formations are beneficial, forcing players to learn patterns and make quick risk-versus-reward decisions on the fly. Delta is especially renowned for its soundtrack by Rob Hubbard. The iconic title theme draws inspiration from Philip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi, while the in-game music echoes the pulsing rhythms of Pink Floyd’s On the Run, creating a moody, driving atmosphere that perfectly complements the action.

video:video.video:title: Derby Day – Could You Beat the Bookies on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Pete G. Curtis and published by CRL Group PLC for the Commodore 64, Derby Day is an early horse racing betting simulation that recreates the excitement of a day at the races in a simple, accessible format. Players are presented with a race card featuring seven fictional horses and must decide how to place their wagers. Gameplay centres on managing a virtual bankroll and choosing between different betting options, including win, each-way, and forecast bets. Once selections are made, an animated race sequence plays out, determining the results and updating the player’s balance based on their predictions. Rather than focusing on complex statistics or deep simulation systems, Derby Day emphasises quick decision-making and the suspense of uncertain outcomes. Success depends on reading form, judging odds, and knowing when to take risks or play it safe.

video:video.video:title: Desert Strike on the Amiga – Running Out of Fuel Was Half the Battle
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Electronic Arts for the Commodore Amiga, Desert Strike: Return to the Gulf is an isometric action-shooter designed by Mike Posehn and John Manley that places players in command of an Apache attack helicopter during a fictional Middle Eastern conflict. Blending fast-paced arcade combat with strategic mission design, the game features large scrolling maps, detailed mission briefings, hostage rescues, and multiple objectives that must be completed in sequence. Players must carefully manage fuel, ammunition, and armour while navigating hostile territory, balancing aggression with planning to survive each operation. The distinctive isometric viewpoint delivers a strong pseudo-3D effect, allowing smooth movement across varied terrain and enhancing spatial awareness during combat. On the Amiga, the game retains the depth and challenge of the original Sega Mega Drive version, standing out as one of the strongest home computer conversions of the era.

video:video.video:title: Die Hard – Did the C64 Game Capture the Battle for Nakatomi Plaza?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 for the Commodore 64, Die Hard is an action-adventure game developed by Silent Software and published by Activision, adapting the blockbuster 1988 film. Players take control of NYPD officer John McClane as he battles terrorists inside the towering Nakatomi Plaza to rescue hostages and stop Hans Gruber’s plan. The game spans multiple floors of the building, presented as interconnected rooms and corridors that must be explored methodically. Players gather weapons, medical supplies, and key items while confronting armed enemies and navigating hazards scattered throughout the tower. Iconic moments from the film are woven directly into the gameplay, including crawling through ventilation shafts, defusing bombs, and escaping danger using improvised tactics. Progress depends on careful exploration, smart item use, and surviving increasingly dangerous encounters. While technically limited by the hardware, the Commodore 64 version captures the tension and structure of the movie well.

video:video.video:title: Dino Eggs – The C64 Platformer That Sent You Back in Time
video:video.video:description: Dino Eggs is a classic platform puzzle originally by David H. Schroeder and published by Micro Fun, with the Commodore 64 version converted by Leonard Bertoni. Many references list the C64 release as 1983, but Commodore 64 database sources record an official February 1984 launch — and I didn’t get my hands on a copy here in the UK until 1984. You play Time Master Tim, journeying into the prehistoric past to collect dinosaur eggs and rescue baby dinos while dodging proto-snakes, spiders and the colossal threat of Dino Mom’s stomp. Gameplay blends platforming precision with thoughtful strategy. You must build and maintain fire to keep Mama Dino at bay while navigating multi-screen levels full of hazards. Planning routes, managing your load of eggs, and timing your retreats to the time warp add tactical depth that sets this title apart from many early 8-bit action games.

video:video.video:title: Dizzy – The C64 Adventure That Launched Codemasters’ Egg-Shaped Hero
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Codemasters for the Commodore 64, Dizzy is the debut adventure of the iconic egg-shaped hero created by The Oliver Twins. Following its success on the ZX Spectrum, the C64 version was carefully adapted to Commodore hardware, introducing Dizzy to a new audience while preserving the spirit that made the original so popular. Players guide Dizzy across a colourful fantasy world on a quest to defeat the evil wizard Zaks. The gameplay blends platforming with inventory-based puzzles, requiring exploration, logical thinking, and precise jumping. Progress often depends on using the right item in the right place, rewarding careful observation and experimentation. The Commodore 64 version features clean sprite work and a memorable SID soundtrack by David Whittaker, adding atmosphere and personality to the adventure. While controls and visuals were tailored to the system, the game retained its charm and challenge, making it instantly recognisable across platforms.

video:video.video:title: Doctor Who and the Mines of Terror – Was the Sixth Doctor Any Good on C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Micro Power, Doctor Who and the Mines of Terror places you in control of the Sixth Doctor as he investigates the dangerous mining complex on the second moon of Rijar. The Master’s plan to exploit the rare mineral Heatonite threatens time itself, and it’s up to you to stop it. Gameplay focuses on exploration, puzzle-solving, and careful movement through a large interconnected map. You guide the Doctor through elevators, tunnels, and industrial chambers, avoiding hazards and enemies while using items to progress. Splinx, the Doctor’s robotic cat companion, adds both flavour and utility to the adventure. The design draws inspiration from Castle Quest on the BBC Micro, emphasising memory and navigation over fast reflexes. On the Commodore 64, the game benefits from refinements such as improved elevator mechanics and in-game music, giving the experience a little more atmosphere.

video:video.video:title: Donald Duck’s Playground – Donald Had to Work FOUR Jobs to Build It on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Sierra On-Line for the Commodore 64, Donald Duck’s Playground is an educational game designed to blend classic Disney character appeal with light problem-solving and learning. Players take control of Donald Duck as he works a series of everyday jobs to earn money for building a playground for his nephews, Huey, Dewey, and Louie. The gameplay is split into a collection of mini-games set across different workplaces, including a greengrocer’s shop, a toy store, a railroad switchboard, and an airport cargo terminal. Each location introduces its own mechanics, from sorting vegetables and stocking shelves to directing trains and matching cargo codes under time pressure. Money earned from each job is carefully managed and spent on playground equipment such as swings and slides, which are then placed piece by piece to complete the final goal.

video:video.video:title: Donkey Kong – Why Did the C64 Get TWO Different Official Arcade Conversions?
video:video.video:description: Donkey Kong is one of the most iconic arcade games of all time, and on the Commodore 64 it arrived in two very different forms. The first port, released in 1983 by Atarisoft, aimed to replicate the arcade original as closely as possible, delivering familiar layouts, bold colours, and a faithful sense of challenge that many players still regard as the most authentic C64 version. In 1986, Ocean Software released their own take on Donkey Kong, featuring more detailed graphics and enhanced sound. While visually more polished, this version takes a few liberties with the arcade feel, making it a fascinating comparison for long-time fans of the game. In both releases, you control Jumpman as he climbs girders, ladders, and elevators to rescue Lady from the clutches of Donkey Kong. Across four classic stages — the Construction Zone, Cement Factory, Elevator Stage, and the Final Rescue — success depends on precise timing, smart movement, and learning enemy patterns under constant pressure.

video:video.video:title: Doriath – A Forgotten C64 Fantasy Adventure Worth Revisiting
video:video.video:description: Doriath (1985), released by Rabbit Software, is an ambitious action-adventure game for the Commodore 64 designed by Dom Ashworth, with programming by Ian Gray and Lee Braine. Players take on the role of Elidaan the Loremaster, a wizard tasked with recovering the legendary Coronet of Arien — an artifact said to grant immortality. The game world is built around a vast 16×16 screen map, encouraging careful exploration, note-taking, and classic hand-drawn mapping. Progress depends on finding the eight fragments of the Riddlescroll of Wurslea, solving environmental puzzles, mastering spells, and defeating powerful enemies including dragons. Doriath places heavy emphasis on non-linear progression, allowing players to tackle challenges in different orders while gradually unlocking new abilities. Its detailed visuals by Richard Murray and atmospheric music by Chris Cox help create a rich fantasy setting rarely seen in budget C64 releases.

video:video.video:title: Double Dare – Could the C64 Recreate TV’s Messiest Obstacle Course?
video:video.video:description: Released for the Commodore 64 in 1988 in the USA and later in 1991 in the UK, Double Dare is an action-adventure game based on the hit television game show. The US version was developed by Rare, while the UK release was handled by Ocean Software, with both aiming to capture the energetic, messy fun that made the show so popular. Gameplay mixes trivia questions with physical challenges and obstacle-course style action. Players alternate between answering questions to build up cash and taking on fast-paced sequences that test timing, movement, and reflexes, mirroring the structure of the TV show itself. Success depends on both knowledge and dexterity, keeping the pace lively and unpredictable. While the two versions share the same core idea, the US release leans into a more cartoon-style presentation and brisk arcade feel, while the UK version introduces small gameplay and pacing differences.

video:video.video:title: Double Dragon – Billy and Jimmy Lee Bring the Arcade Brawl to the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 for the Commodore 64, Double Dragon is a home conversion of Technōs Japan’s hugely influential 1987 arcade hit, published on the C64 by Melbourne House. You take control of martial artist Billy or Jimmy Lee, fighting your way through a hostile city to rescue a kidnapped girl. The game delivers side-scrolling brawling action built around punches, kicks, and stolen enemy weapons like whips and baseball bats. Movement is left-to-right through a series of urban stages, with combat focused on timing, spacing, and crowd control rather than button-mashing. While the C64 version removes cooperative play and some arcade mechanics such as climbing, it still captures the core rhythm of the original. The presentation is scaled back, but the action remains clear and readable, supported by a moody soundtrack composed by Charles Deenen. Today, Double Dragon on the Commodore 64 is remembered as an ambitious arcade conversion.

video:video.video:title: Double Dragon II – Did the C64 Sequel Improve on the Original?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Technōs Japan and ported to the Commodore 64 by Binary Design, Double Dragon II: The Revenge continues the story of Billy and Jimmy Lee as they set out to avenge the death of Marian. Building on the success of the original, the sequel delivers faster combat, tougher enemies, and more varied stage design. The C64 version preserves the core arcade experience, featuring side-scrolling brawling action, cooperative two-player gameplay, and a wide range of martial arts techniques. Players can punch, kick, jump, and use weapons to fight their way through gangs of enemies and imposing boss characters. Each stage introduces new environments and enemy types, gradually increasing the challenge. While occasional slowdown can occur during intense scenes, the smooth scrolling and colourful graphics help maintain the game’s fast-paced momentum. The soundtrack, composed by Dave Lowe, adds energy and atmosphere to the action, reinforcing the dramatic tone of the revenge storyline.

video:video.video:title: Dragon Skulle – Ultimate Sent Sir Arthur Pendragon Into His Final C64 Adventure
video:video.video:description: Released in January 1986 by Ultimate Play the Game and developed by Dave and Bob Thomas, Dragon Skulle is the fourth and final entry in the Sir Arthur Pendragon series. This closing chapter sends Sir Arthur to the ominous Skull Island on a mission to destroy the sinister Skull of Souls. The adventure unfolds in an isometric 3D view, using Ultimate’s Filmation engine to present a network of caverns and underground chambers filled with danger. Exploration and puzzle solving are central, with progress depending on careful navigation and understanding how the environment reacts to your actions. Combat and survival are tightly linked to item use. Tools such as a spade for digging and a veil that grants temporary invisibility play key roles, while environmental hazards like falling stalactites and flooding passages constantly drain energy and increase tension.

video:video.video:title: Dragon’s Lair – How Did a LaserDisc Arcade Game End Up on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Software Projects for the Commodore 64, Dragon’s Lair is a home computer adaptation of Don Bluth’s groundbreaking laserdisc arcade phenomenon. Players guide the heroic knight Dirk the Daring through a series of deadly traps and timing-based challenges as he attempts to rescue Princess Daphne from the evil dragon Singe. Rather than using full-motion video, the C64 version reimagines the cinematic adventure through hand-drawn sprites, animated sequences, and carefully timed gameplay events. This approach allowed the game to function within the system’s technical limits. The game was developed by John Darnell and Steve Birtles, with graphics by Nicole Baikaloff and music composed by Colin Porch. It also features the distinctive “Dragonload” tape-loading system, which enabled its large, multi-stage structure. Gameplay focuses on memorisation, quick reactions, and pattern recognition, requiring players to learn the correct inputs for each sequence in order to progress.

video:video.video:title: Dragon’s Lair II – How Did Eight Arcade-Style Trials Fit on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Software Projects for the Commodore 64, Dragon’s Lair II: Escape from Singe’s Castle is the sequel to the popular fantasy adventure, once again placing players in the role of Dirk the Daring. This time, Dirk sets out to infiltrate the Lizard King’s stronghold in search of a legendary pot of gold, facing a series of dangerous environments and enemies along the way. The game is divided into eight distinct stages, including underground caves, castle walls, and fortified interiors, each demanding quick reactions and careful timing. Gameplay blends action sequences with skill-based mini-games, requiring players to master jumping, combat, and obstacle navigation to survive. Progress depends on learning enemy patterns, refining movement, and reacting precisely to traps and hazards. Visually, the game delivers detailed sprites and atmospheric backgrounds that bring its fantasy setting to life on 8-bit hardware.

video:video.video:title: DreamWeb – The Amiga Adventure Where Your Hero Is Told to Kill Seven People
video:video.video:description: Released in 1994 by Creative Reality for the Commodore Amiga, DreamWeb is a dark cyberpunk adventure that pushes the genre into far more mature territory. You play as Ryan, a troubled bartender haunted by violent dreams of a parallel dimension known as the Dreamweb, where a mysterious monk reveals that Ryan is the “Deliverer” chosen to eliminate seven individuals threatening the balance between worlds. Gameplay is presented from a top-down perspective with static screens, using a contextual verb menu to examine environments, collect items, and interrogate NPCs. Progression is driven by investigation and dialogue, with the story unfolding in a largely linear fashion that emphasises atmosphere and narrative over traditional puzzle complexity. DreamWeb stands out for its uncompromising themes, including psychological trauma, violence, and adult subject matter rarely seen in adventure games of the era.

video:video.video:title: Dropzone – Archer Maclean’s C64 Rescue Mission Still Moves Like Lightning
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by U. S. Gold and developed by Archer Maclean under the Arena Graphics name, Dropzone is one of the Commodore 64’s most celebrated shoot ’em ups. Inspired by the arcade classic Defender, it drops you onto the hostile surface of Jupiter’s moon Io with a jetpack-equipped astronaut and a single objective: rescue stranded scientists while surviving relentless alien attacks. Gameplay is fast, precise, and unforgiving. You fly freely across horizontally scrolling landscapes, blasting enemies with your laser while juggling limited smart bombs and a temporary cloaking device. Every rescue adds pressure, as enemies grow more aggressive and the screen fills with threats from all directions. With 99 progressively tougher levels, Dropzone demands sharp reflexes, spatial awareness, and total control of momentum. Its ultra-smooth scrolling, tight controls, and perfectly tuned difficulty curve make it endlessly playable, even by modern standards.

video:video.video:title: DuckTales: The Quest for Gold – Why Is Scrooge Playing the Stock Market on the Amiga?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Incredible Technologies for the Commodore Amiga, DuckTales: The Quest for Gold is a unique platform-strategy hybrid based on Disney’s popular DuckTales animated series. Players take control of Scrooge McDuck as he accepts a challenge from Flintheart Glomgold to become the world’s richest duck within 30 days. Success depends on smart travel planning, skillful play, and clever money management. The adventure features a variety of mini-games, including mountain climbing, jungle exploration, cave navigation, and wildlife photography. Each location introduces different mechanics that test timing, reflexes, and problem-solving. Travel between destinations takes place in Scrooge’s plane, where players must dodge obstacles and the Beagle Boys. Alternative ways to build wealth include diving into the money bin and experimenting with the in-game stock market. Visually, the game captures the colourful cartoon style of the TV series, with expressive character sprites and lively environments.

video:video.video:title: Dune – The Amiga Game That Blended Adventure and Strategy on Arrakis
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Virgin Interactive and developed by Cryo Interactive, Dune is a bold adventure-strategy hybrid set in Frank Herbert’s iconic sci-fi universe. You step into the role of Paul Atreides, navigating the harsh desert world of Arrakis as rival houses battle for control of the all-important spice. Gameplay blends first-person exploration with strategic management. You travel across the planet, meet key characters, forge alliances with the Fremen, and oversee spice production while making decisions that shape the balance of power. Recruiting warriors, deploying ornithopters, and managing resources are all essential to pushing back the Harkonnen threat. As the story unfolds, Paul’s growing psychic abilities add narrative depth and influence how events play out. Progress isn’t just about military strength, but understanding Arrakis, its people, and the consequences of your choices. On the Amiga, Dune shines with atmospheric visuals, cinematic cutscenes, and a memorable MIDI soundtrack by Stéphane Picq and Philippe Ulrich.

video:video.video:title: Dune II – The Amiga Strategy Game That Helped Define the RTS
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Virgin Games and developed by Westwood Studios, Dune II: The Battle for Arrakis is the game that defined what real-time strategy would become. Set on the harsh desert world of Arrakis, you’re drawn into a war where control of spice means control of everything. You choose to command House Atreides, Harkonnen, or Ordos, each offering distinct units, strengths, and tactical approaches. Your task is to harvest spice, construct and defend a base, manage production, and overwhelm rival forces through careful planning and battlefield awareness. The Amiga version delivers a clear, intuitive interface that makes complex systems accessible, while still offering deep strategic choices. From balancing economy and defence to launching coordinated attacks, every decision matters as the war for Arrakis escalates. With an atmospheric soundtrack by Frank Klepacki and genre-defining mechanics, Dune II remains one of the most influential strategy games ever made.

video:video.video:title: Dynablaster – The Amiga Multiplayer Bomber That Could Ruin Friendships
video:video.video:description: Released in early 1992 by Ubisoft and developed by Hudson Soft, Dynablaster is the Amiga’s take on the legendary Bomberman formula, delivering fast-paced maze action built around timing, positioning, and glorious mayhem. Known as Bomberman on other platforms, this version became a firm favourite for Amiga multiplayer sessions. Gameplay takes place in grid-based arenas where players drop bombs to clear blocks, uncover power-ups, and outmanoeuvre opponents. Power-ups increase bomb range, allow multiple bombs, and boost movement speed, turning each round into a tense battle of prediction and quick thinking. Dynablaster truly shines in multiplayer, supporting up to five players using a joystick adaptor, with four on joysticks and one on the keyboard. Matches are frantic, tactical, and endlessly replayable, making it a staple of living-room gaming during the Amiga’s peak years. Single-player mode offers structured challenges across castle-style labyrinths filled with AI enemies, timers, and increasing difficulty.

video:video.video:title: Dynamite Dan – Infiltrate Dr Blitzen’s Lair and Steal the Laser Plans | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Mirrorsoft and developed by Rod Bowkett, Dynamite Dan is a platform action-adventure that blends secret-agent intrigue with precise exploration. Players step into the shoes of Dan, tasked with infiltrating the lair of the sinister Dr. Blitzen to recover stolen plans for a world-threatening laser weapon. The game unfolds across a large mansion made up of 48 interconnected rooms, demanding careful navigation and route planning. Progress hinges on collecting eight sticks of dynamite to open the central safe, while teleporters, trampolines, lifts, and switches add layers to movement and puzzle-solving. Energy management and enemy avoidance keep the pressure high throughout. Level design is a standout, encouraging methodical exploration and rewarding memory and mastery. Contemporary reviews highlighted the structure of the building and the pull of its gameplay loop, noting its strong visuals and addictive pacing, even if the audio was more restrained on the C64.

video:video.video:title: Eddie Kidd Jump Challenge – How Many C64 Buses Can One Man Clear?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Martech Games Ltd. for the Commodore 64, Eddie Kidd Jump Challenge is a licensed stunt game based on the exploits of British daredevil Eddie Kidd. Players take control of Eddie as he attempts a series of increasingly dangerous jumps, beginning on BMX bikes before progressing to powerful motorbikes. Gameplay is built entirely around timing and precision. Each challenge requires careful control of speed, positioning, and take-off angle in order to clear obstacles such as oil barrels and rows of cars. As the game advances, the jumps become longer and more demanding, leaving little margin for error. Rather than relying on gauges or on-screen indicators, players must judge speed instinctively, using visual cues and engine sound to time each run-up perfectly. This design choice adds tension to every attempt and makes successful landings feel especially rewarding.

video:video.video:title: Elidon – The C64 Fantasy Adventure With Over 300 Screens
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Orpheus, Elidon is an atmospheric fantasy adventure for the Commodore 64 that sends you fluttering through an enormous enchanted world of forests, flowers, strange creatures and hidden pathways. You control a fairy tasked with preparing for the return of the Fairy Queen. Her crown, Finvarra, needs seven magical flowers before the celebrations can begin – but first you must explore Elidon and track down seven bottles of magic water needed to make them bloom. And there is plenty of exploring to do. Elidon contains over 300 flick-screen locations, creating a surprisingly large maze for a C64 game from 1985. Your fairy can walk or fly between screens, squeezing through narrow passages and avoiding enemies and obstacles that gradually drain her energy. Various objects can be collected along the way, although you can only carry three at once.

video:video.video:title: Elite – The C64 Space Game That Made the Universe Feel Massive
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, Elite is a landmark space trading and combat simulation developed by David Braben and Ian Bell. It introduced players to a vast, open-ended universe of 2,040 star systems, each defined by its own economy, political alignment, and opportunities for profit or danger. Starting as a novice pilot with a basic ship, players are free to carve their own path toward the coveted Elite combat rating. Lawful trading, smuggling, piracy, bounty hunting, or a careful mix of all four are viable approaches, with player choice shaping every journey. The procedurally generated galaxy ensures a sense of scale and freedom that was unprecedented at the time. Elite’s technical achievements on the Commodore 64 were extraordinary. Its 3D wireframe vector graphics created a convincing illusion of depth, allowing for space combat, hyperspace travel, and precision docking sequences despite the machine’s limited hardware.

video:video.video:title: Emlyn Hughes International Soccer – The C64 Football Game with Actual Flow
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Audiogenic, Emlyn Hughes International Soccer is widely regarded as one of the finest football games on the Commodore 64. Named after England and Liverpool legend Emlyn Hughes, the game set itself apart by blending fast-paced on-pitch action with detailed management and tactical depth. Matches are presented from a side-on perspective, giving players precise control over passing, shooting, and movement. The control system allows for five-directional passes and shots, diving headers, lobs, slide tackles, and carefully weighted through balls, rewarding skill and positioning over button-mashing. Beyond the action, EHIS introduces an ambitious management layer. Players can tweak formations, adjust player abilities, and take teams through full league and cup campaigns, adding long-term strategy rarely seen in football games of the era. This balance of arcade responsiveness and tactical control helped it stand out against rivals.

video:video.video:title: Entombed – Lost Inside an Egyptian Tomb on the Commodore 64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Ultimate Play the Game and developed by Dave and Rob Thomas, Entombed is the second entry in the Sir Arthur Pendragon series. This time, Sir Arthur finds himself trapped deep beneath the Sphinx in an ancient Egyptian tomb, racing against time as his oxygen supply steadily runs out. The game is presented in an isometric 3D view, with a sprawling maze of corridors and chambers packed with traps, puzzles, and hostile creatures such as mummies and scorpions. Progress depends on careful exploration, spatial awareness, and managing limited resources while navigating the tomb’s many dangers. Combat is more direct than in its predecessor, with Sir Arthur wielding a whip that adds urgency and rhythm to encounters. The focus shifts away from complex spell systems toward exploration-driven problem solving, making the experience more approachable while retaining a strong sense of tension.

video:video.video:title: Escape from Colditz – The Amiga Prison Break That Needed Patience
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 for the Commodore Amiga, Escape from Colditz is a tense stealth-adventure inspired by the famous WWII POW camp and the classic board game that shared its name. You’re tasked with planning and executing a daring escape from Colditz Castle, a fortress designed to hold prisoners considered impossible to contain. You control a team of four Allied officers, each starting in different parts of the castle and bringing unique abilities to the escape effort. Exploration, cooperation, and careful timing are essential as you search for items like disguises, tools, and keys while avoiding guards and routine patrols. Presented in an isometric view, the game focuses on planning rather than action, rewarding patience and observation over quick reflexes. Mistakes can be costly, with limited opportunities to recover if plans unravel at the wrong moment.

video:video.video:title: Escape from the Planet of the Robot Monsters – C64 B-Movie Madness
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Teque Software Development and published by Domark, Escape from the Planet of the Robot Monsters is a multidirectional shooter for the Commodore 64, adapted from Atari Games’ 1989 arcade release. The game embraces a tongue-in-cheek 1950s sci-fi theme, blending action with humour and distinctive presentation. Set on Planet X, players control interplanetary agents Jake and Duke on a mission to rescue Dr. Sarah Bellum and other hostages from the evil Reptilons. Using an isometric viewpoint, the game tasks players with navigating maze-like environments, destroying robotic enemies, and activating switches and mechanisms to progress through each level. Combat introduces an extra layer of strategy, allowing players to crouch, rotate, and fire in eight directions while stationary. This system rewards positioning and timing rather than constant movement, setting it apart from many shooters of the era.

video:video.video:title: Everyone’s a Wally – The C64 Adventure with Multiple Characters and One Big Job
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Everyone’s a Wally is an arcade adventure developed by Chris Hinsley and published by Mikro-Gen. Acting as a follow-up to Pyjamarama, the game expands the world of Wally Week, a builder trying to get through a hectic day alongside his family and friends. The action takes place across a lively town made up of more than 30 locations, including streets, shops, offices, and public buildings. Players can switch between five characters — Wally, his wife Wilma, and friends Tom, Dick, and Harry — each with their own jobs to complete. Progress depends on managing time, energy levels, and movement efficiently across the map. Each completed task earns a letter, and collecting them all reveals the password needed to open the bank safe and collect everyone’s wages. The challenge comes from juggling multiple characters, avoiding hazards, and planning the most efficient order to finish every job before energy runs out.

video:video.video:title: Exile – The Huge C64 Adventure Powered by Physics and Exploration
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Audiogenic for the Commodore 64, Exile is a groundbreaking sci-fi action-adventure developed by Peter Irvin and Jeremy Smith. Originally created for the BBC Micro and Acorn Electron, the C64 version preserves the game’s most ambitious ideas, delivering a remarkably deep experience for an 8-bit system. You play as Mike Finn, a lone pilot sent to the hostile planet Phoebus to rescue a lost research team and stop the rogue scientist Triax. The game blends platforming, exploration, shooting, and puzzle-solving within a vast, interconnected world that can be tackled in multiple ways. What truly sets Exile apart is its advanced physics and simulation systems. Gravity, inertia, heat, pressure, and enemy behaviour all interact dynamically, meaning the environment constantly responds to your actions. Solutions are rarely scripted, encouraging experimentation and emergent gameplay long before it became a common design philosophy.

video:video.video:title: Eye of the Beholder II – Darkmoon’s SSI Dungeon Crawling Comes to the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991, Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Darkmoon is a first-person dungeon-crawling role-playing game developed by Westwood Associates and published by Strategic Simulations, Inc. for the Commodore Amiga and other platforms. Set in the Dungeons & Dragons universe, the game continues the story of the original Eye of the Beholder, sending players deep into the mysterious Temple of Darkmoon. Players assemble a party of adventurers, either creating new characters or importing heroes from the previous game. Exploration unfolds in real time from a first-person perspective, with tactical combat, secret doors, traps, and a strong emphasis on puzzle-solving. Compared to its predecessor, the sequel refines dungeon layouts and introduces more intricate puzzles that reward careful observation and planning. On the Amiga, the game benefits from richer visuals and enhanced audio, helping to build a tense and atmospheric experience throughout the temple’s depths.

video:video.video:title: Face Off! – C64 Ice Hockey with Fights, Skates and Flying Teeth
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by MindSpan Technologies and published by Gamestar for the Commodore 64, Face Off! delivers a fast-paced and distinctive take on ice hockey. It blends accessible arcade action with features that helped it stand apart from other sports games of the era. Players can jump into single-player or head-to-head multiplayer matches, controlling one skater at a time while switching seamlessly during play. Customisation options allow you to tweak match length, team sizes of one, three, or five players, and various rule settings, giving the game flexibility rarely seen on the C64. One of Face Off! ’s most memorable features is the cinematic “Shot-Cam,” which cuts to a dramatic close-up during slapshots to heighten the sense of impact. Penalties can also trigger brief on-ice fights, adding an extra layer of tension and personality to matches.

video:video.video:title: Falcon Patrol – Can You Save All Six Airfields Before the Bombers Arrive? | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Virgin Games and developed by Steve Lee, Falcon Patrol is a fast-paced side-scrolling shoot ’em up for the Commodore 64 that puts players in control of a vertical take-off and landing aircraft. Set above a hostile desert landscape, the mission is simple but demanding: defend six vital airfields from relentless enemy bombers. Gameplay focuses on constant movement and situational awareness as players sweep left and right across the terrain, intercepting enemy jets before they can destroy the runways needed for refuelling and rearming. A radar display at the bottom of the screen tracks hostile aircraft and highlights which airfields remain operational, adding a tactical layer to the action. The two-way scrolling and escalating enemy waves steadily increase the pressure, rewarding sharp reflexes and efficient targeting. While the visuals are straightforward, the pace and structure deliver a tense and engaging experience that captures the spirit of early 80s arcade-inspired design.

video:video.video:title: Fernandez Must Die – C64 Guerrilla Action with No Time to Breathe
video:video.video:description: Fernandez Must Die (1988), developed by Antony Crowther (Ratt) and published by Image Works, is a top-down vertical scrolling shooter for the Commodore 64. You play as a lone commando sent to overthrow the ruthless dictator Fernandez, who has seized control of the Republic of El Diablo. Your mission spans eight enemy bases, where you infiltrate buildings through underground tunnels, rescue prisoners, seize gold bars, and fight through waves of soldiers, vehicles, and landmines. Unlike many shooters of the era, the game mixes on-foot combat with vehicle sections, allowing you to take control of jeeps, motorcycles, and tanks. A standout feature is its cooperative vehicle mode, where two players can work together — one driving while the other fires. The C64 version features unlimited bullets, limited grenades, and large interconnected maps that encourage strategic progression between bases.

video:video.video:title: Feud – The C64 Game Where Two Wizards Fought with Herbs
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Binary Design and published under Mastertronic’s Bulldog Software label, Feud is a unique action-adventure built around magical rivalry and spellcraft. In the Commodore 64 version, you play as the sorcerer Learic, locked in a deadly feud with your evil brother Leanoric. To win, you must explore the map, gather herbs and ingredients, brew powerful spells, and hunt down your rival. Spells range from fireballs and lightning to invisibility and zombification, giving the game a strong tactical element. Success depends on learning spell recipes, managing resources, and predicting your opponent’s movements. The C64 edition differs notably from the Spectrum and Amstrad versions, featuring altered object placement and more unpredictable enemy tracking, which makes each encounter more tense and unpredictable. Visually, Feud features bold character sprites, a striking title screen by Ste Pickford, and an atmospheric soundtrack by David Whittaker that reinforces the game’s mystical tone.

video:video.video:title: Fiendish Freddy’s Big Top O’ Fun – The C64 Circus That Wanted You Humiliated
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Gray Matter and published by Mindscape, Fiendish Freddy’s Big Top o’ Fun brings dark humour and arcade-style action to the Commodore 64. Originally a 16-bit title, the game was later converted to the C64 and became one of the showcase releases for the Commodore 64 Games System, highlighting what the platform could still achieve late in its life. Players are tasked with saving a failing circus from demolition by successfully performing six dangerous circus acts. These include diving, juggling, trapeze, knife throwing, tightrope walking, and the human cannonball, each presented as a distinct mini-game with its own rules, timing, and skill demands. Adding mayhem to every performance is Fiendish Freddy himself, a malicious saboteur who interferes at the worst possible moments. His unpredictable antics turn otherwise straightforward acts into tense, reactive challenges that demand concentration and quick reactions.

video:video.video:title: Fighting Warrior – A Pharaoh, a Kidnapped Princess and One Brutal C64 Rescue
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Melbourne House and developed by Studio B Ltd. , Fighting Warrior drops you into a myth-soaked vision of ancient Egypt where a lone hero sets out to rescue Princess Thaya from a Pharaoh’s temple stronghold. Combat is strictly one-on-one, with enemies drawn from Egyptian-inspired fantasy, including winged beasts, dog-headed warriors, and strange half-human creatures. You control high, middle, and low strikes, along with jumping, ducking, and stepping back, making timing and spacing central to survival. Scattered throughout the levels are magical containers that can either help or hinder your progress, adding an unpredictable edge to each encounter. The game places emphasis on reactions and rhythm rather than crowd control, giving fights a deliberate, almost duel-like feel. Known for its striking character animations and bold visual style on the C64, Fighting Warrior earned a cult following despite its repetitive structure.

video:video.video:title: Final Fight – Why Was Guy Missing from the Amiga Conversion?
video:video.video:description: Final Fight (1991), developed by Capcom and ported to the Amiga by Creative Materials under U. S. Gold, is the home-computer adaptation of the classic 1989 arcade beat ’em up. Players can choose from two of the three main heroes — Mike Haggar, Cody, and Guy — as they battle through Metro City to defeat the Mad Gear gang and rescue Haggar’s daughter, Jessica. Gameplay follows traditional side-scrolling brawler mechanics, featuring punches, kicks, throws, jumping attacks, and waves of on-screen enemies. However, the Amiga conversion is notably less fluid than the arcade original. Animation frames are reduced, certain sections are missing, and performance issues such as slowdown affect the pacing. Some iconic stages and elements are simplified or removed, including parts of the Industrial Area and the elevator sequence. Graphically, the game attempts to preserve the arcade’s pixel-art style, but lacks polish and smoothness.

video:video.video:title: Finders Keepers – The C64 Adventure That Introduced Magic Knight
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Finders Keepers marks the debut of David Jones’ Magic Knight series. Set in a playful fantasy world, the game blends platforming, puzzle-solving, and trading mechanics into an experience that was strikingly original for its time. Players control the Magic Knight, sent by the King of Isbisima into the Castle of Spriteland to find a suitable birthday present for Princess Germintrude. To earn a seat at the Polygon Table, the knight must explore dangerous rooms, collect treasure, and outwit the castle’s strange inhabitants while avoiding traps and hostile creatures. Gameplay combines flip-screen rooms with scrolling maze sections, split between the Castle Gardens and the Castle Dungeons. Items collected throughout the castle can be traded, combined, or sold, adding a light economic layer that rewards curiosity and experimentation.

video:video.video:title: Fire Ant – Eight Scorpion-Filled Caves Before You Can Rescue the Queen on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Victory Software and published by Mogul Communications for the Commodore 64, Fire Ant is an early arcade-style puzzle action game that blends strategy with fast reflexes. Players take control of a determined ant exploring a series of underground chambers in a mission to rescue the captured queen from deadly scorpions. Gameplay centres on navigating maze-like rooms filled with traps, locked doors, and roaming enemies. Players must collect keys, avoid hazards, and carefully plan their routes in order to progress safely through each chamber and reach the next stage. Progression relies on observation, timing, and problem-solving, as each new area introduces different layouts and obstacles. Quick reactions are essential, but success also depends on choosing the right path and managing risks effectively. Visually and aurally, Fire Ant reflects the early era of Commodore 64 gaming, with simple graphics and straightforward sound effects designed to support clear, readable gameplay.

video:video.video:title: Firelord – The C64 Fantasy Adventure Built Around Magic and Bartering
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Hewson Consultants and developed by Stephen Crow, Firelord drops you into the cursed kingdom of Torot as Sir Galaheart, a lone knight tasked with reclaiming the sacred Firestone from the Evil Queen. To restore peace, you must recover four charms of eternal youth while surviving a land filled with danger, temptation, and consequence. The game blends exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving into a surprisingly deep experience. You begin unarmed, forced to explore cautiously until you obtain an enchanted crystal to fight off spectral enemies. As you roam forests, villages, and dungeons, you’ll trade, bargain, steal, or face trials that can end in execution if you fail. Firelord stands out for its layered systems. You must manage health, trading energy, and weapon energy while navigating a dynamic economy and morality system where your choices directly affect outcomes and progression.

video:video.video:title: First Samurai – How Good Was This Huge 1992 C64 Conversion?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Vivid Image for the Commodore 64, First Samurai is a fast-paced hack-and-slash action game that blends intense combat with platforming and exploration. Players step into the role of a lone samurai warrior, travelling through ancient Japan and surreal mystical realms to stop an evil sorcerer threatening the balance of the world. Gameplay centres on precise sword combat, enemy patterns, and careful positioning, with the katana as your primary weapon. Stages are filled with hazards, vertical platforming sections, and environmental challenges that require both quick reactions and thoughtful movement to survive. As the adventure unfolds, the game introduces varied enemies, large animated bosses, and interconnected areas that reward exploration. Progress depends on mastering combat timing, learning level layouts, and using upgrades and items effectively to push deeper into hostile territory. On the Commodore 64, First Samurai delivers fluid animation, bold visuals, and a driving soundtrack that gives the game real energy despite the hardware’s limits.

video:video.video:title: Fist II – The Fighting Sequel That Became a 100-Screen C64 Adventure
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Melbourne House and developed by Beam Software, Fist II: The Legend Continues takes the foundations of The Way of the Exploding Fist and expands them into a far more ambitious experience. Rather than a straight sequence of duels, you’re dropped into a sprawling island adventure where exploration and combat are equally important. You travel across jungles, caves, villages, and ancient temples in search of sacred scrolls, with martial arts battles breaking out whenever rivals challenge your progress. Combat features a deep move set, rewarding timing and technique, while each opponent demands a slightly different approach to win. Between fights, the game slows the pace deliberately, encouraging exploration, memory, and careful route planning. Progression comes not just from winning battles, but from meditation, learning new techniques, and collecting the scrolls needed to unlock the game’s true ending.

video:video.video:title: Flash Gordon – Three Completely Different Challenges in One C64 Budget Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Icon Design and published by Mastertronic under the Added Dimension label, Flash Gordon delivers three very different gameplay styles in a single budget release. Based on the classic comic strip hero, the game throws you into a sequence of action-packed challenges inspired by Flash’s pulpy sci-fi adventures. The opening stage drops you into a hostile jungle maze where survival depends on navigation, timing, and avoiding deadly creatures while searching for Prince Barin’s cave. This is followed by a one-on-one beat ’em up showdown against Barin himself, demanding precise punches and kicks to progress. The final section switches perspective entirely, placing you on a high-speed rocket cycle in a first-person pursuit of Ming the Merciless. Obstacles, enemy fire, and reflex-driven action bring the game to a dramatic close. Praised at the time for its variety and strong production values, Flash Gordon stood out as exceptional value for money.

video:video.video:title: Flashback: The Quest for Identity – Did It Live Up to the Amiga Hype?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Delphine Software International for the Commodore Amiga, Flashback is a landmark cinematic platformer designed by Paul Cuisset. Blending rotoscoped animation, science-fiction storytelling, and methodical puzzle-platforming, it pushed narrative and technical boundaries on home computers. Set in a distant future, players take control of Conrad B. Hart, an agent who awakens on Titan with no memory of his past. As he journeys through futuristic cities, dense jungles, and alien environments, Conrad must survive hostile forces while uncovering a hidden conspiracy involving shape-shifting invaders. Gameplay combines precise movement, environmental puzzles, and tactical combat. Players must carefully time jumps, manage limited ammunition, and use tools like shields and weapons to overcome enemies. Progress often depends on observation, patience, and mastering the game’s deliberate pacing. Visually, Flashback stands out for its smooth rotoscoped character animation and cinematic presentation.

video:video.video:title: Flimbo’s Quest – The C64 Platformer Where Enemies Dropped Pieces of a Spell
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by System 3, Flimbo’s Quest is a colourful platform adventure that arrived late in the Commodore 64’s life and showed just how far the machine could be pushed. Players guide Flimbo on a mission to save his village from an evil sorcerer, exploring imaginative worlds packed with hazards, secrets, and magical items. The gameplay blends traditional platforming with light puzzle elements, requiring careful timing, exploration, and smart use of abilities. Flimbo must navigate traps, avoid enemies, and collect treasures while using magic spells that allow him to transform and bypass obstacles in inventive ways. Level design encourages experimentation rather than rushing headlong forward. Visually, the game stands out with richly detailed backgrounds, smooth animation, and vibrant colour use that gives each area its own identity. The presentation is supported by a memorable soundtrack from Allister Brimble, whose upbeat and playful compositions perfectly match the game’s tone and pacing.

video:video.video:title: Flip & Flop – The C64 Platformer Played on the Ceiling
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64 by State Soft, following its original Atari debut in 1983 from First Star Software, Flip & Flop is an isometric action-platformer created by Jim Nangano that blends arcade reflexes with strategic puzzle design. Players alternate control between Flip the kangaroo and Mitch the ape, each tackling separate stages built around climbing ladders, navigating 3D-style platforms, and flipping marked tiles. The main objective is to activate every highlighted tile by jumping onto them, sometimes requiring precise double-jumps on higher levels while avoiding a relentless pursuer. Depending on the character, players are chased by either a zookeeper or a creeping net, forcing constant movement and quick decision-making. Sticky tiles act as temporary traps, briefly halting enemies and creating vital breathing space to plan routes and recover control. Every five stages, a short circus-themed interlude provides a playful break before the difficulty increases.

video:video.video:title: Floor 13 – The Amiga Game That Put You in Charge of a Secret Government
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Virgin Interactive Entertainment and developed by PSI Software Designers, Floor 13 is a dark political strategy game for the Commodore Amiga that places players at the heart of a shadowy British government agency. Operating from the infamous secret 13th floor, you assume the role of Director General, tasked with keeping the government in power by any means necessary. Gameplay is driven through a menu-based interface styled with a film noir presentation, blending espionage, bureaucracy, and moral compromise. Players issue orders to departments such as surveillance, propaganda, blackmail, and assassination in order to suppress scandals, manipulate public opinion, and neutralise threats to government stability. Every decision carries consequences, often with unpredictable outcomes. Public approval is reviewed every 21 days, and failure to maintain sufficient popularity can result in dismissal, imprisonment, or assassination.

video:video.video:title: Floyd of the Jungle – The C64 Platformer Designed by Sid Meier
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by MicroProse for the Commodore 64, Floyd of the Jungle is a fast-paced action-platformer designed by Sid Meier, making it a fascinating early example of his work outside strategy and simulation. Set in a colourful jungle environment, the game mixes arcade action with competitive scoring. Players control Floyd as he leaps through the jungle, avoiding hazards such as alligators, elephants, and hostile pygmies. The goal is to rescue Janice, but competition is fierce, as rivals George and another Floyd are also racing to impress her. Points are earned by collecting birds and knocking out pygmies, with victory going to the first player to reach the target score. The game supports simultaneous two-player action on the C64, turning each session into a frantic race for points rather than a simple rescue mission. This competitive twist gives Floyd of the Jungle a unique identity compared to more traditional single-player platformers of the era.

video:video.video:title: Flunky – The C64 Game That Made You Serve the Royal Family
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Piranha Software for the Commodore 64, Flunky is a satirical adventure game developed by Don Priestley that puts players in the role of a long-suffering butler serving the British Royal Family. Blending British humour with light action and puzzle-solving, the game offers a deliberately eccentric take on palace life. Gameplay revolves around navigating Buckingham Palace while carrying out tasks assigned by various royal family members. Jobs range from simple errands to more demanding challenges that require quick reactions, careful timing, and learning the palace layout to move efficiently between rooms. The game mixes exploration with arcade-style action, often catching players off guard with sudden demands or hazards. Success depends on memorising routes, prioritising tasks, and coping with the unpredictable nature of royal service. Visually, Flunky stands out thanks to Don Priestley’s distinctive, colourful art style, giving the palace and its inhabitants a playful, exaggerated look.

video:video.video:title: Flying Feathers – Can You Stop the Eagles Stealing Every Fish? | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by T. Owen and published by Bubble Bus Software for the Commodore 64, Flying Feathers is a fast-paced arcade-style shooter that challenges players to protect helpless fish from relentless swooping eagles. Taking control of a warden in a small boat, players use a crosshair to shoot down incoming birds before they can steal their prey. Gameplay takes place on a single screen, where quick reactions and accurate shooting are essential. Players begin with five fish to defend, and even if an eagle manages to grab one, well-timed shots can force it to drop the fish back into the water. After a set time, a passing duck and her family provide an extra fish, giving players a valuable second chance to extend their run. At the start of each session, players can choose from eight different skill levels, allowing the game to scale from accessible arcade fun to a demanding test of reflexes.

video:video.video:title: Forbidden Forest – The C64 Game That Genuinely Unsettled Us
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Cosmi and developed by Paul Norman, Forbidden Forest is one of the earliest and most influential horror-themed action games on the Commodore 64. You take on the role of a lone archer venturing into a dark, hostile forest where every step forward brings new danger. Gameplay revolves around careful positioning, precise timing, and strict arrow management as you face off against giant spiders, bees, mutated frogs, dragons, and other nightmarish creatures. Each enemy has distinct movement patterns, forcing you to react quickly while conserving ammunition and avoiding lethal contact. What truly sets Forbidden Forest apart is its atmosphere. Parallax scrolling gives depth to the forest, a dynamic day-to-night cycle steadily ramps up the tension, and context-sensitive music shifts as threats appear on screen. The game was also one of the first to feature animated blood, pushing boundaries and helping define the visual language of survival horror.

video:video.video:title: Force 7 – The C64 Squad Shooter That Mixed Strategy with Alien Combat
video:video.video:description: Released in October 1987 by Superior Quality Software and published by Datasoft, Force 7 is a unique hybrid of arcade shooting and squad-based strategy on the Commodore 64. In this sci-fi action game, you command a crack special-forces team of seven operatives sent to infiltrate an alien-infested energy facility on the planet Karis and rescue trapped Earth colonists. Only one operative is active at a time, and each squad member has specialised abilities — including welding tools, flame-throwers, hydro-guns, and demolition equipment — requiring tactical switching to survive. Gameplay focuses on navigating multi-level rooms using teleporters, collecting ammo and health packs, battling alien “mother” units, and deploying the powerful Battle Unit (BU) mech turret for temporary invincibility. The C64 version delivers strong graphics for the platform and features an atmospheric soundtrack by Rob Sisinni that builds tension throughout each mission.

video:video.video:title: Fort Apocalypse – Rescue 16 Prisoners, Blow the Reactor… Then Escape on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1982 by Synapse Software, Fort Apocalypse is a demanding multi-directional scrolling shooter for the Commodore 64. Developed by Steve Hales and ported by Joe Vierra, the game drops players into a vast underground fortress with a single goal: rescue prisoners and dismantle enemy installations while surviving relentless opposition. Players pilot a highly manoeuvrable rocket copter through sprawling caverns, contending with tight passages, gun turrets, and hostile forces attacking from all directions. Movement and combat require precision, as weapon controls change depending on the helicopter’s orientation, forcing players to think carefully about positioning and timing. A standout feature is the Navatron system, which provides a radar-style preview of upcoming threats beyond the visible screen. This adds a strategic layer rarely seen at the time, allowing players to plan routes and prepare for ambushes before entering dangerous areas.

video:video.video:title: Frak! – A Caveman with a Yo-Yo… Then the Entire C64 Screen Turns Upside Down
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by StateSoft and created by Nick Pelling, Frak! is an unconventional platform game for the Commodore 64 that stands apart thanks to its unusual mechanics and offbeat presentation. Players take control of Trogg, a caveman armed not with clubs or spears, but a yo-yo, on a mission to retrieve three keys from each increasingly hazardous level. Gameplay focuses on careful movement across ladders and platforms arranged in deliberately awkward layouts. Trogg’s yo-yo acts as both a weapon and a tool, used to dispatch enemies and interact with the environment, demanding precision and timing rather than speed alone. Each level is packed with strange hazards, including static enemies such as Scrubbly, Poglet, and Hooter, alongside moving threats like balloons and flying daggers. Touching any obstacle results in instant death, and a strict time limit keeps pressure high.

video:video.video:title: Frankie Goes to Hollywood – Solve a Murder Before You Reach the Pleasuredome on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Ocean Software and developed by Denton Designs, Frankie Goes to Hollywood is one of the most unconventional and ambitious games ever created for the Commodore 64. Inspired directly by the music, imagery, and themes of the band, it drops you into the bizarre town of Mundanesville on a symbolic journey toward the mythical Pleasuredome. Rather than following a single genre, the game blends exploration, action, puzzles, and narrative experimentation. You play as an anonymous everyman, raising four core personality stats — Sex, War, Love, and Faith — by collecting key items and completing more than 60 wildly varied mini-games. These range from arcade-style challenges and logic puzzles to a full murder mystery subplot that adds an unexpectedly dark investigative edge. Progression is non-linear and often cryptic, encouraging experimentation and curiosity rather than brute force.

video:video.video:title: Freak Factory – A C64 Arcade Oddity with a Name You Don’t Forget
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Firebird Software and developed by Simon W. Sorsbie, Freak Factory casts you as Agent One of the Galactic Police Force on a mission to shut down a deranged scientist and his monster-producing laboratory. It’s a strange, experimental title that blends action, platforming, and endurance testing. The game is split into two distinct sections. First, you navigate a multi-level factory, carefully avoiding electrified barriers, spikes, and roaming gargoyles that steadily drain your energy. Progress demands patience and precise movement as you work your way deeper into the complex. Once inside the laboratory, the focus shifts to direct confrontation. Here, you face the professor’s assistants in close-quarters encounters that rely on rapid joystick movement to overpower them, turning survival into a test of stamina as much as skill. Visually, Freak Factory leans into an eerie sci-fi tone, with purple and blue laboratory environments and an abstract player sprite that adds to the surreal feel.

video:video.video:title: Friday the 13th – Find Jason Before He Kills Your Friends | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Domark for the Commodore 64, Friday the 13th: The Computer Game is a survival horror action-adventure inspired by the iconic slasher film series. Set at the ominous Camp Crystal Lake, players must hunt down and eliminate the masked killer, Jason Voorhees, before he wipes out the camp’s counselors. Gameplay places you in control of multiple counselors, each with different strengths, as you explore cabins, paths, and interiors while scavenging weapons such as machetes and chainsaws. Survival depends on careful exploration, quick reactions, and protecting other counselors from sudden attacks. A key twist is Jason’s ability to disguise himself as ordinary characters, forcing players to identify him through observation and risky confrontation. The game uses a pseudo-3D perspective to enhance tension and atmosphere, supported by a distinctive fear meter that rises as panic sets in.

video:video.video:title: Fright Night – You Play the Vampire… and Dawn Is Coming | Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by MicroDeal for the Commodore Amiga, Fright Night is an arcade-style action game inspired by the 1985 horror-comedy film of the same name. Players take on the role of vampire Jerry Dandridge, stalking the rooms of his mansion in search of victims while racing against the coming sunrise. Gameplay focuses on room-to-room exploration, draining victims to maintain health while avoiding supernatural hazards such as crucifixes, snakes, and grasping zombie hands. Careful timing and movement are essential, as players must always ensure they can return to their coffin before daylight to recover and continue the night’s hunt. The Amiga version features bold, colourful visuals and an atmospheric soundtrack by David Whittaker, helping to create a moody but playful horror tone. While the core loop can feel repetitive over time and lacks a defined ending, the game’s unusual perspective and theme give it a distinctive personality.

video:video.video:title: Frightmare – Can You Survive This C64 Nightmare Until 8:12 AM?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 for the Commodore 64, Frightmare is a surreal platform game developed by Floppy and published by Cascade Games. Set within a disturbing dreamscape, the game tasks players with surviving a series of nightmarish encounters until the alarm clock finally rings at 8:12 AM. Gameplay unfolds across a collection of interconnected rooms, each filled with strange creatures, traps, and hazards. Progress is measured not by reaching an ending, but by endurance, with every room visited advancing the alarm clock by six minutes. Players must rely on sharp reflexes, careful movement, and quick decision-making to stay alive for as long as possible. Enemies range from ghosts to ghoulies, reinforcing the game’s uneasy tone. The lack of traditional goals or rewards heightens the sense of dread, making survival itself the only objective. This structure gives Frightmare a distinctive rhythm that sets it apart from more conventional platformers.

video:video.video:title: Fruit Machine Simulator – When the C64 Turned into a Pub Corner
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Codemasters for the Commodore 64, Fruit Machine Simulator gives you the full British fruit machine experience without risking your pocket money. Designed for one to four players, everyone starts with £1.50 and takes turns testing their luck on a virtual slot machine packed with familiar features. Gameplay focuses on mastering the mechanics rather than pure chance. You can nudge reels, hold symbols, climb skill ladders, gamble winnings, and trigger features like Cash Box, Mega-hold, Winning Streak, and more. Knowing when to play safe and when to push your luck is key to keeping your credits alive. Rather than flashy presentation, the game leans into authenticity, closely mimicking the logic and tension of real pub fruit machines. Every spin feels deliberate, and learning the feature behaviour becomes part of the challenge.

video:video.video:title: Future Wars – The Amiga Adventure That Started with a Window Cleaner
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Delphine Software International for the Commodore Amiga, Future Wars is an ambitious point-and-click adventure that marked the studio’s first step into cinematic storytelling. Created by Paul Cuisset and Éric Chahi, who would later go on to develop Another World, the game runs on Delphine’s proprietary Cinematique engine and laid the groundwork for their distinctive narrative style. Players take on the role of an unlikely hero—a humble window cleaner—who stumbles upon a time machine and is thrown into a battle against the alien Crughons. His journey spans multiple eras, including medieval Europe, the distant 44th century, and the Cretaceous period, each offering unique environments, puzzles, and narrative twists. Gameplay is driven by a streamlined interface designed to keep the screen uncluttered. Left-click controls movement, while right-click opens a verb menu featuring commands such as Operate, Examine, Take, Use, and Inventory.

video:video.video:title: Galactic Gardener – The C64 Game About Rescuing Flowers in a Flying Chair
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Software Projects and designed by David Caballero, Galactic Gardener is a distinctive arcade action game for the Commodore 64 that blends fast reflex gameplay with offbeat sci-fi style. Players take on the role of a galactic gardener piloting a flying chair through dangerous underground caverns to recover ten stolen power-flowers. Gameplay centres on careful navigation through side-scrolling caves packed with hazards such as forcefields, moving gates, and aggressive snapdragons. Before collecting each power-flower, players must first locate an empty pot—touching a flower without one costs a life. Fuel management adds another layer of tension, forcing players to plan routes efficiently. Strategic use of teleporters allows recovery from mistakes, letting players return to safe locations after crashes or misjudged manoeuvres. This balance of action and planning gives the game a deliberate pace beneath its arcade exterior.

video:video.video:title: Gary Lineker’s Superstar Soccer – Did the C64 Get a Golden Boot or a Sliced Clearance?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Gremlin Graphics, Gary Lineker’s Superstar Soccer delivers a fast-paced arcade football experience with an unusual managerial twist. Rather than controlling the whole team, you take charge of a single on-field player, usually the centre-forward, while also acting as manager behind the scenes. On the pitch, the game focuses on quick reactions, sharp movement, and well-timed passes and shots. The action is immediate and fluid, with smooth scrolling and responsive controls that keep matches fast and engaging on the Commodore 64.
