Away from the action, you manage your squad by hiring players, setting training routines, and making key decisions that affect performance. This blend of arcade football and light management gives the game a depth that sets it apart from many sports titles of the era. Although it lacks official team licenses, Gary Lineker’s Superstar Soccer is fondly remembered for its originality, strong gameplay, and memorable presentation, making it a standout football game on the C64.

video:video.video:title: Gateway to Apshai – One of the C64’s Earliest Action RPGs
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Epyx for the Commodore 64, Gateway to Apshai is a pioneering action role-playing game developed by The Connelley Group and designed as a prequel to the classic Temple of Apshai. Players take on the role of the heir to Apshai’s greatest warrior, embarking on a dangerous journey through a vast network of dungeons in search of treasure, power, and survival. The game features eight main levels, each containing multiple interconnected dungeons and over sixty individual rooms. Armed initially with basic equipment, players must battle monsters, collect gold, and discover magical items such as potions and scrolls. Unlike many early RPGs, Gateway to Apshai uses real-time combat and movement, combining arcade-style action with traditional dungeon exploration. Each level is also governed by a time limit, adding pressure and urgency to every expedition.

video:video.video:title: Gauntlet on C64 – Food, Monsters and Four-Player Arcade Envy
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 and brought to the Commodore 64 by U. S. Gold, Gauntlet delivers a faithful home version of Atari’s iconic arcade dungeon crawler. You choose from four classic heroes—Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard, or Elf—and dive into a relentless maze of monsters, traps, and treasure. The action is fast and unforgiving, with health constantly draining as you battle through room after room in search of food, keys, and the all-important exit. Cooperation is at the heart of the experience, especially in two-player mode, where sharing resources and covering each other becomes essential as the difficulty ramps up. While the C64 hardware required some compromises, the game captures the spirit of the arcade original with chunky sprites, colourful dungeons, and nonstop pressure. The sense of urgency and constant enemy spawns keep every run tense and addictive.

video:video.video:title: Gemstone Warrior – Early C64 Dungeon Action Before RPGs Got Cosy
video:video.video:description: Gemstone Warrior (1985) is a 2D action-adventure game developed by Paradigm Creators and published by Strategic Simulations, Inc. , originally released on the Apple II before being ported to the Commodore 64. Set within a dangerous labyrinth beneath a volcanic fortress, you guide an armoured hero armed with a crossbow and limited magical attacks in search of five hidden gemstone fragments. Each run takes place across randomly generated dungeon rooms filled with skeletal warriors, demons, gas-trap plants, and deadly hazards. Supplies and magical items can be looted from chests, coffins, and fallen enemies. Useful tools include healing goblets, screen-clearing crystal balls, illusion spells, invisibility, and freezing magic, all of which must be used carefully. Mapping, saving, and strategic planning are essential for survival. One of the game’s most memorable features is its haunting title-screen music, a variation of J.

video:video.video:title: Ghetto Blaster – Walking the C64 Streets with a Boombox and a Mission
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Virgin Games, Ghettoblaster is one of the Commodore 64’s most unusual and inventive titles, blending street exploration with rhythm-based gameplay. Developed by Tony Gibson and Mark Harrison, it casts you as Rockin’ Rodney, a courier tasked with spreading the latest dance music across a stylised urban landscape. Instead of combat, progress comes from timing and groove. You roam the streets collecting cassette demos and use your boombox to get the right people dancing, triggering events and opening up new areas. Success depends on understanding rhythm, positioning yourself correctly, and knowing when to drop the beat. The city itself is packed with musical personality, from street names inspired by famous songs to a soundtrack featuring twelve original funky tunes that drive the entire experience. The emphasis on music and atmosphere gives the game a strong identity unlike anything else on the platform.

video:video.video:title: Ghost Hunters – Budget C64 Ghostbusting Without the Famous Theme Tune
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Codemasters, Ghost Hunters is a distinctive single-screen platform shooter developed by the Oliver Twins for the Commodore 64. Set inside the spooky Nightmare Mansion, the game blends precision platforming with crosshair-based shooting for a tense, arcade-style experience. Players take control of Chuck Studbuckle on a mission to rescue his brother, Hunk, from a mansion overrun by ghosts and supernatural threats. Each room is packed with platforms, hazards, and roaming spirits, requiring careful movement and accurate shooting to survive. A key gameplay twist is the dual management of Macho Energy and the Terrorometer. While blasting ghosts keeps the mansion under control, allowing fear to rise too high can quickly end the mission, adding pressure to every encounter. The C64 version stands out for its colourful graphics, smooth animation, and responsive controls. The eerie sound effects and music reinforce the haunted atmosphere, making each room feel dangerous and unpredictable.

video:video.video:title: Ghostbusters – David Crane Turned the Movie into a C64 Classic
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64, Ghostbusters was developed by David Crane and published by Activision, redefining what a movie tie-in game could be. Rather than following a simple arcade formula, it blends action, strategy, and light simulation into a surprisingly deep and memorable experience. Players take charge of a Ghostbusters team, managing money, hiring staff, buying equipment, and responding to supernatural outbreaks across New York City. Choosing when to upgrade gear or invest in better vehicles directly affects success, especially as ghost activity escalates toward the endgame. The city map and Ecto-1 driving sequences introduce a strategic layer, forcing careful planning as players balance risk, cost, and time before the final confrontation at the Temple of Zuul. Iconic digitised speech, including famous catchphrases from the film, adds atmosphere and was a technical standout on the C64.

video:video.video:title: Ghostbusters II – Slime, Sewers and Three Very Different C64 Stages
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 and developed by Foursfield, Ghostbusters II is a top-down action game for the Commodore 64, published by Activision and based on the hit movie sequel. Rather than a single gameplay style, the game is structured around several distinct stages that recreate key moments from the film. The action begins in the sewers beneath New York, where players guide a Ghostbuster down vertical shafts to collect slime samples while avoiding or neutralising ghosts. This is followed by a top-down driving section through the streets of Manhattan, piloting the Ecto-1 to trap roaming spirits while dodging traffic and obstacles. The final stage shifts perspective again, delivering a side-scrolling shooter set inside the museum as players confront the game’s main threat. Each section demands a different skill set, keeping the experience varied while staying faithful to the film’s locations and tone.

video:video.video:title: Ghosts ’N Goblins – Could Capcom’s Brutal Arcade Classic Survive on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Ghosts ’N Goblins on the Commodore 64 delivers Capcom’s brutal arcade platformer in full side-scrolling form, challenging you across six punishing levels packed with relentless enemies and hazards. Each stage must be cleared within a strict time limit, or a life is lost, keeping the pressure high from start to finish. You play as Arthur, a brave knight on a desperate mission to rescue his beloved Princess from the Demon King Astaroth. Along the way, you face waves of undead horrors including ghosts, zombies, bats, ogres, and goblins, all while navigating ladders, moving platforms, and deadly fire and water traps. Combat and movement demand absolute precision. Weapon upgrades help, but even the best gear offers little mercy, and losing your armour leaves Arthur painfully vulnerable. Memorisation, timing, and patience are essential to survive the game’s famously unforgiving design.

video:video.video:title: Give My Regards to Broad Street – Paul McCartney’s C64 Game Actually Happened
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Argus Press Software under the Mind Games label, Give My Regards to Broad Street is a distinctive puzzle-adventure inspired by the film of the same name starring Paul McCartney. Rather than traditional action, the game focuses on planning, navigation, and time management, wrapped in a strong musical theme. Players step into the role of McCartney, navigating a top-down map of London in a race against time to reconstruct a missing track from his latest album. By driving across the city, following clues, and predicting where band members will be, players must collect individual music segments before the midnight deadline. When a band member is found, the game shifts perspective to a side-scrolling sequence where the missing section of the track is retrieved. Traffic avoidance, route planning, and efficient use of time are key, making each decision feel important as the clock steadily ticks down.

video:video.video:title: Go For The Gold – The £2.99 C64 Game That Reached UK No.1
video:video.video:description: Released by Americana in 1986, Go For The Gold is a multi-event Commodore 64 sports game featuring sprinting, hurdles, long jump, archery, diving and weightlifting. You can practice individual events or compete across the full programme, with up to six participants battling for the best scores. Some events demand the traditional left-and-right joystick treatment, while archery, diving and weightlifting rely more heavily on timing and technique. The game originally appeared in America as HESGames in 1984. That version was only available on disk in the UK and cost £27.95, leaving it competing with considerably cheaper sports games such as Daley Thompson’s Decathlon and Summer Games. Two years later, Americana brought it back under the new title Go For The Gold. The revised version was released on cassette for just £2.99, transforming a largely overlooked game into one of the biggest C64 budget successes of 1986.

video:video.video:title: Gobliiins – Three Little Idiots Made One Very Strange Amiga Puzzle Adventure
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Coktel Vision, Gobliiins is a point-and-click puzzle adventure for the Commodore Amiga that blends surreal humour with inventive problem-solving. Players are tasked with curing King Angoulafre of madness after he falls victim to a voodoo curse, guided by a trio of mischievous goblins sent on a bizarre rescue mission. The game’s core mechanic revolves around controlling three characters at once, each with a distinct role. Oups handles object interaction, Ignatius casts unpredictable spells, and Asgard relies on brute strength to manipulate the environment. Solving each of the game’s 22 single-screen puzzles requires careful coordination, experimentation, and sometimes intentionally wrong choices to discover the right solution. Mistakes come at a cost, as the goblins share a single energy bar that drains when actions backfire. This adds tension to the puzzle-solving, forcing players to think ahead rather than click blindly through each scene.

video:video.video:title: Gods – Why Did Pirated Amiga Copies Make the First Boss Nearly Impossible
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by The Bitmap Brothers and published by Renegade Software, Gods is a demanding action-platform adventure that casts you as Hercules on a quest for immortality. Progress unfolds across four expansive realms packed with enemies, traps, secrets, and carefully layered puzzles. Every move matters. Precise jumping, measured combat, and deliberate pacing are essential, especially with limited inventory space forcing tough choices about keys, weapons, and upgrades. Weapons range from throwing knives to fireballs and bouncing axes, each suited to different situations and enemy patterns, rewarding experimentation and planning. Levels are built to be learned and mastered, with clever layouts that encourage observation and route optimisation. Certain enemies react to your behaviour, adding tension and pushing you to adapt rather than brute-force your way through. Visually striking with its stone-carved mythological backdrops and paired with an atmospheric soundtrack by Nation 12, Gods earned a reputation for depth and difficulty.

video:video.video:title: Golden Axe – Could Sega’s Fantasy Brawler Survive the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990, Golden Axe brings Sega’s iconic fantasy brawler to the Commodore 64, tasking you with saving the land of Yuria from the evil Death Adder. You choose between Ax Battler, Tyris Flare, or Gilius Thunderhead, each offering different strengths and devastating magic attacks as you fight to reclaim the legendary Golden Axe. The core beat ’em up action remains intact, with side-scrolling combat, melee attacks, screen-clearing magic spells, and the ability to ride dragons for extra firepower. While the C64 version is single-player only and simplifies some elements from the arcade, the moment-to-moment combat still delivers that familiar Golden Axe rhythm. Hardware limitations mean fewer enemies on screen and reduced variety, but the fantasy atmosphere survives thanks to solid visuals and a strong soundtrack by Jeroen Tel. His take on the Golden Axe theme adds weight and nostalgia to the adventure.

video:video.video:title: Gorf – Commodore’s C64 Cartridge Shooter with Arcade Swagger
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 for the Commodore 64, GORF is a home conversion of the 1981 arcade hit originally developed by Dave Nutting Associates and produced by Midway, with its name standing for Galactic Orbiting Robot Force. Players pilot a starship in a series of fixed-screen shooting missions, combining fast reflexes with tactical positioning in the lower portion of the screen. The game features four distinct mission styles inspired by classics such as Space Invaders, Galaxian, and Phoenix, creating a varied and constantly evolving arcade experience. A unique gameplay mechanic allows the quark laser to cancel existing shots when fired again, adding an extra layer of strategy to defensive play. Stages range from classic alien formations to hyperspace warp sequences and intense boss encounters, keeping each round fresh and challenging. The Commodore 64 version is especially notable for supporting speech synthesis via the Magic Voice or Votrax module, making it the only home port to feature in-game voice effects.

video:video.video:title: Grand Prix Circuit – McLaren, Ferrari or Williams: Which Ruled the C64 Circuit?
video:video.video:description: Grand Prix Circuit (1988), developed by Distinctive Software and published by Accolade, is one of the most advanced Formula One racing simulations ever released on the Commodore 64. Players can choose between three licensed F1 cars — the McLaren MP4/4, Williams FW12, and Ferrari 187/88C — each offering a different balance of speed, grip, and handling. The game features practice, qualifying, single races, and a full championship mode across real-world circuits including Monaco, Hockenheim, Suzuka, Canada, and Monza. A detailed damage system adds realism, with collisions and off-track driving affecting handling and potentially forcing retirement if damage becomes too severe. Visually, the C64 version delivers sharp sprite-based graphics with impressive roadside detail and smooth scrolling, while Kris Hatlelid’s energetic soundtrack enhances the racing atmosphere. Grand Prix Circuit is widely regarded as one of the finest motorsport titles on the platform, praised for its sense of speed, technical ambition, and immersive Formula One experience.

video:video.video:title: Grand Prix Simulator – Overhead Racing, Oil Slicks and Two Players… Was It a Simulator? | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Codemasters, Grand Prix Simulator delivers fast, accessible top-down racing on the Commodore 64. Developed by the Oliver Twins, it captures the thrill of high-speed circuit racing with a stripped-back design that focuses on precision, positioning, and momentum rather than realism. Races are viewed from above, giving you a clear view of upcoming corners, hazards, and rival cars. Steering and throttle control are easy to grasp, but mastering tight turns and avoiding costly collisions takes practice, especially as track layouts become more demanding. The C64 version stands out with bold colours, smooth scrolling, and plainly defined circuits that reward clean racing lines. Tracks feature sharp bends and narrow sections that punish mistakes, keeping races tense even with simple mechanics. A two-player mode adds to the fun, allowing head-to-head competition and making it ideal for quick, competitive sessions.

video:video.video:title: Grange Hill – Find Gonch’s Confiscated Walkman Before Midnight | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Argus Press Software, Grange Hill: The Computer Game brings the much-loved British TV series to the Commodore 64 in the form of a school-based adventure. You play as Luke “Gonch” Gardner, on a mission to recover his confiscated Walkman from the staffroom before midnight, with best mate Hollo tagging along for support. The game blends graphic and text adventure elements, with a side-scrolling view of streets and school corridors paired with a text window for descriptions, inventory, and actions. Progress depends on exploration, item use, and avoiding trouble as you sneak through familiar locations after hours. Rather than fast action, the focus is on puzzle-solving and atmosphere, capturing the everyday mischief and tension of school life. The C64 version is enhanced by a soundtrack from David Whittaker, helping ground the game in its late-80s home computer style.

video:video.video:title: Granny’s Garden – The C64 School Game That Made a Witch Terrifying
video:video.video:description: Released on the Commodore 64 in 1987, Granny’s Garden is an educational adventure game developed by 4Mation Educational Resources and published by the Angle Park Computing Centre in South Australia. Originally created for the BBC Micro in 1983, it was later ported to multiple platforms and became a familiar sight in UK schools throughout the 1980s and 1990s. Players embark on a text-driven quest to rescue six missing children from the clutches of an evil witch. Progress is made by navigating locations, answering questions, and solving logic-based puzzles using one-word typed responses, encouraging problem-solving, reading comprehension, and memory skills. The Commodore 64 version preserves the simplicity and structure of the original, with minimal graphics and sound used effectively to support the atmosphere. Despite its educational purpose, the game is remembered for its unsettling tone, particularly the sudden appearances of the witch, which left a lasting impression on many players.

video:video.video:title: Green Beret – Four Enemy Bases, One Knife and Almost No Mercy | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Konami and published on the Commodore 64 by Imagine Software, Green Beret is a fast-moving side-scrolling action game set against a Cold War backdrop. Players take control of an elite soldier tasked with infiltrating enemy territory and rescuing prisoners of war from heavily guarded installations. Gameplay focuses on forward momentum and precision combat. Starting with only a knife, players must defeat enemy troops, avoid traps, and survive relentless attacks while pushing through locations such as missile bases, harbours, bridges, and prison camps. Additional weapons including grenades, bazookas, and flamethrowers provide brief power boosts, but timing and positioning remain critical throughout. The Commodore 64 version delivers confident scrolling and tightly tuned enemy patterns that keep the pressure high. Martin Galway’s powerful soundtrack adds urgency and atmosphere, driving the action forward and standing out as one of the game’s most memorable elements.

video:video.video:title: Gribbly’s Day Out – Rescue Eight Gribblets on Every One of 16 Alien Levels | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Hewson Consultants and developed by Andrew Braybrook, Gribbly’s Day Out is a highly original action-platform game for the Commodore 64. Set on the alien world of Blabgor, players take control of Gribbly Grobbly, a strange one-footed creature gifted with psychic powers and tasked with rescuing eight baby Gribblets scattered across a dangerous landscape. Gameplay blends platform action with shooting mechanics. Gribbly hops and levitates through multi-screen scrolling levels, using psychic bubble shots to fend off enemies and clear hazards. Each area is tightly designed, filled with precision jumps, environmental threats, and the ever-present energy web created to contain the mutated Blabgorian Seon. Progression demands accuracy and patience, as enemy placement and level layouts leave little room for error. The controls and difficulty reward mastery, making each successful rescue feel hard-earned and satisfying.

video:video.video:title: Gryzor – Contra Had a Different Name in Europe… But Could the C64 Cope?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Gryzor is the European home conversion of Konami’s arcade smash Contra. Developed under official licence, it brings explosive run-and-gun action and cooperative gameplay to the 8-bit platform. Players take control of elite soldiers Lance and Bill as they battle through hostile environments to stop an alien invasion. The gameplay delivers relentless side-scrolling action, precise platforming, and intense enemy waves, capped off with imposing boss encounters that test reflexes and timing. Power-ups are central to survival, with rapid-fire weapons, spread shots, and lasers dramatically changing how each section is tackled. The C64 version captures the arcade spirit with fast scrolling, bold sprite work, and atmospheric music by Jason C. Brooke, even if some visual compromises and flicker were unavoidable on the hardware. Despite these limitations, Gryzor remains one of the most celebrated action titles on the Commodore 64.

video:video.video:title: Guzzler – Keys, Food and a Very Hungry Mouse in This Forgotten C64 Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Interceptor Software for the Commodore 64, Guzzler is a charming top-down maze action game that puts a clever twist on the classic arcade formula. Players control a hungry mouse navigating colourful labyrinths to collect keys and unlock food cells scattered throughout each level. The core gameplay revolves around a unique “weight” mechanic. Every time the mouse eats, it grows fatter, making it impossible to squeeze through narrow passages until it gradually deflates over time. This creates a constant strategic balancing act between eating for points and staying slim enough to move freely through the maze. Progression depends on careful route planning, timing, and risk management. Patrolling enemies add pressure to every decision, while Bonus Barry appears carrying letters that spell “GUZZLER”, rewarding exploration and skilful play with valuable extra points. Visually, Guzzler stands out with bright, friendly graphics and clear maze layouts that keep the action easy to follow.

video:video.video:title: Gyropod – The C64 Shooter That Took You from Space to Alien Planets
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Taskset Ltd. , Gyropod is a distinctive multi-stage shoot ’em up for the Commodore 64 that blends space combat with planetary exploration. Players take control of the Galaxy Ranger, a heavily armed spacecraft sent to eradicate hostile alien worlds in a distant star system. The action begins in space, where players rotate around the rim of the Galaxy Ranger, using a movable cannon to fend off incoming waves of alien attackers. Precision aiming and positioning are essential as enemy patterns intensify and pressure builds. Once space defences are cleared, the game shifts into a Lunar Lander-style sequence, requiring careful control to detach and land the supply pod safely on the planet’s surface. The final phase sees players guiding a lone spaceman across the terrain, collecting valuable resources while avoiding aggressive alien lifeforms.

video:video.video:title: Hacker – Activision Gave You “LOGON PLEASE”… and Almost Nothing Else on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Activision and developed by Steve Cartwright for the Commodore 64, Hacker is a distinctive graphic adventure that places players in the role of a digital spy infiltrating secret computer systems. Opening with the now-iconic “Logon Please” prompt, the game immediately sets a tense, puzzle-driven tone that defines the entire experience. Gameplay blends text-based interaction with strategic exploration as players guide a small robot through a complex underground tunnel network. The objective is to locate and assemble fragments of a classified document hidden across multiple global locations, all while managing limited money, time, and access privileges. Progression depends on careful planning, memory, and precision. Surveillance systems, security checkpoints, and restricted routes force players to think several steps ahead, especially since the absence of a save feature means that mistakes can result in starting over from the beginning.

video:video.video:title: Halls of the Things – Survive Seven Floors of a Deadly C64 Tower
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Crystal Computing and developed by Design Design, Halls of the Things is a tense action-adventure that drops you into a mysterious seven-floor tower packed with danger. Programmed by Neil Mottershead, Simon Brattel, and Martin S. Horsley, the game quickly built a reputation for depth, atmosphere, and replay value. You explore each floor from a top-down perspective, navigating intricate mazes in search of seven magical rings hidden throughout the tower. Once collected, you must locate a magical key deep within the dungeon to unlock the drawbridge and escape alive. What truly sets the game apart is its randomly generated maze layout, ensuring every run feels different. You’re armed with a mix of sword combat, arrows, fireballs, and lightning spells, all while facing “Things” — enemies that roam the halls and can disguise themselves as harmless objects to catch you off guard.

video:video.video:title: Hawkeye – The C64 Shooter That Sent a Cybernetic Warrior Into an Alien War
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Thalamus and developed by Boys Without Brains, Hawkeye is a visually striking side-scrolling platform shooter set in a bleak post-apocalyptic future. You take control of a cybernetic warrior battling through a ruined world, fighting to reclaim the planet from alien forces across a series of tightly designed levels. Gameplay blends fast arcade shooting with methodical exploration. Each stage requires you to hunt down hidden puzzle pieces while managing enemy patterns, hazards, and precise platforming. Multiple weapon types keep combat varied, and progression depends on fully mastering each environment rather than simply rushing forward. The game’s presentation is a major part of its identity. Parallax scrolling adds depth to the landscapes, while detailed sprites and smooth movement give the action a polished, high-end feel that became synonymous with Thalamus releases. Sound is where Hawkeye truly shines.

video:video.video:title: He-Man: The Ilearth Stone – When He-Man Needed an Atom Smasher on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by U. S. Gold and developed by Adventure Soft, He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: The Ilearth Stone brings the world of Eternia to the Commodore 64 in a side-scrolling platform adventure. Also known as Masters of the Universe: The Arcade Game, it casts players as He-Man in a race to stop Skeletor and recover the powerful Ilearth Stone. The adventure takes you through Castle Grayskull and its surrounding regions as you gather the ingredients required for Orko’s spell. Gameplay mixes platforming and exploration, with lifts, traps, enemies, and branching routes encouraging steady progression rather than pure speed. He-Man wields his iconic Power Sword to defeat Skeletor’s forces and can collect power-ups that enhance his abilities along the way. The Commodore 64 version stands out for its detailed environments and strong visual design, bringing familiar locations and characters to life on the system.

video:video.video:title: Masters of the Universe: The Movie – He-Man Needed EIGHT Cosmic Key Chords on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Gremlin Graphics, Masters of the Universe: The Movie brings the live-action film to the Commodore 64 in an ambitious multi-genre action adventure. Players step into the role of He-Man on a mission to recover the eight chords of the Cosmic Key and stop Skeletor from conquering Eternia. Gameplay shifts between several styles, including top-down exploration, side-scrolling beat ’em up combat, and first-person shooting sections. This variety reflects the film’s set pieces and keeps the pace moving as players travel between locations and objectives. A standout feature is the ability to switch between characters, with He-Man joined by Teela and Gwildor, each offering different strengths and abilities. This adds a tactical layer to combat and exploration, encouraging players to choose the right character for each situation. The game’s visuals capture the look and locations of the movie within the limits of the Commodore 64, while Ben Daglish’s energetic soundtrack drives the action forward.

video:video.video:title: Head Over Heels – Two C64 Heroes Who Could Literally Combine into ONE
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Head Over Heels is a landmark isometric action-adventure created by Jon Ritman and Bernie Drummond. Building on the ideas introduced in Batman, it pushed the genre forward with a clever dual-character system and a vast, interconnected world to explore. You control two very different heroes. Head can leap higher and fire doughnuts to temporarily paralyse enemies, while Heels runs faster, climbs certain staircases, and carries objects. Progress depends on knowing when to switch between them, using their unique abilities to solve puzzles, avoid traps, and outsmart enemies across hundreds of rooms. The game’s surreal environments, precise isometric design, and thoughtful room layouts reward patience and planning. On the C64, the colourful visuals and atmospheric soundtrack by Guy Stevens help give each area its own identity, drawing you deeper into its strange, offbeat universe.

video:video.video:title: Heart of Africa C64 Review – An 8-Bit Expedition That Refuses to Rush
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Ozark Softscape and published by Electronic Arts for the Commodore 64, Heart of Africa is a deep strategy adventure that builds on the foundations of The Seven Cities of Gold. Set in 1890, the game places players in the role of an ambitious explorer searching for the lost tomb of Pharaoh Ahnk Ahnk somewhere in the vast African continent. Beginning at a port near Cairo with limited supplies, players must carefully plan expeditions across deserts, mountains, rivers, and jungles. Success depends on managing resources, trading goods, and building relationships with indigenous tribes to gather vital clues, maps, and equipment needed to continue the journey. Progression is driven by exploration, diplomacy, and information gathering. Interactions can involve negotiation, gift-giving, trade, or intimidation, with each approach affecting future encounters. A detailed diary, world map, and inventory system help players track discoveries and organise their expedition.

video:video.video:title: Heartland – Odin’s Forgotten Fantasy Adventure on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986, Heartland is a distinctive fantasy platform adventure for the Commodore 64 developed by Odin Computer Graphics. Players take control of a hapless wizard on a race against time to restore a magical book by recovering six missing white pages and destroying six corrupted black pages scattered across a dangerous, storybook world. The adventure unfolds across six themed areas made up of interconnected screens. Players must dodge enemies such as rival wizards and gooches while exploring carefully, as the wizard begins completely unarmed. Weapons and items like hats, knives, and fireballs can be discovered and managed via an on-screen inventory system, adding light strategy to the platforming. Heartland’s structure encourages exploration and planning rather than simple left-to-right progression. Each level has its own challenges and layout, requiring players to learn routes, manage resources, and balance speed against survival as the clock steadily ticks down.

video:video.video:title: Heimdall – Viking Mythology, Amiga Ambition and Some Very Odd Trials
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by The 8th Day and published by Core Design, Heimdall is an ambitious action role-playing game steeped in Norse mythology. Designed for the Commodore Amiga, it blends exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving into a richly imagined mythological journey. Players step into the role of Heimdall, charged with recovering powerful artefacts stolen by Loki to prevent the coming of Ragnarok. The adventure unfolds across three vast realms—Midgard, Utgard, and Asgard—each made up of multiple islands filled with quests, enemies, and environmental challenges. Progress requires careful navigation, smart combat decisions, and puzzle-solving across interconnected locations. A standout feature is the character creation sequence, where a series of mini-games determine Heimdall’s starting attributes and influence which companions can later join your quest. This adds strategic depth from the very beginning and makes each playthrough feel slightly different.

video:video.video:title: Henry’s House – Tiny C64 Platforming Inside One Very Dangerous Home
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by English Software and developed by Chris Murray for the Commodore 64, Henry’s House is a charming single-screen platform game that transforms everyday household spaces into imaginative obstacle courses. Players take control of Little Henry as he explores the rooms of his home, collecting items and avoiding quirky domestic hazards. Gameplay revolves around clearing each room by gathering all scattered objects, which causes a key to appear. Once collected, the key unlocks the exit and allows progression to the next area. With no time limit in place, players are encouraged to move carefully, study enemy patterns, and plan safe routes through each level. Across eight distinct rooms, Henry must dodge moving toothbrushes, toasters, coffee machines, and other animated appliances that threaten to knock him off course. Precise jumping and smart positioning are essential, as even small mistakes can send players back to the start of a room.

video:video.video:title: Herbert’s Dummy Run – The C64 Baby Rescue Mission Nobody Prepared For
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Herbert’s Dummy Run is a 2D arcade-adventure developed by David Perry and published by Mikro-Gen. The fourth entry in the Wally Week series shifts the spotlight away from Wally himself and places players in control of his adventurous infant son, Herbert. Set inside a vast multi-floor department store, the game tasks players with guiding Herbert through more than 25 interconnected rooms after becoming separated from his parents. Progress depends on exploration, careful timing, and logical problem-solving as players collect and use items to overcome obstacles before the store closes at 5:30 PM. A standout feature is the inclusion of clever mini-games that parody classic arcade hits such as Breakout, Space Invaders, and Duck Shoot. These sequences are woven directly into the puzzles, adding variety and a playful sense of humour to the overall experience.

video:video.video:title: H.E.R.O. – A Helicopter Backpack, Dynamite and Trapped Miners on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Activision and developed by John Van Ryzin, H. E. R. O. (Helicopter Emergency Rescue Operation) is a standout action-platformer that blends fast reflex gameplay with careful planning. Players step into the boots of Roderrick Hero, an elite rescue operative sent deep underground to save trapped miners. Equipped with a helicopter backpack, laser helmet, and a limited supply of dynamite, Roderrick must navigate a series of multi-screen cave systems packed with hazards. Falling rocks, toxic gas, lava pits, and hostile creatures all stand between you and the miners, demanding precise movement and smart use of resources. Each level introduces new dangers and layouts, encouraging players to think ahead rather than rush forward. Fuel management, timing, and positioning are crucial, turning every rescue into a tense balancing act between speed and survival. H.

video:video.video:title: Hero of the Golden Talisman – Budget C64 Adventuring with Big Ambition
video:video.video:description: Hero of the Golden Talisman (1985) is an action-adventure game developed by Mr Chip Software and published by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64. You explore a vast labyrinth of 64 interconnected rooms across five levels, searching for five fragments of a magical talisman needed to lift a deadly curse from your town. Each area is filled with hazards and enemies, from jumping pits and climbing ropes to battling fire-breathing dragons and bouncing eyeballs. Progress depends on collecting useful items such as keys, lanterns, ropes, and strength-enhancing flags. While its graphics and sound are modest, the game stands out for its responsive controls and clever level design. A built-in mini-map and inventory system add strategic depth and encourage careful exploration. Its balanced difficulty and rewarding progression make it especially appealing to players who enjoy mapping and methodical gameplay.

video:video.video:title: HeroQuest – Games Workshop’s Board Game Became a Four-Hero C64 Dungeon Crawl
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Gremlin Graphics for the Commodore 64, HeroQuest is a faithful digital adaptation of the hugely popular Games Workshop board game. Developed by 221B Software Development, it brings classic fantasy dungeon crawling and tabletop strategy to the 8-bit home computer. Players command a party of four iconic heroes — the Barbarian, Dwarf, Elf, and Wizard — as they venture into grid-based dungeons to defeat monsters, uncover treasure, and ultimately thwart the evil sorcerer Morcar. Gameplay closely mirrors the board game, blending turn-based movement, combat, exploration, and character progression across a series of structured quests. Despite the C64’s limitations, HeroQuest delivers atmospheric visuals with detailed sprites and dungeon layouts that successfully capture the look and feel of the tabletop experience. The music and sound effects reinforce the fantasy setting, adding tension and drama as each room is revealed.

video:video.video:title: High Noon – C64 Gunslinging Where the Streets Were Never Safe
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, High Noon is a fast-paced western-themed shoot ’em up that puts players in the boots of a lone sheriff defending a frontier town from relentless outlaw attacks. Action unfolds on a single screen as bandits attempt to rob the bank, kidnap townsfolk, and overrun the streets. Gameplay focuses on sharp reflexes and positioning, with the sheriff able to fire in eight directions to counter threats arriving from all sides. Each of the five stages ramps up the challenge, introducing mounted enemies, dynamite throwers, and outlaws firing from windows, keeping the pressure constant. Between levels, players face tense quick-draw bonus duels against bandit leaders, testing reaction speed under pressure. A memorable touch of dark humour comes from the undertaker, Riga Mortis, who periodically clears fallen bodies from the street while the action continues.

video:video.video:title: Highlander – Ocean Turned Connor MacLeod Into a C64 One-on-One Fighter
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Highlander is a one-on-one fighting game based on the cult classic fantasy film. Developed by Canvas, the game puts players in control of Connor MacLeod, the immortal swordsman, as he faces key opponents from the movie in a bid to claim “The Prize.” Combat is presented as a series of duels against Ramírez, Fasil, and the Kurgan. Each encounter focuses on sword-based fighting, with the goal of defeating every opponent in turn. While the premise promises cinematic clashes, the gameplay itself is very limited, offering a small move set and little tactical depth. Controls are awkward and unresponsive, making combat feel sluggish and unrefined. Movement and attacks lack precision, which often turns fights into drawn-out exchanges rather than tense duels. Presentation does little to elevate the experience, with stiff character animation and basic arenas that fail to convey the atmosphere of the film.

video:video.video:title: Hollywood or Bust – Chasing Fame Through C64 Arcade Weirdness
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Hollywood or Bust is a light-hearted action-adventure that draws heavily on the mayhem and humour of the silent movie era. Players take on the role of Buster Baloney, a would-be film star navigating a frantic studio complex in a bid to collect five Oscar statues and make it big in Hollywood. Gameplay blends arcade platforming with resource management and quick decision-making. Buster defends himself by hurling custard pies at enemies, with supplies replenished via a strategically placed cream tap. The studio itself is a maze of interconnected rooms, doors, and hazards, with some exits leading to hectic street scenes filled with fast-moving policemen that demand sharp reflexes and careful timing. The isometric presentation gives the game a strong sense of depth and movement, while colourful visuals help sell its cartoonish, slapstick tone.

video:video.video:title: Home Alone – Could You Stop the Wet Bandits on the Commodore Amiga?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Manley & Associates and published by Capstone Software, Home Alone brings the hit holiday film to the Commodore Amiga with a distinctive mix of strategy and action. Players step into the shoes of Kevin McCallister as he defends his house from the infamous Wet Bandits, Harry and Marv. The game is split into two clear phases. During the preparation stage, players are given a limited amount of time to explore the house and set traps using everyday household items such as marbles, paint cans, and a BB gun. Planning and placement are key, as every room can be turned into a defensive advantage. Once the burglars arrive, the game shifts into the action phase. Kevin must move through the house, baiting the intruders into carefully placed traps while avoiding capture. Success depends on timing, knowledge of the layout, and efficient use of the tools prepared earlier.

video:video.video:title: Hostages – Three Snipers Outside, Three Men Inside the Embassy | Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Infogrames, Hostages is a tense tactical shooter inspired by the real-life Iranian Embassy siege. You take command of an elite six-man GIGN unit, tasked with rescuing hostages from a heavily guarded embassy using planning, precision, and restraint rather than brute force. The operation unfolds across three carefully linked phases. First, you position snipers across the street to silently remove threats without endangering civilians. Next comes helicopter insertion, where assault team members rappel through embassy windows under strict timing. Finally, the mission shifts to a first-person interior assault, clearing rooms, neutralising terrorists, and securing hostages one by one. Hostages blends strategy, stealth, and action in a way that was ambitious for its time. Every mistake carries consequences, and success depends on patience, observation, and controlled execution rather than fast reflexes alone. On the Amiga, the game delivers strong atmosphere and mounting tension through its sound design and methodical pacing.

video:video.video:title: Hover Bovver – Jeff Minter Turned Mowing the Lawn into C64 Trouble
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Llamasoft for the Commodore 64, Hover Bovver is an offbeat maze-action game designed by Jeff Minter that blends humour with fast-paced arcade gameplay. Players take on the role of a mischievous homeowner who “borrows” his neighbour’s lawnmower to cut his own overgrown garden. The objective is to mow every patch of grass while avoiding flowerbeds and escaping angry pursuers. Gameplay revolves around navigating tight garden layouts while being chased by an enraged neighbour and gardener. Quick reactions and careful route planning are essential to avoid capture and complete each level. A unique feature is the player’s dog, which can be commanded to distract enemies and create escape routes. However, misuse can cause the dog to turn hostile, adding an extra layer of risk and strategy. Visually, the game features simple but charming character sprites and plainly defined playfields.

video:video.video:title: How to Be a Complete Bastard – The C64 Party Game Built Around Being Awful
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Virgin Games and developed by Sentient Software, How to Be a Complete Bastard is one of the most unconventional adventure games on the Commodore 64. Based on Adrian Edmondson’s book, it drops you into a house party with a single goal: cause as much mayhem as possible and drive every guest away. Played from an isometric perspective, the game revolves around exploring rooms, interacting with objects, and performing increasingly antisocial actions to rack up “bastard points.” You’ll need to juggle meters such as the Weeometer, Drunkometer, and Fartometer, balancing maximum disruption with personal survival. Rather than traditional puzzles, progress comes from experimentation and timing, learning how different actions affect guests and the party atmosphere. Its humour leans heavily into satire, mocking social etiquette and pushing boundaries far beyond typical 8-bit adventures.

video:video.video:title: Hudson Hawk – Steal Leonardo da Vinci’s Art from an Auction House AND the Vatican | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Hudson Hawk is a movie tie-in platform game based on the Bruce Willis action-comedy film. Developed during the height of licensed game adaptations, it combines stealth, precision platforming, and light puzzle-solving to reflect the film’s art thief storyline. Players take control of Hudson Hawk as he infiltrates museums, mansions, and secret facilities, avoiding guards, security cameras, dogs, and deadly traps while collecting valuable treasures. Each level is presented as a single-screen challenge, demanding careful timing, sharp reactions, and smart route planning. The gameplay follows Ocean’s well-known platforming formula, delivering tight controls, responsive movement, and cleverly designed obstacle layouts. Success depends on learning enemy patterns, using hiding spots effectively, and mastering difficult jumps under pressure. Visually, the game features a distinctive and polished presentation, with detailed environments and clear sprite work that keeps the action readable.

video:video.video:title: Hunchback – C64 Bell-Ringing, Rope-Swinging and Old-School Pain
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Hunchback is a fast-paced platform game inspired by Victor Hugo’s The Hunchback of Notre-Dame. Players take control of Quasimodo as he scales the castle walls of Notre Dame, determined to rescue Esmeralda from captivity. Gameplay unfolds across 15 single-screen levels packed with hazards including pits, swinging ropes, fireballs, arrows, and patrolling knights. Precise timing is essential as Quasimodo jumps, swings, and dodges his way toward the bell at the end of each screen. Adding constant pressure, a pursuing knight steadily climbs the wall, forcing players to keep moving. Collecting bells rewards progress, with a super bonus awarded after every five bells. Completing all levels rescues Esmeralda, after which the game restarts at a faster speed, significantly increasing the difficulty and testing player reflexes even further.

video:video.video:title: Hunchback II – Was Quasimodo’s C64 Revenge Worth the Climb?
video:video.video:description: Hunchback II: Quasimodo’s Revenge is a 1985 arcade platform game for the Commodore 64, published by Ocean Software and developed by Choice Software. Building on the success of the original Hunchback, this sequel expands the formula into a series of varied, skill-based challenge stages rather than a single looping screen. It was designed specifically to showcase the strengths of the C64. You once again control Quasimodo as he navigates swinging ropes, collapsing platforms, arrow traps, and precision jumps across multiple distinct events. Each stage introduces new mechanics, demanding fast reactions, sharp timing, and strong memorisation. One of the game’s standout features is its atmospheric soundtrack by Martin Galway, whose SID composition elevates the experience and remains one of the most memorable pieces of C64 music of the era. Visually, the game delivers clean sprite work, smooth scrolling, and plainly readable hazards — essential for high-speed arcade gameplay and competitive score-chasing.

video:video.video:title: Hunchback at the Olympics – Quasimodo Really Got His Own C64 Sports Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Seatongrove and published by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Hunchback at the Olympics puts Quasimodo centre stage in a tongue-in-cheek take on Olympic competition. Competing to impress Esmeralda, players guide the famous hunchback through a series of athletic events with a clear focus on humour over realism. The game features a selection of Olympic disciplines including the 100m sprint, long jump, shot put, discus, javelin, hurdles, and high jump. Each event requires players to meet qualification standards using fast joystick movements or carefully timed inputs, emphasising reflexes and rhythm rather than detailed simulation. Presentation is simple and direct, with straightforward animations and arcade-style mechanics typical of mid-1980s sports titles. While the physics are intentionally loose and events can feel repetitive, the exaggerated performances and Esmeralda’s reactions add personality and light relief throughout the competition.

video:video.video:title: Hunter – Activision Gave the Amiga a 3D Open World in 1991
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991, Hunter was developed by Paul Holmes and published by Activision, delivering a level of freedom rarely seen in games of its era. Designed for the Amiga and Atari ST, it places players in control of a lone soldier dropped into a vast archipelago under enemy control, with no fixed path to success. The game’s defining feature is its open-ended structure. Players can explore freely on foot or by swimming, and can commandeer a wide range of vehicles including cars, tanks, helicopters, boats, and even surfboards. Missions can be tackled in multiple ways, rewarding experimentation, planning, and improvisation rather than rigid solutions. Hunter’s world feels alive and reactive. Buildings can be entered, civilians and enemies move independently, and player actions can influence future encounters. This dynamic design creates a strong sense of immersion and scale, especially impressive given the hardware limitations of the time.

video:video.video:title: Hyper Sports – Another C64 Sports Game Your Joystick Feared
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Konami for the Commodore 64, Hyper Sports is the sequel to the hugely popular Track & Field and delivers a fast-paced collection of Olympic-themed events straight from the arcade. You compete across a series of demanding challenges, pushing for qualifying scores just to stay in the competition. The game features a varied lineup of events including swimming, skeet shooting, vaulting, archery, triple jump, and weightlifting, each with its own timing-based mechanics. Success depends on precision, rhythm, and endurance, with difficulty ramping up sharply as you progress through the tournament. On the C64, Hyper Sports stands out as a strong arcade conversion, offering smooth movement, responsive controls, and clear event visuals that keep the action readable even under pressure. Every event tests a different skill, keeping the experience tense and competitive throughout.

video:video.video:title: IK+ on the Amiga – Still One of the Slickest Fighting Games of Its Era?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by System 3 and developed by Archer MacLean for the Commodore Amiga, International Karate Plus—commonly known as IK+—is a refined and expanded sequel to the original International Karate. This fast-paced top-down fighting game introduced the unique concept of three fighters battling simultaneously on a single screen, creating constant tension and chaotic fun. Gameplay focuses on precise joystick control, responsive combat, and smart positioning, as players must defend themselves from two opponents at once. A wide range of punches, kicks, and special moves encourages aggressive play, while careful timing and spacing are essential for survival in later rounds. Progression is driven by skill mastery and adaptability, as enemy fighters become faster and more unpredictable. Alongside its competitive mechanics, the Amiga version adds playful background animations and hidden gags, including roaming Pac-Man characters, periscopes, spiders, and cheeky visual tricks that give the game its distinctive personality.

video:video.video:title: IK+ – Three Fighters, One Beach and Rob Hubbard at Full Blast | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by System 3, International Karate + is one of the most celebrated fighting games on the Commodore 64. Designed by Archer Maclean, with a legendary soundtrack by Rob Hubbard, IK+ refined and expanded the original International Karate formula into a faster, deeper, and far more distinctive experience. The game’s standout feature is its unique three-player combat system, where fighters battle simultaneously on a single screen. Matches are scored through well-timed punches, kicks, sweeps, and acrobatic flips, rewarding precision and positioning rather than button mashing. Controls are tight and responsive, making every exchange feel deliberate and skill-based. Between bouts, IK+ introduces bonus rounds such as deflecting bouncing balls, adding variety and extra challenge. Smooth animation, humorous background details, and expressive character movement give the game a lively personality that still holds up decades later.

video:video.video:title: Ikari Warriors – Why Were There Two Different C64 Versions?
video:video.video:description: Originally released in arcades in 1986 by SNK, Ikari Warriors became one of the defining run-and-gun shooters of the era, and its Commodore 64 history is notable for having two very different home conversions. The first C64 version arrived in 1986 via Data East and Quicksilver Software, offering a single-player experience split into four phases. This early take delivers straightforward vertical shooting with basic visuals and limited enemy variety, capturing the core idea of the arcade but in a stripped-back form. A later and far more ambitious 1988 release by Elite Systems refined the formula significantly. This version supports both solo play and two-player simultaneous action, with improved graphics, stronger sound, and more varied enemy behaviour. You fight your way through jungles, rivers, and fortified positions, using power-ups, tanks, and helicopters to survive the onslaught.

video:video.video:title: Impossible Mission – Stay Awhile, Stay Forever… and Search Every Room
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Epyx and developed by Dennis Caswell, Impossible Mission is one of the most influential and technically impressive games on the Commodore 64. It famously pushed boundaries with digitised speech, instantly setting the tone with one of the most memorable villain introductions in 8-bit history. You play as Agent 4125, infiltrating the underground fortress of the deranged Professor Elvin Atombender. Your mission is to stop a nuclear launch by locating scattered fragments of a secret password hidden throughout a vast network of rooms beneath his complex. Gameplay blends precise platforming with methodical puzzle-solving. You explore interconnected rooms, evade lethal robots, and search furniture for vital clues, all while racing against a strict six-hour time limit. Every mistake costs precious minutes, turning patience and planning into essential survival skills. The atmosphere is driven by tense music, clever room design, and constant pressure rather than raw action.

video:video.video:title: Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis – How Did This Huge Adventure Fit on C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by LucasArts for the Commodore 64, Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis is an ambitious action-adventure that sends Indy on a globe-trotting race against the Nazis to uncover the secrets of the legendary lost city. Packed with exploration, puzzle-solving, and tense encounters, it delivers a cinematic adventure true to the spirit of the films. Players guide Indiana Jones through exotic locations, using his whip, fists, and wits to overcome enemies and environmental challenges. The game allows different approaches to progression, encouraging players to choose how they tackle obstacles and solve puzzles, with decisions shaping the flow of the adventure. While the Commodore 64 version is more constrained than its counterparts on more powerful systems, it retains the core gameplay ideas and memorable moments that define Fate of Atlantis. Atmospheric music, sound effects, and a strong narrative help carry the experience, making it a notable late-era C64 release.

video:video.video:title: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade – The Amiga Adventure Worth Digging Up?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Lucasfilm Games for the Commodore Amiga, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Graphic Adventure is a landmark point-and-click adventure built on the SCUMM engine. Designed by Ron Gilbert, Noah Falstein, and David Fox, the game expands on the events of the film, allowing players to guide Indy and his father through iconic locations including Venice, Brunwald Castle, and Berlin in a race to secure the Holy Grail. Gameplay centres on puzzle-solving, exploration, and narrative-driven progression, with multiple ways to approach and complete many challenges. The introduction of the “Indy Quotient” (IQ) scoring system rewards experimentation and creative thinking, encouraging players to discover alternative solutions and aim for the maximum 800-point score. Progression is shaped by player choice, observation, and careful interaction with the environment. Conversations, item combinations, and branching puzzle paths give the adventure a high level of replayability, setting it apart from many linear titles of the era.

video:video.video:title: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade – Did the C64 Action Game Miss the Grail?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by U. S. Gold and developed by Tiertex, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Action Game brings the blockbuster film to the Commodore 64 as a fast-moving platform adventure. You take control of Indy as he races across iconic locations in a quest to recover the Holy Grail and save his father. The game is split into five stages inspired directly by the movie, including the caves of Utah, the circus train, Venetian catacombs, Castle Grunwald, a zeppelin showdown, and the final Grail challenge. Each level mixes combat, timing-based platforming, and light puzzle elements. Indy’s whip is central to gameplay, used both as a weapon and a traversal tool for swinging across gaps. Hand-to-hand combat and environmental hazards keep pressure high, while exploration is needed to progress safely through each section.

video:video.video:title: Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom – Arcade Whip-Cracking on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by US Gold and developed by Paragon Programming, Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom brings the Atari arcade hit to the Commodore 64, itself based on the 1984 film. You step into Indy’s boots to relive key moments from the movie, from perilous temples to high-risk escapes. Gameplay blends platforming, combat, and light puzzle elements as you use Indy’s whip to defeat enemies, avoid traps, and interact with the environment. The game is split into three distinct stages: the Mine Cart Escape, the Temple of Doom, and the Bridge of Death, each offering its own mechanics and challenges. On the Commodore 64, the focus is on atmosphere and fidelity to the source material, supported by Martin Galway’s soundtrack. While the slower pace, repetitive sections, and long loading times drew criticism at the time, the ambition of the conversion is clear.

video:video.video:title: Indiana Jones in the Lost Kingdom – The C64 Indy Game People Forget Exists
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Mindscape and developed by Michael J. Hanson, Indiana Jones in the Lost Kingdom is a puzzle-driven adventure for the Commodore 64 that stands apart from other Indy games by telling a completely original story. Rather than following a film plot, you guide Indiana Jones through a mysterious lost kingdom in a race against rival archaeologist Ivar Reiss to recover a powerful artifact. The game is deliberately cryptic, offering almost no instructions and expecting you to work things out through experimentation and observation. Each of the six levels introduces new ideas and challenges, forcing you to think logically, test assumptions, and adapt your approach as the rules subtly change. Unlike many puzzle games of the era, progress depends less on reflexes and more on insight. Success comes from paying attention to how each screen behaves and learning from failure, making every breakthrough feel earned rather than handed to you.

video:video.video:title: Infernal Runner – The C64 Platformer Where Dying Was Half the Attraction
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Loriciels, Infernal Runner is a darkly satirical platform game for the Commodore 64 developed by Michel Koell and Yves Korta. Set inside a nightmarish labyrinth, the game drops players into a surreal world of deadly traps, grotesque surprises, and pitch-black humour, where survival is never guaranteed. Gameplay is deliberately non-linear, allowing players to move freely between interconnected rooms packed with hazards. The objective is to locate keys and open chests in order to escape, all while managing a constantly draining hunger meter that forces you to hunt for food scattered throughout the maze. Every screen introduces new ways to die, often suddenly and brutally. Infernal Runner became infamous for its exaggerated death animations and macabre tone, which were strikingly graphic for the mid-1980s. Rather than discouraging failure, the game almost revels in it, turning death into part of the learning process.

video:video.video:title: Infiltrator – Fly the Chopper, Forge the Papers, Bluff the Guards | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Chris Gray Enterprises and published by Mindscape and U. S. Gold, Infiltrator is a unique combat flight simulation and stealth action game for the Commodore 64. Players step into the role of Johnny “Jimbo Baby” McGibbits, piloting the advanced Gizmo DHX-3 helicopter to infiltrate enemy territory and stop the plans of the mysterious Mad Leader. Each mission is divided into two phases: an aerial combat section and a ground-based infiltration segment. During flight missions, players navigate hostile airspace, identify friendly aircraft, and deploy missiles while using whisper mode for stealth. Ground missions focus on careful planning and disguise, requiring players to use fake documents, gas grenades, security cards, and explosives to bypass guards and complete objectives without raising alarms. This blend of flight simulation and espionage gameplay was highly innovative for its time, offering a level of depth and variety rarely seen on 8-bit systems.

video:video.video:title: Insects In Space – The Bizarre C64 Defender Clone That Scored 94%
video:video.video:description: Insects in Space is a 1989 Commodore 64 side-scrolling shooter published by Hewson and created by Sensible Software, with Chris Yates credited for the design and programming. Its structure recalls Defender: the player patrols a horizontally scrolling landscape while hostile insects descend to capture the babies scattered below. Abducted survivors must be rescued before the insects carry them away and transform them, so watching the radar and deciding when to attack or recover a captive is as important as firing accurately. The playfield wraps around and supports rapid changes of direction, creating a continuous defence mission rather than a fixed procession of stages. A simultaneous two-player option lets both pilots share the rescue effort, adding coordination to a game already built around speed, prioritisation and constant movement.

video:video.video:title: International Basketball – Was This the C64’s First Great Basketball Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Andrew B. Spencer and published by Commodore for the Commodore 64, International Basketball is an early attempt to bring the speed and excitement of basketball to home computers. Focusing on arcade-style action rather than deep simulation, it delivers quick matches that are easy to pick up and play. Games are played in a 3-on-3 format using a side-scrolling view, with support for both single-player and two-player modes. Players can select different difficulty levels and choose between NBA, NCAA, or international rule sets, adding welcome variety to each match. Passing, shooting, and stealing all rely on sharp timing and positioning, keeping the action lively and competitive. The controls are simple and responsive, making the game accessible to newcomers while still offering enough challenge to reward practice. Visually, the presentation keeps the court and players clear and readable, while sound effects help sell the on-court action.

video:video.video:title: International Soccer – The C64 Cartridge Football Game Everyone Recognised
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Commodore International for the Commodore 64, International Soccer is a pioneering football game developed by Andrew Spencer. Known in some regions as Cup Final or Voetbal 64, it was one of the first soccer titles to present the action from a realistic side-on perspective, helping to shape the future of sports games on home computers. Matches feature two teams of six players and can be played solo against the computer or head-to-head with a second player. Games are split into two 200-second halves, with no fouls or offside rules, keeping the focus firmly on fast, uninterrupted play. Players can choose from six kit colours and even switch to a grayscale mode designed for black-and-white televisions. The gameplay is smooth and responsive, with flowing scrolling and intuitive controls that made it instantly accessible.

video:video.video:title: International Tennis – Did the C64 Serve Up a Decent Match?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Zeppelin Games for the Commodore 64, International Tennis is a late-era sports title that delivers a polished, arcade-leaning take on tennis. Programmed by Jason Benham, it arrived during the C64’s twilight years and stood out for its smooth presentation and accessible, competitive gameplay. Players can take part in singles or doubles matches against the computer or a human opponent, with responsive controls allowing for serves, volleys, lobs, and powerful smashes. The pacing encourages longer rallies, while the ball physics feel tight and predictable, rewarding smart positioning and shot placement over button-mashing. Visually, International Tennis makes confident use of the C64’s colour palette and sprite handling, featuring clean court layouts and fluid player animations. The audio is understated but effective, with catchy title music and subtle sound effects that keep the focus firmly on the action.

video:video.video:title: Into the Eagle’s Nest – Rescue the Saboteurs… Then Blow the Fortress | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Pandora for the Commodore 64, Into the Eagle’s Nest is a World War II–themed action-adventure that blends shooting, exploration, and tactical decision-making. Players step into the boots of an Allied soldier sent behind enemy lines to infiltrate the heavily guarded Eagle’s Nest fortress. The mission objectives are clear but demanding: rescue three captured comrades, recover stolen art treasures, and plant explosives to destroy the stronghold from within. Gameplay is viewed from a top-down perspective, with interconnected levels filled with enemy patrols, locked doors, hidden items, and limited resources. Progression relies on careful planning rather than constant firepower. Ammunition, keys, and explosives must be managed wisely, while reckless movement can quickly lead to failure. The emphasis on stealth and route planning gives the game a tense, methodical pace that rewards patience and awareness.

video:video.video:title: Invade-A-Load – The C64 Loading Game That Made Waiting Less Painful
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Mastertronic and developed by Richard Aplin, Invade-a-Load is one of the most inventive ideas to appear on the Commodore 64. Rather than staring at a static loading screen, you’re dropped straight into a Space Invaders-style shooter that runs while the main game loads from cassette in the background. You control a small ship at the bottom of the screen, blasting descending alien waves as they speed up and become more aggressive. It’s simple, immediate, and surprisingly addictive, turning unavoidable loading time into a playable challenge instead of dead air. What makes Invade-a-Load truly special is how seamlessly it integrates with the fast loader itself, running without slowing the loading process. Add Rob Hubbard’s unmistakable SID music into the mix and you’ve got a loading screen that became more memorable than some full games.

video:video.video:title: Iridis Alpha – Jeff Minter’s C64 Shooter That Refuses to Behave Normally
video:video.video:description: Iridis Alpha (1986), developed by Jeff Minter and released by Hewson, is one of the most distinctive and unconventional shoot ’em ups on the Commodore 64. Players control Gilby, a robotic spacecraft capable of both aerial and ground-based movement, as they explore the alien world of Iridis Alpha. A defining feature is the dual-universe system, where players must switch between parallel screens to manage threats and maintain energy balance. Energy management is central to survival — having too much or too little power leads to destruction, forcing constant tactical adjustments. The game blends fast-paced shooting with strategic resource control, creating a demanding and highly original gameplay experience. Renowned for its difficulty, hypnotic visuals, and innovative mechanics, Iridis Alpha has earned cult status among fans of Jeff Minter’s experimental design philosophy.

video:video.video:title: It Came from the Desert – B-Movie Giant Ants Invade the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Cinemaware for the Commodore Amiga, It Came from the Desert is a cinematic action-adventure inspired by 1950s B-movie monster films, most notably Them!. Players take on the role of Dr. Greg Bradley, a geologist investigating a mysterious meteor crash near the desert town of Lizard Breath, only to uncover a terrifying mutant ant invasion. Gameplay blends exploration, investigation, puzzle-solving, and tense action sequences within a strict real-time structure. Over the course of just 15 in-game days, players must gather clues, question townsfolk, explore underground tunnels, and fend off giant ants in order to prevent an impending catastrophe. A dynamic day-and-night cycle drives the narrative forward, with events unfolding whether the player is ready or not. The Amiga version stands out for its detailed artwork, atmospheric sound design, and cinematic presentation, alongside varied mini-games that reinforce the sense of urgency and storytelling.

video:video.video:title: Ivan ‘Ironman’ Stewart’s Super Off Road – Still Great on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Graftgold and published by Virgin Mastertronic, Ivan ‘Ironman’ Stewart’s Super Off Road brings the hugely popular arcade racer to the Commodore 64 with fast, top-down off-road action. You race chunky trucks around tight dirt circuits, battling rivals while sliding through corners and launching over jumps. The heart of the game is its cash-based upgrade system. Winning races earns money that you can spend on improving speed, handling, and nitro boosts, adding a layer of strategy between events. Choosing where to invest can make the difference between staying competitive or being left in the dust. Tracks are packed with sharp bends, hazards, and elevation changes, keeping races tense and chaotic. Support for up to three players makes it especially memorable, turning every race into a loud, competitive scramble for position. On the Commodore 64, the game captures the spirit of the arcade original with bold colours, clear sprites, and a strong sense of speed.

video:video.video:title: Jack the Nipper – Fill the Naughtyometer Before Mum Catches You | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Gremlin Graphics, Jack the Nipper puts you in control of a mischievous toddler determined to cause as much mayhem as possible. Instead of saving the day, your goal is to be as naughty as you can without getting caught. The game unfolds across 50 flip-screen locations including kindergartens, police stations, museums, and back streets. Each screen becomes a playground for mischief as you jump on objects, move items around, and set up pranks to push your naughtyometer ever higher. Avoiding adults is critical, as getting caught results in a spanking that fills Jack’s nappy rash meter. Monsters and ghosts add extra danger, forcing you to balance reckless behaviour with careful movement and timing. On the Commodore 64, Jack the Nipper stands out for its colourful presentation and memorable soundtrack by Ben Daglish.

video:video.video:title: Jack the Nipper II – His Nappy Was Literally a Parachute on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Gremlin Graphics for the Commodore 64, Jack the Nipper II: In Coconut Capers continues the misadventures of gaming’s most troublesome toddler. This time, Jack parachutes into the African jungle, determined to cause mayhem while staying out of reach of his relentlessly chasing father. The game spans a huge 192 screens packed with obstacles, enemies, and environmental puzzles. Jack can climb ropes, swing from vines, and hurl coconuts to distract or defeat enemies, with progress relying on exploration, timing, and problem-solving rather than simple reflexes. A key feature is the Naughty-O-Meter, which tracks how much mischief Jack causes. Creative pranks and clever interactions increase your score, encouraging experimentation and rewarding players who embrace Jack’s mischievous nature. On the C64, the game delivers colourful jungle environments with varied locations including caves, swamps, and temples.

video:video.video:title: James Pond: Underwater Agent – The Amiga Spy Parody That Started a Series
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Vectordean and published by Millennium Interactive for the Commodore Amiga, James Pond: Underwater Agent introduces a humorous aquatic spy adventure inspired by the world of James Bond. Players take control of James Pond, a suave mudskipper secret agent, as he embarks on a series of eco-themed missions to protect the underwater world from pollution and danger. The game features twelve varied levels where objectives include rescuing trapped sea creatures, sealing toxic leaks, and escorting fish to safety, all while racing against the clock. Gameplay centres on trapping enemies inside bubbles and then popping them to turn foes into useful collectibles. Exploration is encouraged through branching tunnels, hidden rooms, and interconnected pipe systems. Visually, the Amiga version stands out for its bright cartoon-style graphics, detailed sprites, and parallax-scrolling backgrounds. Humorous level titles such as “Licence to Bubble” and “A View to a Spill” reinforce the game’s playful tone.

video:video.video:title: Jammin’ – The C64 Music Game That Turned the Top 20 Into a Maze
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Taskset Ltd. , Jammin’ is a distinctive action-puzzle game for the Commodore 64 that fuses maze navigation with a strong musical theme. Players take control of Rankin Rodney, working their way through 20 levels inspired by the Top 20 music charts. Each stage challenges players to collect four musical instruments and deliver them to their correct locations. Movement is restricted to paths of the same colour, forcing careful route planning, while moving platforms are used to switch between colour zones. Roaming musical notes and other hazards add pressure, demanding precision and timing to complete each level safely. One of Jammin’s standout features is its evolving soundtrack, which changes dynamically as instruments are collected, reinforcing the game’s musical identity and adding a satisfying sense of progression. The combination of audio feedback and puzzle mechanics gives the game a character all its own.

video:video.video:title: Jet Set Willy – 60 Rooms of Housework Before Maria Lets You Sleep on the C64
