video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Software Projects and designed by Matthew Smith, Jet Set Willy is a defining non-linear platform game that pushed 8-bit ambition to its limits. On the Commodore 64, you guide Willy through a vast mansion of 60 interconnected rooms, collecting glowing objects while surviving a maze of hazards and roaming guardians. Controls are deceptively simple—left, right, jump—but the challenge lies in precision. You’re free to explore in almost any order, climbing ropes, tackling awkward staircases, timing jumps perfectly, and learning how each room behaves. Progress demands memory, patience, and an understanding of how the mansion fits together. The C64 version carries over many of the quirks that made the game legendary. Respawning behaviour can be unforgiving, some layouts border on the cruel, and the infamous Attic Bug originally made the game impossible to complete until later fixes appeared.

video:video.video:title: Jimmy White’s Whirlwind Snooker – The Amiga Table That Made Pool Games Look Old
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Virgin Games and developed by Archer Maclean for the Commodore Amiga, Jimmy White’s Whirlwind Snooker set a new standard for cue sports on home computers. Endorsed by professional snooker legend Jimmy White, the game delivers a remarkably authentic and feature-rich snooker experience. Players are given complete control over the table, with the ability to rotate the view, zoom in on any ball, and apply spin or swerve to shots. Multiple modes are included, ranging from competitive one- and two-player matches to practice sessions, trick shots, and demo play, all supported by four adjustable skill levels. What truly sets the game apart is its smooth 3D presentation and highly accurate ball physics. Each break-off plays differently, maximum 147 breaks are possible, and games can be saved mid-frame. Digitised crowd applause and sound effects add to the atmosphere, while playful visual touches appear if players take too long to line up a shot.

video:video.video:title: Joe Blade – Budget C64 Action with a One-Man Army Attitude
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Players Software under the Interceptor Micros label, Joe Blade is a side-scrolling action platform game for the Commodore 64 developed by Colin Swinbourne. Players take on the role of Joe Blade, a lone commando sent deep into an enemy complex to rescue six kidnapped world leaders from the grip of the villainous Crax Bloodfinger. The game unfolds across a maze of flip-screen rooms packed with guards, traps, and explosives. Armed with a machine gun and working against a strict time limit, players must carefully explore the complex, disable bombs, and locate hostages while conserving limited ammunition. Progress depends on learning the layout, planning efficient routes, and avoiding costly mistakes. Each room presents its own hazards, encouraging methodical movement and memorisation rather than reckless action. The emphasis on exploration and timing gives Joe Blade a tense rhythm, where every wrong turn can waste precious seconds or resources.

video:video.video:title: Joe Blade II – More Bombs, More Rooms and More C64 Trouble
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Colin Swinbourne and published by Players Software for the Commodore 64, Joe Blade II shifts the series away from military infiltration and drops its vigilante hero into the crime-ridden streets of the city. This time, Joe must rescue kidnapped civilians while taking on gangs and urban hazards across a series of side-scrolling levels. Gameplay focuses on timing and movement rather than weapon-based combat. Joe defeats enemies by jumping on their heads, giving the game a distinctive twist compared to traditional beat-’em-ups. Progression hinges on rescuing trapped citizens, each of which triggers one of four fast-paced sub-games that test reflexes, memory, and problem-solving under strict time limits. The city environments are bright and expressive, with large character sprites and a cartoon-like presentation that suits the game’s lighter tone. Music by Mike Brown drives the action with energetic tunes that keep the pace lively as pressure mounts during rescues and timed challenges.

video:video.video:title: Judge Dredd – Why Did the C64 Get TWO Different Mega-City One Games?
video:video.video:description: Judge Dredd made his Commodore 64 debut in 1986, with a later reimagined version released in 1991, both drawing on the iconic 2000 AD comic and its dystopian vision of Mega-City One. Each game offers a different interpretation of the lawman, reflecting changing design trends across the late 1980s and early 1990s. The 1986 release from Melbourne House, developed by Beam Software, mixes arcade action with light strategy. Players patrol the city via a crime map before tackling flick-screen platform levels, choosing how to deal with perps using commands like Halt, Warn, or Kill. The Lawgiver’s multiple ammo types add tactical flexibility, reinforcing Dredd’s role as judge, jury, and executioner. In contrast, the 1991 version from Virgin Mastertronic and Random Access shifts to a scrolling platform format with structured missions spread across Mega-City One. Each assignment focuses on eliminating threats or objectives while keeping the city’s crime rate under control, blending fast action with time pressure and forward planning.

video:video.video:title: Jumpman – C64 Platform Puzzles Before Everyone Called Them Retro
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Epyx for the Commodore 64, Jumpman is a pioneering platform game developed by Randy Glover that helped define precision-based action on home computers. Players take on the role of Jumpman, a bomb disposal expert racing to save Jupiter Headquarters after it has been sabotaged by terrorists. The objective is clear but demanding: navigate each level and defuse every bomb while avoiding a variety of hazards. Gameplay focuses on carefully timed jumps, climbing ladders, and swinging from ropes as the screen scrolls vertically to reveal multiple floors. Enemies such as smart darts react to Jumpman’s position, adding constant pressure and forcing players to plan every move. Risk and reward are central to the experience. Players can adjust Jumpman’s running speed, choosing between safer, slower movement or faster runs that increase danger but improve scoring potential.

video:video.video:title: Jungle Hunt – Swinging, Swimming and Stabbing Crocodiles on C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Taito Corporation and published by Atarisoft for the Commodore 64, Jungle Hunt is a faithful home conversion of the arcade hit originally known as Jungle King. Due to copyright issues, the game was rebranded, but its fast-paced jungle action remained intact. Players take on the role of a daring explorer racing to rescue a captured woman from hostile cannibals. The adventure is split across four varied stages, each testing different skills. Vine swinging demands precise timing, the crocodile-infested river requires sharp reactions and careful knife use, rock dodging pushes climbing reflexes, and the final leap over cannibals brings the rescue mission to a tense conclusion. The game supports single-player and two-player alternating modes, with difficulty steadily increasing as stages repeat. While the Commodore 64 version lacks some of the arcade’s music, it captures the structure, challenge, and rhythm of the original experience.

video:video.video:title: Jupiter Lander – Commodore’s C64 Cartridge Where Landing Was the Whole Battle
video:video.video:description: Released in 1982 by Commodore and developed by HAL Laboratory, Jupiter Lander is one of the earliest arcade-style titles available for the Commodore 64. As a launch-era game, it played a key role in demonstrating the system’s technical potential and introducing players to physics-based gameplay on home computers. The objective is simple but demanding. Players pilot a spacecraft descending toward the surface of Jupiter, carefully managing thrust to counter gravity and line up with one of three landing platforms, each offering different levels of difficulty. Safe landings reward points and replenish fuel, while hard impacts or collisions with the terrain result in instant failure. Fuel management is central to the challenge. Every burst of thrust must be carefully judged, as running out of fuel brings the mission to an abrupt end. Precision, timing, and restraint are essential, turning each descent into a tense balancing act between control and momentum.

video:video.video:title: Kamikaze – A Late C64 Shooter with Old-School Arcade Teeth
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Codemasters and developed by Digital Design for the Commodore 64, Kamikaze is a fast-moving horizontal shoot-’em-up that puts players in control of a nimble biplane flying deep into enemy territory. Drawing inspiration from arcade favourites like Sky Kid, it delivers classic side-scrolling action with a light tactical twist. Players can manoeuvre freely in all directions, dodging incoming fire while taking out enemy aircraft, ground troops, tanks, and defensive installations. Rather than pure shooting, the game encourages smart positioning and timing to survive the increasingly busy screens. Kamikaze adds extra depth through mission-style objectives, including rescuing hostages and bombing key enemy targets. These elements reward careful play and awareness of the level layout, helping the game stand out from more straightforward shooters on the system. On the C64, the game features bright, colourful graphics and smooth scrolling that keep the action flowing at a brisk pace.

video:video.video:title: Kane & Kane 2 – Cowboys, Shooting Galleries and C64 Western Oddness
video:video.video:description: Released by Mastertronic in 1986 and 1988, Kane and Kane II are Western-themed arcade action games developed by John Darnell for the Commodore 64. Both titles place you in the boots of lawman Marshall McGraw as he rides into danger to restore order across the frontier. The original Kane mixes fast-paced shooting with horseback riding stages, throwing a variety of arcade-style challenges your way. Gunfights test reflexes and positioning, while the riding sections demand precision and timing, earning a reputation for being tough but memorable. Kane II follows the same structure, offering more shootouts and riding sequences with familiar mechanics. While it sticks closely to the formula of the first game, it expands on the action and delivers another dose of Wild West arcade gameplay. Neither game set out to reinvent the genre, but together they represent a distinctive slice of budget-era Commodore 64 action.

video:video.video:title: Karateka – Jordan Mechner’s First Published Game Before Prince of Persia | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Broderbund and developed by Jordan Mechner, Karateka is a landmark martial arts action game that pushed the Commodore 64 far beyond expectations. It was Mechner’s first published title and laid the groundwork for ideas he would later refine in Prince of Persia. Players control a lone martial artist on a side-scrolling quest to rescue Princess Mariko from the warlord Akuma. Combat unfolds in a deliberate, almost cinematic rhythm, requiring players to switch stances and time punches and kicks at different heights to defeat guards and avoid instant defeat. What truly set Karateka apart was its animation. Using rotoscoping techniques, Mechner captured realistic human movement, giving the game a fluidity and sense of weight rarely seen on home computers at the time. Combined with dramatic pacing and atmosphere, it created an experience that felt closer to a film than a typical arcade brawler.

video:video.video:title: Kawasaki Rhythm Rocker – The C64 Music Game Nobody Expects
video:video.video:description: Released in June 1984 by Sight & Sound Music for the Commodore 64, Kawasaki Rhythm Rocker is a unique interactive music-making tool created by jazz fusion musician and programmer Ryo Kawasaki. Rather than focusing on traditional gameplay, the software allows users to compose and perform music in real time using four independent tracks: drums, bass, synthesiser, and vocal-style effects. Players select an instrument channel, input rhythms and notes, and loop their creations while adjusting tempo, bass levels, and dub-style effects on the fly. The interface is designed to be intuitive and expressive, encouraging experimentation and live-style performance rather than rigid composition. High-resolution animated visuals pulse and react to the music, creating a hypnotic, psychedelic display that enhances the creative experience. Powered by the SID chip, Rhythm Rocker showcases the sound hardware’s expressive range, blending sequencing, synthesis, and performance into one package.

video:video.video:title: KGB – One Wrong Decision Could Wreck This Cold War Amiga Thriller
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Cryo Interactive and published by Virgin Games, KGB is a dark and demanding point-and-click adventure for the Commodore Amiga, set against the backdrop of the collapsing Soviet Union in the summer of 1991. Players take on the role of Captain Maksim Rukov, a newly assigned KGB officer drawn into a murder investigation that quickly spirals into a far-reaching political conspiracy. The game is built around realism and consequence. Actions unfold in real time, with events continuing whether the player is ready or not. A single poor decision can lead to immediate failure or trigger consequences that surface hours later, forcing players to think carefully, manage time, and pay close attention to dialogue, documents, and subtle clues. Using the same engine as Cryo’s Dune, KGB features detailed hand-drawn locations and an interface designed to support complex investigation and interaction.

video:video.video:title: Kickman – Catching Balloons on a Unicycle Because Early C64 Said So
video:video.video:description: Released in 1982, Kickman is an arcade action game developed by Midway and published by Commodore that puts a playful spin on the classic catch-and-balance formula. Players control a unicycle-riding clown tasked with catching falling balloons on his head, carefully stacking them higher and higher without letting the pile topple over. As the game progresses, the pace increases and the challenge ramps up. Balloons fall faster, the stack becomes harder to control, and quick reactions are essential. A clever kick mechanic allows players to punt falling balloons back into the air for a second chance, adding both strategy and tension to the action. Adding to the mayhem are surprise elements such as Pac-Man-style characters and ghost-like enemies that appear during play, alongside bonus rounds that offer extra points and lives. These twists keep the gameplay fresh and unpredictable, rewarding skill and timing rather than pure luck.

video:video.video:title: Kikstart II – The C64 Motorbike Game That Let You Build Your Own Tracks
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Kikstart II is the sequel to the hugely popular motorcycle trials racer, developed by Mr. Chip Software. It builds directly on the original’s foundations while adding deeper mechanics and one of the most influential features of its era — a full track construction set. The game includes 24 challenging pre-designed courses packed with ramps, gates, fences, mud pits, and precision jumps that demand careful throttle control and balance. Players can race against the clock or go head-to-head in split-screen two-player mode, where mastering momentum and timing is key to victory. Kikstart II’s standout feature is its track editor, which allows players to design, save, and replay custom courses. This dramatically extends replay value and turns the game into a creative sandbox, encouraging experimentation and competitive custom challenges long after the built-in tracks are mastered.

video:video.video:title: Kingpin – Was Team17’s Amiga Bowling Game Any Good?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1995 by Team17 for the Commodore Amiga, Kingpin: Arcade Sports Series Bowling is a dedicated ten-pin bowling simulation designed for both solo players and multiplayer groups. You can control up to six bowlers, customise player names and shirt colours, and compete in full matches against friends or AI opponents. The gameplay focuses on timing, spin, and angle, delivering a surprisingly authentic bowling experience. Visually, the game features smooth ball and pin animations, with realistic reactions as strikes and spares unfold. The sound effects recreate the atmosphere of a real bowling alley, although the full CD-audio soundtrack is exclusive to the Amiga CD32 version. While modest in scope compared to larger sports titles, Kingpin stands out in the Amiga library for filling a rare niche. Bowling games were uncommon on the platform, and this remains one of the most polished examples.

video:video.video:title: King’s Bounty – The C64 Strategy RPG Before Heroes of Might and Magic
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by New World Computing, King’s Bounty is a landmark turn-based strategy game designed by Jon Van Caneghem and widely recognised as the foundation for the later Heroes of Might and Magic series. On the Commodore 64, it delivers a deep fantasy adventure built around exploration, planning, and tactical combat. Players take on the role of a hero tasked by King Maximus with recovering the stolen Sceptre of Order from the dragon Arech Dragonbreath. The quest spans four large continents, each filled with castles, towns, enemies, and secrets. Choosing between the Knight, Paladin, Barbarian, or Sorceress shapes how battles unfold and how armies are built. Gameplay combines open-world exploration with turn-based battles, as players recruit creatures, manage gold, and decide when to fight or avoid danger. Systems such as villain contracts and map fragments that reveal the Sceptre’s location add structure and long-term goals, encouraging careful strategy rather than brute force.

video:video.video:title: Klax – Did Atari’s Addictive Arcade Puzzle Work on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Atari Games and published by Domark for the Commodore 64, Klax is a fast-thinking puzzle game that puts reflexes and pattern recognition to the test. Adapted from the arcade hit, it delivers a fresh twist on tile-matching at a time when the genre was rapidly evolving. Gameplay revolves around catching coloured tiles as they slide down a conveyor belt and stacking them to form rows, columns, or diagonals of matching colours. Points are awarded for completed patterns, but poor placement can quickly lead to stack overflow and an abrupt game over. As levels progress, speed increases and decision-making becomes increasingly demanding. The Commodore 64 version successfully captures the addictive core of the arcade original, combining simple controls with rising pressure and satisfying scoring chains. Quick reactions must be balanced with careful planning to survive the later stages.

video:video.video:title: Knight Games – The C64 Medieval Tournament with Eight Different Events
video:video.video:description: Released for the Commodore 64, Knight Games is a medieval-themed multi-event title that combines precision shooting challenges with intense one-on-one combat. Rather than a single adventure, the game is made up of eight distinct events, each testing different skills and reflexes. Two of the events focus on ranged accuracy. Crossbow tasks players with moving a crosshair to hit rotating targets, while Archery raises the difficulty with targets moving horizontally, demanding careful timing and anticipation. These events reward precision and patience over brute force. The remaining six events are all close-combat duels fought head-to-head. Sword fighting, quarterstaff battles on a log, and weapon-based contests using ball and chain, axe, and pike all follow a similar structure. Players must land repeated, well-timed hits while blocking incoming attacks, with victory achieved through consistency and timing rather than button-mashing.

video:video.video:title: Knight Tyme – How Did Magic Knight End Up in the 25th Century? | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by David Jones and published by Mastertronic under the Added Dimension label, Knight Tyme is a graphic adventure for the Commodore 64 and the third entry in the Magic Knight series. Picking up after the rescue of the wizard Gimbal, Magic Knight is unexpectedly transported to the 25th century aboard the starship USS Pisces, far from his medieval roots. The adventure blends fantasy and science fiction as players explore futuristic locations, interact with crew members and aliens, and work toward assembling the Golden Sundial to return home. Progress depends on careful exploration, logical puzzle-solving, and understanding how the game’s world fits together. Knight Tyme uses the Windimation system, a menu-driven interface that allows players to select actions and objects rather than type commands. This approach makes interaction clear and accessible while still offering layered puzzles, inventory management, and meaningful choices that affect progress.

video:video.video:title: Knightmare – Six Spells, One Dungeon and No Easy Way Out | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by MD Software and published by Activision for the Commodore 64, Knightmare is an adventure game based on the hugely popular British television series of the same name. Players are cast into the dangerous medieval world of Damonia, trapped inside the infamous Knightmare Castle and tasked with finding a way to escape its many deadly traps. Gameplay blends traditional adventure mechanics with puzzle-solving and spellcasting. Players explore interconnected rooms, interact with objects using a verb–noun command system, and deploy a range of magical spells including Anvil, Casper, Alchemy, Ice, Toad, and Metamorph, each designed to overcome specific obstacles or enemies. The game uses a distinctive semi-3D presentation, with castle locations displayed like illustrated pages in a book, giving it a strong sense of atmosphere and structure. While there is no background music, the sound effects reinforce actions and events, keeping the focus firmly on exploration and problem-solving.

video:video.video:title: Kobyashi Naru – The C64 Adventure Inspired by Star Trek’s No-Win Test
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Kobyashi Naru is a science-fiction themed adventure that takes its inspiration from the famous no-win test of Star Trek lore. Designed by Clive Wilson and Les Hogarth, the game challenges players to prove their worth by surviving a sequence of cerebral trials rather than relying on action or reflexes. Gameplay is divided into three distinct sections—Knowledge, Wisdom, and Understanding—each presenting puzzles that test logic, observation, and reasoning. Instead of a traditional text parser, the game uses an icon-based interface, allowing players to interact with objects and environments in a more visual and accessible way for the time. The challenge is deliberately unforgiving. Incorrect decisions can lead to sudden failure, and progress often demands experimentation and lateral thinking. This difficulty split opinion on release, but it also gave the game a reputation as a demanding experience aimed squarely at players who enjoyed tough mental challenges.

video:video.video:title: Koronis Rift – Lucasfilm’s C64 Alien Salvage Hunt Scored 96% in Zzap!64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Lucasfilm Games, Koronis Rift is a pioneering 3D action-strategy game that pushed the Commodore 64 into bold new territory. Set in the year 2049, players take on the role of a rover pilot exploring the dangerous Koronis Rift on an alien world, tasked with uncovering the remains of an ancient civilisation hidden deep within hostile terrain. Gameplay blends real-time exploration with careful planning. Players must descend into twenty increasingly dangerous rifts, locating long-lost alien hulks and salvaging powerful modules to upgrade the rover. Each module serves a specific function, from improved shields and weapons to navigation and mapping tools, making preparation just as important as piloting skill. A core mechanic is the colour-coded module system, which determines compatibility and effectiveness against enemy saucers guarding the hulks. With limited space to carry equipment, players are forced to make tactical choices, adapting their loadout to survive each mission and uncover deeper secrets.

video:video.video:title: Kung-Fu Master – Did One of Arcade Gaming’s First Beat ’Em Ups Work on C64?
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Irem and released in arcades in 1984, Kung-Fu Master arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1985 via a conversion by Berkeley Softworks, with Chris Hawley handling the port. Published by U. S. Gold in Europe, it brought one of arcade gaming’s most influential action titles to home computers. Players step into the role of Thomas, a martial arts expert fighting his way through the five floors of the Devil’s Temple to rescue his kidnapped girlfriend, Sylvia. Each level throws relentless waves of enemies into the action, from knife throwers and grippers to powerful end-of-floor bosses that test timing and positioning. The gameplay is fast, direct, and demanding, relying on punches, kicks, jumps, and crouches to survive the constant pressure. Despite the Commodore 64’s technical limits, the conversion delivers colourful visuals and a tense background soundtrack that maintain the urgency of the arcade experience.

video:video.video:title: Labyrinth – The C64 Adventure Starts as Text… Then Pulls You Into the Film
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Lucasfilm Games and published by Activision for the Commodore 64, Labyrinth: The Computer Game is a graphic adventure inspired by Jim Henson’s fantasy film. Players are dropped into a sprawling maze filled with traps, riddles, and strange characters, racing against time to confront Jareth and escape. The adventure unfolds under a strict 13-hour real-time limit, adding tension and urgency to every decision. Gameplay begins with a text-based sequence before shifting into a graphical exploration format, featuring side-scrolling corridors, interactive environments, and a radar bar that maps each area. A standout feature is the innovative “word wheel” interface, which replaces traditional text parsers with rotating menus of verbs and nouns. This system streamlines command input, reduces frustration, and makes experimentation more accessible for players new to adventure games. Visually, Labyrinth delivers detailed environments and expressive animations that were highly regarded at the time.

video:video.video:title: Las Vegas Casino – Could You Beat the House on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Zeppelin Games for the Commodore 64, Las Vegas Casino is a single-player casino simulation designed by Kevin Franklin, with graphics by Michael Owens and music by Adam Gilmore. The game brings the atmosphere of a casino floor to the C64, offering faithful digital versions of four popular gambling games. Players can choose between Blackjack, Baccarat, Roulette, and Craps, each presented with clear rules and accessible controls. Blackjack and Baccarat use a first-person viewpoint, placing you directly opposite the dealer, while Roulette and Craps are shown from a top-down perspective that makes betting and table interaction easy to follow. The gameplay focuses on straightforward, pick-up-and-play mechanics rather than complex systems. Joystick-driven menus and clean layouts keep things moving smoothly, making it easy to jump between games and chase a winning streak without lengthy setup or explanations.

video:video.video:title: Laser Squad – Before X-COM, Julian Gollop Was Waging War on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Target Games and designed by Julian Gollop, Laser Squad is a landmark turn-based tactical strategy game that helped define the genre on home computers. Often described as the spiritual forerunner to X-COM, it introduced ideas and systems that would influence tactical design for decades. Players command a small squad of elite soldiers across a range of mission scenarios, including hostage rescues, search-and-destroy operations, and item recovery. Viewed from an isometric perspective, each mission demands careful positioning, awareness of enemy movement, and smart use of cover. Every unit operates using a limited pool of action points per turn, forcing players to plan movement, attacks, and reactions with precision. A wide selection of weapons and equipment—each with distinct strengths and limitations—allows for varied tactical approaches, while line-of-sight rules and fog of war keep tension high.

video:video.video:title: Last Ninja 2 – System 3 Sent the C64’s Ninja to New York
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by System 3 for the Commodore 64, Last Ninja 2: Back with a Vengeance boldly shifts the series from feudal Japan to the streets of modern-day New York City. Armakuni is torn from his own time and dropped into an urban battleground where his ancient enemy Kunitoki has rebuilt his power in a new era. The game expands on the original’s isometric design, letting you move freely in eight directions while navigating locations such as Central Park, city streets, sewers, and hidden laboratories. Progress depends on careful exploration, precise movement, and understanding how each area connects to the next. Combat plays a major role, with Armakuni using shuriken, nunchaku, staffs, and other tools to overcome enemies. Some foes require specific weapons, encouraging tactical thinking rather than brute force. Alongside fighting, puzzles and item use are essential, with keys, ropes, maps, and other objects needed to unlock new paths.

video:video.video:title: Law of the West – On the C64, Every Conversation Could End in a Gunfight
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Accolade and designed by Alan Miller, Law of the West is one of the earliest video games to place storytelling and player choice at the centre of the experience. Rather than relying on constant action, it delivers tension through conversation, decision-making, and the threat of sudden violence. Set in the frontier town of Gold Gulch, you play the role of the local sheriff, dealing with a rotating cast of townsfolk throughout a single in-game day. Each encounter unfolds through branching dialogue choices, where your words can calm a situation, provoke hostility, or trigger a deadly gunfight. Every response matters, and no two playthroughs feel quite the same. Gameplay blends slow, deliberate interaction with fast-draw shootouts that demand sharp reflexes. Unlike traditional arcade shooters, success depends as much on reading people and choosing the right tone as it does on pulling the trigger at the right moment.

video:video.video:title: Lazarian – Five Space Trials and a Giant Flying Eye on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Commodore for the Commodore 64, Lazarian is an early arcade-style shoot-’em-up programmed and scored by Andy Finkel and inspired by Bally Midway’s 1981 arcade title. Players pilot a spacecraft through a series of increasingly challenging combat zones, battling waves of alien enemies, navigating dense meteor fields, and surviving fast-paced attack patterns. The game unfolds across five distinct stages, each introducing new mechanics and enemy behaviours. Progression requires sharp reflexes, precise movement, and careful positioning. The final phase culminates in a showdown with the powerful “Evil Eye” boss, providing a demanding conclusion to the multi-stage campaign. Visually, Lazarian delivers simple but effective space-themed graphics that suit its fast-moving gameplay. Enemy formations and environmental hazards are plainly presented, allowing players to react quickly. Sound design and music by Andy Finkel enhance the experience, adding tension and atmosphere to each stage.

video:video.video:title: Lazy Jones – 15 Mini-Games Hidden Inside One Commodore 64 Hotel
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Terminal Software, Lazy Jones is a brilliantly inventive Commodore 64 title that wraps a collection of arcade-style mini-games inside a single cohesive world. You play as Lazy Jones, a hotel janitor wandering corridors and rooms that each hide a different arcade challenge waiting to be played. The hotel acts as the hub, with doors leading to 14 distinct mini-games inspired by classic shooters, platformers, and puzzle games. Progression comes from mastering these short, fast-paced challenges, each with its own rules, hazards, and scoring systems, all stitched together by exploration rather than menus. What truly elevates Lazy Jones is its presentation. Designed and programmed by David Whittaker, the game features an unforgettable soundtrack that includes clever SID reinterpretations of popular early-80s tunes, giving every room its own identity and mood. Over time, Lazy Jones has earned cult status for its creativity and forward-thinking design.

video:video.video:title: Le Mans – HAL Laboratory’s Forgotten C64 Racing Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1982 by HAL Laboratory and published by Commodore, LeMans is one of the earliest racing games available for the Commodore 64 and a showcase of forward-thinking arcade design. Presented from a bird’s-eye view, the game challenges players to overtake traffic at speed while managing risk and precision under constant pressure. The goal is simple but demanding: pass as many cars as possible within a 60-second time limit. Overtaking ten cars cleanly earns a 1,000-point bonus, while reaching 20,000 points extends the race by another minute. Crashes force a pit stop on the left side of the track, resetting your overtake count and costing valuable seconds. LeMans keeps things fresh with changing conditions, including icy roads that affect handling, night stages lit only by headlights, and the notorious LeMans Esses that test steering control.

video:video.video:title: Leader Board – Was This the C64’s Best Early Golf Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Access Software, Leader Board is a landmark golf simulation that redefined realism in sports games on home computers. Originally developed for the Commodore 64 and later enhanced on the Amiga, the game introduced precision mechanics and presentation that set a new benchmark for virtual golf. Gameplay is built around four full 18-hole courses, viewed from behind the golfer for a realistic perspective of the fairways and greens. Players control shot power and direction using a timing bar, with carefully timed inputs allowing shots to hook or slice. This added a layer of skill and finesse that rewarded practice and consistency rather than guesswork. The Amiga version benefits from smoother animation and improved visuals, making courses feel more alive and immersive. Water hazards, bunkers, and varied terrain demand thoughtful club selection and strategic play, while subtle risk-and-reward decisions keep every hole engaging.

video:video.video:title: Lemmings – Did This Amiga Classic Change Puzzle Games Forever?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by DMA Design and published by Psygnosis for the Commodore Amiga, Lemmings is a landmark puzzle-strategy game built around a deceptively simple idea. A group of lemmings march blindly forward, and it’s your job to guide as many as possible safely to the exit using a limited set of skills. Gameplay revolves around assigning roles such as digger, builder, blocker, and climber to individual lemmings in real time. Each level becomes a carefully balanced logic puzzle where timing, placement, and forward planning are essential to success. One wrong decision can doom the entire group. With over 100 levels included, the difficulty steadily ramps up, introducing new hazards and tighter constraints that demand increasingly creative solutions. The intuitive interface and expressive animations make the game easy to understand, while the puzzle design provides long-lasting depth and challenge.

video:video.video:title: Little Computer People – Every Original C64 Disk Could Create a Different Person
video:video.video:description: Released in October 1985 for the Commodore 64, Little Computer People is a groundbreaking life simulation game developed by David Crane and published by Activision. Long before virtual pets became mainstream, this title offered a novel idea: sharing your computer with a living digital companion. After loading, players are presented with a three-storey house and, after a short wait, a Little Computer Person moves in and begins living an independent daily routine. The character cooks meals, watches television, reads, and relaxes, all without direct control. Interaction is subtle, with players influencing behaviour through gifts, card games, and observation rather than commands. A defining feature is that each copy of the game generates a unique character with its own name and personality traits. The LCP responds to care and neglect, encouraging a sense of responsibility and long-term engagement rather than traditional goals or scoring systems.

video:video.video:title: Live and Let Die – The C64 James Bond Game That Started Life as Aquablast
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Elite Systems and published by Domark for the Commodore 64, Live and Let Die is a fast-paced action game loosely inspired by the 1973 James Bond film. Originally developed as an original title called Aquablast, the game was later rebranded after Domark recognised its similarity to the movie’s famous speedboat chase sequence. Players take control of a heavily armed high-speed boat and race through a variety of global locations, including the Florida Everglades, Arctic waters, and desert regions of the Sahara. The main objective is to battle enemy forces, avoid environmental hazards, and ultimately destroy Dr. Kananga’s heroin refinery. Gameplay blends high-speed racing with arcade-style shooting, drawing comparisons to titles such as RoadBlasters and Overlander. Players must balance aggressive combat with careful fuel management, precise steering, and quick reactions to survive increasingly intense stages.

video:video.video:title: Lode Runner – The C64 Puzzle Platformer That Gave You 150 Levels to Beat
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Broderbund for the Commodore 64 and created by Doug Smith, Lode Runner is a landmark puzzle-platformer that redefined the genre. Players control a lone runner tasked with collecting all the gold in each level while avoiding relentless enemy guards. The core mechanic that sets Lode Runner apart is the ability to dig temporary holes in the floor. These holes can trap enemies, open new routes, or create vital escape paths, turning every level into a strategic puzzle rather than a test of reflexes alone. Success depends on planning, timing, and understanding enemy behaviour. The Commodore 64 version includes an impressive 150 levels, each introducing new challenges and layouts. Adding to its longevity is a built-in level editor, allowing players to design, save, and share their own creations, greatly expanding replay value and creativity.

video:video.video:title: Loom – Lucasfilm Threw Away the Inventory and Made Music Your Commands on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Lucasfilm Games for the Commodore Amiga, Loom is a beautifully crafted graphic adventure led by Brian Moriarty, set in a mysterious fantasy world ruled by the ancient Guild of Weavers. Players follow young Bobbin Threadbare on a personal and emotional journey to uncover the secrets of the Great Loom and rescue his disappearing guild. Instead of traditional inventory puzzles, the game introduces a unique spell-casting system based on musical drafts played on a magical distaff, allowing players to reshape the world through sound. These musical spells can open paths, transform objects, reverse effects, and solve environmental puzzles through experimentation and logic. True to Lucasfilm’s design philosophy, Loom removes player death and dead ends, encouraging relaxed exploration and story-driven discovery. Visually, the game features striking high-resolution artwork with distinctive EGA and VGA dithering that gives Fantasia a painterly, dreamlike quality.

video:video.video:title: Lotus Turbo Challenge 2 – Still the Amiga’s Greatest Arcade Racer?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 and developed by Magnetic Fields, Lotus Turbo Challenge 2 is the high-octane sequel that redefined the series on the Commodore Amiga. Moving away from traditional circuit racing, the game embraces checkpoint-based, arcade-style action inspired by classics like OutRun. Players race against the clock across a wide range of global locations, alternating between two Lotus cars: the Elan SE on odd-numbered stages and the Esprit SE on even-numbered ones. Each course demands speed, precision, and split-second reactions as traffic, sharp bends, and environmental hazards stand between you and the next checkpoint. The Amiga version is especially celebrated for its fluid scrolling, varied scenery, and dynamic weather effects that keep races visually fresh and challenging. Barry Leitch’s iconic soundtrack, particularly the instantly recognisable intro theme, adds an extra layer of energy and remains one of the most memorable pieces of Amiga game music.

video:video.video:title: Lure of the Temptress – The Amiga Adventure Where NPCs Had Lives of Their Own
video:video.video:description: Lure of the Temptress (1992) is a classic point-and-click adventure game developed by Revolution Software and published by Virgin Interactive. Set in the medieval kingdom of Turnvale, you play as Diermot, a young peasant who must overthrow the evil sorceress known as the Temptress. Using the innovative Virtual Theatre engine, the game features a dynamic world where NPCs follow their own routines. The unique “Tell” command allows players to issue detailed instructions, adding depth to puzzle-solving and interaction. Its atmospheric graphics, ambient sound design, and engaging narrative set it apart from many contemporaries. While Diermot himself may lack depth, the rich world-building and clever mechanics have earned the game a loyal following. Lure of the Temptress remains an important title in the adventure genre, showcasing early advances in interactive storytelling and game design.

video:video.video:title: Mad Doctor – The C64 Horror Game About Building Your Own Monster
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Creative Sparks and developed by James Allen, Mad Doctor is a darkly inventive action-adventure for the Commodore 64 that blends horror themes with open-ended gameplay. Players step into the role of Professor Franz Johann Blockenspiel, an unhinged scientist determined to create life by assembling and reanimating a creature from stolen body parts. Set in the eerie village of Struddleberg, the game unfolds across six interconnected areas including a castle, graveyard, forest, village districts, and Lightning Hill. Exploration is key, as players search for tools, ingredients, and body parts while navigating hostile villagers who become increasingly suspicious of your activities. The game runs from a top-down, fixed-screen perspective and introduces survival elements such as hunger, thirst, and health management. A day-and-night cycle adds further tension, forcing players to carefully plan movements and actions to avoid capture or attack.

video:video.video:title: Mad Nurse – Saving Babies from a Hospital That Should Be Closed
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Simon Pick and published by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, Mad Nurse is a distinctive platform arcade game set inside a chaotic hospital maternity ward. Players take on the role of a nurse tasked with rescuing wandering babies before they meet a variety of dangerous hazards. Each level presents a multi-storey hospital layout filled with elevators, platforms, and environmental threats such as electrical sockets, medicine bottles, and open shafts. The challenge escalates as more babies appear simultaneously, requiring quick reactions and careful route planning to return them safely to their cribs. A key gameplay mechanic is the nurse’s limited supply of stun gas, which temporarily freezes all babies in place and offers a brief moment to regain control. Using it too often, however, comes at a cost, reinforcing the game’s risk-versus-reward structure.

video:video.video:title: Magic Carpet – Early C64 Flying With Just Enough Weirdness to Notice
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by David and Richard Darling and published by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Magic Carpet is a fast-paced arcade-style action game that challenges players to guide a carpet-riding hero through a series of dangerous underground caverns. Presented in a side-scrolling format, the game tasks players with dodging falling rocks, stalactites, and hostile enemies while collecting treasure and useful power-ups. Each stage demands sharp reactions and careful timing, with hazards often appearing suddenly and leaving little room for error. As progress is made, the level layouts become more complex and the pace intensifies, pushing players to master precise movement and pattern recognition. Success relies on memorising trap placements and maintaining control under pressure. Visually, Magic Carpet makes effective use of colour and smooth animation to create lively cave environments within the limits of the C64 hardware.

video:video.video:title: Mail Order Monsters – Build a Beast, Train It, Then Let It Loose on C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Electronic Arts for the Commodore 64, Mail Order Monsters is an innovative action-strategy game designed by Paul Reiche III, Evan Robinson, and Nicky Robinson. The game places creativity at the centre of its design, allowing players to construct and customise their own combat creatures, known as morphs, before sending them into brutal arena battles. Gameplay revolves around three distinct modes that cater to different skill levels. Free Trial mode introduces pre-built morphs and basic combat mechanics, while Rental mode gives players a limited budget of psychons to assemble a creature for a single fight. Tournament mode offers the deepest experience, challenging players to build, upgrade, and evolve their morph across multiple battles while managing resources and long-term strategy. Combat takes place in a variety of arena formats, including Destruction, Capture the Flag, and The Horde, each demanding different tactics and loadouts.

video:video.video:title: Maniac Mansion – The C64 Adventure That Gave Lucasfilm Its SCUMM Engine
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Lucasfilm Games for the Commodore 64, Maniac Mansion is a landmark graphic adventure that redefined how games told stories. Built on the newly created SCUMM engine, it introduced a point-and-click interface that made interaction more intuitive and opened the door to deeper, more expressive game narratives. Players control Dave Miller and choose two friends from a cast of six unique characters, each with different abilities, as they infiltrate the bizarre mansion of Dr. Fred Edison to rescue Dave’s kidnapped girlfriend, Sandy Pantz. The non-linear design allows multiple solutions to puzzles, encouraging experimentation and replayability as different character combinations unlock new paths and outcomes. The Commodore 64 version delivers colourful visuals, atmospheric music, and animated cutscenes that push the story forward, helping the mansion feel alive and unpredictable. Its humour, strange characters, and occasional danger create a tone that balances comedy with tension, something rarely seen at the time.

video:video.video:title: Manic Miner – 20 Caverns Before the Oxygen Runs Out on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 for the Commodore 64, Manic Miner is a landmark platform game developed by Matthew Smith that helped define the genre. You take control of Miner Willy as he explores a series of increasingly hostile caverns, racing against a constantly draining oxygen supply. Each of the 20 caverns demands exact timing and pixel-perfect jumps. Progress depends on collecting every flashing item in each level while avoiding enemies and environmental hazards that punish even the smallest mistake. The challenge is relentless, turning every successful run into a genuine achievement. The Commodore 64 version stays faithful to the game’s original design, featuring simple backdrops and distinctive sprites that keep the focus firmly on gameplay. Its stark presentation only adds to the tension, stripping away distractions and leaving nowhere to hide from the difficulty. A defining feature is the use of Edvard Grieg’s “In the Hall of the Mountain King”, which plays throughout and steadily builds pressure as your oxygen runs low.

video:video.video:title: Maria’s Christmas Box – Barbarian’s Cover Star Returned for C64 Strip Poker
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Anco Software for the Commodore 64, Maria’s Christmas Box is an adult-themed strip poker game that arrived during the festive season, tapping into the popularity of celebrity-inspired titles of the era. The game features British model Maria Whittaker, well known to Commodore fans for her appearance in Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior. Gameplay centres on a one-on-one strip poker match, with Maria initially dressed in a Santa Claus outfit to fit the Christmas theme. Players wager credits, bluff, and trade clothing items in familiar fashion, closely following the mechanics established in Anco’s earlier Strip Poker II+. Two difficulty levels are available, with the harder mode offering a more aggressive and challenging AI opponent. Presentation is basic, using static pixel artwork, limited animation, and a very simple interface built around the standard C64 system font.

video:video.video:title: Master of Magic – The C64 Dungeon Adventure with a Legendary Rob Hubbard Soundtrack
video:video.video:description: Released in December 1985 by Richard Darling and published by Mastertronic under its M. A. D. label, Master of Magic is a fast-paced dungeon adventure that drops players into a dangerous high-fantasy world of spells, monsters, and maze-like peril. Transported by the mysterious Thelric, your unnamed hero must recover the legendary Amulet of Immortality before being trapped forever. Gameplay blends action-oriented role-playing with constant exploration. Players navigate interconnected mazes while battling creatures such as skeletons, bats, and spiders, carefully managing health and magical energy as danger escalates. Progress depends on learning layouts, reacting quickly in combat, and making smart decisions under pressure. The screen layout is clean and functional, combining a live map, text messages, command options, and clear visual representations of enemies and items. This structure keeps the action flowing while allowing tactical choices during exploration and combat.

video:video.video:title: Master of the Lamps – The C64 Game That Turned Music Into the Challenge
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Master of the Lamps is a highly original title developed by Peter Kaminski and Russell Lieblich and published by Activision. Blending action, rhythm, and puzzle-solving, the game offers a calm yet demanding experience that stood apart from the more aggressive arcade releases of the era. Players take on the role of an Eastern prince on a mystical journey to restore three shattered magical lamps and reclaim his palace. Gameplay alternates between two very different challenges. The first involves piloting a magic carpet through winding tunnels, passing precisely through diamond-shaped gates where even a single mistake sends you back to the start. The second core mechanic introduces rhythm and memory-based gameplay. Players face musical duels with genies, repeating increasingly complex sequences of tones. Across three sets of seven genie dens, the challenge escalates from audio and visual cues, to visual-only prompts, and finally to sound alone, testing timing, memory, and pitch recognition.

video:video.video:title: Match Day II – Was This Ocean’s Best C64 Football Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Ocean Software, Match Day II is a landmark football simulation for the Commodore 64 that built upon and refined the foundations laid by the original Match Day. Developed by Jon Ritman, with graphics by Bernie Drummond and music by Guy Stevens, the game introduced new systems that significantly raised the bar for 8-bit sports titles. The game offers league and cup competitions for up to eight teams, alongside quick exhibition matches. Played with seven players per side, Match Day II allows direct control of the goalkeeper, adding an extra tactical layer rarely seen at the time. The action is fast, fluid, and highly responsive, rewarding anticipation and positioning rather than simple button-bashing. A defining innovation is the Diamond Deflection System, which calculates realistic ball rebounds based on angle and impact, creating unpredictable and natural-feeling play.

video:video.video:title: Max Headroom – Rescue Max from the Top 11 Floors of Network 23 on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Quicksilva and developed by Binary Design, Max Headroom brings the dystopian world of the British TV movie and series to the Commodore 64. Set in a future ruled by ruthless media corporations, players take on the role of investigative journalist Edison Carter on a dangerous mission inside Network 23. Gameplay blends isometric exploration with cerebral puzzle-solving as players climb the corporation’s towering 211-floor headquarters to rescue Max Headroom, Edison’s digital alter ego. Progress requires hacking security systems, evading guards, and solving abstract challenges such as elevator control puzzles and memory-based light and sound sequences. The interface centres around icon-driven actions, allowing players to access surveillance cameras, manipulate building systems, and rest to recover energy. Tension builds steadily as resources are limited and mistakes can quickly derail progress through the tower. While reception on release was mixed, Max Headroom stood out for its ambition and thematic consistency.

video:video.video:title: Mean Streets – Tex Murphy Was a Detective Game AND a 3D Flight Sim on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Access Software for the Commodore 64, Mean Streets introduced players to Tex Murphy, a down-on-his-luck private investigator navigating a bleak, cyberpunk vision of post-apocalyptic San Francisco. Hired to uncover the truth behind the suspicious death of scientist Dr. Carl Linsky, Tex is drawn into a conspiracy involving advanced technology, corruption, and corporate secrecy. Gameplay blends classic adventure mechanics with several innovative ideas. Players explore the city using Tex’s flying car, travelling between locations to gather clues and piece together the investigation. Conversations with suspects and informants require careful dialogue choices to extract useful information, while certain moments escalate into side-scrolling combat sequences that demand quick reactions and careful positioning. One of the game’s most ambitious features is its use of digitised imagery and sound, including early full-motion video elements and Access Software’s RealSound technology, which delivered sampled voices and audio without extra hardware.

video:video.video:title: Mega Lo Mania – Start in 9500 BC… End with Nukes on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Sensible Software for the Commodore Amiga, Mega Lo Mania is a distinctive real-time strategy game that fuses god-game concepts with tactical warfare. Players take control of one of four rival deities—Scarlet, Oberon, Caesar, or Madcap—each leading their civilisation through ten technological epochs, from 9500 BC into the far future. Gameplay revolves around managing people, resources, and progression while competing gods fight for dominance across a series of islands. Each map is divided into sectors, forcing careful decisions about where to gather minerals, develop weapons, and position armies. Timing is critical, as advancing through epochs unlocks stronger units and new capabilities that can quickly shift the balance of power. Combat plays out in real time, with players deploying forces to attack enemy territory or defend their own sectors. Success depends on striking the right balance between expansion, defence, and technological advancement, as neglecting any one area can leave a civilisation vulnerable.

video:video.video:title: Miami Vice – One Million-Dollar Drug Deal, Four Days to Find Mr J on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64 and developed by Canvas Software, Miami Vice is an action-adventure title inspired by the hugely popular 1980s television series. Players take on the roles of detectives Sonny Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs as they attempt to dismantle a major drug operation led by the mysterious criminal known as “Mr. J.” Gameplay is split into two distinct sections. The first involves top-down driving sequences, where players navigate a city map to reach crime scenes and suspect hideouts. These segments are notoriously challenging, with awkward steering, tight time limits, and frequent crashes making navigation a major test of patience and precision. Once a destination is reached, the game shifts into side-scrolling action stages. Here, players confront criminals using basic combat mechanics and simple shooting elements. While functional, these sections lack depth and variety, contributing to the game’s mixed critical reception.

video:video.video:title: Micro Mouse Goes De-Bugging – The C64 Game That Made You Repair BASIC Code
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by MC Lothlorien, Micro Mouse Goes De-Bugging is a distinctive action-educational title for the Commodore 64 that blends arcade gameplay with early programming concepts. Players take control of Micro Mouse, a digital fixer tasked with repairing corrupted BASIC code inside a malfunctioning computer system. The action unfolds across side-view, flip-screen stages where players must retrieve missing characters from cages positioned around the screen and return them to their correct places in the code. At the same time, hostile bugs roam the area, attempting to steal characters and undo progress, forcing players to balance speed, accuracy, and survival. A key mechanic is resource management. Micro Mouse can either carry a code character or a can of “datakill” to eliminate bugs, but never both at once. This simple restriction adds tension and strategy, requiring careful decision-making as threats increase and screens grow more chaotic.

video:video.video:title: MicroProse Soccer – The C64 Football Game That Led to Sensible Soccer
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988, MicroProse Soccer is an arcade-style football game developed by Sensible Software and published by MicroProse for the Commodore 64. Often seen as the foundation of the legendary Sensible Soccer series, it redefined how football games felt on 8-bit systems with speed, flow, and immediate control. The game offers both full 11-a-side outdoor matches and fast-paced 6-a-side indoor soccer, alongside single matches, tournaments, and full World Cup campaigns. Players can save progress and customise teams using the Name Bank, adding long-term appeal rarely seen in football games of the era. Controls are simple yet expressive, allowing crisp passing, chipped balls, powerful shots, and the famous “banana kick” for curling efforts on goal. The top-down scrolling pitch is enhanced by weather effects, player fatigue, and dynamic replays that mimic video rewinding, adding style and atmosphere to every match.

video:video.video:title: Midnight Resistance – Ocean’s C64 Run-and-Gun Rescue Mission Revisited
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Ocean Software and developed by Special FX, Midnight Resistance is a hard-hitting side-scrolling run-and-gun game set in a brutal dystopian future. You play as a lone resistance fighter battling through enemy territory to rescue your kidnapped family from the ruthless King Crimson. The action is fast, relentless, and plainly inspired by arcade classics like Contra. You fight through waves of soldiers, tanks, and airborne enemies, grabbing red keys dropped by foes along the way. These keys are vital, letting you buy powerful weapons and upgrades between stages, including flamethrowers, homing missiles, and multi-directional guns with limited ammo. Levels are tightly designed and scroll smoothly, keeping the pressure high as enemy patterns and hazards escalate. While the Commodore 64 version can’t quite match the detail of more powerful systems, it delivers impressive animation, strong pacing, and a solid sense of scale throughout.

video:video.video:title: Mike Read’s Computer Pop Quiz – How Tough Was This 1988 C64 Music Quiz?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Elite Systems for the Commodore 64 and re-released by Encore in 1989, Mike Read’s Computer Pop Quiz brings the popular BBC Radio 1 quiz show to home computers, hosted by Mike Read and packed with music trivia from the 1950s through the 1980s. The game recreates a full TV-style quiz format, guiding players through multiple themed rounds that test knowledge of artists, songs, dates, and pop culture history. Round One challenges players to select questions from a jukebox, while later rounds introduce clue-based star guessing, category choices, and year-identification challenges. The fast-paced Quickfire Round adds pressure with timed questions and penalties for wrong answers, rewarding speed and accuracy under pressure. A final jukebox segment offers one last chance to boost your score, keeping tension high right to the end. Players can compete solo or against a friend, choosing music categories and animated team-mates that add personality and charm to each match.

video:video.video:title: Mikie – Konami’s Schoolyard Arcade Game Comes to the Commodore 64
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Konami and released in arcades in 1984, Mikie arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1986 via Imagine Software, bringing its unusual school-based action to home computers. Instead of battling aliens or monsters, players take control of Mikie, a lovestruck student determined to deliver a heartfelt letter to his girlfriend. Gameplay unfolds across a series of school locations including classrooms, locker rooms, the cafeteria, dance studio, and the playground. Mikie must collect scattered hearts to complete his message, all while avoiding or dealing with teachers, janitors, and other authority figures who are determined to stop his romantic mission. Each room presents its own hazards and opportunities, encouraging careful movement, timing, and quick thinking. Doors can be opened to reveal surprises, items can be collected for points, and some staff members can be temporarily neutralised, adding a light strategic layer to the action.

video:video.video:title: Milk Race – The C64 Cycling Game Based on Britain’s Famous Road Race
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987, Milk Race is a cycling simulation for the Commodore 64 developed by Icon Design and published by Mastertronic. Designed by Phil Berry and Stuart Ruecroft, with music by David Whittaker, the game is based on the famous British Milk Race, now known as the Tour of Britain. Despite its budget price, it delivers a surprisingly deep and energetic sports experience. Players take control of a cyclist competing in a gruelling 1,000-mile race across England. Gameplay focuses on maintaining speed, managing stamina, avoiding hazards such as potholes and rival riders, and collecting milk bottles to restore energy. Each stage demands concentration as the pace rarely lets up. A key mechanic is gear management, with 12 gears available to adapt to terrain and race conditions. Time trial sections introduce additional pressure, requiring players to hit checkpoints within strict limits while balancing speed against exhaustion.

video:video.video:title: Miner 2049er – Early C64 Platforming That Still Looks Like Hard Work
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 for the Commodore 64, Miner 2049er is a landmark platform game developed by Bill Hogue and published by Big Five Software. Players take on the role of Bounty Bob, a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, sent deep into an abandoned uranium mine to capture the criminal Yukon Yohan. Gameplay is built around precision movement and route planning. Each level is cleared by walking over every section of the mine’s platforms while avoiding radioactive enemies and environmental hazards. Timing is critical, as each stage is governed by a strict time limit that pushes players to balance speed with accuracy. Strategic depth comes from collectible items such as drills and candles, which temporarily turn enemies harmless and allow Bob to defeat them on contact. Learning enemy patterns and choosing the safest order to claim platforms becomes essential as the levels grow more complex.

video:video.video:title: Monkey Island 2: LeChuck’s Revenge – Guybrush Returns for a Bigger Amiga Adventure
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by LucasArts for the Commodore Amiga, Monkey Island 2: LeChuck’s Revenge continues the legendary adventures of Guybrush Threepwood in one of the most celebrated sequels in gaming history. Picking up after the events of The Secret of Monkey Island, you set off on a globe-trotting quest to uncover the mythical treasure of Big Whoop, all while dealing with pirates, curses, and unfinished business with LeChuck. Built using the SCUMM engine, the game refines the point-and-click formula with deeper puzzles, sharper writing, and a much larger world to explore. You travel between multiple islands, combining inventory items, outwitting rivals, and engaging in some of the most memorable dialogue ever written for an adventure game. The Amiga version shines with richly detailed hand-painted visuals and smooth presentation, while the innovative iMUSE system dynamically adjusts the music to match on-screen action, creating a seamless and immersive atmosphere.

video:video.video:title: Montezuma’s Revenge – Panama Joe Had 99 Rooms to Survive on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Parker Brothers and developed by Robert Jaeger, Montezuma’s Revenge is a landmark 2D platformer for the Commodore 64 that blends fast reflexes with methodical exploration. Players take on the role of Panama Joe, a fearless treasure hunter descending into the ancient catacombs of Emperor Montezuma II in search of priceless jewels. The game is structured across nine increasingly difficult levels, each made up of 100 interconnected rooms arranged in a pyramid layout. Progress requires careful navigation, collecting keys to unlock colour-coded doors, and avoiding a wide range of hazards including rolling skulls, fire pits, collapsing floors, and deadly spiders. Items such as torches, swords, and protective gear add tactical depth, allowing players to access darker areas or temporarily defend themselves. Success depends on precise timing, route planning, and knowing when to push forward or retreat to safety.

video:video.video:title: Monty on the Run – Pick the Wrong Five Items and You Can’t Finish It | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Gremlin Graphics, Monty on the Run is the third game in the Monty Mole series and one of the most celebrated platformers on the Commodore 64. The game follows Monty as he escapes from Scudmore Prison and attempts a perilous journey to France, dodging capture while navigating a hostile world packed with hazards. Gameplay is built around fast-paced, multi-screen platforming that demands sharp reflexes and careful planning. Players must learn enemy patterns, master precise jumps, and make smart use of collected items to progress through the game’s varied environments. A defining feature is the opening item selection screen, where players choose five items from a larger list—some of which are essential to complete later sections—adding strategy and replay value while also acting as subtle copy protection. The presentation makes full use of the C64’s strengths, with colourful, detailed backdrops and fluid character movement.

video:video.video:title: Moon Shuttle – How Good Was This Nichibutsu Shooter on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Datasoft and developed by John Butrovich, Moon Shuttle is a fast-paced shoot-’em-up that blends arcade reflexes with strategic navigation. In the game, you pilot a sleek Moon Shuttle spacecraft through layered asteroid fields and hostile alien formations, blasting narrow pathways while avoiding deadly collisions. Gameplay alternates between navigating dense asteroid belts and fighting bizarre alien enemies, including beetles, “brains”, phasmidæ, and seaweed-like creatures. Moon Shuttle’s design is deceptively simple but highly tactical. Players must fire upwards to clear tight corridors, manage positioning carefully, and react quickly to shifting hazards. Visually, the game features clean, minimalist graphics with functional sprites. There is no background music, relying instead on sound effects to heighten the arcade-style intensity. Despite its simplicity, Moon Shuttle stands out among early C64 shooters for its multi-layered challenge and rewarding difficulty curve.

video:video.video:title: Moonstone – Four Knights, One Moonstone and a Literal GORE Switch on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Mindscape for the Commodore Amiga, Moonstone: A Hard Days Knight is a distinctive hybrid of action, strategy, and role-playing designed by Rob Anderson. Set in a grim fantasy version of Britain, the game casts you as a knight chosen by druids to recover the mystical Moonstone and return it safely to Stonehenge. Gameplay alternates between turn-based movement on a world map and brutal real-time combat encounters. Knights travel across the land visiting villages, forests, and monster-guarded dolmens, collecting treasures and keys while racing rival knights who are also pursuing the Moonstone. When enemies are encountered, the game shifts into one-on-one combat reminiscent of Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior. Timing, positioning, and aggression are key, with battles often ending in graphic and decisive fashion. Victories reward gold and experience points, which can be invested into attributes such as strength, constitution, and endurance.

video:video.video:title: Mountie Mick’s Death Ride – The C64 Game That Put You on Top of a Moving Train
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Timedata Ltd and published by Ariolasoft for the Commodore 64, Mountie Mick’s Death Ride is a fast-paced action-platformer that casts players as a Royal Canadian Mounted Police officer battling criminals aboard speeding freight trains. Players must run, jump, and fight across the tops and undersides of moving wagons, carefully timing leaps between carriages while managing a limited supply of bullets and grenades. Survival depends on collecting key items such as gas masks and torches, which are essential for navigating hazardous sections including gas-filled compartments and dark tunnels. The game features side-scrolling stages with parallax backgrounds that enhance the illusion of high-speed travel, adding a strong sense of motion and urgency to each level. Progress is challenged by demanding level design and sometimes unreliable controls, with certain stages containing bugs that can block advancement.

video:video.video:title: Mr. Robot and His Robot Factory – The C64 Platformer That Let You Build Levels
video:video.video:description: Mr. Robot and His Robot Factory (1983), developed by Ron Rosen and published by Datamost, is a classic platform game that was later ported to the Commodore 64. Players guide a humanoid robot through 22 built-in factory screens, collecting white power pills while navigating ladders, conveyor belts, escalators, traps, and roaming fireball enemies. Each stage begins with a limited energy meter that constantly drains, creating urgency and forcing players to plan their movements carefully. Touching hazards or falling too far costs a life, while collecting a pulsing white ring grants temporary invulnerability and allows enemies to be destroyed. One of the game’s standout features is its built-in level editor, known as the “Robot Factory,” which lets players design, save, and load up to 26 custom levels — greatly extending replay value. Visually, the game features crisp sprites and clear platform layouts typical of early 1980s home computer titles, while the sound design supports the fast-paced gameplay.

video:video.video:title: The Astonishing Adventures of Mr. Weems – The C64’s Bizarre Vampire Hunt!
video:video.video:description: The Astonishing Adventures of Mr. Weems and the She Vampires is a 1987 Commodore 64 action game published by Piranha. Viewed from above, it sends Mr. Weems through six maze-like levels filled with vampires, monsters, locked routes and hazards. His garlic gun provides the main defence, while keys open doors and garlic pills grant temporary protection. Each stage also hides part of the equipment needed for the final confrontation: a stake, mallet, mega-garlic, mirror and crucifix. Collecting those objects and surviving long enough to reach the Great She Vampire gives the arcade action a persistent objective. The design is often compared with Gauntlet, but its horror-comedy theme, limited resources and emphasis on assembling a vampire-hunting kit give the game its own identity.

video:video.video:title: M.U.L.E. – Compete for Wealth, Cooperate to Save the Colony | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Ozark Softscape and published by Electronic Arts, M. U. L. E. is a landmark multiplayer strategy game designed by Danielle Bunten (credited as Dan Bunten). Set on the fictional planet Irata, players become rival colonists competing to build a thriving economy through careful planning, negotiation, and cooperation. Gameplay is split between two contrasting phases. In the real-time auction, players bid aggressively for plots of land, while the turn-based phase focuses on managing resources using M. U. L. E. s to produce food, energy, smithore, and crystite. Balancing production with market demand is essential, especially as unexpected events such as pirate raids and meteor showers disrupt even the best-laid plans. Supporting up to four players, M. U. L. E. shines as a social experience, encouraging deals, rivalries, and shifting alliances. Success depends not only on strategy, but on reading opponents and adapting to an ever-changing economy.

video:video.video:title: Murder on the Mississippi – Three Days, One Corpse and a Killer on the C64
video:video.video:description: Murder on the Mississippi is a classic detective adventure for the Commodore 64 that places players aboard the luxury paddle steamer Delta Princess. While enjoying a holiday cruise, renowned detective Sir Charles Foxworth and his loyal servant Regis stumble upon a grim discovery: the body of Raleigh Cartwright III. With the ship due to arrive in New Orleans in just three days, time is running out to catch the killer before they escape. Gameplay blends exploration with investigation, using joystick-controlled movement and a context-sensitive command menu. Players walk the decks, inspect cabins, examine evidence, and interact with passengers and crew, all of whom may be suspects. Early progress depends on locating the body, after which characters become far more forthcoming with information. The heart of the game lies in careful note-taking and deduction. Players must gather statements, share information between characters, and piece together contradictions and motives.

video:video.video:title: Mutant Monty – Collect the Gold and Survive This Forgotten C64 Arcade Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64, Mutant Monty is a fixed-screen arcade game developed by John Prince and published by Artic Computing. Players take control of Monty, an ambitious adventurer determined to become rich and heroic by collecting gold nuggets scattered across a series of increasingly demanding levels. The game is built around 40 single-screen rooms, each packed with enemies, hazards, and tight time limits. To progress, Monty must collect every gold nugget on the screen and reach the exit door before time runs out. Contact with enemies or failure to escape in time costs one of Monty’s limited lives. Movement is a key part of the challenge. Monty continues moving in the chosen joystick direction until he hits an obstacle, with longer joystick holds increasing his speed. This creates a risk-and-reward balance, where precision and planning are just as important as quick reactions.

video:video.video:title: Myth: History in the Making – Greek, Norse AND Egyptian Legends in One C64 Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by System 3 for the Commodore 64, MYTH: History in the Making is an ambitious side-scrolling action platformer that blends modern storytelling with ancient legend. You play a present-day teenager thrown through time into the “Time of Legends,” where restoring balance means confronting gods, monsters, and the Dark Angel of Time himself. Gameplay spans a series of large, varied levels inspired by Greek, Norse, and Egyptian mythology. You explore locations such as Hades, Asgard, and the Valley of the Kings, combining precise platforming with combat and item-based puzzles that directly reference their mythological roots. Progress often depends on using the right artefact in the right place, rewarding observation and experimentation. The game makes striking use of the C64’s capabilities, with detailed environments, smooth character animation, and a strong sense of scale. Jeroen Tel’s atmospheric soundtrack reinforces the epic tone, giving each mythological setting its own weight and mood.

video:video.video:title: NARC – Arrest the Drug Dealers… or Use the Rocket Launcher on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990, NARC is a hard-hitting run-and-gun action game developed by Williams Electronics and brought to the Commodore 64 by Ocean Software. Players take on the roles of elite narcotics officers Max Force and Hit Man, tasked with dismantling the criminal empire of the notorious Mr. Big. Gameplay focuses on fast-paced side-scrolling action, blasting through city streets packed with gang members, dealers, and heavily armed enemies.
