Players are encouraged not only to eliminate criminals but also to arrest them where possible, adding a risk-versus-reward scoring element to the relentless shooting. The Commodore 64 conversion captures the structure and intensity of the arcade original, featuring smooth movement, responsive controls, and large character sprites. While visually toned down compared to the coin-op, the game still delivers a strong sense of impact, backed by a soundtrack composed by Paul Tonge that drives the action forward.

video:video.video:title: Nebulus – The C64 Platformer That Rotated the Entire Tower Around You
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Hewson Consultants and developed by John M. Phillips, Nebulus is a standout platform-puzzle game that pushed the Commodore 64 in bold new directions. Also known as Tower Toppler in the U. S. , it introduced a striking visual concept that made it instantly recognisable. Players control Pogo, a small green alien sent to the planet Nebulus to dismantle a series of towering structures. Each level tasks you with climbing a cylindrical tower while avoiding enemies, navigating platforms, and dealing with hazards that demand careful timing and positioning. The game’s defining feature is its rotating tower effect. As Pogo moves left or right, the tower appears to spin in 3D, creating a constantly shifting sense of perspective that adds both challenge and tension. A single misstep can send you plunging into the water below, costing a precious life.

video:video.video:title: Nemesis – Could the C64 Handle Konami’s Legendary Gradius Arcade Shooter?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Konami for the Commodore 64, Nemesis is the European home-computer release of the arcade classic known worldwide as Gradius. Players take control of the iconic Vic Viper starfighter, battling through hostile alien territory to defeat the Bacterion forces in a relentless side-scrolling assault. Gameplay unfolds across horizontally scrolling stages packed with enemy formations, terrain hazards, and screen-filling bosses. A defining feature is Nemesis’s revolutionary power-up system, where collected capsules activate upgrades along a selectable meter, including speed boosts, missiles, double shots, lasers, and defensive shields. Choosing when to trigger each upgrade adds a strong tactical layer to the fast-paced action. The Commodore 64 version was coded by Simon Pick, with graphics by Bob Stevenson, and is widely praised for capturing the feel of the arcade original despite hardware constraints. Smooth scrolling, precise controls, and well-judged difficulty helped deliver an authentic and challenging shooter experience on 8-bit hardware.

video:video.video:title: Nemesis the Warlock – Dead Enemies Literally Become Your Platforms on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Martech for the Commodore 64, Nemesis the Warlock is an action platform game based on the iconic 2000 AD comic series created by Pat Mills and Kevin O’Neill. Developed by Creative Reality, the game brings the dark sci-fi world of Nemesis to life in fast-paced 8-bit form. Players take control of Nemesis, a powerful alien warrior armed with both a gun and a sword, battling through 30 single-screen levels packed with enemies and hazards. Progress depends on defeating a required number of Terminators on each stage, encouraging aggressive and tactical play. One of the game’s most distinctive mechanics is the ability to pile up defeated enemies and use their bodies as makeshift platforms. This unusual feature adds a strategic layer to level navigation and sets Nemesis apart from traditional platformers of the era.

video:video.video:title: Neuromancer – William Gibson, DEVO and Cyberspace on the Commodore 64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Interplay Productions and published by Electronic Arts for the Commodore 64, Neuromancer is an ambitious adventure game inspired by William Gibson’s groundbreaking cyberpunk novel. Blending hacking simulation, role-playing, and narrative exploration, it delivers one of the most immersive sci-fi experiences of the 8-bit era. Set in 2058 in Chiba City, Japan, players take on the role of a struggling hacker trying to regain access to the Matrix after being cut off from cyberspace. The journey unfolds across neon-lit streets, shady bars, corporate offices, and virtual networks filled with danger and opportunity. Gameplay is divided between real-world exploration and cyberspace infiltration. In the physical world, players gather information, earn money, buy equipment, and install skill chips that enhance abilities. In cyberspace, they battle hostile ICE programs, evade security systems, and confront powerful artificial intelligences guarding valuable data.

video:video.video:title: Nexus – The C64 Espionage Game with Remarkable Digitised Faces
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Nexus Productions Ltd and developed by Paul Voysey and Tayo Olowu, Nexus is a distinctive action-adventure title that blends espionage, investigation, and arcade-style tension. Casting the player as a journalist for The Clarion, the game sets up a serious narrative rarely seen on the Commodore 64 at the time. Your mission is to infiltrate a Colombian drug lord’s heavily guarded headquarters, rescue a kidnapped colleague, and uncover vital information hidden throughout the complex. Progress depends on answering 32 key questions, each unlocked by discovering clues scattered across the building, giving the game a strong investigative core. Gameplay combines stealth, exploration, and combat, drawing comparisons with Impossible Mission and Kung Fu Master. You move between multiple floors, interact with characters, avoid detection, and fight only when necessary. The balance between careful movement and sudden action keeps tension high throughout.

video:video.video:title: Night Driver – HAL Laboratory Was Doing First-Person Racing on the C64 in 1982
video:video.video:description: Released in 1982 by HAL Laboratory and published by Commodore for the Commodore 64, Night Driver is an early milestone in racing games, bringing first-person driving to home computers. Originally debuting as a 1976 Atari arcade title, it helped define the foundations of the genre long before modern racing sims existed. Gameplay drops you behind the wheel on a pitch-black road, guided only by glowing roadside reflectors. The aim is simple but demanding: cover as much distance as possible within a strict 90-second time limit without crashing. Four track modes—beginner, pro, expert, and random—gradually increase the challenge, while manual gear shifting adds an extra layer of skill and tension. The Commodore 64 version improves on the arcade original with higher resolution visuals and smoother scrolling, enhancing the sensation of speed as the road twists ahead.

video:video.video:title: Nightbreed: The Action Game – Could Clive Barker’s Horror Work on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Ocean Software and developed by Impact Software, Nightbreed: The Action Game brings Clive Barker’s dark cinematic world to the Commodore 64. Set in the shadowy realm of Midian, the game leans heavily into atmosphere, mystery, and unsettling horror themes. You play as Boone, a hunted man seeking refuge among the Nightbreed, navigating five distinct stages filled with hostile enemies, traps, and exploration challenges. Progress revolves around collecting keys, battling the sinister Mask, and rescuing Lori, while uncovering the secrets of the Necropolis. Reaching Baphomet grants Boone the power to transform into Cabal, shifting the balance of play and adding narrative weight to your journey. Gameplay blends side-scrolling platforming with combat and light exploration. Boone can punch, jump, crouch, and make use of weapons such as pistols and grenades, while careful positioning and timing are vital to survive the game’s tougher encounters.

video:video.video:title: Nightbreed: The Interactive Movie – Why Did Clive Barker’s Film Get TWO Amiga Games?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Ocean Software and developed by Impact Software for the Commodore Amiga, Clive Barker’s Nightbreed: The Interactive Movie adapts the dark fantasy world of Barker’s film and novella Cabal into a cinematic arcade adventure set in the underground city of Midian. Players take on the role of Aaron Boone, navigating graveyards, crypts, and the twisted corridors of Midian while confronting enemies and the menacing Dr. Decker. The game presents a sequence of arcade-style scenes inspired directly by the film, blending platforming, combat, and light puzzle elements to progress the story. A major focus is atmosphere, with gothic visuals, stylised character designs, and digitised speech helping to reinforce the horror tone. The Amiga hardware is used to deliver moody presentation and cinematic flair, aiming to blur the line between film and game.

video:video.video:title: Nightshade – Could Ultimate’s Filmation Style Work on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Ultimate Play the Game and published by Firebird, Nightshade is an isometric action-adventure for the Commodore 64, ported by Shahid Ahmad. Built using the advanced Filmation II engine, the game introduced smooth scrolling 3D environments, marking a major step forward from earlier static-screen isometric designs. Players take on the role of a lone knight tasked with freeing a plague-ravaged village from the grip of four demonic overlords. Exploration is key as you navigate a maze-like medieval town, battling monsters, avoiding traps, and carefully managing health while progressing deeper into enemy territory. The gameplay blends combat and strategy, allowing players to throw objects at enemies and make use of a distinctive colour-based health system. The isometric viewpoint and layered environments demand precise movement and spatial awareness, giving the game a tense and methodical pace.

video:video.video:title: Ninja – Swords, Shuriken and Magic Lamps for £2.99 on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Ninja is a side-scrolling beat ’em up that delivers straightforward arcade-style combat. Players take control of a lone ninja battling through enemy-filled stages, relying on timing, positioning, and simple but effective attacks to survive. Gameplay focuses on direct hand-to-hand combat, with enemies approaching from both sides as players punch, kick, and use basic weapons to clear each area. The structure is immediately accessible, making it easy to pick up and play while still offering a steady challenge as enemy placement and numbers increase. True to its budget roots, Ninja features a clean and functional presentation that keeps the emphasis firmly on action rather than spectacle. The sound and visuals support the gameplay without distraction, reinforcing the fast, no-nonsense feel typical of mid-80s C64 arcade titles.

video:video.video:title: Ninja Massacre – The £1.99 C64 Gauntlet Clone You Probably Missed
video:video.video:description: Developed by TAG Computer Games and published by Codemasters in 1989, Ninja Massacre is a fast-paced top-down action game for the Commodore 64, plainly inspired by the arcade hit Gauntlet. Players take control of a ninja battling through a series of dangerous, maze-like levels packed with enemies, traps, and hidden rewards. Gameplay focuses on quick reflexes and smart positioning. Armed with throwing stars, players must clear rooms of enemies while navigating tight corridors and avoiding hazards. Each level is completed by locating the staircase to the next area, with passwords provided to allow progress to be resumed later. The game supports two-player co-operative play, adding a strategic edge as players work together to survive tougher stages. Destructible scenery, secret passages, and power-ups such as smart bombs and reflective shots introduce tactical choices and keep the action varied across its 50 levels.

video:video.video:title: Ninja Rabbits – The C64 Beat ’Em Up with a Mutant Martial-Arts Rabbit
video:video.video:description: Ninja Rabbits is a 1991 beat ’em up developed by MicroValue for the Commodore 64, also released on Amiga and DOS. This quirky arcade-style fighter puts you in control of a martial-arts-trained rabbit on a mission to save his world from destruction, blending humour with side-scrolling combat. The game takes you across three main environments — countryside, city streets, and underground sewer sections — where you battle waves of mutant enemies including badgers, frogs, and other bizarre creatures. On the Commodore 64, Ninja Rabbits is best known for its surprisingly impressive graphics. Large, detailed sprites and colourful backgrounds were uncommon for many budget releases of the era. However, gameplay is often criticised for sluggish movement, limited sound design, and repetitive combat, which prevents it from reaching the heights of top-tier C64 beat ’em ups. Despite these flaws, the game remains memorable as a quirky example of early ’90s experimentation on the Commodore 64 and has earned cult status among retro gaming fans.

video:video.video:title: Nippon Safes Inc. – Three Heroes, One Very Strange Amiga Adventure
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Italian studio Dynabyte for the Commodore Amiga, Nippon Safes Inc. is a distinctive point-and-click adventure that blends European humour with a satirical take on Japanese pop culture. Set in the fictional city of Tyoko, the game follows three eccentric protagonists: Doug Nuts, a socially awkward safecracker; Dino Fagioli, a dim-witted former boxer; and Donna Fatale, a glamorous club dancer. Each character pursues their own storyline while becoming entangled in a larger criminal plot. The game runs on the Parallaction engine, allowing players to switch between characters and tackle puzzles from multiple perspectives. Progression is largely non-linear, with each storyline offering unique locations, challenges, and interactions. Gameplay uses an intuitive icon-based interface, encouraging exploration, item experimentation, and logical problem-solving. The interconnected narrative structure gives the adventure a dynamic, replayable feel. Visually, the Amiga version stands out for its colourful, comic-style graphics and expressive character animations.

video:video.video:title: Nodes of Yesod – Catch a Mole Before You Can Save the Moon on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Odin Computer Graphics for the Commodore 64, Nodes of Yesod is a side-scrolling platform adventure set on a mysterious lunar landscape. Players take control of astronaut Charlemagne “Charlie” Fotheringham-Grunes, sent to investigate strange signals coming from a towering black monolith buried deep beneath the Moon’s surface. Gameplay focuses on careful exploration and puzzle-solving as Charlie navigates interconnected caverns filled with hazards, enemies, and hidden routes. The main objective is to locate and collect eight coloured crystals known as alchiems, each required to progress deeper into the underground maze. A defining feature is the ability to capture and release lunar moles, which can burrow through walls to open new paths and uncover secrets. This mechanic adds a strong strategic layer, forcing players to think ahead rather than rely purely on reflexes. Red astronaut-like enemies known as muggers increase the tension by stealing collected alchiems on contact, making safe traversal just as important as discovery.

video:video.video:title: North & South – The Amiga Civil War Game You Didn’t Know Came from a Belgian Comic
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Infogrames for the Commodore Amiga, North & South is a distinctive blend of strategy and action inspired by the Belgian comic series Les Tuniques Bleues. It presents a lighthearted and humorous take on the American Civil War, combining tactical planning with fast-paced arcade-style challenges. Gameplay is divided into two interconnected phases. On the strategic map, players move armies across the United States, capturing states, forts, and railway lines in order to weaken the opposition and secure vital resources. Careful positioning and timing play a major role in long-term success. When opposing forces meet, the game shifts into real-time action sequences. These include battlefield skirmishes, fort assaults, and train-capture missions, each requiring quick reflexes and smart use of infantry, cavalry, and artillery units with distinct strengths and weaknesses. Throughout the campaign, humorous animations and unexpected events reflect the game’s comic book roots, adding personality and charm to every encounter.

video:video.video:title: Nosferatu the Vampyre – Play Jonathan, Van Helsing AND Lucy on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Design Design and published by Piranha Software for the Commodore 64, Nosferatu the Vampyre is an atmospheric action-adventure inspired by Werner Herzog’s 1979 film. Set in a bleak, gothic world, the game blends exploration, tension, and narrative-driven objectives across multiple characters. The adventure unfolds over three distinct stages. First, players control Jonathan Harker as he explores Count Dracula’s castle, searching for vital documents while evading supernatural dangers. The second stage shifts to the town of Wismar, where Van Helsing and Jonathan battle the spreading vampire threat using tools such as garlic and stakes. In the final act, players take control of Lucy, the only character capable of confronting Dracula directly, attempting to lure him into a deadly trap. Presented in an isometric perspective, the game delivers a striking visual style that reinforces its eerie tone.

video:video.video:title: Omega Race – The 1982 C64 Cartridge You Could Play with a Paddle
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Ron Haliburton and released by Midway in 1981, Omega Race arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1982 as a remarkably faithful home conversion of the arcade original. It delivers fast, precision-based shooting action built around clean vector-style visuals and tight arena combat. Players pilot an Omegan Fighter within a rectangular arena, rotating and thrusting freely in any direction while battling hostile droid ships and avoiding deadly mines. Movement has a deliberate, momentum-driven feel similar to Asteroids, demanding careful control and spatial awareness at all times. The arena itself adds to the challenge, with invisible force-field walls that punish reckless movement and force players to master positioning and timing. Success depends on understanding enemy patterns, conserving momentum, and keeping full control of the ship under pressure. The Commodore 64 version captures the spirit of the arcade machine with striking monochrome vector graphics and responsive controls.

video:video.video:title: One Man and His Droid – Herding Alien Sheep with a Robot on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Mastertronic and developed by Clive Brooker, One Man and His Droid is a clever puzzle-action game that puts a futuristic spin on herding. Set on the alien world of Andromadous, you control a droid tasked with rounding up strange sheep-like creatures known as Ramboids and guiding them safely into teleporters. Each of the game’s 20 levels is split into two distinct phases. First, you navigate maze-like caverns filled with roaming Ramboids and environmental hazards. Then the real challenge begins, herding them into teleporters in the correct order against a strict time limit. The ability to dig and tunnel through the terrain adds a strategic layer, letting you reshape levels to manage the Ramboids’ unpredictable movement. The Commodore 64 version is especially memorable thanks to its colourful presentation and smooth animation, but it’s Rob Hubbard’s outstanding SID soundtrack that truly elevates the experience.

video:video.video:title: Operation Wolf – Could Ocean Bring Taito’s Arcade Gun Game to the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988, Operation Wolf is Taito’s explosive arcade hit brought to the Commodore 64 by Ocean Software. Casting players as a lone Special Forces operative, the game drops you straight into high-risk rescue missions deep behind enemy lines, capturing the intensity and urgency of the original coin-op experience. Gameplay unfolds from a first-person perspective with horizontally scrolling stages set across jungles, villages, and fortified enemy bases. Enemies attack from all directions, including soldiers, helicopters, tanks, and boats, keeping the pressure constant as the screen fills with targets and incoming fire. Strategy plays a key role alongside fast reactions. Ammunition and grenades are limited, hostages must be protected, and power-ups such as health packs and extra ammo are revealed by shooting specific objects in the environment. Destructible scenery, including windows and barrels, adds an extra layer of interaction and spectacle.

video:video.video:title: Orc Attack – Defend the Castle Before the Orcs Reach the Walls | C64
video:video.video:description: Orc Attack (1984) is a frantic fixed-screen action game for the Commodore 64, developed by Chris James with graphics by Dean M. Lock, and published by Creative Sparks under the Thorn EMI label. Set during a fantasy siege, you control a lone defender standing atop a castle wall, moving across icy battlements to drop rocks on invading orcs or drawing a sword when enemies breach the ramparts. As each wave escalates, new threats appear, including ladder-less ninja orcs, evil sorcerers summoning spirits, and demon trolls casting lightning. Later stages introduce boiling oil, allowing you to incinerate large groups and clear the round. The game’s difficulty steadily increases, demanding careful positioning, precise timing, and smart use of limited resources to survive the onslaught. Despite its simple presentation, Orc Attack delivers tense, addictive gameplay and remains a memorable challenge from the golden age of C64 arcade action.

video:video.video:title: Outlaws – The Forgotten C64 Western That Turned You into a Gunslinger
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Ultimate Play the Game for the Commodore 64, Outlaws is a Wild West–themed action shooter developed by Dave and Robert Thomas that puts players in the role of the mysterious Lone Rider. Riding on horseback across prairie landscapes and frontier towns, players must take down roaming bandits and hostile threats before they cause mayhem. Gameplay combines fast scrolling movement with shooting, jumping, and obstacle avoidance. Players gallop through varied environments, ducking under hazards, leaping over barriers, and firing on enemies in cabins, streets, and open terrain. The balance of movement and combat delivers a classic arcade-style challenge. Visually, the game features crisp sprite work and detailed Western-inspired scenery that helps establish its frontier atmosphere. The SID soundtrack and sound effects further enhance the game’s gritty tone. While some contemporary reviews noted repetitive gameplay, Outlaws remains a noteworthy entry in the Commodore 64 library.

video:video.video:title: Painterboy – A Finnish Paint Company Really Made This C64 Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Chart Top Design and published by Finnish paint company Tikkurila for the Commodore 64, Painterboy is one of the earliest examples of an advergame. Based on the company’s “Father and Son” television commercials, it stars a master painter and his apprentice in a lighthearted promotional adventure. The game is structured around three main gameplay sections. First, players must select the correct type of paint for each job, with mistakes resulting in stern feedback from the Father. Choosing wisely is essential before progressing to the next stage. The second phase places players behind the wheel of a pickup truck in a top-down driving sequence. Navigating to the job site requires careful steering and obstacle avoidance, including dodging trains, buildings, and environmental hazards along the route. Once on location, the focus shifts to painting the building itself.

video:video.video:title: Paperboy – Deliver to Subscribers… Trash Everyone Else’s House on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Atari Games and ported to the Commodore 64 by Elite Systems, Paperboy turns a simple daily job into frantic arcade mayhem. You take control of a newspaper delivery kid pedalling through suburban streets, trying to complete your route while everything around you seems determined to knock you off your bike. Gameplay revolves around accurate newspaper throwing and quick reactions. You must deliver papers to subscribers, avoid smashing windows at non-subscribers’ houses, and steer clear of traffic, pedestrians, dogs, lawnmowers, and other unpredictable hazards. Balancing speed, accuracy, and survival is the key to making it through each day. The C64 version captures the spirit of the arcade original, translating its distinctive diagonal viewpoint and fast-paced action to home hardware. While visuals and animation are pared back, the colourful presentation and recognisable layouts keep the experience instantly familiar.

video:video.video:title: Paradroid – Hijack Enemy Robots Across Eight Space Freighters on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Hewson Consultants and developed by Andrew Braybrook for the Commodore 64, Paradroid is a landmark action-strategy game that places players in control of an Influence Device known as the 001 Droid. Your mission is to reclaim a spaceship overrun by rogue robots, using skill, tactics, and calculated risk to survive. Gameplay blends fast-paced top-down shooting with a unique takeover mechanic that sets Paradroid apart. Instead of simply destroying enemies, players can attempt to hack and possess other droids through a tense mini-game, allowing access to stronger units with different abilities, weapons, and movement speeds. Each robot type introduces new strategic decisions, forcing players to balance firepower against energy efficiency and survivability. The smooth scrolling, precise controls, and layered ship design create a constant sense of momentum and pressure as you push deeper into enemy territory.

video:video.video:title: Park Patrol – The C64 Game That Put You in Charge of an Entire Lakeside Park
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Activision for the Commodore 64, Park Patrol is a refreshingly original action game designed by Tony Ngo, with music by Russell Lieblich. Later released in Europe under Firebird’s Silverbird budget label, it puts you in charge of keeping a busy lakeside park clean, safe, and under control. You play as a park ranger, choosing a male or female character, travelling by foot and inflatable dinghy to collect litter, rescue swimmers, and deal with wildlife hazards. Tasks range from warding off snakes with repellent to recovering food stolen by ants, all while managing a constantly draining energy meter. The gameplay blends fast-moving action with light strategy, encouraging efficient routes and smart use of resources. Bonus sections, including a logrolling mini-game, add variety and reward skilled play, while returning to your hut restores energy and keeps the patrol going.

video:video.video:title: Pinball Dreams – Did This Amiga Classic Change Computer Pinball Forever?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Digital Illusions for the Commodore Amiga, Pinball Dreams is a landmark pinball simulation and one of the earliest titles from the studio that would later become DICE. It set a new standard for realism, presentation, and table design on home computers. The game features four expertly crafted tables, each with its own theme and rule set. Ignition is built around space travel and rocket launches, Steel Wheel takes inspiration from the Old West with steam trains and frontier imagery, Beat Box reflects the music industry with charts and touring bands, while Nightmare delivers a dark graveyard setting filled with supernatural elements. Gameplay focuses on precise flipper control, table knowledge, and chaining bonuses through skilful shots. Each table introduces unique mechanics and scoring strategies, encouraging players to learn layouts thoroughly and aim for high-risk, high-reward play.

video:video.video:title: Pit-Fighter – Could the Commodore 64 Handle Atari’s Brutal Arcade Brawler?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 for the Commodore 64, Pit-Fighter brings the raw intensity of underground combat to home computers. Developed by Atari Games and ported by Ocean Software, it delivers a gritty, arcade-style brawler where brutal one-on-one fights take place in hostile arenas packed with danger. The game mixes classic beat-’em-up mechanics with digitised fighters, a bold technical move at the time. You can choose from three distinct characters, each with their own fighting style and special moves, and battle through a roster of hard-hitting opponents ranging from street brawlers to trained martial artists. While the C64 version can’t fully match the visual impact of the arcade machine, it still captures the aggressive feel and fast-paced combat that made Pit-Fighter stand out. The action remains fluid, with colourful sprites and punchy animations keeping fights lively and unpredictable.

video:video.video:title: Pitfall! – 32 Treasures, 20 Minutes… Could You Do It on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Activision and designed by David Crane for the Commodore 64, Pitfall! is one of the most influential platform adventures of the early home computer era. Players take control of Pitfall Harry, a fearless treasure hunter racing through a dangerous jungle to collect 32 hidden treasures within a strict 20-minute time limit. Gameplay unfolds across 256 horizontally connected screens packed with hazards including bottomless pits, quicksand, rolling logs, fire, rattlesnakes, scorpions, and snapping crocodiles. Using precise jumping, ladder climbing, and vine swinging, players must carefully time every movement to survive and keep momentum. Progression is driven by exploration, memory, and risk management. Treasures such as bags of money, gold and silver bars, and diamond rings boost the player’s score, while mistakes cost valuable points and time. Achieving the perfect score of 114,000 points requires flawless play and complete mastery of the jungle.

video:video.video:title: Pitfall II – The C64 Platformer Where You Couldn’t Actually Die
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Activision for the Commodore 64, Pitfall II: Lost Caverns is the acclaimed sequel to the original Pitfall! , developed by David Crane and designed around exploration and discovery rather than simple score chasing. Players take control of Pitfall Harry as he ventures deep into the caverns of the Andes to rescue his niece Rhonda and her pet mountain lion, Quickclaw, while searching for the legendary Raj Diamond. The game features a vast interconnected world of over 100 screens, encouraging free exploration through swimming tunnels, climbing ropes, riding balloons, and navigating hidden passages. Progress depends on careful observation and learning the map layout. A major innovation is the checkpoint system, which allows players to restart from the last red cross reached after losing a life. This makes the adventure more forgiving and supports longer play sessions.

video:video.video:title: Pitstop II – The C64 Racer That Made Split-Screen Feel Revolutionary
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Epyx for the Commodore 64, Pitstop II is a landmark racing game that redefined multiplayer competition on home computers. Designed by Dennis Caswell and Stephen Landrum, it famously introduced split-screen racing, allowing two players to compete head-to-head simultaneously—an innovation that set it apart from its contemporaries. Players race across six international circuits, including Brands Hatch, Hockenheim, Sebring, and Watkins Glen, choosing from multiple difficulty levels and race lengths. On track, success depends on precision driving, careful braking, and learning each circuit’s flow as speeds and pressure increase. What truly elevates Pitstop II is its strategic depth. Fuel consumption and tyre wear must be monitored closely, with pit stops playing a crucial role. Rather than being automated, players take direct control of the pit crew, manually changing tyres and refuelling as quickly as possible, turning every stop into a tense, skill-based mini-game.

video:video.video:title: Platoon – Four Completely Different Games Hidden Inside One C64 Licence
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Ocean Software and published by Data East for the Commodore 64, Platoon is an ambitious action-adventure game based on Oliver Stone’s acclaimed Vietnam War film. Rather than focusing on a single gameplay style, the game attempts to capture the mayhem and intensity of combat through multiple distinct scenarios. The experience is split across four varied segments. Jungle Trek plays as a side-scrolling shooter through hostile terrain filled with traps and enemy patrols. Tunnel Exploration shifts to a tense first-person perspective as you navigate claustrophobic underground passages. Night Ambush uses a fixed-screen viewpoint with limited visibility, forcing careful positioning and awareness, while the Final Assault presents an isometric shooter climax inside an enemy bunker. A unique morale system underpins the gameplay, dropping if civilians are harmed or objectives are failed, which directly impacts progression.

video:video.video:title: Pneumatic Hammers – Stop the Mine Collapsing Before Time Runs Out | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Andromeda Software and published by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, Pneumatic Hammers places players in the role of Red O’Blair, a mining engineer racing against time to prevent a disastrous collapse inside a malfunctioning mining facility. The game blends platform action with puzzle-solving and light resource management. Players must navigate a complex, multi-level structure while avoiding falling debris, hazardous machinery, and environmental dangers. Progress depends on collecting gold nuggets needed to repair a critical switch that controls the rogue pneumatic hammers threatening the mine. A constant sense of pressure defines the gameplay. Time and resources must be managed carefully, as delays can worsen the situation and make navigation increasingly dangerous. Success relies on learning the layout, planning efficient routes, and reacting quickly to changing conditions. Visually, the C64 version uses a distinctive split-screen display.

video:video.video:title: Pole Position – Could the Commodore 64 Handle Namco’s Arcade Racing Classic?
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Namco and released in arcades in 1982, Pole Position arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1984 as a home conversion of one of the most influential racing games ever made. Players take control of a Formula One car and attempt to qualify for pole position by completing a fast, clean lap of the iconic Fuji Racetrack. Gameplay is split into two phases, beginning with a solo time trial where precision and memorisation are essential. Successfully qualifying unlocks the main race, where players must compete against rival cars while managing speed, positioning, and a strict time limit. Collisions with other vehicles or trackside objects quickly end a promising run. The Commodore 64 version recreates the arcade’s behind-the-car perspective with smooth forward scrolling and recognisable track landmarks. While simplified compared to the original cabinet, the core mechanics remain intact, focusing on rhythm, reaction time, and learning the course layout corner by corner.

video:video.video:title: Popeye – Parker Brothers Turned Spinach and Olive Oyl Into a C64 Arcade Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64, Popeye is a faithful home conversion of Nintendo’s hugely popular arcade hit, published by Parker Brothers. It brings the spinach-powered sailor to home computers with fast, single-screen platform action that closely mirrors the original coin-op experience. You control Popeye as he navigates a series of compact arenas, collecting musical notes, hearts, and other items thrown by Olive Oyl while dodging enemies like Bluto and the Sea Hag. The goal is simple but demanding: collect everything on screen before the timer runs out. Spinach plays a crucial role, temporarily turning the tables and allowing Popeye to defeat enemies rather than avoid them. This risk-and-reward loop keeps the action lively, forcing you to decide when to play it safe and when to go on the offensive. The Commodore 64 version captures the arcade feel with responsive controls, colourful character sprites, and instantly recognisable tunes that enhance the light-hearted but frantic pace of play.

video:video.video:title: Popeye – Don Priestley Ditched the Arcade Look for Giant C64 Sprites
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Piranha Software for the Commodore 64, Popeye is a distinctive reinterpretation of the classic arcade game, developed by Don Priestley. Rather than aiming for a direct conversion, this version embraces Priestley’s signature visual style, delivering oversized cartoon sprites and a pseudo-3D playfield that immediately sets it apart from other C64 platformers. Players guide Popeye through interconnected screens, collecting hearts and items thrown by Olive Oyl while avoiding hazards and adversaries such as Bluto. Movement and timing are central to success, as the environments demand careful positioning rather than constant speed. Picking up a can of spinach grants temporary invincibility, allowing Popeye to defeat enemies and push forward safely. The gameplay unfolds at a deliberate pace, encouraging strategic decisions over twitch reflexes. Navigating the layered environments and planning routes between screens adds a puzzle-like feel to the action, rewarding players who learn the layouts and enemy patterns.

video:video.video:title: Populous – The Amiga Game That Let You Play God
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Bullfrog Productions for the Commodore Amiga, Populous is widely regarded as the first true “god game,” placing players in the role of a deity guiding their followers toward domination. Instead of controlling individual units, players shape the world itself to influence the fate of their civilisation. Gameplay is presented in an isometric view, where players raise and lower terrain to create habitable land for their people. As populations grow, followers build settlements that increase their power, allowing them to expand, defend territory, and prepare for conflict with rival gods. Strategic depth comes from balancing population growth, land management, and divine intervention. Players can unleash powerful abilities such as earthquakes, floods, and volcanoes to disrupt enemies, destroy settlements, and shift the balance of power. With over 500 unique levels, each featuring different landscapes and challenges, Populous offers enormous variety and long-term replay value.

video:video.video:title: Poster Paster – The C64 Game That Made Putting Up Billboards Dangerous
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Taskset for the Commodore 64, Poster Paster is a quirky arcade-style platform game designed by Andy Walker, with music composed by Paul Hodgson. You play as Bill Stickers, a hard-working billboard poster racing against time to plaster advertisements across a series of increasingly hazardous cityscapes. Each fixed-screen level challenges you to position ladders and apply poster sections in the correct order, all while dodging a cast of mischievous troublemakers including Gnurds, Wazzocks, and Brain Drains. Careful planning is essential, as poor ladder placement or mistimed movement can quickly bring your shift to a sticky end. A unique twist comes in the form of the Paste Consistency Gauge, which forces you to manage how thick or thin your paste is before applying posters. Get it wrong and the poster won’t stick, adding an extra layer of strategy to what initially looks like simple arcade action.

video:video.video:title: Power Drift – How Did Chris Butler Pull Off Sega’s 3D Racer on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Sega AM2 for arcades in 1988, Power Drift roared onto the Commodore 64 in 1990 thanks to an ambitious conversion by Chris Butler, published by Activision. Against the odds, it delivers a bold, high-speed take on 3D arcade racing on 8-bit hardware. You choose from a colourful roster of drivers and tackle five circuits, each made up of five increasingly demanding tracks. Races unfold across wild, roller-coaster-style courses packed with jumps, tight corners, and dramatic elevation changes, where mastering drifting and momentum is key to staying in the top three and qualifying for the next stage. The C64 version is a technical showcase, using clever programming tricks to create a convincing sense of depth and speed. While backgrounds are simplified and corners can appear suddenly, the fast, responsive handling keeps the action flowing.

video:video.video:title: Predator – The C64 Game That Suddenly Put YOU in the Predator’s Heat Vision
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Activision and developed by Source the Software House, Predator brings the tension of the 1987 action film to the Commodore 64. You step into the boots of Major Dutch Schaefer, fighting your way through hostile Central American jungle terrain against armed soldiers and an unseen alien hunter. The game plays as a side-scrolling action shooter spread across five stages. You begin lightly equipped, but fallen teammates allow you to swap weapons along the way, including the iconic Minigun and grenade launcher. Choosing when to change firepower matters, as only one weapon can be carried at a time. A standout feature is the sudden shift into the Predator’s infrared viewpoint, where the hunter stalks you with its targeting system. These moments heighten the sense of danger and reinforce the film’s cat-and-mouse suspense within the game’s structure.

video:video.video:title: Prince Clumsy – Codemasters Filled This C64 Platformer with Ghosts, Goblins and Bad Luck
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Codemasters, Prince Clumsy is a tongue-in-cheek platformer that playfully pokes fun at the Ghosts ’n Goblins formula. You guide the hopelessly accident-prone Prince Clumsy on a quest to rescue the princess from her evil sister, armed with an unlimited supply of throwing daggers and very little dignity. The game keeps things approachable with smooth, forgiving jumping and straightforward combat, making it far less punishing than its inspirations. Along the way you’ll battle zombies, grim reapers, and other familiar foes while collecting bread and ale to restore health and avoiding hazards like poison and sticky traps. Levels are designed to be readable and welcoming, encouraging steady progress rather than memorisation. The light-hearted tone runs throughout, helped along by Allister Brimble’s upbeat music, which perfectly matches the game’s playful mood. Simple, fun, and self-aware, Prince Clumsy remains a fondly remembered C64 platformer, celebrated for its humour, accessibility, and relaxed take on a famously brutal genre.

video:video.video:title: Prince of Persia – Did Jordan Mechner’s Rotoscoped Classic Shine on the Amiga?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 for the Commodore Amiga, Prince of Persia is a cinematic platformer created by Jordan Mechner and published by Brøderbund. Based on the original 1989 Apple II release, it set new standards with its rotoscoped animation, grounded movement, and dramatic presentation. You guide a nameless Prince through deadly palace dungeons in a race against time, battling guards, avoiding traps, and solving environmental puzzles to rescue the Princess from the evil Vizier Jaffar. Every jump, sword fight, and switch pull demands precision, with a strict 60-minute countdown adding constant pressure. The Amiga version elevates the experience with smoother visuals, richer sound, and responsive controls, making combat and platforming feel deliberate and weighty. Traps like spike pits, collapsing floors, and timed gates force you to learn the environment and respect the game’s careful pacing. Today, Prince of Persia is recognised as one of the most influential platform games ever made.

video:video.video:title: Project Firestart – Survival Horror on the C64 Seven Years Before Resident Evil
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Electronic Arts and developed by Dynamix, Project Firestart is widely regarded as one of the earliest true survival horror games on the Commodore 64. Set aboard the orbital research station Prometheus above Titan in the year 2061, you play government agent Jon Hawking, sent to investigate a catastrophic loss of contact. Exploration unfolds through side-scrolling corridors with clever pseudo-3D depth, as you move between decks, access computer terminals, and uncover logs detailing a genetic experiment that has spiralled out of control. The station is no longer abandoned, and every encounter forces you to balance survival, limited resources, and time pressure. Tension is driven by deliberate pacing, atmospheric music, and cinematic scripted moments that build dread rather than relying on constant action. Player choices affect outcomes, leading to multiple endings and giving the experience lasting replay value.

video:video.video:title: Project Stealth Fighter – The C64 Sim That Later Became F-19 Stealth Fighter
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by MicroProse for the Commodore 64, Project Stealth Fighter is an ambitious combat flight simulator developed by Jim Synoski and Arnold Hendrick. Set against the backdrop of Cold War tensions, the game places players in the cockpit of a fictional stealth aircraft tasked with high-risk missions across global hotspots including Libya, the Persian Gulf, Scandinavia, and Central Europe. Before take-off, players engage in detailed mission planning, selecting weapons, fuel loads, flight routes, and tactics. Conflict levels ranging from Cold War to Conventional War alter enemy behaviour and engagement rules, giving each mission a different strategic flavour and level of risk. Once airborne, the simulation focuses on immersion and tactical awareness. The cockpit view features a comprehensive HUD, external 3D perspectives, reconnaissance systems, and electronic countermeasures. A key gameplay mechanic is managing radar exposure, as enemy detection strength is constantly measured against the aircraft’s stealth profile.

video:video.video:title: Project-X – Team17’s Amiga Shooter That Refused to Go Easy on You
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Team17 for the Commodore Amiga, Project-X is a brutally challenging horizontally scrolling shoot ’em up set in a futuristic war against rogue military droids that have turned on humanity. It quickly earned a reputation as one of the toughest shooters of the 16-bit era. Players pilot a heavily armed spacecraft equipped with seven distinct weapon systems, including Guns, Buildup, Side Shots, Homing Missiles, Plasma, Magma, and Laserbeam. Choosing the right loadout and managing upgrades is essential, as enemy placement and bullet patterns leave little room for error. The game spans five lengthy levels, each ending with large, multi-phase boss encounters. Difficulty is relentless, with many players struggling to progress beyond the early stages. In response, Team17 released Project-X Special Edition in 1993, offering a reduced difficulty option while preserving the core experience.

video:video.video:title: Psycho Hopper – The C64 Game Where You Explored a Castle on a Space Hopper
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Mastertronic and developed by M. C. Lothlorien, Psycho Hopper is one of the Commodore 64’s more unconventional action games. Set on the bizarre planetoid Dreams in the Belt of Unreality, you explore a surreal fantasy castle in search of valuable artefacts. You move through each level perched on a floating “bouncebubble” filled with poisonous gas, bouncing from left to right while blasting enemies with a blunderbuss. Contact with enemies drains the gas supply, and if it runs out, you lose a life. A constant countdown timer adds pressure, as letting it reach zero causes the bubble to explode instantly. Progress depends on collecting all parts of a valuable object in each stage, combining careful movement with accurate shooting. The unusual physics and control scheme demand patience and practice, making early moments challenging but distinctive.

video:video.video:title: Psycho Santa – Bullfrog Really Made This Bizarre Amiga Christmas Shooter
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Bullfrog Productions as a coverdisk title for The One Amiga magazine, Psycho Santa is a playful horizontal-scrolling shoot-’em-up with a distinctly festive twist. Players take control of a heavily armed Santa Claus battling waves of mischievous elves and other Christmas-themed enemies in a mission to save the holiday season. The gameplay sticks to classic side-scrolling shooter conventions, focusing on fast reactions, enemy patterns, and screen control. Levels are compact and action-packed, making the game easy to jump into while still delivering satisfying arcade-style challenge. Psycho Santa stands out thanks to its colourful presentation and tongue-in-cheek tone. The experience is boosted by a lively ProTracker soundtrack by Kevin Earl, which adds energy and personality to the festive mayhem. Although short in length, Psycho Santa became a memorable Amiga oddity, fondly remembered for its humour, polish, and seasonal novelty.

video:video.video:title: Push-Over – The Amiga Puzzle Game Built Around Quavers and Dominoes
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Red Rat Software and published by Ocean Software for the Commodore Amiga, Push-Over is a clever puzzle-platform game that puts players in control of G. I. Ant on a mission to recover lost packets of Quavers crisps from a sprawling ant hill. The core gameplay revolves around arranging domino-like slabs to trigger a precise chain reaction. Each level requires careful planning, as every slab must fall in the correct order, with the final domino opening the exit to the next stage. One wrong move can halt progress completely. Across 100 levels set in nine themed worlds, including industrial complexes, Aztec temples, space stations, and medieval castles, the game introduces slabs with special properties such as delays, split paths, and vertical ascents. These mechanics add depth and variety, gradually increasing the challenge as players advance.

video:video.video:title: Pyjamarama – Wally Week Had to Escape His Own Dream on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Mikro-Gen, Pyjamarama is the second game in the Wally Week series and places you inside a bizarre dream version of Wally’s own house. Still fast asleep, Wally must navigate this surreal landscape to wind up his alarm clock and wake up in time for work. Gameplay blends platforming with puzzle-solving as you explore interconnected rooms filled with strange hazards, moving platforms, and oddball enemies. You can only carry two items at once, forcing careful planning and experimentation to work out how each object fits into the wider puzzle. The Commodore 64 version stands out for its bold use of colour and its imaginative level design, creating a dreamlike atmosphere that feels playful and slightly unsettling. Progress relies on memory, logic, and patience rather than fast reactions. Pyjamarama is fondly remembered as one of the more creative adventure-platform hybrids of the early 1980s, and a defining entry in the Wally Week series that still rewards thoughtful exploration today.

video:video.video:title: Q*Bert – Change Every Cube Before Coily Catches You | C64
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Gottlieb and ported to the Commodore 64 by Parker Brothers in 1983, Q*Bert is a landmark arcade game that blends fast reactions with puzzle-like precision. You guide the instantly recognisable orange hero across a pyramid of cubes, aiming to change every tile to the correct colour. The challenge comes from timing and spatial awareness. Each hop alters the cube beneath you, but enemies, flying discs, and awkward jump angles constantly threaten to knock you off course. As stages progress, new hazards are introduced, turning simple movement into a tense test of nerve and planning. The isometric perspective gives the game its distinctive pseudo-3D look, making depth and direction part of the challenge. On the Commodore 64, the conversion stays faithful to the arcade original, with bright colours, smooth animation, and the same addictive difficulty curve.

video:video.video:title: Quick Draw McGraw – The C64 Game That Put a Cartoon Horse on a Moving Train
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Hi-Tec Software and developed by PAL Developments, Quick Draw McGraw brings the classic Hanna-Barbera cartoon star to the Commodore 64 in a fast-moving western action adventure. You step into the hooves of the fastest gun in the West, racing across moving trains to keep them safe from bandits and outlaws. Gameplay mixes horizontal side-scrolling action with constant forward momentum as you run along carriage roofs and sides, leaping gaps and dodging hazards like smoke plumes and swooping birds. Timing and positioning are key, as one mistimed jump can quickly bring your train-top heroics to an end. At key moments, the game switches perspective inside the train carriages, dropping you into first-person shooting sections where quick reactions matter most. Clearing these interiors and reaching the engine allows you to face off against the boss controlling each train, before moving on to the next challenge.

video:video.video:title: Quinx – The Bizarre C64 Game Set Inside a Student’s Exam Nightmare
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Supersoft for the Commodore 64, Quinx is a bizarre and memorable arcade game built around a dreamlike premise. Players take on the role of Arthur Crown, a student at the London School of Economics, trapped in a nightmare where ink worms threaten to consume the very paper he stands on. Gameplay takes place on a single screen viewed from above, with worms emerging from the edges and leaving trails of ink as they move. The goal is simple but demanding: squash the worms before they hatch. If a worm survives too long, it destroys part of the paper, steadily shrinking the playable area and pushing the game toward failure. The challenge comes from speed and positioning, as multiple worms can appear at once and hesitation quickly leads to irreversible damage. There are no power-ups or complex mechanics, just constant pressure to react quickly and stay in control as the screen becomes more chaotic.

video:video.video:title: Radar Rat Race – Commodore’s C64 Take on Rally-X with Rats
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Commodore, Radar Rat Race first appeared on the VIC-20 in 1981 before being ported to the Commodore 64 in 1982. This maze-chase title is a licensed reworking of Namco’s Rally-X, reimagined with a playful rodent theme and home-computer flair. Players control a mouse navigating maze-like arenas, collecting pieces of cheese while evading relentless rats and avoiding stationary cats that block escape routes. A built-in radar screen reveals the full maze layout, allowing players to plan routes and anticipate danger rather than relying purely on reflexes. A key tactical feature is the limited-use star screen, which temporarily confuses pursuing rats and offers a brief window to escape or grab remaining cheese. As stages progress, the action intensifies with more enemies and increasingly complex layouts, pushing both strategic thinking and execution.

video:video.video:title: Raging Beast – C64 Bullfighting That Feels Like It Shouldn’t Exist
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, Raging Beast—originally titled Olé! is a lighthearted arcade-style game that puts a playful spin on the traditional bullfighting spectacle. Developed by François Lionet, with graphics by Frédéric Pinlet and music by Jim Cuomo, the game focuses on timing, nerve, and quick reactions rather than violence. Players step into the arena as a torero, using a red cloak to lure and dodge a charging bull within a fixed-perspective playfield. Points are awarded for well-timed evasions, but progress depends on waiting for a ring to be thrown into the arena and successfully placing it onto the bull’s horns. A mistimed dodge sends the torero flying, and failing to recover quickly can end the round in spectacular fashion. The tone is deliberately comical, with colourful visuals and exaggerated animations keeping things playful and accessible.

video:video.video:title: Rags to Riches – Can You Climb from Broke to Loaded on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985, Rags to Riches is an ambitious life simulation for the Commodore 64 developed by Bob Keener and published by Melody Hall Publishing. Unusually for its time, the game places players in the role of a homeless character with a single long-term objective: work your way up from nothing and accumulate one million dollars. The journey begins on the streets, where survival comes first. Players collect bottles, search for spare change, and take on low-paying jobs to build a small income. Gradual progression allows lifestyle upgrades such as getting a haircut, pursuing education, and securing better employment, turning small decisions into meaningful long-term consequences. The city is divided into distinct districts, each presenting its own opportunities and risks. Navigating these areas requires careful planning, as threats like police, thieves, and the IRS can quickly undo progress.

video:video.video:title: Raid on Bungeling Bay – The C64 Helicopter Raid with a Bigger Legacy
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Brøderbund and designed by Will Wright, Raid on Bungeling Bay is a distinctive shoot ’em up that blends fast-paced action with strategic depth. Players pilot a helicopter launched from an aircraft carrier, striking at the Bungeling Empire by bombing factories scattered across multiple islands on a small planetoid. Gameplay revolves around repeated attack runs against enemy infrastructure while defending the aircraft carrier, which serves as the player’s home base. As missions progress, resistance intensifies with gun turrets, fighter jets, guided missiles, and even a battleship hunting the player down. A hidden island provides a vital opportunity to rearm and refuel, rewarding exploration and careful planning. What truly sets the game apart is its underlying simulation-style design. Factories evolve over time, developing new defences and technologies if left unchecked, while supply boats visibly move between islands, reinforcing their interdependence.

video:video.video:title: Raid Over Moscow – The C64 Cold War Game That Caused Real Controversy
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Access Software, Raid Over Moscow is a tense Cold War–themed action game for the Commodore 64 that puts you in the cockpit of an American fighter pilot facing a global crisis. With diplomacy off the table, you’re tasked with stopping a Soviet nuclear strike and carrying the fight deep into enemy territory. The game unfolds across multiple distinct stages, each demanding different skills. You begin by intercepting incoming missiles, then move on to attacking heavily defended missile silos from the air. The final sequence raises the stakes even further, sending you into the Kremlin to destroy a nuclear reactor and prevent worldwide catastrophe. What makes Raid Over Moscow stand out is its constant shift in gameplay. Each phase feels different, keeping tension high and forcing you to adapt quickly. Combined with its stark presentation and high-pressure objectives, the game delivers a strong sense of urgency rarely seen at the time.

video:video.video:title: Rainbow Islands on Amiga – Cute, Colourful and Harder Than It Looks
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990, Rainbow Islands is the colourful sequel to Bubble Bobble, developed by Taito and expertly ported to the Commodore Amiga by Graftgold, with publishing duties handled by Ocean Software. Bub and Bob return in human form, setting out to free the Rainbow Islands from an evil wizard in a joyful but demanding platforming quest. Gameplay shifts to vertically scrolling stages where progress is all about momentum and positioning. You create rainbows that double as weapons and platforms, trapping enemies beneath them or using them to climb higher. Mastery comes from chaining jumps, controlling enemy movement, and collecting power-ups that enhance speed, range, and scoring potential. The adventure spans seven main islands, each ending with a boss encounter, while skilled players can unlock secret islands by collecting all seven rainbow-coloured diamonds. This adds depth and replay value for those aiming to see everything the game has to offer.

video:video.video:title: Rambo – Ocean Turned First Blood Part II Into a Tactical C64 Jungle Mission
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Ocean Software and developed by Platinum Productions, Rambo: First Blood Part II adapts the 1985 action film into a tense top-down action-adventure for the Commodore 64. Rather than straightforward run-and-gun mayhem, the game leans into survival, stealth, and tactical decision-making. Players guide Rambo through dense jungle environments on a mission to rescue prisoners of war from enemy camps. Progress requires careful navigation, avoiding patrols, and choosing when to strike. Rambo can arm himself with a knife, bow and arrows—including explosive variants—and an M16 rifle, each weapon offering different risks and rewards. A standout mechanic is how noise affects enemy behaviour. Loud weapons attract reinforcements, encouraging a more considered approach and rewarding players who balance stealth with aggression. Limited lives and tough enemy placement make every encounter feel high stakes. The Commodore 64 version is elevated by a powerful soundtrack from Martin Galway, featuring themes inspired by the film’s score and adding intensity to the action.

video:video.video:title: Rampage – Three Monsters, One Goal: Flatten the City | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Rampage is the home computer adaptation of Bally Midway’s hugely popular arcade destruction game. Developed by Monarch Development and published by Activision, it delivers chaotic monster mayhem straight to the 8-bit era. You take control of one of three unfortunate humans transformed into towering monsters: George the giant ape, Lizzie the colossal reptile, or Ralph the werewolf-like brute. The goal is gloriously simple—smash buildings, eat civilians, and survive relentless attacks from military forces as cities crumble beneath you. Each city brings escalating pressure as enemies become tougher and damage mounts, forcing you to balance destruction with survival. The C64 version supports up to three players, making it perfect for shared mayhem, whether you’re working together or racing to cause the most destruction. Despite hardware limitations, Rampage on the Commodore 64 stays true to the arcade’s spirit with smooth animation, responsive controls, and addictive gameplay.

video:video.video:title: Rampart on C64 – Build the Walls, Fire the Cannons, Panic Anyway
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Atari Games and released on the Commodore 64 by Domark in 1992, Rampart delivers a distinctive blend of real-time strategy, action, and puzzle gameplay. Rather than traditional armies or units, the focus here is on building, repairing, and defending medieval castles under constant threat. Gameplay is split into two intense phases. During the building phase, players use a limited supply of wall pieces to repair damage and expand their fortress layout, deciding how best to enclose space for cannons and protection. Once time runs out, the battle phase begins, with players firing cannons to repel waves of attacking enemies and rival castles. Success depends on fast thinking and smart planning. Poor wall placement leaves cannons exposed, while inefficient repairs can spell disaster when the next assault begins. As levels progress, enemy pressure increases, forcing players to refine both construction and combat tactics.

video:video.video:title: Rastan – Can Taito’s Barbarian Arcade Hit Survive an 8-Bit Conversion? | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Rastan is a side-scrolling hack-and-slash action game developed by Taito and brought to home computers by Imagine Software. You step into the role of Rastan, a sword-wielding barbarian on a brutal quest through the land of Ceim, battling mythical creatures to save the kingdom. Gameplay blends fast-paced combat with precise platforming as you fight through forests, deserts, and castles, each stage ending in a demanding boss encounter. Along the way you can upgrade your arsenal with weapons like maces and axes, plus shields and body armour that subtly change how you survive each encounter. The Commodore 64 version features six distinct stages and leans heavily on timing and positioning, rewarding confident, aggressive play while punishing mistakes. While its difficulty and collision quirks divided opinion at the time, Rastan still delivers a raw, arcade-style challenge that captures the spirit of classic fantasy action.

video:video.video:title: Realm of Impossibility – A C64 Dungeon Game That Earns Its Name Quickly
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by BRAM Inc. and published by Electronic Arts, Realm of Impossibility is an isometric action-adventure for the Commodore 64 that plunges players into a surreal, illusion-filled nightmare. Originally released as Zombies on the Atari 8-bit, this enhanced version challenges players to recover seven mystical crowns and defeat the evil cleric Wistrik. Gameplay blends fast reflexes with tactical thinking as you explore 13 labyrinthine dungeons crawling with zombies, snakes, spiders, and other horrors. Players can place crosses to temporarily block enemies and collect scrolls to unleash spells, adding layers of strategy to the constant pressure of survival. The standout feature is its disorienting isometric world, inspired by impossible architecture that twists perception and navigation. Each room demands careful planning and spatial awareness, turning movement itself into a puzzle as deadly as the monsters.

video:video.video:title: Rebel – The C64 Puzzle Game That Sounds Bigger Than It Looks
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Virgin Games and developed by Gang of Five, Rebel is a distinctive top-down, multi-directional scrolling shooter for the Commodore 64 with a strong tactical edge. You play as THX2240, a worker who has stolen a Crowd Control Vehicle and turned against the oppressive Agri-dustrial Combine. Across thirteen large levels, progression depends on more than pure reflexes. You must rotate and align solar reflectors to redirect powerful laser beams, blasting enemies, clearing barriers, and reshaping the environment itself. Destructible scenery allows you to carve new routes or temporarily escape relentless pursuit, adding a strategic layer rarely seen in shooters of the era. The challenge level is high, with demanding controls and tightly designed stages that punish mistakes and reward planning. Success comes from understanding enemy patterns, managing space, and using the laser mechanics efficiently rather than charging in blindly.

video:video.video:title: Red Heat – Schwarzenegger’s Soviet Beat ’Em Up Comes to the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Ocean Software and developed by Special FX, Red Heat is a side-scrolling beat ’em up based on the 1988 action film starring Arnold Schwarzenegger and James Belushi. The game aims to translate the film’s hard-edged tone to the Commodore 64, placing story and presentation firmly at the forefront. You take control of Soviet police officer Viktor Rostavili as he teams up with Chicago detective Art Ridzik, moving through a series of stages inspired by key moments from the movie. Progression is linear, with each section focused on clearing enemies using punches, kicks, and occasional weapons. Visually, Red Heat was impressive for its time, featuring large character sprites and smooth animation that gave the game a cinematic feel. Jonathan Dunn’s soundtrack adds atmosphere and weight to the action, reinforcing the gritty setting even as it repeats during longer play sessions.

video:video.video:title: Renegade – The C64 Beat ’Em Up That Took Fighting to the Streets
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Renegade is a home computer adaptation of Technōs Japan’s 1986 arcade hit, developed by Ocean Software under the Imagine label. The C64 version features programming by Max Taylor, graphics by Stephen Wahid and Jane Lowe, and a hard-hitting soundtrack by Fred Gray. Players take on the role of a lone street fighter battling through five distinct stages to rescue a kidnapped girlfriend. Action unfolds across gritty locations such as subways, docks, and alleyways, with waves of enemies attacking from both sides. Combat allows for punches, kicks, jump attacks, and grabs, giving players a surprising amount of tactical freedom for the time. The Commodore 64 conversion was widely praised for capturing the feel of the arcade original, delivering fluid animation and responsive movement. While the control scheme required use of the space bar for certain actions, many players appreciated the depth and challenge this added to the fighting system.

video:video.video:title: Rescue on Fractalus! – The C64 Rescue Mission with One Nasty Surprise
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Lucasfilm Games, Rescue on Fractalus! is a groundbreaking 3D space combat and rescue simulator that pushed the Commodore 64 to its limits. Set on the hostile alien world of Fractalus, players pilot a Valkyrie fighter tasked with locating and rescuing downed pilots scattered across a dangerous mountain landscape. The game blends first-person flight action with careful navigation and tense decision-making. Players must skim across jagged terrain, manage fuel and shields, evade enemy fire, and land safely to collect stranded pilots. Adding to the suspense, not every rescue is what it seems, with some pilots revealing themselves as hostile aliens once aboard. One of the game’s most celebrated achievements is its use of fractal-generated landscapes, creating rolling mountain ranges that felt genuinely three-dimensional at a time when such visuals were almost unheard of on home computers.

video:video.video:title: Revenge of the Mutant Camels – Jeff Minter Gets Even Weirder on C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Llamasoft and developed by Jeff Minter, Revenge of the Mutant Camels is a horizontally scrolling shoot ’em up that cranks the absurdity to full blast. A direct sequel to Attack of the Mutant Camels, the game puts players in control of a heavily armed camel battling through 42 waves of surreal and unpredictable enemies. Gameplay is fast, frantic, and deliberately offbeat. Players fire basic blue shots while weaving through enemies that range from falling umbrellas and vending machines to flying toilets, all rendered in Minter’s unmistakable psychedelic style. Power-ups boost firepower, but danger also comes in the form of tokens that can poison the player or reverse controls, keeping every moment unpredictable. A standout feature is the optional two-player mode, where a second player controls a bipedal goat riding atop the camel, doubling firepower and adding a unique cooperative twist rarely seen in shooters of the era.

video:video.video:title: Rick Dangerous on Amiga – Traps, Deaths and That Smug Little Hero
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Core Design for the Commodore Amiga, Rick Dangerous is a notoriously unforgiving platform adventure inspired by the spirit of Indiana Jones. You step into the boots of Rick, a British agent whose jungle expedition quickly turns into a deadly obstacle course packed with traps, enemies, and cruel surprises. Gameplay focuses on careful movement, memory, and restraint. Hidden spikes, collapsing floors, darts, and instant-death hazards are everywhere, forcing you to learn each level through trial and error. Rick’s limited ammo and dynamite mean every shot counts, and rushing forward without caution is almost always punished. Each location introduces new dangers and layouts, from the Amazon jungle to ancient Egyptian ruins, with level design that rewards patience and observation. Success comes from anticipating traps, mastering timing, and accepting that death is part of the learning process.

video:video.video:title: River Raid – Carol Shaw’s Fuel-Hungry Shooter Reaches the Commodore 64
video:video.video:description: Released on the Commodore 64 in 1984, River Raid is a vertically scrolling shooter developed by Micro Projects Engineering and published by Activision. Originally designed by Carol Shaw for the Atari 2600, this C64 version brings the same intense aerial combat and precision gameplay to Commodore’s 8-bit hardware. Players pilot the B-1 StratoWing Assault Jet along the perilous “River of No Return,” blasting enemy helicopters, jets, tankers, bridges, and fuel depots while navigating ever-narrowing river passages. Movement is restricted to horizontal control and speed adjustment, demanding sharp reflexes and careful positioning at all times. A defining feature is fuel management. Supplies constantly drain as you fly, forcing players to skim over fuel depots to stay airborne. This simple mechanic adds strategic tension to the action, rewarding risk-taking and route planning alongside shooting accuracy. Praised for its smooth scrolling, responsive controls, and endlessly replayable design, River Raid became one of the most recognisable shooters of the 8-bit era.

video:video.video:title: Road Runner – Could the C64 Keep Up with Atari’s Arcade Cartoon Chase?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by U. S. Gold for the Commodore 64, Road Runner brings Warner Bros. ’ iconic cartoon rivalry to life in fast-paced arcade form. Players take control of the lightning-fast Road Runner, constantly outpacing the ever-unlucky Wile E. Coyote across a series of hazard-filled routes. Gameplay focuses on speed, timing, and anticipation as you sprint along roads while dodging trucks, landmines, falling rocks, and other obstacles. Collecting birdseed helps maintain top speed, while cleverly luring Wile E. Coyote into danger earns bonus points and adds a playful risk–reward element. The C64 version features smooth scrolling, bold colours, and animations that closely reflect the cartoon’s slapstick style. Catchy music and clear visual feedback keep the action readable even at high speed, making it immediately accessible. While the core loop is simple, Road Runner is fondly remembered for its faithful presentation and pure arcade energy.

video:video.video:title: Robin of the Wood – Find Three Magic Arrows to Beat the Sheriff on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Odin Computer Graphics for the Commodore 64, Robin of the Wood is an atmospheric action-adventure maze game programmed by Marc Dawson, featuring graphics by Stuart Fotheringham and music by Fred Gray. Players step into the role of Robin Hood, exploring the depths of Sherwood Forest in search of the legendary Silver Arrow, which has been seized by the Sheriff of Nottingham. Progress begins by collecting gold to purchase essential equipment, including swords and bows, from the mysterious forest Ent before venturing deeper into hostile territory. The game unfolds across a vast 16×20 screen maze populated by Norman soldiers, wild boars, witches, a wise Hermit, and surprise encounters with high-ranking medieval figures. Navigation relies on careful exploration, memory, and timing, with screen-by-screen progression rewarding patient and methodical play. Visually, the game delivers richly detailed 2D environments and smoothly animated sprites that bring the forest to life.

video:video.video:title: Robinson’s Requiem – Survival Gaming Before the Genre Took Over | Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1994 by Silmarils for the Commodore Amiga, Robinson’s Requiem is a deeply ambitious survival RPG that drops players onto a hostile alien planet with little more than their wits. Controlling two stranded astronauts, the goal is simple in theory but brutal in practice: survive. Gameplay revolves around a complex survival simulation rarely seen at the time. Players must manage hunger, thirst, fatigue, injuries, infections, and even detailed medical treatment, alongside exploration, crafting, and combat. Every decision carries weight, and mistakes can spiral into life-threatening consequences. The isometric presentation reinforces the sense of isolation, with bleak alien landscapes and threatening wildlife creating constant tension. Sound design and ambient effects further heighten the atmosphere, making exploration feel dangerous and unpredictable rather than heroic. Notorious for its steep learning curve, Robinson’s Requiem rewards patience and persistence.

video:video.video:title: Robocop on the C64 – Did Ocean Give Murphy the Game He Deserved?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 for the Commodore 64 by Ocean Software, RoboCop is a side-scrolling action game based on Paul Verhoeven’s iconic sci-fi film. Developed under license from Orion Pictures, the home computer versions were produced by Ocean in collaboration with Data East, aiming to bring the film’s gritty atmosphere to 8-bit hardware. Players step into the metal boots of RoboCop, patrolling the crime-ridden streets of Detroit across seven scrolling levels. Gameplay blends beat ’em up combat with run-and-gun shooting, as RoboCop uses punches and his Auto-9 pistol to clear enemies. Bonus shooting galleries add variety, rewarding accuracy and timing between the main stages. On the Commodore 64, RoboCop delivers moody visuals and a strong sense of atmosphere that reflects the film’s tone. Jonathan Dunn’s powerful soundtrack is a standout feature, driving the action and becoming one of the most recognisable C64 game themes of the era.

video:video.video:title: RoboCop 3 – Digital Image Design Took Murphy Into 3D on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Ocean Software and developed by Digital Image Design, RoboCop 3 brings a bold 3D action experience to the Commodore Amiga, inspired by the film’s dystopian vision of Detroit.
