You step into RoboCop’s role as he fights to stop corporate plans to evict citizens and rebuild the city for profit. The game is split into five varied gameplay styles, including first-person shooting, driving missions, hand-to-hand combat, jetpack flying, and confrontations with a deadly robot ninja. This constant shift in perspective keeps the action fresh and reinforces the cinematic scope of the adventure. Two modes are available: Movie Adventure delivers a narrative-driven structure with branching missions, while Arcade Action lets you jump straight into individual scenarios. Between missions, in-game news reports help flesh out the story and give the game a strong sense of atmosphere.

video:video.video:title: Rock’n Wrestle – Big Hair, Bigger Slams and C64 Grappling
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Melbourne House and developed by Beam Software, Rock’n Wrestle is one of the earliest attempts to bring professional wrestling to home computers using a 3D-style presentation. Players step into the boots of Gorgeous Greg, the tenth-ranked challenger battling his way toward the World Championship Belt. Matches take place in a single-screen arena where timing and positioning are key. Players face a roster of exaggerated wrestling personalities, each with their own strengths, weaknesses, and move sets. The objective is simple but tense: pin your opponent within the time limit, with the final championship bout removing the clock entirely. Combat revolves around classic wrestling manoeuvres such as body slams, flying tackles, elbow drops, and throws. Controls are accessible via joystick or keyboard, with customisable options that make the game easy to pick up while still demanding precision to master.

video:video.video:title: Rock Star Ate My Hamster – The C64 Band Manager Game with an Unforgettable Title
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Codemasters for the Commodore 64, Rock Star Ate My Hamster is a tongue-in-cheek music management simulation inspired by a notorious tabloid headline. Blending sharp humour with strategy, it puts a satirical spin on the excesses and absurdities of the pop music industry. Players step into the role of Cecil Pitt, an ambitious music manager guided by his assistant Clive, with the goal of earning four gold discs within a single year. Gameplay is menu-driven, focusing on decisions such as rehearsals, gigs, publicity stunts, recording sessions, and handling scandals as they arise. The band members are exaggerated parodies of real-world pop stars, each with their own strengths, weaknesses, and weekly costs. Success is tracked through a dynamic Top 10 chart system, forcing players to balance creativity, money, reputation, and internal band politics to stay competitive.

video:video.video:title: Rocket Ball – The C64 Sports Game Set in the Distant Future of 2010
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Rocket Ball is a futuristic sports-action game developed by IJK Software and coded by John S. Sinclair. Set in the then-future year of 2010, the game imagines a world where international disputes are settled through a violent, high-energy arena sport. The action blends elements of roller derby and American football. Teams of five skaters battle it out in a circular arena, aiming to score by launching a heavy metal ball into a cone-shaped goal while physically overpowering their opponents. Elbows, knees, and fists are all fair game as mayhem unfolds at high speed. Players must skate quickly, collect the ball, and time their shots carefully while defending against relentless attacks. Four teams are available — Houston, Tokyo, Moscow, and Madrid — each with different strengths, adding variety and tactical choice to matches that last a tense ten minutes.

video:video.video:title: Rocket Ranger – Jetpacks, Villains and Cinemaware Ambition on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released for the Commodore 64 by Cinemaware, Rocket Ranger drops players into an alternate-history 1940s where the Nazis have established a secret base on the Moon. Using a mysterious substance called Lunarium, they plan to reduce global intelligence levels and secure world domination. Humanity’s last hope comes from the future, as advanced jetpack technology, powerful weapons, and code-breaking tools are sent back in time for you to change the course of history. The game follows Cinemaware’s trademark cinematic structure, blending dramatic animated sequences with a mix of action and strategy. Players must manage limited resources, deploy spies across Europe to uncover enemy rocket factories, and decide how much Lunarium to expend at each stage while avoiding capture. Strategic choices directly affect your chances of success. Action sequences punctuate the experience, including brutal hand-to-hand combat with Nazi guards, high-speed jetpack dogfights against enemy aircraft, and daring assaults on Zeppelins and secret installations.

video:video.video:title: Rodland – The Amiga Cute ’Em Up Built for Two Players
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Random Access and published by Storm for the Commodore Amiga, Rodland is a charming single-screen platformer based on Jaleco’s popular arcade hit. The Amiga version expands on the original with extra levels, enhanced visuals, and a highly enjoyable two-player cooperative mode. Players take control of the fairy sisters Tam and Rit, who wield magical rods on a quest to rescue their mother from the towering stronghold of Maboots. Each stage challenges players to defeat enemies, collect flowers, and clear the screen in order to progress, blending action with light puzzle elements. Gameplay draws clear inspiration from classics like Bubble Bobble, focusing on precise movement, clever enemy manipulation, and tactical use of special abilities. Mastering timing and coordination becomes especially important in later stages, particularly when playing cooperatively. Visually, the Amiga port shines with colourful environments, smooth animations, and expressive character sprites that capture the playful spirit of the arcade original.

video:video.video:title: Rollercoaster Rumbler – The C64 Shooter Played from a Moving Roller Coaster
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Tynesoft and developed by Subway Software for the Commodore 64, Roller Coaster Rumbler is a distinctive rail shooter that puts players on a high-speed roller coaster armed with a mounted machine gun. Unlike the Amiga and Atari ST versions, the C64 release takes a unique approach with a split-screen presentation. Gameplay combines a first-person shooting view with an isometric perspective showing the roller coaster’s twisting track. As the ride climbs, dips, and swerves, players must blast waves of flying targets, all while compensating for the constant motion of the coaster itself. The challenge lies in accuracy and timing, with players required to hit a set number of targets within a limited time window. The shifting viewpoint and relentless movement add an extra layer of difficulty, keeping the action tense despite the simple core mechanics.

video:video.video:title: Rolling Thunder – Could Tiertex Pull Off Namco’s Arcade Hit on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Rolling Thunder is a side-scrolling run-and-gun action game originally developed by Namco and brought to home computers by Tiertex under U. S. Gold. Players take on the role of Agent Albatross of the World Intelligence Network, fighting to rescue his partner, Leila Blitz, from the terrorist organisation Geldra. Gameplay unfolds across multi-level stages where movement, positioning, and timing are just as important as shooting. Players battle Maskers and other enemies while using doors, platforms, and vertical layers for cover, creating a more tactical feel than simple left-to-right shooters. The Commodore 64 version aims to replicate the structure and pacing of the arcade original, though compromises were inevitable due to hardware limits. While the action remains recognisable, the visuals and audio are more restrained, and the difficulty is unforgiving, with tough enemy patterns and limited margin for error.

video:video.video:title: R-Type – How Did Manfred Trenz Fit Irem’s Arcade Shooter Into the C64?
video:video.video:description: R-Type is the 1988 Commodore 64 port of Irem’s legendary arcade “force-ship” shooter, published by Electric Dreams / Rainbow Arts and coded by Manfred Trenz. In the game, you pilot the iconic R-9 “Arrowhead” spacecraft through eight intense horizontally-scrolling stages, battling the alien Bydo Empire, navigating hazardous terrain, and facing massive biomechanical bosses. Your arsenal includes rapid-fire shots, a powerful chargeable wave cannon, and the game’s signature feature — the indestructible “Force” orb. Attach it, detach it, or deploy it freely to act as both shield and weapon platform. The C64 conversion delivers fast gameplay and smooth scrolling, outperforming many other 8-bit shooters of its era. Atmospheric visuals, detailed sci-fi environments, and an outstanding soundtrack by Chris Hülsbeck and Ramiro Vaca add to the experience. Remarkably, the port was reportedly developed in just a few weeks, yet it remains one of the finest technical showcases on the Commodore 64.

video:video.video:title: Saboteur – The C64 Ninja Mission That Still Feels Tense
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Durell Software, Saboteur is a landmark stealth-action game developed by Clive Townsend and brought to the Commodore 64 by Branko Spoljaric. Players assume the role of a lone ninja infiltrating a heavily guarded warehouse complex to recover a disk containing the names of rebel leaders. Gameplay takes place across a large network of interconnected rooms, tunnels, and hidden areas. Success relies on careful movement, observation, and timing as players avoid or confront guards, dogs, and automated gun turrets. The ninja can crouch, climb, sprint, and attack using punches, drop-kicks, and weapons such as shurikens, with improvised tools discovered along the way adding tactical variety. An energy system governs every action, draining through combat, falls, and swimming. Resting in safe zones is essential to survive longer infiltrations, while selectable difficulty levels alter enemy density, security systems, and time pressure, allowing players to tailor the challenge.

video:video.video:title: Saboteur II – Did the C64 Sequel Improve the Mission?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Durell Software, Saboteur II: Avenging Angel is a side-scrolling action-adventure for the Commodore 64 and the sequel to the cult hit Saboteur!. Developed by Clive Townsend with music by Rob Hubbard, the game introduces Nina, sister of the original protagonist, on a mission driven by revenge and infiltration rather than brute force. The game unfolds across nine missions spanning more than 700 interconnected screens, forming a vast industrial compound filled with hazards and security systems. Progress depends on exploration and careful planning as players collect punched tape fragments to disable defences and work towards a daring motorcycle escape. Combat is deliberately de-emphasised in favour of stealth and evasion. Robotic guards, wild animals, electrified fences, and surveillance systems force players to observe enemy patterns, choose routes wisely, and solve environmental challenges rather than rely on direct confrontation.

video:video.video:title: Saint Dragon – The C64 Shooter Where Your Weapon Was a Cyborg Dragon
video:video.video:description: Released on the Commodore 64 in 1990 and ported by Random Access from NMK’s arcade original, Saint Dragon is a horizontally scrolling shoot ’em up that immediately stands out thanks to its biomechanical dragon protagonist. Set in a dark sci-fi future, you control Saint Dragon as it rebels against a ruthless cyborg empire. Action unfolds across five steadily escalating stages, each ending with a huge screen-filling guardian that tests positioning and firepower. Movement is deliberate and weighty, demanding careful control as enemy patterns close in from all angles. The weapon system takes clear inspiration from R-Type, with collectible power-ups that upgrade pulse shots, lasers, and the dragon’s distinctive segmented tail, which can be used defensively as a shield. A temporary hyper mode boosts firepower and grants brief invulnerability, adding a risk-reward layer to the combat.

video:video.video:title: Samantha Fox Strip Poker – The C64 Game That Could Only Have Happened in the 80s
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Software Communications and published by Martech Games for the Commodore 64, Samantha Fox Strip Poker is an early adult-themed poker simulation featuring British model Samantha Fox. Players compete in 5-card or 7-card stud matches, with opponents adapting their play style as each game progresses and victories unlocking progressively revealing images. Despite its provocative premise, the game focuses heavily on genuine card strategy, requiring careful betting, bluffing, and risk management to succeed. The minimalist presentation keeps attention firmly on the gameplay loop, blending gambling mechanics with reward-based progression. A standout feature is the soundtrack by Rob Hubbard, credited as John York, including SID chip versions of “The Entertainer” and “The Stripper,” which became legendary among C64 music fans. These distinctive tunes helped elevate the experience and remain one of the game’s most memorable elements.

video:video.video:title: Samurai Warrior – The C64 Comic-Book Adventure with Honour and Blades
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 for the Commodore 64, Samurai Warrior: The Battles of Usagi Yojimbo is an action-adventure developed by Beam Software and published by Firebird, based on Stan Sakai’s acclaimed comic series. Players step into the sandals of Miyamoto Usagi, a wandering rabbit samurai navigating a dangerous world shaped as much by ethics as by steel. Gameplay unfolds in a side-scrolling format, blending sword combat with exploration and interaction. Usagi faces bandits, ninjas, and deceptive enemies who may appear as harmless villagers or monks, requiring constant vigilance and careful judgment during encounters. A defining feature is the game’s karma system. Honorable actions raise Usagi’s standing, while attacking innocents or acting dishonorably reduces it. Let karma fall too low and Usagi is forced into seppuku, bringing the journey to an abrupt end. Between battles, players can gamble at inns for money and purchase food to restore health, adding a strategic layer to survival.

video:video.video:title: Santa’s Xmas Caper – An Amiga Christmas Shooter That Sounds Like a Threat
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Reflective Designs and published by Zeppelin Games, Santa’s Xmas Caper is a holiday-themed side-scrolling shooter that puts a mischievous twist on Christmas cheer. After having his Christmas pudding spiked by rogue elves, Santa takes to the skies to rescue the festive season the only way he knows how. Gameplay unfolds across three themed stages, beginning in snowy Lapland, moving over the Atlantic Ocean, and ending with Santa delivering presents under fire. Players must dodge bombs, hostile toys, and enemy elves while firing an endless supply of gift-wrapped projectiles to clear the way forward. The game’s festive presentation is a major highlight, with colourful visuals that lean fully into the Christmas theme. The soundtrack features chiptune renditions of classic carols such as We Wish You a Merry Christmas and Silent Night, composed by Mark Wilson, giving the game a cheerful seasonal identity.

video:video.video:title: Sanxion – The C64 Shooter That Showed the Battle from Two Angles at Once
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 for the Commodore 64, Sanxion was developed by Stavros Fasoulas and published by Thalamus as the company’s very first release. From the outset, it established Thalamus as a publisher willing to push technical and design boundaries, delivering a shoot-’em-up that felt fresh and ambitious. Players pilot a futuristic aircraft through horizontally scrolling stages packed with enemies and hazards. Sanxion’s most distinctive feature is its split-screen presentation: the upper section shows an overhead tactical view, while the lower portion displays the traditional side-on action. This dual perspective allows players to anticipate threats ahead while reacting to immediate danger, adding an extra layer of strategy rarely seen in the genre. Another standout mechanic is the adjustable scrolling speed. Movement accelerates as the player ship approaches the centre of the screen, forcing constant judgment calls between speed, control, and survival.

video:video.video:title: SAS Combat Simulator – Was This Budget C64 Action Harder Than Expected?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Optimus Software and published by Codemasters for the Commodore 64, SAS Combat Simulator delivers a hard-edged military action experience inspired by elite special forces operations. Rather than sticking to a single style, the game blends two distinct action formats into one fast-moving campaign. Each of the four levels is split into two phases. The first drops players into a top-down shooter where constant movement and enemy management are key, echoing classic arcade run-and-gun design. The second phase switches perspective to a side-scrolling beat ’em up, demanding close-quarters combat and careful positioning as enemy soldiers swarm in. Across jungle, desert, and swamp environments, players make use of machine guns, grenades, and heavy firepower, with the added ability to commandeer vehicles such as jeeps and tanks. This variety helps keep the pace aggressive while giving brief moments of power amid the mayhem.

video:video.video:title: Savage Pond – The C64 Game Where the Pond Fights Back
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Argus Press Software and developed by Gwyll Jones, Savage Pond is an unusual arcade action game for the Commodore 64 that places players inside a hostile but fascinating pond ecosystem. Rather than shooting waves of enemies, the focus here is survival, growth, and adaptation. Players begin life as a vulnerable tadpole, navigating a side-view, flip-screen pond while avoiding predators such as dragonflies, water spiders, and other natural dangers. Progress depends on careful movement and feeding, as consuming food allows the tadpole to grow and eventually transform into a frog. Once evolved, the challenge shifts toward survival at the top of the food chain, with the longer-term goal of establishing a thriving frog colony. The game’s mechanics reflect a simplified but thoughtful take on biology and natural progression, blending educational ideas with arcade-style tension.

video:video.video:title: The C64 Tomb Adventure That Was Years Ahead of Its Time | Scarabaeus
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Hungarian studio Andromeda Software and published by Ariolasoft for the Commodore 64, Scarabaeus is a pioneering first-person 3D maze adventure set deep within a mysterious Egyptian tomb. Known as Invaders of the Lost Tomb in North America, the game blends exploration, puzzle-solving, and survival into a tense and atmospheric experience. The adventure unfolds across three distinct stages. Players first navigate a sprawling maze to capture wandering ghosts, each revealing a hieroglyphic symbol. These symbols become essential clues in the second phase, where logic puzzles involving alcoves, medicinal vials, and zombie traps must be solved through careful deduction. In the final stage, knowledge gathered earlier is put to the test as players confront zombies and solve a central puzzle to access the inner sanctum and recover the sacred jewel. Success depends on observation, memory, and understanding how each element connects across the game’s structure.

video:video.video:title: Schizofrenia – A Strange C64 Puzzle Game with a Name You Don’t Forget
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Quicksilva for the Commodore 64 and developed by Terry P. Watts, Schizofrenia is a single-screen puzzle platformer built around a clever and unusual concept. Players take control of Alphonse T. Nurd, a lab assistant who accidentally creates a duplicate of himself after activating a malfunctioning machine. The objective is to reunite with this mischievous double by navigating five increasingly complex laboratory stages. Gameplay centres on puzzle-platform mechanics, requiring careful use of switches, elevators, and timing-based movement to progress through each room. What sets Schizofrenia apart is the behaviour of the duplicate, which actively interferes with the player’s plans. This constant disruption forces strategic thinking and precise execution, as even small mistakes can undo progress. The tight controls and escalating difficulty demand patience and concentration. While reviews at the time were mixed—some praising the originality and challenge, others criticising the steep learning curve—Schizofrenia has since earned a small but dedicated following.

video:video.video:title: Seaside Special – The C64 Arcade Game That Feels Very British
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Taskset and published by Argus Press Software for the Commodore 64, Seaside Special is a politically charged action-adventure that blends arcade gameplay with sharp British satire. Players take on the role of Radium Rodney, battling alien invaders known as the Polytikians who have secretly taken control of the UK government. Gameplay is split across two main locations. On the beach, Rodney must collect radioactive seaweed while avoiding hazards such as jellyfish, crabs, sandpits, rising tides, and increasing radiation levels. Once enough seaweed is gathered, the action shifts to 10 Downing Street, where players hurl it through the windows to drive out the Polytikians while dodging enemy fire. The challenge steadily escalates as environmental dangers intensify and enemies become more aggressive. This mix of item collection and precision throwing gives the game a distinctive rhythm, setting it apart from more straightforward arcade titles of the time.

video:video.video:title: Seek & Destroy – The Amiga Helicopter Shooter Few People Remember
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Vision Software and published by Mindscape for the Commodore Amiga, Seek & Destroy is a fast-paced top-down helicopter shoot-’em-up that delivers arcade-style military action with strategic depth. Players take control of a heavily armed Apache helicopter and are sent into hostile territory across a series of combat missions set in a fictional Middle Eastern conflict. The game features a dynamic 360-degree scrolling playfield, allowing free movement in all directions and encouraging tactical positioning during intense firefights. A wide range of weapons is available, including missiles, bombs, and machine guns, which can be used to engage tanks, enemy helicopters, ground forces, and defensive installations. Success depends on balancing aggression with careful navigation, managing ammunition, and choosing the right weapons for each situation. Visually, Seek & Destroy delivers detailed sprites and smooth scrolling environments, with the AGA-enhanced Amiga 1200 version offering improved colour depth and sharper presentation.

video:video.video:title: Sensible Golf – Did Sensible Software’s Amiga Style Work on the Green?
video:video.video:description: Sensible Golf (1995) is a 2D arcade-style golf game developed by Sensible Software and published by Virgin Interactive for the Commodore Amiga. Featuring the familiar “pin-like” characters seen in Sensible Soccer and Cannon Fodder, the game delivers a fast-paced, no-frills take on golf that focuses on fun over realism. Gameplay is built around a simple three-click system — aim, set power and curve, then strike — with automatic club suggestions and slope indicators to help guide each shot. Rather than simulating wind and terrain height, the game concentrates on hazards such as water and sand across 25 imaginative courses, totalling 72 holes. This makes it ideal for quick rounds, full seasons, or tournament play with large groups. Despite its charm, Sensible Golf received mixed reviews at release, including a 66% score from Amiga Power, and proved to be one of Sensible Software’s weaker commercial performers.

video:video.video:title: Sensible Soccer – How Sensible Software Reinvented Football on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Sensible Software, Sensible Soccer redefined football games on the Commodore Amiga with its instantly recognisable top-down view and lightning-fast gameplay. You control compact teams of tiny players in matches that prioritise speed, precision, and pure fun over complicated simulation. On the pitch, the game is all about sharp passing, quick shots, and fluid movement. Controls are intuitive yet deep, letting you pull off one-touch football, curling shots, and last-ditch tackles with ease. Matches flow at a blistering pace, making every goal feel earned and every mistake costly. The success of the original led to refined updates like Sensible Soccer 92/93 and ultimately Sensible World of Soccer, which expanded the formula with transfers, management depth, and a staggering number of teams and players. Across the series, the balance between arcade action and tactical awareness kept matches endlessly replayable.

video:video.video:title: Serenade – A Forgotten C64 Puzzle Game with an Odd Little Hook
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by VIFI International for the Commodore 64, Serenade is a highly unusual and experimental title developed by French studio Jawx. Players take on the role of a lovesick troubadour, depicted as a silhouetted figure, attempting to win the affection of a lady by performing music with a selection of instruments. The game is presented entirely in French, adding to its distinctive atmosphere and reinforcing its European art-game sensibility. Rather than following traditional arcade or adventure conventions, Serenade focuses on mood and presentation. Gameplay revolves around choosing musical pieces and attempting to perform them using four available instruments. However, interaction is deliberately minimal, and progress can feel ambiguous or even confusing. Many players find it difficult to produce clear musical results, leading some to interpret the game as more of an interactive demo or artistic experiment than a conventional game.

video:video.video:title: Shadow Dancer – Did Sega’s Ninja Arcade Hit Survive the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by U. S. Gold and developed by Images Design, Shadow Dancer brings Sega’s arcade follow-up to Shinobi onto the Commodore 64. You play as a masked ninja warrior fighting through hostile urban environments, taking down terrorists and rescuing hostages under constant pressure. The gameplay focuses on fast side-scrolling combat, combining shuriken attacks with close-range strikes and the unique support of a loyal attack dog. Timing your moves and knowing when to deploy the dog becomes essential as enemy patterns tighten and levels grow more demanding. Despite the limitations of the 8-bit hardware, the C64 version delivers fluid animation and well-structured level design that keeps the action flowing. The darker colour palette suits the urban ninja theme, while Allister Brimble’s driving soundtrack adds energy and urgency to every encounter.

video:video.video:title: Shadow Fighter – The Amiga Fighting Game That Pushed the Hardware
video:video.video:description: Shadow Fighter (1994), developed by the Italian NAPS Team and published by Gremlin Interactive, is one of the most technically impressive 2D beat ’em ups on the Commodore Amiga. Designed for standard OCS/ECS hardware, the game delivers smooth animation, vibrant sprites, and impressive multi-layer parallax scrolling that pushes the platform to its limits. With 17 playable fighters, each featuring unique moves and backgrounds, the game uses a simple one-button control system that allows players to perform over 25 attacks per character through intuitive joystick motions. A dedicated training mode introduces “Pupazz,” a practice opponent designed to help players master advanced techniques and special moves. Graphically, Shadow Fighter stands out with its rich colour palette and dynamic arenas, while Patrick Phelan’s energetic soundtrack enhances the intensity of each battle. Although later AGA and CD32 versions offered visual upgrades, the original OCS/ECS release remains a showcase of expert Amiga programming and fast-paced arcade-style combat.

video:video.video:title: Shadow of the Beast – 12 Layers of Parallax: This Was the Amiga Showing Off
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Reflections Interactive and published by Psygnosis for the Commodore Amiga, Shadow of the Beast casts players as Aarbron, a once-human warrior transformed into a monstrous servant of the evil Maletoth. After fragments of his past resurface, Aarbron sets out on a brutal journey of revenge across a hostile and surreal world. Gameplay unfolds across more than 350 side-scrolling screens filled with enemies, traps, and environmental hazards. Progress relies heavily on precise movement, sharp reflexes, and memorisation, with limited room for error. Combat is deliberate and punishing, reinforcing the game’s unforgiving tone and demanding mastery from the player. The game is renowned for pushing the Amiga hardware to its limits, featuring stunning multi-layer parallax scrolling and rich 128-colour visuals that give its alien landscapes a distinctive, dreamlike quality. David Whittaker’s atmospheric soundtrack adds emotional weight, perfectly complementing the dark fantasy setting.

video:video.video:title: Shao-Lin’s Road – Did Konami’s Arcade Fighter Survive the Move to C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Konami and ported to the Commodore 64 by The Edge, Shao-Lin’s Road is a martial arts platform beat ’em up inspired by the arcade hit Yie Ar Kung-Fu. Players take control of Lee, a skilled warrior trapped inside a hostile temple after the murder of his master. The game is structured across five multi-tiered stages filled with enemy fighters, traps, and challenging boss encounters. Movement combines side-scrolling action with vertical platforming, requiring precise jumps and well-timed attacks. Combat focuses on jumping kicks, rapid strikes, and positioning to control crowds. Defeating certain enemies releases special power-ups, including the meteor hammer, fireballs, and protective energy orbs. These temporary abilities add variety and strategy, encouraging players to adapt their playstyle as they progress through each level. On the Commodore 64, Shao-Lin’s Road delivers colourful sprites, smooth animation, and responsive controls that capture much of the arcade’s intensity.

video:video.video:title: Sheep in Space – Jeff Minter, C64 Shooting and Pure Woolly Madness
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Llamasoft and developed by Jeff Minter, Sheep in Space is a horizontally scrolling shoot-’em-up that puts a surreal twist on classic arcade action. Players control a genetically engineered combat sheep defending a planetary colony from waves of invading droids. Inspired by Defender, the game spans 48 levels, each requiring the destruction of 16 enemies before progressing. Alongside a standard blaster and shield, the sheep can perform a “DJump,” instantly warping to the nearest hostile for rapid attacks and emergency escapes. A distinctive survival mechanic adds pressure, as the sheep must regularly land on grassy areas to feed when hunger levels drop. Managing energy is critical, as becoming famished weakens the player, while overeating leads to an explosive end. This balance between combat and survival creates a rhythm that keeps players constantly engaged.

video:video.video:title: Short Circuit – Did Number 5 Survive His C64 Film Licence?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Virgin Games and developed by The Sales Curve, Shinobi brings Sega’s legendary arcade ninja action to the Commodore 64. You take control of Joe Musashi, a master ninja on a mission to dismantle the Zeed crime syndicate and rescue captured hostages across a series of dangerous locations. Gameplay blends fast side-scrolling combat with precision timing. You fight waves of enemies using shurikens, close-range attacks, and powerful ninja magic, while keeping a close eye on hostage appearances. Rescuing them not only boosts your score but also rewards you with vital power-ups, adding tension and urgency to every encounter. Each stage introduces new enemy patterns and hazards, demanding sharp reactions and careful positioning. While the controls can feel unforgiving at times, success comes from learning enemy behaviour and committing to confident, decisive moves.

video:video.video:title: Shoot-Out – Miss ONE Tin Can and It’s Game Over on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Martech for the Commodore 64, Shoot-Out is a crosshair-based shooting game set in the dusty frontier town of Gulch Creek. Players take on the role of Quick Hand Luke, a skilled gunslinger determined to restore order to the Wild West. The game unfolds across a series of increasingly demanding scenarios. It begins with precision-based target practice, where players must shoot appearing cans without missing a single shot. As the game progresses, moving enemies, obstacles, and time pressure are introduced, requiring fast reactions and steady aim. Gameplay focuses on accuracy, rhythm, and memorisation, with little margin for error. Each stage demands perfect timing, making Shoot-Out a test of concentration as much as reflexes. One mistake can often mean restarting the challenge. Visually, the game uses a fixed-screen, top-down perspective with simple yet effective Western-themed backdrops.

video:video.video:title: Short Circuit – Was the Commodore 64 Movie Game Any Good?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Ocean Software, Short Circuit is an action-adventure game for the Commodore 64 based on the popular 1986 sci-fi comedy film. Players take control of Number 5, a military robot accidentally brought to life by a lightning strike and determined to escape captivity without harming humans. The game is split into two contrasting gameplay styles. The first section is a top-down adventure set inside a laboratory complex, where players search for items, avoid guards, and solve puzzles to build a robot decoy. Careful exploration and planning are essential, reflecting Number 5’s ethical refusal to cause harm. Once outside, the game shifts into a side-scrolling action phase focused on speed and precision. Players must guide Number 5 through hazardous environments while avoiding security forces, obstacles, and enemy robots as the difficulty steadily increases.

video:video.video:title: Sid Meier’s Pirates! – Trade, Fight, Marry and Hunt Treasure Across the Caribbean | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by MicroProse and designed by Sid Meier, Sid Meier’s Pirates! is one of the most ambitious and influential games ever released on the Commodore 64. Set across the Caribbean during the golden age of piracy, it drops you into a living world shaped by exploration, politics, and personal ambition. You take command of a pirate ship and choose how to carve out your legend, whether that means serving European powers, turning rogue against everyone, or switching allegiances as fortunes change. Naval battles, trading, treasure hunting, and information gathering all feed into a constantly shifting political landscape that makes every playthrough feel different. Beyond sailing and combat, Pirates! layers in memorable side activities including sword duels, dancing at governors’ balls to gain favour, rescuing lost family members, and uncovering buried treasure maps. These systems combine strategy, action, and role-playing elements in a way that was far ahead of its time.

video:video.video:title: Silent Service – Sid Meier’s C64 Submarine Sim Made Every Torpedo Matter
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Sid Meier and published by MicroProse for the Commodore 64, Silent Service is a landmark submarine simulation set in the Pacific Theater of World War II. Players take command of a U. S. Navy Gato-class submarine, embarking on tense war patrols against Japanese shipping with survival depending on patience, planning, and precision. Gameplay is split between strategic navigation and high-stakes combat. During patrols, players plot courses, manage fuel and systems, and decide when to engage or evade. Combat brings torpedo targeting, sonar interpretation, periscope tracking, and evasive manoeuvres as enemy escorts hunt you down. Weather conditions, day-night cycles, and detection mechanics all play a critical role in each encounter. The simulation places strong emphasis on realism, featuring authentic instrumentation, damage modelling, and multiple difficulty levels that cater to both newcomers and experienced players.

video:video.video:title: Silkworm – The C64 Co-op Shooter with a Helicopter and a Jeep
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 for the Commodore 64 and developed by The Sales Curve under licence from Tecmo, Silkworm is a fast-paced horizontal-scrolling shoot ’em up that pairs a helicopter with an armed jeep. Players can choose to pilot either the chopper or the jeep, while two-player mode allows cooperative play with one player controlling each vehicle. Together, you battle waves of tanks, aircraft, and ground forces as they flood in from all directions. The C64 conversion retains the arcade feel with smooth scrolling, power-up shields, destructible scenery, and intense enemy patterns. The port was programmed by Warren Mills, with graphics by Edward Langman and music by Barry Leitch. Although less technically advanced than the arcade and Amiga versions, the Commodore 64 edition stands out as one of the system’s strongest co-op shooters, delivering true simultaneous two-player action.

video:video.video:title: SimCity – How Did Will Wright Squeeze an Entire City Builder into the C64?
video:video.video:description: SimCity (1989), developed by Maxis and designed by Will Wright, is the groundbreaking city-building simulation that helped define the genre on home computers. The Commodore 64 version condenses the full SimCity experience into just 64 KB of memory — a remarkable technical achievement for the time. You build and manage your city zone by zone, laying residential, commercial, and industrial areas, constructing roads and waterways, setting taxes, balancing budgets, and responding to disasters such as earthquakes. To fit within tight memory limits, features like police stations, fire departments, stadiums, railways, and advanced statistics were removed. However, core systems such as pollution tracking, growth charts, water systems, and tax controls remained intact — with some elements appearing on C64 before the PC version. Despite its minimalist, mostly monochrome visuals, performance is smooth and responsive, turning technical limitations into part of the game’s charm.

video:video.video:title: Simon the Sorcerer – Why Didn’t the Original Amiga Version Have Chris Barrie?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Adventure Soft for the Commodore Amiga, Simon the Sorcerer is a classic point-and-click adventure that places players in the role of Simon, a sarcastic teenage wizard-in-training unexpectedly pulled into a colourful fantasy world. His task is to rescue the imprisoned wizard Calypso from the grip of the villainous sorcerer Sordid. Gameplay follows a traditional verb-based adventure interface, featuring twelve commands that allow players to explore environments, manipulate objects, and solve layered puzzles. Progress depends on observation, logic, and creative item use rather than reflexes, rewarding patience and experimentation. The Amiga version stands out for its richly detailed hand-drawn graphics and vibrant colour palette, bringing its fairy-tale world to life. The game is especially well remembered for its sharp dialogue, playful humour, and frequent nods to classic fantasy stories, delivered with a distinctly British tone.

video:video.video:title: Skate or Die – Was This the C64’s Best Skateboarding Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Electronic Arts, Skate or Die! is a landmark skateboarding game for the Commodore 64 and a defining slice of 1980s gaming culture. Notably, it was EA’s first internally developed title, helping establish the publisher’s early reputation for polished, personality-driven sports games. The game offers five distinct skateboarding events, each focusing on a different skill set. Players can compete in Freestyle half-pipe trick sessions, test timing in the High Jump, race downhill at speed, battle opponents in Downhill Jam, or knock rivals off their boards in the chaotic Joust mode. This variety gives the game an arcade-style structure that keeps play sessions fast and competitive. One of Skate or Die! ’s standout features is its multiplayer support, allowing up to eight players to compete by rotating turns, making it a popular choice for social gaming.

video:video.video:title: Skate Rock – Ten C64 Skateboarding Courses and One Very ’80s Soundtrack
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Bubble Bus Software and developed by Zig Zag Creations, Skate Rock blends arcade skateboarding with a loud, energetic rock aesthetic. Also known as Awesome Earl in SkateRock, the game drops you into busy urban courses where speed, precision, and nerve are everything. You skate through ten increasingly demanding levels, racing against the clock to collect flags while dodging pedestrians, traffic, and roadworks. Tight control and route planning are essential, as one mistake can quickly derail a run. Progression is driven by mastery, with the ultimate goal of earning your place among the elite Slime Rat Skaters. Each course has its own visual identity, filled with animated hazards that bring the city streets to life. The experience is powered by Ben Daglish’s driving soundtrack, which reinforces the game’s pace and attitude throughout.

video:video.video:title: Skidmarks – Link Two Amigas for Four-Player Racing AND a Chat Line for Abuse
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Acid Software for the Commodore Amiga, Skidmarks is a fast-paced isometric racing game inspired by arcade classics such as Super Sprint. It blends accessible pick-up-and-play controls with tactical racing elements, creating a distinctive and highly competitive experience. Players can choose from four different vehicles, including a rally sports car, a high-wheeled muscle car, a monster truck, and a buggy, each offering unique handling, acceleration, and top-speed characteristics. Mastering these differences is key to dominating the game’s demanding circuits. The game features twelve expansive tracks filled with tight corners, ramps, and shortcuts, all designed to test precision driving and racecraft. The isometric viewpoint provides excellent visibility, allowing players to anticipate hazards and plan overtaking moves effectively. One of Skidmarks’ defining features is its multiplayer support, allowing up to four players to compete via modem link.

video:video.video:title: Skool Daze – Get the Report Card Before the Headmaster Sends It Home | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Skool Daze is an open-world action-adventure developed by Microsphere and designed by David Reidy, with graphics by Keith Warrington. Players take control of Eric, a mischievous schoolboy on a mission to retrieve his disastrous report card from the headmaster’s safe before it’s sent home. To succeed, Eric must explore a fully interactive school building, attending lessons, sneaking through corridors, and outwitting teachers. The safe’s combination is uncovered by firing a catapult at shields around the school, each linked to a letter held by a different member of staff. Timing, planning, and clever mischief are essential. What sets Skool Daze apart is its pioneering sandbox design. Teachers and pupils follow their own routines, creating a living, unpredictable environment. Eric must balance rule-breaking with caution, as accumulating too many “lines” leads to expulsion and game over.

video:video.video:title: Skull & Crossbones – Why Did the C64 Lose the Arcade’s Two-Player Swordfights?
video:video.video:description: Skull & Crossbones (1991), developed by Walking Circles and published by Domark / Tengen, is a pirate-themed side-scrolling beat ’em up for the Commodore 64. Players choose between One Eye or Red Dog, two swashbuckling heroes on a mission to recover stolen treasure and rescue a kidnapped princess from an evil wizard. The adventure takes you through ships, castles, caves, and other exotic locations, battling waves of enemies and powerful bosses along the way. Between stages, collected loot can be traded to upgrade weapons such as cutlasses, knives, and flintlock pistols, adding a light role-playing element to progression. The C64 conversion removes some arcade features, including true simultaneous co-op, replacing it with alternating turns. Controls are often criticised for feeling sluggish, with certain actions requiring awkward inputs. One standout feature is the soundtrack by Matt Furniss, which delivers a memorable high-seas theme — though players must choose between music and sound effects.

video:video.video:title: Sláine – The C64 Adventure Where Your Commands Disappeared Before You Picked Them
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Martech for the Commodore 64, Sláine is a distinctive adventure game developed by Creative Reality and based on the British comic series Sláine from 2000 AD. Drawing heavily from its graphic novel roots, the game blends interactive fiction, real-time action, and strong narrative elements into a uniquely challenging experience. At the heart of the game is the unusual REFLEX command system, where actions scroll across the screen and must be selected quickly, reflecting the hero’s split-second decision-making. This mechanic demands fast reactions and mental agility, setting Sláine apart from traditional menu-driven adventures of the era. Players control Sláine, a barbarian warrior on a quest through a mythic fantasy world to rescue a captive princess. Gameplay mixes real-time combat, inventory use, and puzzle-solving, with the story delivered through descriptive text and stark monochrome illustrations that echo the tone of the original comic.

video:video.video:title: Slalom! – How Fast Could You Survive This 1983 C64 Skiing Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Tronix Publishing Inc. for the Commodore 64, Slalom! is a fast-paced downhill skiing game that focuses on speed, precision, and tight control. Players guide a skier through a series of slalom gates, racing against the clock while avoiding rocks, trees, and other hazards scattered across the slope. The game features five runs of increasing difficulty, each demanding sharper reactions and more accurate steering. Success depends on clean lines through the gates and maintaining momentum, as even small mistakes can cost valuable time. On the Commodore 64, Slalom! stands out for its smooth scrolling and responsive controls, creating a convincing sense of downhill motion. The soundtrack by Arti Haroutunian adds atmosphere and energy to each run, enhancing the intensity of the race. While simple by modern standards, Slalom! was an impressive early sports title that showcased what the C64 could deliver in terms of speed and fluid movement.

video:video.video:title: Slicks – Did Codemasters Save One of the C64’s Best Racers Until 1992?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 by Digital Design and published by Codemasters for the Commodore 64, Slicks is a fast-paced overhead Formula One racing game designed by Ashley Routledge and David Saunders, with music composed by Allister Brimble. It delivers an arcade-driven racing experience that pushes the C64 hard in its later years. Players choose from six racing teams, each with different performance characteristics, and compete across circuits inspired by real-world Formula 1 tracks. The focus is on speed, precision, and maintaining control through tight corners while jostling for position against rival cars. While the handling is immediate and accessible, Slicks adds a strategic layer through fuel consumption and tyre wear. Knowing when to push hard and when to drive conservatively becomes key to finishing races successfully, especially over longer events. The game is widely praised for its smooth scrolling, responsive controls, and energetic presentation.

video:video.video:title: Smash T.V. – Cash, Prizes and a Deadly Twin-Stick Game Show | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Ocean Software and developed by Probe Software, Smash T. V. brings the explosive Williams arcade hit to the Commodore 64. Set in a dystopian future where ultra-violent game shows rule television, you step into a deadly arena battling for cash, prizes, and survival. The action is relentless. Enemies pour in from all directions across compact, multi-directional arenas, demanding constant movement and sharp reactions. While the C64 lacks dual-stick controls, the conversion smartly adapts movement and firing to joystick directions, delivering fast, playable combat that keeps the pressure high. Pickups such as cash, televisions, and toasters litter the arena, rewarding aggressive play and risk-taking. Despite 8-bit limitations, the game impresses with large sprites, smooth scrolling, and satisfying explosions that capture the arcade’s intensity. Driven by Jonathan Dunn’s punchy soundtrack, Smash T. V.

video:video.video:title: Soccer Boss – Manage the Club, Balance the Books and Chase Promotion | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Alternative Software and developed by Peaksoft, Soccer Boss is a deep football management simulation from the early days of the genre. Originally titled The Boss and later rebranded as Champions! , it focuses entirely on the pressures and decisions of life off the pitch. You take control of a struggling club with the long-term goal of climbing through the divisions and reaching the top of European football. Squad building, tactical choices, and transfer negotiations are central, with finances playing a constant role as you balance wages, gate receipts, and unexpected off-field events. Matches unfold through text-based commentary rather than live action, shifting the emphasis firmly onto strategy and planning. Results, scorers, and league progression reflect the decisions you make behind the scenes, reinforcing the manager-first design. On the Commodore 64, Soccer Boss stands out for its accessible menus and surprising depth.

video:video.video:title: Son of Blagger – Did the C64 Sequel Make Blagger Even Harder?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Alligata Software and developed by Tony Crowther, Son of Blagger is the sequel to the original Blagger and expands the formula into a more demanding scrolling platform experience. Players control Slippery Sid, the son of the infamous burglar, on a mission to collect keys scattered across a large, interconnected landscape. Unlike the single-screen design of its predecessor, the game features continuous scrolling levels that require careful planning and precise movement. Sid must navigate complex platforms, avoid robotic enemies, and manage risky jumps, with long falls and instant-death hazards keeping tension high throughout each stage. The challenge is relentless, as all keys must be collected within a time limit to progress. Route choice and timing are critical, rewarding players who memorise layouts and master movement. The difficulty curve is steep, but it’s this uncompromising design that gives the game its lasting appeal.

video:video.video:title: Southern Belle – Could You Drive a Steam Train from London to Brighton on C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Hewson Consultants for the Commodore 64, Southern Belle is a pioneering train simulation programmed by Mike Male and Bob Hillyer during the height of the 8-bit era. It stands out as one of the earliest serious attempts to recreate the operation of a real steam locomotive on a home computer. Players take on the demanding roles of both driver and fireman aboard a King Arthur class steam passenger locomotive, tasked with completing the famous journey from London Victoria to Brighton. Success depends on carefully managing speed, coal, water levels and braking while keeping to a strict timetable and avoiding derailment. The game uses a first-person, vector-style presentation and focuses on measured control rather than arcade reflexes. Multiple levels of complexity allow players to observe automated runs or take full command of the locomotive, balancing realism with accessibility on limited C64 hardware.

video:video.video:title: Space Harrier – The C64 Somehow Got TWO Different Versions of Sega’s Arcade Hit
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Elite Systems for the Commodore 64, Space Harrier is the home computer adaptation of Sega’s groundbreaking 1985 arcade hit, developed by Sega AM2 using “Super Scaler” technology. Players control Harri as he flies through the surreal world of Dragonland, battling waves of enemies and gigantic bosses using fast-paced shooting and evasive movement. The gameplay centres on constant motion, reflexes, and precise positioning. The C64 version delivers a scaled-down interpretation of the arcade’s pseudo-3D visuals, adapting the experience to 8-bit hardware while preserving the game’s core intensity and pace. Two regional versions were released. The European version features flat terrain and simplified scrolling, while the North American release adds raster effects to simulate movement and includes alternative graphics and sound. Despite technical limitations, the game captures much of the arcade original’s energy.

video:video.video:title: Space Hulk – Freeze Time Before the Genestealers Reach You on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Electronic Arts for the Commodore Amiga, Space Hulk is a tense real-time tactical game set in the dark, brutal universe of Warhammer 40,000. Based on Games Workshop’s 1989 board game, it places players in command of elite Space Marine squads sent into derelict spacecraft infested with deadly Genestealers. Gameplay blends first-person action with strategic squad management. Players control up to five Space Marines simultaneously, each viewed through their own 3D window, while coordinating movement, positioning, and firepower through narrow, claustrophobic corridors. Missions range from extermination and escort duties to data retrieval and object recovery. A key feature is the innovative “freeze-time” system, which allows players to pause the action briefly to issue commands. This mechanic adds vital tactical depth, letting players react to sudden ambushes and carefully plan defensive formations under pressure.

video:video.video:title: Space Taxi – Why C64 Owners Still Remember “Hey Taxi!”
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Muse Software and developed by John F. Kutcher, Space Taxi is a distinctive action-platform game for the Commodore 64 that blends precise flying with light arcade strategy. Players take control of a futuristic flying taxi, tasked with safely transporting passengers between floating platforms across a series of increasingly demanding levels. The core challenge lies in mastering the taxi’s thrusters and landing gear. Smooth take-offs and gentle landings are rewarded with tips, while crashes, fuel waste, and rough handling can quickly end a run. Each of the game’s 24 stages introduces new hazards, including moving platforms, tight caverns, environmental traps, and altered gravity conditions. Space Taxi is especially remembered for its groundbreaking use of digitised speech on the C64. Calls like “Hey taxi!” , “Pad one please”, and “Up please” gave the game a lively personality and helped it stand out immediately on release.

video:video.video:title: Spartacus: The Swordslayer – The C64 Gladiator Game Nobody Remembers
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Players Software and developed by Ian Potts, Spartacus: The Swordslayer is a side-view fighting game that drops you into the brutal arenas of ancient Rome. You take on the role of Spartacus, battling your way through a series of deadly one-on-one encounters in pursuit of freedom. Combat focuses on sword-and-shield fighting, with careful timing needed to attack, block, and reposition against increasingly tough opponents. The game stands out for its large character sprites and varied enemy types, ranging from rival gladiators to Roman soldiers determined to bring your rebellion to an end. To break up the arena duels, Spartacus throws in unusual set pieces such as dodging volleys of arrows and surviving an encounter with a swooping eagle. These moments add variety, even if the controls and collision detection can feel unforgiving at times.

video:video.video:title: Speedball 2 – Why This Amiga Sports Game Still Has No Equal
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by The Bitmap Brothers, Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe is one of the most iconic and fully realised sports games of the 16-bit era. Set in the brutal cyber-future of 2105, it transforms competitive sport into a fast, violent spectacle where precision, tactics, and aggression are equally important. You control a team of nine cybernetic athletes in a high-speed arena sport that blends handball-style scoring with the physical intensity of ice hockey. Matches are frantic and unforgiving, with players smashing into opponents, stealing the ball, and triggering devastating power-ups that can swing momentum in seconds. Success depends not just on reflexes, but on team management, upgrades, and knowing when to play dirty. The Amiga version is widely regarded as definitive, delivering smooth scrolling, sharp visuals, and an intense sense of speed. The atmosphere is elevated by Nation 12’s driving soundtrack, which perfectly matches the game’s cold, industrial tone.

video:video.video:title: Spellbound – The C64 Adventure Where Your Characters Could Starve to Death
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Mastertronic under the Added Dimension label, Spellbound is a graphic adventure developed by David Jones and the second entry in the Magic Knight series. Picking up after the rescue of the wizard Gimbal, the story transports Magic Knight to a strange and dangerous castle filled with puzzles, characters, and hidden dangers. Gameplay is driven by the Windimation system, a menu-based interface that allows players to interact with objects and characters in a structured but flexible way. Exploration and problem-solving take centre stage, with progress tied to logical thinking rather than fast reactions. As Magic Knight explores the castle, players must manage energy and health while uncovering clues, solving environmental puzzles, and dealing with the castle’s inhabitants. Each area introduces new challenges, encouraging careful observation and experimentation. The Commodore 64 version is enhanced by a memorable soundtrack from Rob Hubbard, which adds atmosphere and tension to the game’s detailed locations.

video:video.video:title: Spelunker – The C64 Explorer Who Could Die from the Tiniest Fall
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Timothy G. Martin and published by Brøderbund Software, with the Commodore 64 version distributed in Europe by Ariolasoft, Spelunker is infamous for its unforgiving difficulty and remarkably fragile hero. Few games on the C64 punish carelessness quite like this one. The goal is to descend deep into a sprawling multi-level cave system while collecting keys, treasure, bombs, and flares, all under constant pressure from a limited air supply. Hazards are everywhere, from deadly traps and roaming ghosts to sheer drops where even the smallest fall results in instant death. Every movement demands patience, precision, and absolute caution. Progression relies on mastering elevators, ropes, ladders, and careful item use as you work through six increasingly dangerous stages. The Commodore 64 version delivers smooth scrolling, colourful cave environments, atmospheric sound effects, and an eerie soundtrack that reinforces the sense of isolation and danger.

video:video.video:title: Spiky Harold – Eat Enough Food to Hibernate Before Winter Arrives | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Firebird Software and developed by Andrew Rogers, Spiky Harold is a distinctive single-screen platform adventure for the Commodore 64. You take control of Harold the hedgehog, who must gather enough food to survive hibernation while navigating an underground maze of interconnected screens. The game spans 57 linked areas beneath a hedgerow, each filled with hazards, collectables, and routes that demand careful planning. Food keeps Harold going, coins earn extra lives, and enemies such as wasps, rodents, and drifting sulfur clouds constantly threaten progress. A unique twist comes from the wine glasses scattered throughout the maze. If Harold drinks one, he becomes drunk, making movement unpredictable and turning simple platforming into a risky balancing act. This mechanic adds humour while increasing the challenge at exactly the wrong moment. All of this unfolds against a 24-hour in-game clock, pushing you to memorise routes and move efficiently rather than wandering aimlessly.

video:video.video:title: Spitting Image – Thatcher, Reagan and Gorbachev Settle Politics with Fists | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Domark and developed by Walking Circles, Spitting Image: The Computer Game brings the anarchic British TV satire to the Commodore 64 in the form of a one-on-one fighting game. Inspired by the show’s infamous puppets, it throws global politics into the arena with exaggerated caricatures and unapologetic humour. You can choose from six world leaders, each battling opponents across stages themed around their home countries. Matches play out over three rounds, with basic punches, kicks, and the ability to summon a helper mid-fight, adding a tactical twist to the otherwise straightforward combat. The focus is firmly on satire rather than technical depth. Controls and mechanics are simple, but the exaggerated sprites and familiar faces do the main work, leaning into parody and shock value rather than precision fighting. While opinions were divided on release, Spitting Image stands out as one of the most unusual licensed games on the C64.

video:video.video:title: Split Personalities – Rebuild Famous Faces Before the Clock Beats You | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Domark and developed by Ernieware, Split Personalities is a clever and addictive sliding puzzle game that tasks you with rebuilding the faces of famous figures piece by piece. Played on a 5×5 grid, the goal is to restore each portrait before the clock runs out. Using a flashing cursor, you slide individual pieces into position while referencing a miniature preview of the completed image, which also highlights the active tile. The puzzles feature recognisable personalities including Ronald Reagan, Margaret Thatcher, Marilyn Monroe, and Mick Jagger, adding a playful hook to the brain-teasing challenge. As you progress, the game introduces hazards such as gaps that swallow pieces, bombs that must be pushed off-screen to avoid losing lives, and bonus objects that reward precise movement. These twists elevate the puzzles beyond simple tile-sliding and demand forward planning as well as speed.

video:video.video:title: Spy Hunter – The C64 Spy Car That Could Suddenly Turn into a Speedboat
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64, Spy Hunter is a high-speed vehicular combat game originally developed by Bally Midway and inspired by the style and swagger of classic spy thrillers. You take control of the G-6155 Interceptor, a heavily armed spy car tasked with eliminating enemy agents while keeping innocent civilian traffic intact. Gameplay blends fast driving with precision shooting as the road scrolls relentlessly forward. You’ll deploy machine guns, oil slicks, smoke screens, and missiles, upgrading your loadout mid-run via the iconic weapons van. Success depends on sharp reactions, careful positioning, and knowing when to attack or evade. The Commodore 64 version captures the tension and pace of the arcade original, supported by the instantly recognisable Peter Gunn theme that kicks in as the action heats up. Its clean design and focused mechanics keep the challenge intense without unnecessary complexity.

video:video.video:title: Spy vs. Spy – The C64 Game Built Around Ruining Your Mate’s Day
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by First Star Software for the Commodore 64, Spy vs. Spy brings the anarchic rivalry of the MAD Magazine comic strip to life. You face off as the Black or White Spy in a frantic race to outwit your opponent, gather secret items, and escape the embassy before time runs out. Gameplay is built around exploration, memory, and deception. You search rooms for essential items like passports, money, secret plans, and the all-important airport key, while laying traps to sabotage your rival’s progress. Every mistake costs precious seconds, especially when a deadly trap sends your spy floating off as an angel. The split-screen design keeps both players constantly visible, turning every match into a tense battle of nerves and timing. Traps, bluffing, and last-second reversals create moments of genuine comedy, perfectly capturing the humour and style of Antonio Prohías’ original comic.

video:video.video:title: Spy vs Spy II: The Island Caper – Traps, Treachery and Two-Player Revenge on C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by First Star Software for the Commodore 64, Spy vs. Spy II: The Island Caper expands on the original’s devious formula by moving the action to a dangerous tropical island. You play as either the Black Spy or the White Spy, locked in a race to outwit your rival and escape before disaster strikes. This time, the island scrolls horizontally, opening up the world and introducing new hazards such as quicksand, sharks, and deadly terrain. Your goal is to locate three missile parts hidden across the island, assemble them, and escape via submarine before a volcano erupts. Strategy plays a bigger role thanks to the ability to craft traps using materials found in the environment. Careful planning, timing, and misdirection are just as important as speed, especially when laying traps for your opponent.

video:video.video:title: Spy vs Spy III: Arctic Antics – The C64 Feud That Froze Both Spies Solid
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 for the Commodore 64, Spy vs Spy III: Arctic Antics is the third entry in First Star Software’s classic series inspired by MAD Magazine’s iconic comic strip. This time, the Black Spy and White Spy trade tropical islands for the freezing Arctic, where survival is as important as sabotage. The goal remains familiar: assemble a rocket by locating a Gyroscope, Fuel Canister, and Key Card before your rival does. The icy setting introduces new challenges, including managing body heat, navigating slippery terrain, and avoiding traps hidden beneath the snow. Players must balance exploration with constant interference from the opposing spy. New tools and mechanics add extra depth and humour, such as snowball fights, snowshoes, ice picks, and the plunger detonator. Levels are presented as flip-screen environments with snowy exteriors and warmer interiors like igloos, which provide both shelter and tactical advantages.

video:video.video:title: Stairways – The C64 Pub Game with Drunken Hallucinations
video:video.video:description: Stairways (1985), developed and published by Thor Computer Software, is a quirky and highly distinctive action-shooter for the Commodore 64, set almost entirely inside a chaotic pub. You play as a bar patron on a mission to collect seven fragments of the legendary amulet of the great budgie WONGA — all while trying to avoid being thrown out by the doorman. Gameplay takes place in a side-view scrolling environment where you must balance three key attributes: energy, hunger, and drunkenness. Hallucinations drain your energy, spilled drinks anger staff, and sobering up makes defending yourself more difficult. To survive, you can return to the bar to get more intoxicated, grab food from a burger kiosk, and carefully manage your condition while shooting “thought bubble” enemies. Each level is timed, adding extra pressure to collect all amulet pieces before advancing.

video:video.video:title: Star Wars – Atari’s Vector Death Star Run Rebuilt for the C64 in 1988
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Domark and developed by Vektor Grafix, Star Wars for the Commodore 64 brings the legendary Battle of Yavin to home computers. Inspired by Atari’s iconic arcade machine, this version reimagines the experience within the limits of the C64 while aiming to preserve the feel and structure of the original. The game is split into three distinct sequences. First, players engage in a space battle against swarms of TIE Fighters defending the Death Star. This is followed by a surface assault, flying low across the station while avoiding obstacles and targeting defensive emplacements. The final and most memorable section is the trench run, where precision flying and sharp reflexes are required to survive enemy fire and line up the decisive shot into the exhaust port. While the C64 cannot reproduce true vector graphics, the game’s presentation captures the spirit of the arcade with fast-paced, forward-scrolling action.

video:video.video:title: Star Wars: Droids – R2-D2 and C-3PO’s 1980s Cartoon Became a C64 Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Mastertronic and developed by Binary Design, Star Wars: Droids is a side-scrolling platform game inspired by the animated TV series that followed the adventures of R2-D2 and C-3PO. Rather than retelling the films, the game draws from the lighter, episodic tone of the show, placing the droids in a fresh series of perilous situations. Players guide R2-D2 and C-3PO through multiple levels as they attempt to evade the Fromm Gang. Progress relies on careful movement, timing, and puzzle-solving, with traps, hostile droids, and environmental hazards constantly blocking the way. Success often depends on observation and planning rather than speed alone. The game’s presentation makes strong use of detailed pixel art to convey recognisable Star Wars locations and characters within the limits of the Commodore 64. Its soundtrack supports the atmosphere and helps reinforce the identity of the animated series rather than the cinematic saga.

video:video.video:title: Stardust – The Amiga Asteroids Game That Looked Years Ahead in 1993
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Bloodhouse for the Commodore Amiga, Stardust is a spectacular reimagining of the classic arcade hit Asteroids, created by a Finnish development team determined to push the system to its limits. Players pilot a sleek spacecraft through dangerous asteroid fields and enemy-filled zones, blasting rocks and hostile ships across smooth multi-directional scrolling levels. The game introduces advanced power-ups, boss encounters, and high-speed tunnel sequences, adding depth and variety far beyond traditional arcade shooters. Progress depends on mastering tight controls, managing weapon upgrades, and reacting quickly to dense enemy patterns and environmental hazards. Visually, Stardust is renowned for its real-time ray-traced graphics, impressive particle effects, and smooth scaling animations that showcased the Amiga’s technical power. Its pounding techno soundtrack and atmospheric audio design further enhance the sense of speed and intensity. The combination of cutting-edge presentation and refined gameplay earned Stardust widespread critical acclaim.

video:video.video:title: Starquake – 512 Screens Inside One Dying Planet on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Bubble Bus Software and developed by Stephen Crow, Starquake is an ambitious action-adventure platform game for the Commodore 64. Players control BLOB (Bio-Logically Operated Being), a robotic explorer sent to stabilise a rogue planet whose unstable core threatens to trigger a devastating starquake. The game is built around exploration across a vast world of 512 interconnected screens, each presenting unique layouts, hazards, and hostile alien life. BLOB can walk, shoot, and deploy temporary platforms, allowing players to traverse complex terrain while carefully managing positioning and movement. Progress depends on exploration and problem-solving rather than simple reflexes. Players collect and carry items needed to repair the planet’s core, making inventory management and route planning essential to survival. The environment itself feels alive, filled with remnants of a long-lost civilisation and dangerous native creatures.

video:video.video:title: Stormbringer – How Did the Magic Knight Saga End on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Mastertronic under the M. A. D. (Mastertronic Added Dimension) label, Stormbringer is a fantasy adventure game for the Commodore 64 developed by David Jones. It serves as the fourth and final entry in the Magic Knight series, following Finders Keepers, Spellbound, and Knight Tyme, while shifting the formula toward a more action-focused arcade-adventure style. The story centres on Magic Knight facing his own evil alter ego, the Off-White Knight, also known as Stormbringer. A time travel accident has created this destructive duplicate, and the only way to restore balance is for Magic Knight to confront and ultimately merge with his darker self. This narrative twist gives the game a more personal and dramatic tone than earlier entries in the series. Gameplay takes place across 64 interconnected screens filled with hazards, puzzles, and environmental challenges.

video:video.video:title: Street Fighter – How Bad Was the First Street Fighter on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Capcom and ported to the Commodore 64 by Tiertex, Street Fighter marks the very beginning of one of gaming’s most influential fighting franchises. Players step into the role of Ryu, travelling across the world to face a series of martial artists in traditional one-on-one combat. The gameplay centres on close-range battles using punches, kicks, and signature special moves including the Hadouken and Shoryuken. Each location introduces a new opponent with distinct fighting styles, building towards a final confrontation with Sagat. Timing, spacing, and stamina management are key to surviving each bout. On the Commodore 64, the game presents a simplified take on the arcade original. Visuals and sound are scaled back, animations are limited, and control responsiveness can feel stiff, yet the core structure of the fights and the global tournament concept remain intact.

video:video.video:title: Street Hassle – The C64 Beat ’Em Up That Was Anything but Polite
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987, developed by Beam Software and published by Melbourne House, Street Hassle is a side-scrolling beat ’em up that takes the usual street-fighting formula and makes it considerably stranger. Your job is simple enough: walk through the city and deal with anybody foolish enough to get in your way. The opposition, however, is anything but ordinary. Alongside the expected street thugs you’ll encounter gorillas, towering basketball players, dogs, motorcyclists and elderly ladies armed with handbags. Combat gives you a surprisingly varied selection of attacks, with punches, kicks and some decidedly unconventional moves available as you work your way through each stage. There’s also a two-player option, with players taking turns to tackle the streets. Street Hassle was developed by Australian studio Beam Software and was also released under the names Bop ’N Rumble and Bad Street Brawler in other territories.

video:video.video:title: Strider – Could Tiertex Really Bring Capcom’s Arcade Hit to the C64?
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Capcom and released to home computers in 1989 by U. S. Gold, Strider brings futuristic arcade action to the Commodore 64. Players step into the role of Strider Hiryu, a high-tech ninja sent to dismantle a ruthless regime in a dystopian sci-fi world. Gameplay centres on fast-paced side-scrolling action, combining sword combat with acrobatic movement. Wall climbing, precision jumps, and quick reactions are essential as enemies attack from all directions and hazards fill the screen. The emphasis is firmly on momentum and timing rather than exploration. The Commodore 64 version, programmed by Paul Cole, delivers its own take on the arcade original, adapting the experience to the system’s limitations while retaining the core mechanics. Visuals by Andrew Ingram and James Clark push the hardware with detailed sprites and varied environments, while Mark Tait’s music adds tension and atmosphere throughout the mission.

video:video.video:title: Strip Poker – Be Honest… Were You Really Playing the C64 Version for the Poker?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Artworx Software Company for the Commodore 64, Strip Poker: A Sizzling Game of Chance is a card-based strategy title that blends traditional poker mechanics with novelty-driven presentation. Viewed from a first-person perspective, the game places players at the table against computer-controlled opponents in a straightforward game of five-card draw. Gameplay follows standard poker rules, with players wagering virtual money and relying on hand strength, bluffing, and betting decisions to gain the upper hand. Successful rounds trigger visual progression tied to each opponent, giving the game a clear win–reward structure that goes beyond simple score-chasing. Multiple characters are featured, each with their own reactions and pacing. Technically modest but conceptually distinctive, the game reflects an era when home computers experimented with niche and adult-oriented themes alongside more conventional genres. Its appeal was rooted less in complexity and more in novelty, helping it stand out among early C64 card games.

video:video.video:title: Strontium Dog and the Death Gauntlet – Johnny Alpha Hunts the Stix Brothers on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Quicksilva and developed by Stephen R. Kellett for the Commodore 64, Strontium Dog and the Death Gauntlet brings the world of 2000AD to home computers. Based on the popular comic series, the game stars mutant bounty hunter Johnny Alpha as he battles across a hostile alien landscape in search of his companions, Wulf and Gronk.
