Gameplay is presented as a horizontally scrolling shooter, with players guiding Johnny through dangerous terrain packed with enemies and lethal plant life. Armed with a blaster, electro-flares, and time-bombs, success depends on careful positioning and knowing when to engage or evade. A strength meter adds an extra layer of tension, draining when Johnny takes damage or increases speed. The game includes multiple difficulty levels and a radar display to track progress toward the rendezvous point, encouraging repeated attempts and mastery of its mechanics.

video:video.video:title: Stunt Car Racer – How Did Geoff Crammond Pull Off 3D Racing on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by MicroStyle and developed by Geoff Crammond, Stunt Car Racer is a landmark 3D racing game that pushed the Commodore 64 far beyond expectations. Featuring elevated tracks suspended high above the ground, the game delivers white-knuckle races packed with jumps, narrow turns, and dramatic drop-offs. Players take control of a powerful V8-powered car fitted with a roll cage and turbo boost, competing one-on-one against rival drivers in a league-based structure. Winning races earns points and promotion through divisions, while crashes, rollovers, and falling from the track result in punishing time penalties that can quickly turn victory into defeat. Success depends on precise steering, throttle control, and learning when to push for speed or back off to avoid disaster. The game’s physics-driven handling gives every bump and landing real weight, making each track feel tense and unpredictable.

video:video.video:title: Summer Games – The C64 Classic That Started Epyx’s Greatest Series
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Epyx, Summer Games is a landmark title that helped define the multi-event sports genre on the Commodore 64. Inspired by the unreleased Starpath game Sweat! , it became the first entry in Epyx’s celebrated Games series and set the template for everything that followed. You compete across a range of Olympic-style events including the 100m sprint, pole vault, platform diving, gymnastics, freestyle swimming, and skeet shooting. Each discipline has its own rhythm and control style, rewarding timing, coordination, and practice rather than button-mashing. The game supports up to eight players, each representing a chosen country, making it perfect for competitive multiplayer sessions. Events can be played individually, selected freely, or tackled as a full tournament with medals awarded for top performances. A major step forward for Epyx, Summer Games was one of the first titles to feature a dedicated graphics designer, helping elevate presentation and polish.

video:video.video:title: Summer Games II – Eight More Events, from Triple Jump to Kayaking | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Epyx, Summer Games II expands on the success of the original by delivering a broader and more varied Olympic-style competition on the Commodore 64. It refines the multi-event formula with new disciplines and a strong focus on competitive play. You can take part in eight events including triple jump, high jump, rowing, javelin, equestrian, fencing, kayaking, and cycling. Each event has its own rhythm and control style, rewarding timing, coordination, and practice. The game supports up to eight players, each representing a different country, making it ideal for competitive multiplayer sessions. Presentation plays a big role, with smooth animations, detailed backdrops, and a lively soundtrack that adds momentum to each event. Opening and closing ceremonies featuring fireworks and a blimp help sell the Olympic atmosphere and give the competition a celebratory feel.

video:video.video:title: Super Cars II – The Amiga Racer Where Winning Meant Blowing Up Your Rivals
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991, Super Cars II was developed by Magnetic Fields and published by Gremlin Graphics, expanding on the formula of the original Super Cars with faster action, deeper strategy, and sharper presentation. Designed for the Amiga and other 16-bit platforms, it blends arcade racing with combat and progression systems that keep each championship unpredictable. Gameplay is built around a season-based championship where players race against colourful rivals with tongue-in-cheek names such as Ayrton Sendup and T Hairy Bootson. Tracks span a variety of environments, including snow, grass, and rocky terrain, each influencing grip and handling. Winning races earns cash, which can be spent in the garage on repairs, speed upgrades, and offensive weapons. Combat plays a major role, with missiles, mines, and other gadgets turning every race into a tactical battle. Track layouts feature ramps, shortcuts, and hazards such as trains, rewarding bold driving and quick reactions.

video:video.video:title: Super Cycle – Could Epyx Bring Hang-On Speed to the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Epyx for the Commodore 64, Super Cycle is a high-speed motorcycle racing game inspired by Sega’s arcade hit Hang-On. It delivers an intense sense of speed and urgency as players race against the clock across a variety of challenging courses. The game is presented from a behind-the-bike perspective, allowing players to lean into corners, weave through traffic, and react quickly to changing track conditions. This viewpoint enhances immersion and makes every race feel fast, fluid, and demanding. Players can select from multiple skill levels, each adjusting the available time limits and bonus rewards. As the game progresses, tracks become increasingly complex, introducing hazards such as oil slicks and rival riders that require sharp reflexes and precise control. Super Cycle stands out for its responsive handling, smooth scrolling, and effective use of simple yet expressive graphics to convey speed.

video:video.video:title: Super Gran: The Adventure – Did the Classic TV Heroine Work on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Tynesoft and developed by Brian Howarth, Super Gran: The Adventure brings the popular British children’s TV series to the Commodore 64 as a graphic text adventure. Set in the town of Chisleton, players step into the role of the super-powered grandmother as she sets out to stop her long-time foe, Scunner Campbell. The story revolves around a series of thefts from the local museum and Town Hall. Players must explore Chisleton, recover stolen items, and piece together clues by moving between locations, examining objects, and interacting with characters using text commands. Gameplay combines static illustrated scenes with descriptive text, presenting each location visually while allowing traditional adventure-style input. Puzzle solving and logical exploration drive progress, staying true to the structure of classic 1980s graphic adventures. While opinions at the time were mixed, Super Gran: The Adventure is remembered today for its faithful adaptation and unmistakably British humour.

video:video.video:title: Super Gridder – The Early C64 Arcade Game Inspired by Amidar
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Terminal Software for the Commodore 64, Super Gridder is a minimalist arcade-style puzzle game developed and programmed by R. W. Stevens. Also published by Microdigital Ltd. , it delivers a deceptively simple concept built around precision, timing, and risk management. Gameplay takes place on a single 8×8 grid where players control a character tracing the grid’s boundaries. Successfully enclosing a square fills it in, pushing you closer to completion, but danger lurks within the grid itself. Scorpions roam the interior, and a single touch costs a life, forcing careful planning and steady movement. The challenge comes from balancing speed and accuracy under constant time pressure. Complete the grid before the timer expires to earn bonus points, but rush too much and mistakes can quickly end a run. Every movement matters, turning simple line-drawing into a tense arcade puzzle.

video:video.video:title: Super Pipeline – Protect the Workmen While Everything Bursts on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Taskset and developed by Andy Walker, Super Pipeline is a distinctive puzzle-action game that tasks players with keeping an industrial pipe network running under constant threat. Taking on the role of a pipe foreman, players must prevent leaks, fend off enemies, and coordinate repairs before the system collapses. Gameplay revolves around navigating the pipe layout, shooting hostile creatures that cause damage, and directing workers to fix leaks as they appear. The challenge escalates as pressure builds, enemy behaviour becomes more aggressive, and multiple faults demand attention at once, rewarding quick thinking and efficient movement. On the Commodore 64, Super Pipeline delivers bold, colourful visuals and a catchy soundtrack composed by Paul Hodgson, helping maintain tension as the action intensifies. Its blend of arcade reflexes and strategic prioritisation set it apart from more straightforward shooters of the era.

video:video.video:title: Super Robin Hood – The Oliver Twins’ Forgotten C64 Platform Adventure
video:video.video:description: Super Robin Hood (1987) is a medieval-themed platform game for the Commodore 64, published by Codemasters and designed by the Oliver Twins, with programming by Delvin J. Sorrell and graphics by James Wilson. Featuring an energetic soundtrack by David Whittaker, the game casts you as Robin Hood on a quest to rescue Maid Marian from Nottingham Castle. You progress through scrolling levels, dodging guards, firing arrows, collecting hearts to restore health, and gathering keys that activate lifts and open new areas. The game is praised for its responsive controls, engaging platform mechanics, and memorable 8-bit soundtrack. As the first Codemasters title by the Oliver Twins, it marked the beginning of a legendary developer–publisher partnership. Super Robin Hood holds an important place in Commodore 64 history and remains a much-loved example of classic British platform design.

video:video.video:title: Super Trolley – The C64 Supermarket Game Born from a Jim’ll Fix It Wish
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Mastertronic and developed by Icon Design Ltd. , Super Trolley is one of the most unusual simulation games to appear on the Commodore 64. Inspired by a wish granted on BBC’s Jim’ll Fix It, the original idea came from eight-year-old Andrew Collett, who imagined a game about the everyday realities of working in a supermarket. Viewed from an isometric perspective, you take on the role of a supermarket employee tasked with stocking shelves, labelling goods, collecting stray trolleys, and keeping the store running smoothly. Each working day is timed, and failure to complete your duties efficiently can result in being fired. The aim is to perform well enough to earn promotions across six in-game days, eventually working your way up to store manager. With over 30 different grocery items to handle and multiple store sections to navigate, the game turns mundane retail work into a surprisingly demanding test of organisation and time management.

video:video.video:title: Superfrog – Was Team17’s Amiga Platformer as Good as We Remember?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Team17 for the Commodore Amiga, Superfrog is a colourful side-scrolling platformer that became one of the defining titles of the platform’s golden era. Players control a young prince transformed into a frog by an evil witch, setting out on a quest to rescue his kidnapped princess. The adventure spans six themed worlds, each packed with enemies, hazards, and hidden secrets. Gameplay focuses on precise jumping, projectile attacks, and item collection, including wings for gliding and Lucozade for restoring health. A unique slot machine system allows players to gamble collected credits for bonuses, passwords, and extra lives. One of the game’s standout features is the hidden “Project-F” bonus level, a side-scrolling shoot-’em-up tribute to Team17’s Project-X, adding variety and surprise to the adventure. Visually, Superfrog is renowned for its vibrant colour palette, fluid animation, and smooth scrolling.

video:video.video:title: Switchblade – The C64 Adventure That Sent Hiro into the Deadly Undercity
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Gremlin Graphics for the Commodore 64, Switchblade is an ambitious action-platform adventure that casts you as Hiro, the last surviving Bladeknight warrior. Your mission is to explore the dangerous Undercity, recover the 16 scattered fragments of the legendary Fireblade, and defeat the evil entity Havok. Gameplay focuses on deep exploration across interconnected, multi-screen labyrinths filled with ladders, platforms, traps, and hostile creatures. Players must carefully navigate each area, uncover hidden routes, and collect weapon upgrades and bonus items to survive increasingly dangerous encounters. Progression relies on memory, observation, and precise movement, as new abilities and equipment gradually open up previously unreachable areas. The game blends arcade-style combat with exploration elements, creating a rewarding sense of discovery as the world slowly unfolds. Visually, Switchblade stands out with its distinctive NES-style presentation, detailed environments, and polished animated intro and title screen.

video:video.video:title: S.W.I.V. – Helicopter or Jeep? The C64 Shooter Built for Two
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 for the Commodore 64, S. W. I. V. (Space War: Invasion Force) is a fast-paced vertical scrolling shooter originally developed by Atari Games and ported by The Sales Curve. Players take control of an advanced combat jet tasked with repelling a large-scale alien invasion across hostile territory. The gameplay focuses on relentless forward momentum, heavy enemy waves, and precise positioning as players blast through scrolling levels packed with ground targets, airborne threats, and imposing boss encounters. Weapon upgrades and firepower management play a key role in surviving the escalating difficulty. S. W. I. V. stands out on the C64 for its large, detailed sprites and smooth vertical scrolling, pushing the hardware hard for the time. The action is backed by an energetic soundtrack that maintains intensity throughout, reinforcing the game’s arcade-style pacing and urgency.

video:video.video:title: Syndicate – Bullfrog Put You in Charge of a Cybernetic Hit Squad | Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Bullfrog Productions, Syndicate is a landmark cyberpunk strategy game set in a bleak future where megacorporations control the world through violence, surveillance, and technology. You command a squad of cybernetically enhanced agents, carrying out assassinations, sabotage, and corporate warfare across a global map of sprawling cityscapes. The game unfolds in real time from an isometric top-down view, blending tactical planning with fast, often brutal action. Missions demand careful positioning, weapon choice, and agent upgrades, while urban environments are filled with civilians, enemy operatives, and destructible surroundings that can quickly turn mayhem into opportunity. One of Syndicate’s defining features is the Persuadatron, a mind-control device that allows you to convert civilians and enemies into loyal followers. Used well, it can completely shift the balance of a mission, turning hostile cities into walking armies under your control.

video:video.video:title: System 15000 – The C64 Hacking Game That Came Before Activision’s Hacker
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Craig Communications and developed by A. V. S. for the Commodore 64, System 15000 is one of the earliest video games to realistically simulate computer hacking. Designed by Lee Kristofferson, the game places players in the role of a digital investigator tasked with recovering $1.5 million stolen from Comdata by the criminal organisation Realco. Armed with only a phone number and access code, players must dial into remote systems using a simulated modem interface, decipher passwords, analyse data, and bypass security protocols. Gameplay unfolds as a text-based adventure, carefully recreating the experience of early online computing. Dial tones, slow screen rendering, and realistic command prompts mirror the behaviour of 300-baud modems. Progress depends on logical thinking, careful note-taking, and understanding system structures rather than fast reflexes, making it a uniquely cerebral experience.

video:video.video:title: Tales of the Arabian Nights – The C64 Platformer That Actually Talked in 1984
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Interceptor Software for the Commodore 64, Tales of the Arabian Nights is a richly themed action-platformer created by Ian Gray, produced by Richard Paul Jones, and featuring music by Chris Cox. Players take on the role of Prince Imrahil, racing across eight exotic locations to rescue his sister Anitra from the evil Sultan Saladin. Levels range from Sinbad’s ship and palace gardens to underground caverns and fortified strongholds, delivering constant variety and escalating challenge. Gameplay alternates between single-screen platform stages and side-scrolling sequences, including raft journeys and flying carpet rides. In platform sections, players must collect golden jars spelling ARABIAN in the correct order, adding memory and precision to the action. During scrolling stages, enemies and hazards are tackled using magic lightning bolts, a feature unique to the Commodore 64 version.

video:video.video:title: Tapper – The Budweiser Arcade Game Built for Bars Came Home to the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64, Tapper is an arcade-style action game originally developed by Marvin Glass and Associates and brought to home systems with its fast, reflex-driven gameplay intact. You step behind the bar as a bartender under pressure, racing to keep an ever-growing crowd of thirsty customers satisfied. Gameplay is all about timing and multitasking. You must fill and slide drinks down the bar, catch empty glasses hurled back your way, and stop customers from reaching the end unserved. Every round demands sharper reactions as speed increases and multiple bars need attention at once. The game moves between themed locations including a Wild West saloon, beach bar, punk club, and futuristic space tavern, each adding visual flair and escalating difficulty. The Commodore 64 version captures the arcade’s energy with bright graphics and clear animations that keep the action easy to read even when things get frantic.

video:video.video:title: Target: Renegade – Why Did the C64 Lose the Two-Player Co-op?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Imagine Software under the Ocean label for the Commodore 64, Target: Renegade is a gritty side-scrolling beat ’em up and sequel to the original Renegade. Players step into the role of a lone street fighter on a mission to rescue his kidnapped brother, Matt, from the clutches of the crime lord Mr. Big. The game spans five varied stages set across urban streets, warehouses, docks, and industrial zones, each packed with aggressive enemies including bikers, thugs, and attack dogs. Combat is built around punches, kicks, flying attacks, and the use of improvised weapons such as baseball bats and pool cues found throughout the levels. Progression depends on mastering crowd control, positioning, and precise timing, as enemy numbers and aggression increase rapidly. Careful use of weapons and well-placed attacks becomes essential for surviving the later stages and reaching the final showdown.

video:video.video:title: Tau Ceti – The Remarkable 3D C64 Space Game That Was Years Ahead
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 and developed by Pete Cooke, Tau Ceti is a landmark science-fiction action-adventure published by CRL Group for the Commodore 64. Set on the distant planet Tau Ceti III, the game places you in control of a lone Gal-Corp pilot tasked with shutting down a rogue planetary defence system before it triggers a catastrophic meltdown. Gameplay centres on piloting a skimmer through vast hostile cities, battling robotic defenders while exploring complex urban environments. Progress depends on locating and assembling reactor cooling rods, managing limited fuel and ammunition, and making smart use of tools such as infrared vision, scanners, and flares to survive the planet’s dangers. What truly set Tau Ceti apart was its technical ambition. The game features solid 3D environments with shadow effects and a dynamic day-night cycle, creating a strong sense of scale and atmosphere that was astonishing on 8-bit hardware.

video:video.video:title: Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles – Did the Original Turtles Game Work on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 for the Commodore 64, Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles was developed by Unlimited Software Inc. and published by Ultra Software, bringing the hugely popular animated series to 8-bit home computers. Players take control of Leonardo, Donatello, Michelangelo, and Raphael as they battle through New York City to rescue April O’Neil and Splinter from the clutches of Shredder. The game blends overhead exploration with side-scrolling platform action, allowing players to switch between turtles and make use of their individual weapons and strengths. Streets, sewers, and interior locations are packed with enemies, hazards, and environmental challenges that demand careful character choice and smart resource management. Memorable sections include the notoriously tough underwater stages, vehicle sequences, and boss encounters against familiar villains from the series. Each turtle plays differently, adding a strategic layer as health, weapons, and positioning all influence survival.

video:video.video:title: Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles: The Coin-Op – Could the C64 Handle Konami’s Arcade Hit?
video:video.video:description: Released on the Commodore 64 in 1991, Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles: The Coin-Op brings Konami’s hugely popular arcade brawler into the home. Developed by Konami and converted by Ocean Software, the game lets players take control of Leonardo, Michelangelo, Donatello, or Raphael as they battle through the streets of New York to rescue April O’Neil and stop the Shredder. The gameplay closely follows the arcade original, focusing on side-scrolling beat ’em up action against waves of Foot Soldiers and familiar villains including Bebop and Rocksteady. Combat is fast and direct, rewarding positioning and timing as players punch, kick, and throw enemies across busy urban environments. On the Commodore 64, the game delivers colourful sprites and recognisable characters, with some simplification compared to the arcade machine but enough detail to preserve the look and feel of the original.

video:video.video:title: Terminator 2 – Fight the T-1000… Then Repair the T-800’s Wrist on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 for the Commodore 64, Terminator 2: Judgment Day is an action-heavy arcade shooter based on the blockbuster sci-fi film. Developed by Virgin Games and published by Ocean Software, it puts you in the role of the Terminator, fighting to protect John Connor while Skynet’s forces close in. Gameplay is split across several distinct sections, including a side-scrolling shooter, a high-speed driving sequence, and tense first-person shooting gallery stages. This variety keeps the pace moving and mirrors key moments from the film, even if the C64 version is necessarily scaled back from the arcade original. Despite the hardware limits, the game delivers smooth movement, solid enemy sprites, and a strong sense of momentum. The action feels fast and focused, with each section demanding different skills as you push through the levels. Allister Brimble’s atmospheric soundtrack adds real weight to the experience, driving the action forward and helping capture the darker, relentless tone of the movie.

video:video.video:title: Terror of the Deep – Explore Loch Ness in a Victorian Diving Bell on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Mirrorsoft for the Commodore 64, Terror of the Deep is an atmospheric first-person action-adventure set beneath the dark waters of Loch Ness in the late 19th century. Players take on the role of a submersible pilot investigating mysterious meteorite impacts and the sudden emergence of hostile alien lifeforms deep below the surface. The game is played entirely from the cockpit of a Victorian-era submersible, with hands-on control over navigation, lighting, power systems, and weapons. Progress depends on careful exploration, managing limited oxygen and energy reserves, and reacting quickly to threats lurking in the depths. Combat involves tools such as harpoons and electric defences, all while maintaining control of the vessel under pressure. Terror of the Deep builds tension through its moody presentation, using sound and sparse visuals to reinforce isolation and danger.

video:video.video:title: Thanatos – You’re a Dragon… But Lose the Sorceress and It’s Game Over on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Durell Software for the Commodore 64, Thanatos casts players as Thanatos the Destroyer, a colossal green dragon unleashed across a corrupted fantasy land. Your mission is to rescue the sorceress Eros, carry her safely across hostile terrain, and protect her as she performs the spell needed to cleanse the world of evil. Gameplay blends side-scrolling action with unusual mechanics that set it apart from typical shooters. Thanatos can breathe fire to incinerate enemies, grab and drop objects to crush foes or remove obstacles, and must carefully balance two vital resources: Flame and Heart. Flame powers attacks and can be replenished by consuming witches, while Heart represents the dragon’s life force and drains through damage or reckless high-speed flight. The game’s presentation is enhanced by parallax-scrolling landscapes and detailed dragon animation, giving the world a strong sense of scale and weight.

video:video.video:title: The Activision Decathlon – Before Button Mashing Became a Health Risk
video:video.video:description: The Activision Decathlon is the 1984 Commodore 64 conversion of Activision's athletics game, based on David Crane's original design. Up to four players can contest all ten events in sequence or practise them individually: the 100 metres, long jump, shot put, high jump, 400 metres, 110-metre hurdles, discus, pole vault, javelin and 1500 metres. Running events demand fast, steady joystick movement, while jumps and throws add a precisely timed fire-button press to set the angle or release point. Each performance earns points according to its time, height or distance, and the highest combined score wins the decathlon. The C64 edition retains the multiplayer rivalry and demanding physical controls that made the game famous, while adding colourful presentation, animated athletes and crowd effects suited to Commodore hardware.

video:video.video:title: The Adventures of Robin Hood – Was This Amiga Adventure Worth Revisiting?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Millennium Interactive for the Commodore Amiga, The Adventures of Robin Hood is an action-adventure title that brings the legendary outlaw to life through exploration, combat, and platform-based gameplay. Players take control of Robin as he navigates forests, castles, and medieval villages while battling the Sheriff of Nottingham’s guards using bows, arrows, swords, and careful positioning. The gameplay blends fast reflexes with thoughtful movement and light puzzle-solving. Levels are vertically layered and encourage exploration, rewarding players who master timing and enemy patterns. Combat and traversal are closely linked, making positioning just as important as raw skill. Visually, the game features detailed character sprites, atmospheric backgrounds, and a moody colour palette that reflects its medieval setting. Period-appropriate music and sound effects help reinforce the tone, while smooth scrolling keeps gameplay responsive. While many licensed games of the era were rushed, Robin Hood stands out as a thoughtfully designed title that makes good use of the Amiga’s hardware.

video:video.video:title: The Captive – Trapped in the Glen of Coloured Corpses on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in June 1985 by Mastertronic and developed by Nigel P. Johnstone, The Captive is a tense top-down action-adventure that blends exploration, puzzle-solving, and careful planning. From the creator of The Prisoner, it delivers an unsettling atmosphere and an unusual sense of vulnerability for a Commodore 64 title. The game is set on a mysterious island known as the Glen of Coloured Corpses. Players begin in a small town and must explore the surrounding areas in search of a way to escape. Progress is gated by colour-coded keys used to unlock doors scattered across the island, forcing players to think carefully about route planning and item usage. Inventory management plays a central role, with only three items carriable at any time. Objects range from practical tools like guns and shovels to stranger items such as mushrooms, scrolls, and even a helicopter.

video:video.video:title: The Castles of Dr. Creep – The C64 Puzzle Game Built Around Traps
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Brøderbund and created by Edward R. Hobbs, The Castles of Dr. Creep is a distinctive puzzle-platform game that challenges players to escape a series of devious medieval castles. Each of the thirteen castles is packed with traps, enemies, and mechanical contraptions designed to test logic and timing rather than reflexes alone. Gameplay focuses on experimentation and problem-solving. Players manipulate conveyor belts, force fields, switches, teleports, and other devices to open paths and avoid deadly hazards. Progress often requires understanding how multiple systems interact, encouraging careful observation and planning. Enemies such as mummies and Frankenstein-style monsters roam the castles, adding pressure to every move. The game also supports two-player cooperative play, allowing players to work together to solve puzzles and coordinate actions across different parts of a castle. Praised for its inventive design and depth, The Castles of Dr.

video:video.video:title: The Chaos Engine on Amiga – Does This Top-Down Shooter Still Hit Hard?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by The Bitmap Brothers, The mayhem Engine is a top-down run-and-gun action game set in a twisted steampunk version of Victorian Britain. A sentient machine has warped time and space, turning the population into hostile creatures, and a team of hired mercenaries is sent in to shut it down. You choose two characters from a roster of six, each with distinct weapons and abilities, and fight your way through four worlds made up of dense, enemy-filled levels. Progress requires careful movement, managing choke points, activating nodes, and uncovering hidden routes while enemies flood the screen from every direction. Gold collected during missions can be spent on upgrades, adding a strategic layer to the relentless action. Played solo or cooperatively, the game rewards coordination, positioning, and smart character choices as difficulty steadily ramps up.

video:video.video:title: The Dolphin’s Rune – Was This More Interactive Art Than C64 Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Mindscape for the Commodore 64 and developed by John O’Neill under the Admacadiam label, The Dolphin’s Rune: A Poetic Odyssey is a highly unconventional action-puzzle game that prioritises atmosphere and reflection over traditional arcade thrills. Designed as an interactive art experience, it stands apart from most titles of its era. Players take control of a dolphin swimming through a vast ocean environment, where survival depends on awareness and restraint rather than speed. Avoiding sharks, surfacing for air, and steering clear of dangerous fishing nets form the core challenges, encouraging slow, thoughtful exploration from the dolphin’s perspective. Progression is shaped by observation, rhythm, and environmental understanding. Instead of score-chasing or time pressure, the game rewards patience and immersion, inviting players to absorb its unusual tone and subtle mechanics. Visually, the game employs minimalist graphics that evoke the scale and emptiness of the open sea.

video:video.video:title: The Eidolon – Lucasfilm’s Strange C64 Cave Adventure Still Feels Alien
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Lucasfilm Games for the Commodore 64, The Eidolon is a pioneering first-person adventure that blends exploration, combat, and surreal science fantasy. Set in a mysterious, steampunk-inspired world, players discover a strange 19th-century machine and are transported into a vast network of otherworldly caves guarded by powerful creatures. Gameplay focuses on navigating fractal-generated labyrinths, collecting coloured energy orbs, and battling hostile enemies. Each orb provides unique abilities, such as freezing time, transforming foes, or boosting attack power, encouraging players to experiment and adapt their strategy to survive. Progression depends on careful resource management and tactical combat, as players must gather the right combination of orbs to defeat the fearsome dragon guardians that block advancement. With no save feature, every decision carries weight, making concentration and planning essential. Visually, The Eidolon stands out for its use of fractal technology, previously seen in Rescue on Fractalus!

video:video.video:title: The Evil Dead – The C64 Horror Game That Trapped You in the Cabin
video:video.video:description: Developed by Palace Software and released in 1984 for the Commodore 64, The Evil Dead is an early licensed horror game based on Sam Raimi’s cult 1981 film. Players step into the role of Ash Williams, defending a remote woodland cabin from relentless demonic forces. Gameplay is presented from a top-down perspective, focusing on fast reactions and constant pressure. Players must move around the cabin sealing doors and windows to stop creatures breaking in, while simultaneously fighting off enemies that slip through the defences. Ash can wield a range of weapons including axes, shovels, and shotguns, but survival also depends on careful energy management. As enemy waves increase in speed and number, players are forced to balance offence, defence, and positioning to stay alive. Despite the limitations of the Commodore 64 hardware, the game delivers a tense atmosphere through eerie sound effects and moody presentation.

video:video.video:title: The Faces of Haarne – Why Are You Defending a Giant Face with a Flying Hat? | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Software Projects, The Faces of Haarne is an unusual arcade shooter for the Commodore 64 designed, coded, and illustrated by Shahid Ahmad, with music by George Neophytou. The game leans heavily into surreal imagery and abstract design, setting it apart from more conventional shooters of the era. Action takes place on a fixed single screen where players control a strange creature tasked with defending a central face from waves of bizarre attackers. Offence and defence are handled via an unconventional weapon: a hat used to strike or repel enemies, requiring careful positioning and timing to survive the onslaught. The presentation is memorable and eccentric, highlighted by a soundtrack inspired by Johann Sebastian Bach’s Brandenburg Concerto No. 3, lending a classical and unexpected tone to the action. While the core gameplay can feel repetitive, the combination of visuals, audio, and concept gives the game a distinctive personality.

video:video.video:title: The Goonies on C64 – Film Licence, Puzzle Rooms and 80s Treasure Hunting
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Datasoft for the Commodore 64, The Goonies delivers a distinctive take on the hit movie, focusing on puzzle-solving and exploration rather than pure action. Instead of controlling a single character, you switch between two of the Goonies, using their combined abilities to progress through trap-filled environments inspired by the film. Each stage is built around problem-solving, requiring careful movement, timing, and cooperation between characters to bypass hazards, navigate maze-like layouts, and recreate memorable moments such as the infamous bone organ sequence. Progress comes from thinking ahead rather than rushing forward. The game’s colourful visuals capture the adventurous tone of the movie, while the SID soundtrack includes an 8-bit rendition of The Goonies ‘R’ Good Enough, adding instant nostalgia. While challenging, the experience is rewarding for players who enjoy methodical puzzle-platform gameplay.

video:video.video:title: The Great Escape – Follow the Camp Routine… Then Plan Your C64 Breakout
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Ocean Software and developed by Denton Designs, The Great Escape is an isometric action-adventure for the Commodore 64 inspired by the classic 1963 war film. Players take on the role of a prisoner of war held in a heavily guarded German camp during World War II, with one goal in mind: escape without raising suspicion. The game centres around a strict daily routine. Roll calls, exercise periods, and mealtimes must all be attended, and ignoring camp rules quickly draws the attention of guards. Within these constraints, players must carefully plan their breakout, balancing obedience with secret preparation. Multiple escape routes are available, including digging tunnels, forging documents, bribing guards, or navigating underground drains. Each method requires patience, exploration, and clever use of limited resources, creating a constant sense of tension and risk.

video:video.video:title: The Great Giana Sisters – The C64 Mario Rival Nintendo Forced Off Shelves
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Rainbow Arts and developed by Time Warp, The Great Giana Sisters is one of the most famous and talked-about platform games on the Commodore 64. Players guide Giana through a surreal dream world packed with hazards, enemies, and precision jumps, all in a quest to reach a giant diamond and wake from her dream. The gameplay is classic side-scrolling platform action spread across 33 increasingly demanding levels. Giana can jump on enemies, collect gems, and use power-ups that grant new abilities such as projectile attacks or temporarily disabling foes. Tight controls and fast-paced level design demand accuracy, timing, and memorisation to progress. On the C64, the game stood out for its smooth scrolling and colourful visuals, pushing the hardware impressively hard. Chris Hülsbeck’s soundtrack became legendary, with its energetic and memorable tunes playing a huge role in the game’s enduring reputation.

video:video.video:title: The Guild of Thieves – Your Amiga Entrance Exam? Rob a Castle AND a Bank
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Magnetic Scrolls for the Commodore Amiga, The Guild of Thieves is a landmark interactive fiction adventure set in the richly imagined medieval world of Kerovnia. You play as an aspiring thief seeking admission to the notorious Guild, tasked with proving your skill by stealing priceless treasures from heavily guarded locations. Gameplay is driven by a powerful text parser that allows detailed and flexible interaction with the environment. Players must carefully explore towns, castles, and vaults, using observation, logic, and precise timing to overcome devious puzzles and security systems. Every command matters, and experimentation is often the key to progress. The Amiga version enhances the experience with around 30 high-quality illustrations that bring key moments and locations to life, adding atmosphere without breaking the flow of the text-driven gameplay. Puzzle design is demanding but fair, rewarding patience and careful thinking rather than trial and error alone.

video:video.video:title: The Happiest Days Of Your Life – C64 Gameplay & Review | Cheeky Commodore Gamer
video:video.video:description: The Happiest Days of Your Life is a 1986 Commodore 64 school adventure published by Firebird. Schoolboy G. McFat has been accused of stealing the headmaster's wallet, so he must search the school for both the missing wallet and photographic evidence that identifies the real culprit. Play combines flick-screen platform movement with object-based puzzles as McFat explores classrooms, corridors and staff areas, avoids hazards and works out where each collected item should be used. The deliberately unruly school setting gives the game a comic British character, but progress depends on careful mapping and experimentation rather than simple arcade action. It is a single-player title designed around exploration, memory and puzzle solving, with the central mystery providing a goal beyond merely reaching the next screen.

video:video.video:title: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy – Could You Survive Infocom’s C64 Adventure?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Infocom and designed by Douglas Adams alongside Steve Meretzky, The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy arrived on the Commodore 64 as one of the most ambitious interactive fiction titles of the 8-bit era. Based directly on Adams’ bestselling novel, the C64 version faithfully recreated the absurd humour and unpredictable sci-fi storytelling that made the book a cult phenomenon. On the Commodore 64, gameplay is entirely text-driven, powered by Infocom’s advanced Z-machine engine. Players must type precise commands to explore environments, solve layered puzzles, and survive increasingly bizarre situations — from escaping a bulldozer to navigating interstellar travel. The parser is famously demanding, often requiring exact phrasing and lateral thinking, making experimentation essential. The C64 release also shipped with Infocom’s signature “feelies” in the box, physical props that enhanced immersion and reinforced its narrative depth.

video:video.video:title: The Human Race – C64 Evolution with Cavemen, Lasers and Head-Scratching
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985, The Human Race is a single-player platform game for the Commodore 64 developed by John D. Ferrari and published by Mastertronic. The game takes a bold and unusual approach, charting a journey through human evolution that begins with the player controlling an ape and progresses through different stages of humanity. Each level represents a distinct era, with gameplay mechanics and environments changing dramatically as you advance. Early stages feature jungle-based platforming with banana collecting and prehistoric hazards, while later levels introduce lava-filled landscapes, rolling logs, and fast-paced sequences set in a modern city. This constant reinvention keeps the experience unpredictable and varied. A major highlight is the dynamic soundtrack by Rob Hubbard, whose music shifts between levels to reflect each evolutionary stage. The score plays a huge role in setting the tone and is often cited as one of the game’s most memorable features.

video:video.video:title: The Immortal – The Amiga Dungeon Crawler That Wanted You Dead
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990, The Immortal is a dark isometric action-adventure game developed by Sandcastle and published by Electronic Arts for the Commodore 64. Players take on the role of an ageing wizard descending into a deadly dungeon to rescue his mentor, Mordamir, uncovering a grim story of ancient civilizations, betrayal, and the pursuit of immortality along the way. The game spans eight perilous dungeon levels packed with traps, puzzles, monsters, and environmental hazards. Progress relies heavily on experimentation and learning from failure, with death often serving as a lesson rather than a setback. Exploration rewards careful observation, item collection, and cautious movement through the labyrinthine rooms. Combat is slow, deliberate, and unforgiving, requiring precise timing and smart use of magic rather than button-mashing. Encounters are tense and often brutal, with graphic death animations reinforcing the constant sense of danger and vulnerability that defines the experience.

video:video.video:title: The Last Ninja – C64 Combat, Puzzles… and That Bloody River Jump
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by System 3 for the Commodore 64, The Last Ninja is a landmark action-adventure that pushed the machine to its limits. You play as Armakuni, the sole survivor of a destroyed ninja clan, on a quest for revenge against the evil shogun Kunitoki and the recovery of a sacred scroll. The adventure unfolds across six large isometric levels, ranging from serene gardens to dangerous wastelands, underground dungeons, and Kunitoki’s heavily guarded palace. Movement is deliberate and precise, with narrow paths, traps, and environmental hazards demanding careful control and spatial awareness. Combat is unusually deep for its time, allowing you to strike enemies at different body areas using a combination of direction and timing. A wide selection of ninja weapons—including the ninjato, nunchaku, staff, shuriken, and smoke bombs—adds tactical variety, while puzzles and hidden items encourage exploration and observation.

video:video.video:title: The Last V8 – One Crash and Your Post-Apocalyptic C64 Drive Was Over
video:video.video:description: The Last V8 (1985) is a futuristic, post-apocalyptic racing game for the Commodore 64, developed by David Darling, with graphics by Jim Wilson and music by Rob Hubbard. Released under Mastertronic’s MAD label, you pilot a radiation-shielded V8 through a nuclear wasteland, balancing speed, fuel, and shield power in a race for survival. Gameplay features a split-screen display with action view and dashboard, precise steering, and a steep difficulty curve. The famous “V8, return to base immediately” intro sets the tone. Rob Hubbard’s soundtrack is a highlight, despite a small sync glitch later fixed in the HVSC archive. Visually, the game delivers striking post-apocalyptic imagery. Despite its flaws, The Last V8 remains a cult classic, remembered for its atmosphere, soundtrack, and brutal challenge.

video:video.video:title: The Lords of Midnight – Win the War OR Destroy the Ice Crown | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Mindscape for the Commodore 64, The Lords of Midnight is a groundbreaking blend of strategy and role-playing developed by Mike Singleton and set in a vast, atmospheric fantasy world. Players command heroes such as Luxor the Moonprince and his son Morkin in a quest to defeat the evil Witchking Doomdark, who has plunged the Land of Midnight into eternal winter. The game offers multiple paths to victory, including destroying the Ice Crown, conquering Doomdark’s fortress of Ushgarak with assembled armies, or completing both objectives in Epic mode. This freedom of approach was highly innovative for its time. A standout feature is the “landscaping” engine, which presents the world from a first-person perspective across more than 4,000 unique locations. This creates a strong sense of scale, immersion, and exploration rarely seen on 8-bit systems.

video:video.video:title: The Lost Patrol – Seven Men, 58 Miles and Barely Any Supplies on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released for the Commodore Amiga, Lost Patrol places you in command of a stranded U. S. infantry squad after a helicopter crash in the Central Highlands of Vietnam. Cut off from support and deep in hostile territory, your mission is simple in theory but brutal in execution: lead the survivors safely to the nearest U. S. base while an unseen enemy hunts you at every step. Most of the game unfolds on a strategic map of Vietnam, where you guide your squad across dangerous terrain. Managing morale, health, food, water, ammunition, and rest is essential, as exhaustion and poor decisions can be just as deadly as enemy fire. Every move carries risk, forcing you to weigh speed against safety. When the patrol reaches key locations such as villages, rivers, or jungle clearings, the game shifts into illustrated scenario screens that present critical decisions.

video:video.video:title: The C64 Game That Let You Destroy an Entire City | Movie Monster Game
video:video.video:description: Released by Epyx as a follow-up to Crush, Crumble and Chomp! , The Movie Monster Game flips the formula by putting players directly in control of the monster. Choose from six giant creatures, including officially licensed icons like Godzilla, alongside classics such as Tarantula and a towering Robot, then unleash mayhem across cities including London, Paris, New York, Moscow, and San Francisco. Rather than relying on turn-based strategy commands, the game adopts a more immediate arcade-style control system. Players can freely roam the city streets, smashing buildings, battling military forces, and completing one of five scenario-based objectives ranging from escape and rescue missions to total landmark destruction. Tiny humans fight back with tanks, jets, missiles, and other defences, forcing players to balance raw destruction with survival. While the strategic layer of the original game is reduced, the faster pace and hands-on control give The Movie Monster Game a more action-focused feel that suits its over-the-top theme perfectly.

video:video.video:title: The Muncher – Was This Gremlin’s C64 Answer to Rampage?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Beam Software and published by Gremlin Graphics for the Commodore 64, The Muncher is a destructive side-scrolling action game inspired by arcade smash hit Rampage. Players take control of Muncher, a giant Godzilla-style creature rising from the sea to reclaim his stolen eggs from invading explorers. Gameplay centres on pure mayhem as you rampage through cities, military installations, and industrial areas, tearing down buildings and battling waves of enemies. Muncher can climb structures, punch and kick opponents, and unleash powerful fireballs to clear the screen. Collectibles play an important role in survival. Eggs and radioactive barrels restore health or allow players to continue after losing a life, encouraging aggressive play and constant forward momentum. The action is simple and immediate, focusing on destruction rather than complex mechanics. Visually, the game delivers chunky sprites and clear animation that sell the scale of Muncher’s rampage on the C64.

video:video.video:title: The Neverending Story – Fight The Nothing One Typed Command at a Time on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Ocean Software and published by Datasoft for the Commodore 64, The Neverending Story is a graphics-text adventure based on the beloved fantasy film, placing players in the role of Atreyu on a quest to save Fantasia. The journey involves exploring story-rich locations, solving puzzles, and confronting the growing threat of The Nothing while restoring hope and belief to the realm. Each scene is supported by small illustrated panels showing your surroundings, inventory, and companions such as Falkor and Artax, blending visual storytelling with interactive fiction. Gameplay relies on a streamlined text parser with a limited vocabulary, encouraging players to think carefully about commands and interactions. This minimalist approach allows more memory to be devoted to narrative depth and atmospheric presentation. A major highlight is the title theme composed by Martin Galway, who adapted the film’s iconic melody into a memorable SID soundtrack.

video:video.video:title: The New Zealand Story – Did Ocean Get the Arcade Adventure Right on C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, The New Zealand Story is a colourful arcade-style platformer based on Taito’s popular coin-op hit starring Tiki the Kiwi. Players take control of Tiki as he journeys across varied landscapes to rescue his kidnapped friends from cages and enemy creatures before time runs out. Gameplay combines precise jumping with a quirky selection of weapons, tools, and hidden routes. Levels encourage exploration and experimentation, rewarding players who uncover secret paths and power-ups. Tight controls and clever level layouts help balance the game’s increasing difficulty. Visually, the C64 version features vibrant sprite work and cheerful backgrounds that closely reflect the arcade original. The presentation is enhanced by standout music composed by Jonathan Dunn, which remains one of the game’s most memorable features. Despite hardware limitations, Ocean delivered a faithful and engaging conversion.

video:video.video:title: The Official Father Christmas – How Good Was This 1989 C64 Christmas Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Alternative Software for the Commodore 64, The Official Father Christmas is a cheerful seasonal arcade game designed to capture the fun and magic of Christmas. Aimed at younger players and families, it delivers light-hearted gameplay wrapped in festive charm. Players take control of Father Christmas as he delivers presents across a snow-covered town. The game is split into short arcade-style sequences, including loading gifts, running across rooftops, and dropping presents down chimneys while avoiding hazards such as icy ledges and troublesome animals. Each section is simple to understand and quick to play, making it ideal for pick-up-and-play sessions. On the C64, the game features colourful winter-themed graphics and bright, friendly sprites that give it a strong festive identity. The jolly soundtrack and sound effects reinforce the Christmas atmosphere without overcomplicating the experience.

video:video.video:title: The Prince – Rescue the Princess from the Black Castle on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Firebird Software and developed by Marcus Charleville, The Prince is a fantasy-themed action-adventure for the Commodore 64 that blends arcade-style challenges with light puzzle elements. Players take on the role of a wealthy prince determined to rescue his captive princess from the depths of the ominous Black Castle. Gameplay unfolds from a side-scrolling perspective as the prince navigates dangerous corridors filled with traps, enemies, and environmental hazards. Progress depends on precise timing, quick reactions, and careful movement, as mistakes are often punished immediately. The castle’s layout encourages exploration and memorisation, with each area presenting new threats and requiring players to balance risk and caution. While combat is straightforward, positioning and agility play a key role in surviving the castle’s many dangers. Though modest in presentation, The Prince stands out for its atmosphere and focused design.

video:video.video:title: The Rats – The C64 Horror Strategy Game Where London Gets Overrun
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Five Ways Software and published by Hodder & Stoughton for the Commodore 64, The Rats is an unusual hybrid of strategy and interactive fiction based on James Herbert’s best-selling horror novel. Players take on the role of Harris, head of the rat extermination commission, as London faces a devastating invasion of genetically mutated rats. Using a detailed city map, players must deploy emergency services, manage resources, and fund research into advanced extermination technologies. Strategic planning is balanced with crisis management, as rising panic levels and civilian casualties can quickly overwhelm your efforts. Careful coordination and long-term investment are essential for survival. At key moments, the game shifts into real-time, text-based scenarios where players experience the invasion from the perspective of trapped civilians. These sequences present tense decision-making situations supported by eerie sound effects and minimalist visuals.

video:video.video:title: Ghostbusters Returned to the C64 – But Was It Any Good?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Activision, The Real Ghostbusters brings the animated series to the Commodore 64 with fast-paced, top-down, multi-scrolling action. You take control of one of the four Ghostbusters—Peter, Ray, Egon, or Winston—tasked with clearing New York City of spectral trouble. Gameplay revolves around navigating maze-like locations, stunning ghosts with the Proton Pack, and collecting items to progress. Each area introduces new hazards, tighter layouts, and tougher enemies, pushing you to balance movement, positioning, and quick reactions. The inclusion of a two-player cooperative mode adds an extra layer of mayhem and teamwork. Visually, the game captures the look and feel of the cartoon with colourful sprites and detailed environments, while David Whittaker’s music delivers a memorable take on the iconic Ghostbusters theme. Though the controls can feel demanding at times, the challenge keeps the pressure high.

video:video.video:title: The Rocky Horror Show – How Did This Cult Musical Become a C64 Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by CRL Group, The Rocky Horror Show is a side-scrolling adventure game for the Commodore 64 based on Richard O’Brien’s cult musical. Players are dropped into the bizarre world of Dr. Frank-N-Furter’s castle, where nothing is quite as it seems and danger lurks around every corner. You can choose to play as either Brad or Janet, with the goal of rescuing your partner after they’ve been turned to stone by the Medusa machine. Progress requires careful exploration of the castle, collecting the scattered parts of the de-Medusa machine and reassembling it in the theatre room to reverse the petrification. Gameplay focuses on puzzle-solving and navigation, with keys, force fields, and hostile characters standing in your way. Familiar faces from the musical—including Riff-Raff, Magenta, Columbia, Eddie, and Frank-N-Furter himself—add constant pressure as you move through the castle.

video:video.video:title: The Running Man – Could Schwarzenegger Survive the C64 Game Show?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Grandslam and developed by Emerald Software, The Running Man is a side-scrolling action game for the Commodore 64 inspired by the 1987 dystopian film starring Arnold Schwarzenegger. You play as Ben Richards, forced to survive a brutal televised game show where contestants are hunted for public entertainment. The gameplay focuses on moving through a series of scrolling levels, each ending in a showdown with one of the show’s stalkers. Combat is simple and direct, placing emphasis on positioning and survival rather than complex move sets. Between stages, a brief puzzle-based mini-game offers a chance to recover health before the next encounter. As a movie tie-in, the game leans heavily on its concept rather than technical ambition. Controls and repetition were widely criticised at the time, but the structure still reflects late-80s licensed design, with clear stages, boss battles, and a relentless push forward.

video:video.video:title: The Sacred Armour of Antiriad – C64 Sci-Fi Adventuring with Big Box Energy
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Palace Software, The Sacred Armour of Antiriad is a landmark action-adventure on the Commodore 64, blending exploration, combat, and progression in a way that was ahead of its time. Set in a distant post-apocalyptic future, the game casts players as Tal, a lone warrior facing an alien threat that has devastated the world. Progression is driven by exploration across interconnected environments, with access to new areas tied directly to abilities gained along the way. Central to this is the legendary Antiriad battlesuit, which grants Tal the power to fly, survive radiation zones, and engage enemies more effectively. Recovering and upgrading the suit transforms both movement and combat, encouraging careful backtracking and discovery. Energy management plays a key role, as both Tal and the armour draw from limited reserves. Players must balance exploration, combat, and survival, adding a strategic edge to what might otherwise be straightforward action.

video:video.video:title: The Secret of Monkey Island – How Guybrush Threepwood Became an Amiga Legend
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Lucasfilm Games, The Secret of Monkey Island is a landmark point-and-click adventure set in a playful, offbeat Caribbean during the golden age of piracy. You follow the misadventures of Guybrush Threepwood, an eager but hopelessly inexperienced wannabe pirate determined to prove himself on Melee Island. Gameplay revolves around exploration, puzzle-solving, and sharp dialogue choices, with challenges built around logic, experimentation, and comedy rather than punishment. The game’s design encourages curiosity, rewarding players who talk to everyone, try everything, and embrace its absurd sense of humour. Powered by the SCUMM engine, the Amiga version delivers expressive visuals and a rich MIDI soundtrack that perfectly supports the game’s tone. Memorable characters, clever writing, and inventive puzzles combine to create an experience that feels effortlessly timeless.

video:video.video:title: The Sentinel – The C64 Strategy Game That Watches You Back
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Firebird Software and developed by Geoff Crammond, The Sentinel is a groundbreaking puzzle strategy game that pushed the Commodore 64 into entirely new territory. It was one of the first home computer games to use solid-filled 3D graphics, delivering a surreal and unsettling experience unlike anything else at the time. Players control a synthoid exploring abstract, chessboard-like landscapes rendered in a striking pseudo-3D perspective. The objective is to climb the terrain by absorbing energy from trees, rocks, and other objects, creating new synthoids and strategically relocating across the landscape until the Sentinel itself can be absorbed. Tension comes from the Sentinel’s constant surveillance. If it spots the player, it begins draining energy, forcing careful planning, positioning, and timing. Energy management is central to survival, with every move carrying risk and long-term consequences.

video:video.video:title: The Settlers – Why This Amiga Strategy Game Ate Entire Weekends
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by Blue Byte for the Commodore Amiga, The Settlers is a landmark city-building and real-time strategy game designed by Volker Wertich. Set in a richly detailed medieval world, the game challenges players to balance economic growth with territorial expansion in order to build a thriving settlement. Gameplay revolves around managing complex supply chains, with resources such as wood, stone, and food feeding into interconnected production systems. Every settler performs a specific role, from woodcutters and miners to bakers and soldiers, making careful planning and logistics essential to long-term success. Progression is driven by smart infrastructure design, efficient road networks, and the steady development of military strength. As settlements grow, players must optimise workflows, expand into new territories, and defend their borders against increasingly capable opponents. The game features a 30-mission campaign that gradually introduces advanced mechanics and tougher AI rivals, alongside a free-play mode that supports two-player split-screen multiplayer.

video:video.video:title: The Smiths Are Dead – A New C64 Adventure About Morrissey After The Smiths
video:video.video:description: Released in 2023 by Commodore Plus for the Commodore 64, The Smiths Are Dead is an illustrated text adventure that blends interactive fiction with British music history. This unofficial release places players in the role of Steven Patrick Morrissey during the uncertain period following The Smiths’ breakup in 1987, with the goal of recovering the lost sheet music for his debut solo single, Suedehead. Gameplay uses a classic text parser interface, with commands such as GO, EXAMINE, and TALK driving exploration and conversation. Players visit key locations and interact with real figures from Morrissey’s early solo career, piecing together clues through dialogue, observation, and careful decision-making. The experience is enhanced by high-resolution illustrations and an atmospheric SID soundtrack, including a rendition of Oscillate Wildly, which reinforces the tone and period setting. Attention to detail and authentic references make the narrative feel grounded and deliberate.

video:video.video:title: The Snowman – Build Him Before the Gas Flames Melt Your Snow on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Quicksilva for the Commodore 64, The Snowman is a charming single-screen platform game inspired by Raymond Briggs’ beloved picture book and its iconic animated adaptation. Rather than focusing on action, the game delivers a gentle, thoughtful experience that reflects the warmth and magic of the original story. Gameplay centres on collecting items such as snow, clothing, toys, and ice to assemble the snowman piece by piece. Players must carefully navigate layered platform layouts while avoiding hazards, particularly gas flames that can melt collected snow. Strategic use of items like ice lollies allows flames to be frozen, adding a subtle puzzle element to progression. The presentation plays a huge role in the game’s appeal. Festive visuals capture a cosy winter atmosphere, while the inclusion of Howard Blake’s Walking in the Air gives the game a strong emotional connection to the animated film and elevates it above many licensed titles of the era.

video:video.video:title: The Staff of Karnath – Find 16 Key Pieces Before Midnight or the World Ends | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Ultimate Play the Game and developed by Dave and Bob Thomas, The Staff of Karnath introduced Commodore 64 players to the dark and dangerous world of Sir Arthur Pendragon. Set inside a vast haunted castle, the game tasks you with stopping an ancient evil before it can consume the world. Exploration is presented in an isometric 3D view, with Sir Arthur navigating rooms and corridors filled with hostile creatures, deadly traps, and hidden secrets. Your primary objective is to locate the 16 scattered pieces of a pentacle and deliver them to the tomb in the castle basement, where the Staff of Karnath can finally be destroyed. Magic plays a central role in survival. Sir Arthur has access to ten spells, each serving a specific purpose, from revealing hidden items to eliminating enemies or manipulating objects.

video:video.video:title: Sword of Fargoal – One of the C64’s Earliest Dungeon Crawlers
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by Epyx and designed by Jeff McCord, Sword of Fargoal is one of the most influential dungeon-crawling RPGs on the Commodore 64. Players descend into a deadly, ever-changing dungeon on a quest to recover the legendary Sword of Fargoal, stolen by the evil wizard Umla. Each playthrough features randomly generated dungeon layouts, ensuring no two adventures are ever the same. Players explore between 15 and 20 levels, facing over 30 different monster types including ogres, trolls, wyverns, and fearsome shadow dragons. A key feature is the fog-of-war system, which hides unexplored areas and creates constant tension as new threats emerge from the darkness. Progression is driven by experience, levelling, and careful resource management, with temples on each level offering healing, protection, or experience in exchange for gold. Known for its unforgiving difficulty and permanent death mechanic, Sword of Fargoal rewards cautious exploration and strategic decision-making.

video:video.video:title: The Three Stooges – Could You Save the Orphanage on the Commodore Amiga?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Cinemaware for the Commodore Amiga, The Three Stooges is an adventure-driven collection of mini-games built around the anarchic humour of Moe, Larry, and Curly. The goal is simple: raise enough money to save an orphanage from foreclosure, using a board-game style structure to move between challenges inspired by classic Stooges routines. Gameplay unfolds as players land on tiles that trigger a variety of slapstick mini-games, including pie fights, reflex challenges, and timing-based obstacles. Success depends on quick reactions and pattern recognition, with each activity capturing the physical comedy that defined the trio’s films. Presentation is a major strength, with expressive animations, digitised voice clips, and a strong cinematic feel that reflects Cinemaware’s trademark style. The humour is front and centre, making each task feel like a playable gag rather than a traditional arcade challenge.

video:video.video:title: The Train: Escape to Normandy – Steal Back France’s Art and Drive It to Freedom on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, The Train: Escape to Normandy is an action-simulation title developed by Artech Digital Entertainment and published by Accolade. Inspired by the 1964 film The Train, the game places players in the role of French Resistance fighter Pierre LeFeu during a daring World War II mission to hijack a Nazi-controlled steam train carrying priceless artworks. Gameplay unfolds across multiple interconnected phases. The opening sequence involves a tense shootout as Pierre covers his ally Le Duc while critical track switches are thrown. Once the train is moving, players must manage the steam locomotive itself, balancing speed, pressure, and water levels while navigating hostile territory. Combat adds another layer of pressure, with German fighter planes and gunboats attacking at key moments. Players take control of defensive weapons to repel these assaults, while station stops require securing enemy-held locations to resupply and gather intelligence.

video:video.video:title: The Transformers – The FIRST Transformers Video Game Arrived on the C64 in 1985
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Ocean Software and developed by Denton Designs, The Transformers brings the hugely popular toy line and animated series to the Commodore 64 in an ambitious action-platform adventure. You control a team of five Autobots—Optimus Prime, Hound, Jazz, Mirage, and Bumblebee—tasked with stopping the Decepticons by recovering the scattered parts of an energon cube. Gameplay unfolds across a sprawling cityscape filled with platforms, ladders, and hostile enemies. Each Autobot has distinct strengths in power, shields, and weapons, encouraging strategic switching via Defensa-Pods placed throughout the map. Choosing the right character at the right time is key, whether it’s Optimus Prime’s brute strength or Bumblebee’s ability to access tighter spaces. Combat is relentless, with Decepticons such as Megatron, Starscream, and Soundwave constantly respawning to apply pressure. The ability to transform between robot and vehicle forms adds variety to both movement and combat, giving the game a unique rhythm compared to standard platform shooters.

video:video.video:title: The Trap Door – Five Jobs Before the Thing Upstairs Loses His Temper | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Piranha Software for the Commodore 64, The Trap Door is a wonderfully odd puzzle-adventure based on the British animated TV series. You play as Berk, a nervous blue servant tasked with preparing increasingly bizarre meals for the unseen and very impatient “Thing Upstairs.” Gameplay revolves around exploration and problem-solving inside a gloomy castle. You move between rooms, collect strange items, and deal with creatures that emerge from the trap door, all while working out how each task fits together. Boni the talking skull offers helpful hints, but Drutt the pet has a habit of eating things you actually need, adding mayhem to every objective. Time pressure keeps the tension high, as each task must be completed before the Thing Upstairs loses patience. The flip-screen, pseudo-3D presentation lets Berk move into the depth of rooms, while expressive animations and dark humour capture the atmosphere of the TV show perfectly.

video:video.video:title: The Untouchables – Did Ocean Turn the Gangster Film Into a Great C64 Game?
video:video.video:description: The Untouchables (1989), developed by Ocean Software, is a licensed video game adaptation of the 1987 film, putting you in the role of Eliot Ness as you attempt to dismantle Al Capone’s criminal empire. The game blends multiple arcade and shooter styles across six cinematic levels, including a scrolling warehouse shootout, a sniper-style bridge sequence, and cover-based alley and rooftop battles leading to a final confrontation with Frank Nitti. Each section offers a different gameplay experience, keeping the action varied while demanding precision and fast reactions from the player. The game stands out with its detailed sprites, smooth level transitions, and atmospheric 1930s-inspired soundtrack composed by Jonathan Dunn. While its high difficulty — especially in the opening warehouse stage — frustrated many players, its ambition and strong movie licence earned widespread praise. It was highly rated by magazines such as Zzap!

video:video.video:title: The Way of the Exploding Fist – 18 Moves from ONE Button on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Beam Software for the Commodore 64, The Way of the Exploding Fist is a landmark martial arts fighting game that helped define the genre on home computers. Inspired by the arcade hit Karate Champ, it introduced a more measured, skill-based approach to one-on-one combat, placing emphasis on timing, spacing, and precise control. Players compete in karate matches where victory is achieved by scoring two full points, represented by yin-yang symbols. The control system offers 18 distinct moves, including punches, kicks, blocks, and acrobatic somersaults, all executed through deliberate joystick movements. As the game progresses, opponents become faster and more disciplined, testing both reflexes and technique across a range of atmospheric locations. A memorable highlight is the bonus stage, where players attempt to defeat a charging bull with a single perfectly timed strike—a direct nod to martial arts legend Mas Oyama.

video:video.video:title: Willow Pattern – The Beautiful C64 Adventure Inspired by a Chinese Legend
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Mr. Micro Ltd. and published by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, Willow Pattern is an atmospheric action-maze game inspired by the famous Chinese porcelain design of the same name. Known in some regions as The Willow Pattern Adventure, the game blends exploration, timing, and tension with a distinctive oriental visual style. Players control Chang, a humble clerk navigating a multi-screen garden maze filled with danger. The objective is to locate the key, rescue Princess Koong-Shee, and escape by boat, all while avoiding relentless samurai enemies who hurl swords that can be dodged, collected, and reused as weapons. Resource management and positioning are crucial to survival. Gameplay alternates between overhead maze exploration and focused action sequences. One of the most memorable sections is the bridge-jump sequence, where Chang must leap across stepping stones as giant hands reach up from the water below, adding pressure and variety to the pacing.

video:video.video:title: The Wombles – Was This the Strangest C64 TV Tie-In of 1990?
video:video.video:description: The Wombles is a 1990 action-adventure game for the Commodore 64, developed by Enigma Variations and published by Alternative Software. In this charming licensed title, you play as Orinoco — one of the famous Wombles — exploring Wimbledon Common and the underground burrow to collect litter and special items, including a television, suitcase, telephone, and even a copy of The Times. Along the way, you must avoid humans, squirrels, rats, bees, and the mischievous Womble Wellington, who is racing you to grab items first. Gameplay blends exploration with timed fetch-quests and item collection. The screen scrolls through a horizontally laid-out maze, where you navigate with the joystick, collect objects, and return them before the clock runs out. Collisions with enemies or running out of time cost you valuable pie-slice lives. Visually, The Wombles delivers colourful 8-bit graphics that capture the spirit of the TV series, with detailed sprites, environmental features, and a handy minimap.

video:video.video:title: The Young Ones – Find Your Stuff Before Balowski Comes for the Rent on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Orpheus Software, The Young Ones is a single-screen adventure game for the Commodore 64 based on the anarchic BBC sitcom. You choose one of the housemates and attempt to gather all your belongings before the landlord turns up demanding the rent, all while the student house descends into predictable madness. Gameplay centres on exploring the house room by room, solving light puzzles, and managing objects through a menu-driven interface. The remaining housemates are controlled by the computer, each behaving in ways that reflect their TV personalities and frequently disrupting your plans rather than helping them. While the game aims to capture the humour and mayhem of the series, technical limitations and bugs can make progress frustrating. Licensing restrictions also meant the iconic theme tune was replaced, slightly dulling the show’s distinctive energy.

video:video.video:title: Theme Park – Did Bullfrog’s Amiga Classic Make Business Management Fun?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1994 by Bullfrog Productions and published by Electronic Arts, Theme Park is a landmark construction and management simulation for the Commodore Amiga. As the first title in Bullfrog’s Designer Series, it challenged players to balance creativity, strategy, and business sense in order to build a successful amusement park. Players begin by choosing a country to build in, each presenting different economic conditions and gameplay challenges. From there, the task is to design rides, set entrance fees, manage food and souvenir prices, hire staff, and keep visitors happy—all while staying profitable. Three gameplay modes, Sandbox, Sim, and Full, allow players to tailor the level of complexity to their preferred play style. The depth of the simulation is where Theme Park truly shines. Ride popularity, queue times, park layout, staff efficiency, and research all play crucial roles in long-term success.

video:video.video:title: They Stole a Million – Could You Plan the Perfect Heist on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by 39 Steps and published by Ariolasoft for the Commodore 64, They Stole a Million puts you in control of “The Boss”, a criminal mastermind planning and executing complex, high-risk heists against well-guarded targets. The game is split into two distinct phases: planning and execution. During planning, you choose a target, purchase blueprints, gather intelligence, and recruit a specialist team, each member offering unique skills such as lock-picking, alarm disabling, or getaway driving.
