Every decision matters, as team fees, profit cuts, and timing must be carefully balanced to avoid disaster. Once the plan is set, the execution phase unfolds in real time from a top-down perspective. You watch your crew carry out their roles while monitoring the operation, stepping in directly if things start to go wrong. Success depends on precise coordination, smart intervention, and flawless timing, with even small mistakes leading to failure.

video:video.video:title: Thing on a Spring – The C64 Platformer with a Legendary Rob Hubbard SID Tune
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Micro Projects and published by Gremlin Graphics, Thing on a Spring is a distinctive side-scrolling platformer that immediately stands out on the Commodore 64. You control Thing, a spring-based character sent into a chaotic toy factory to recover stolen puzzle pieces while surviving a maze of hazards. Movement is the heart of the game. Thing’s ability to bounce to extreme heights transforms every screen into a timing and positioning puzzle, forcing you to think carefully about momentum, landing points, and enemy patterns rather than relying on simple jumps. Each factory section introduces new dangers such as conveyor belts, collapsing platforms, and aggressive toy enemies. Alongside this, you must collect all nine puzzle pieces while keeping an eye on the oil meter, which drains through enemy contact and environmental traps, adding constant pressure to every decision.

video:video.video:title: Through the Trap Door – Can Berk Rescue Boni Beneath the Castle? | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Piranha Software and developed by Don Priestley, Through the Trap Door is a charming puzzle-adventure based on the much-loved British stop-motion TV series. Acting as a sequel to The Trap Door, the game sends you deep into the castle’s underbelly on a rescue mission to save Boni the talking skull. You control Berk, the friendly blue creature, alongside his unpredictable spider companion Drutt. Exploration is key as you move between rooms, collect and use items, and work out how to deal with the bizarre creatures that regularly emerge from the trap door. Progress depends on observation, experimentation, and timing rather than quick reflexes alone. Faithful to the TV show, the game leans heavily into humour and personality. Its bold, cartoon-style graphics and playful animations capture the look and feel of the series, while the puzzles strike a balance between light-hearted fun and genuine challenge.

video:video.video:title: Thrusta – Software Projects’ Forgotten C64 Gravity Shooter
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Software Projects, Thrusta is a demanding gravity-based space shooter inspired by arcade classics like Gravitar. You pilot a small spacecraft through tightly designed caverns, with smooth 360-degree scrolling that evokes the feel of vector-based games such as Asteroids. The objective is deceptively simple: collect a bomb and deliver it to the target zone. In practice, every movement is affected by gravity, forcing you to carefully manage thrust, momentum, and fuel while avoiding walls, hazards, and tight passages. Precision control is essential, and even small mistakes can quickly end a run. Thrusta builds constant tension through its physics-driven gameplay, rewarding patience, skill, and mastery rather than quick reflex shooting. Each level increases the challenge, pushing you to refine your control and plan every manoeuvre. Widely praised for its design and difficulty, Thrusta earned strong critical acclaim and remains one of the Commodore 64’s most respected skill-based space games.

video:video.video:title: Thunder Blade – Could the C64 Handle Sega’s 3D Helicopter Arcade Hit?
video:video.video:description: Originally released by Sega in 1987, Thunder Blade is a high-energy shoot-’em-up that puts you in control of a heavily armed attack helicopter blasting through enemy territory. Famous in the arcades for its pseudo-3D visuals and dramatic motion cabinets, the game later made its way to home computers with mixed but fascinating results. On the Commodore 64, published by U. S. Gold in 1988, Thunder Blade takes a top-down approach combined with behind-the-helicopter stages. You pilot the Gunship Gladiator through vertically scrolling combat zones, taking out tanks, gun turrets, and enemy helicopters. Clever programming techniques attempt to recreate depth and scale, delivering fast action even if movement and detail can feel rough at times. The Amiga version, also released in 1988 by U. S. Gold, offers smoother scrolling and richer visuals, making better use of the hardware while keeping the arcade’s alternating perspectives intact.

video:video.video:title: Thunderbirds – Did International Rescue Work on the Commodore 64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Thunderbirds is a puzzle-adventure game developed by Teque Software and published by Firebird Software. Based on Gerry Anderson’s iconic 1960s TV series, the game places players in control of International Rescue’s most famous vehicles as they tackle a series of logic-based rescue scenarios. Gameplay centres on controlling Thunderbird 1 and Thunderbird 2 within maze-like environments. Progress depends on manipulating coloured blocks to clear routes and solve puzzles, with each vehicle limited to moving specific block types. This creates a deliberate, strategic pace where careful planning is essential to avoid dead ends and complete each screen. The presentation uses a clear top-down perspective, making puzzle layouts easy to read and understand. While the visuals are functional rather than flashy, they suit the methodical gameplay well. The inclusion of a rendition of the Thunderbirds theme adds a strong sense of identity and nostalgia, especially for fans of the original series.

video:video.video:title: Thundercats – Lion-O Takes on Mumm-Ra in Elite’s C64 Action Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Elite Systems, ThunderCats brings the hit animated series to the Commodore 64, casting you as Lion-O on a mission to reclaim the Eye of Thundera from the evil Mumm-Ra. The game translates the show’s fantasy setting into a side-scrolling action adventure built around urgency and exploration. Each level represents a different elemental environment, with strict time limits pushing you forward as enemies and hazards close in. Combat is straightforward, but survival depends on learning layouts, managing momentum, and reacting quickly before time runs out. Progression is tied to rescuing fellow ThunderCats, including Tygra, Panthro, and WilyKit, who play a role in advancing the quest. While the mechanics remain simple, the game leans heavily into atmosphere, using bold colours and moody music to capture the tone of the TV series. Often debated but fondly remembered, ThunderCats stands as a classic example of 8-bit licensed gaming.

video:video.video:title: Tilt – The Codemasters C64 Puzzle That Made You Move the Entire Maze
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Codemasters, Tilt is a distinctive action-puzzle game for the Commodore 64 that puts physics and precision front and centre. Players guide a marble through a series of maze-like levels by tilting the entire playfield, aiming to reach the exit without smashing into obstacles or running out of energy. Rather than moving the marble directly, the screen itself is rotated to influence momentum. As levels progress, the challenge increases with tighter layouts, gates, traps, and changes to the marble’s size, all of which demand careful control and forward planning rather than brute force reactions. Technically, Tilt is an impressive showcase for the C64. The marble physics feel convincing, movement is smooth, and the controls are responsive, making success feel earned rather than random. The experience is backed by a fitting soundtrack composed by Steve Barrett, which complements the calm-but-tense puzzle action.

video:video.video:title: Time Tunnel – The C64 Adventure That Sent a Gnome Through History
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Applied Systems Engineering and published by U. S. Gold for the Commodore 64, Time Tunnel is an atmospheric puzzle-adventure that casts players as a gnome on a quest to become King of the Gnomes. To succeed, you must recover seven fragments of a magical scroll, each hidden in a different time period. The adventure begins in the gnome’s mansion, where activating a time machine opens portals to wildly different eras, including the Stone Age, Ancient Persia, Mythological Greece, Colonial Salem, the California Gold Rush, an intergalactic spaceship, and a distant black hole in the year 9999. Each setting presents its own logic, hazards, and item-based puzzles that must be solved to progress. A defining feature is the “virtual room” inventory system, accessed by holding the fire button, allowing items to be stored and reused across timelines.

video:video.video:title: Times of Lore – The Vast C64 RPG That Helped Inspire Ultima VI
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Origin Systems, Times of Lore is an ambitious action role-playing game for the Commodore 64 designed by Chris Roberts. Set in the troubled medieval kingdom of Albareth, the story begins with the mysterious disappearance of High King Valwyn, plunging the land into unrest as rival factions battle for control. Players choose between three distinct heroes: a powerful barbarian, a heavily armoured knight, or a swift and agile valkyrie, each offering different strengths and playstyles. The game is presented from a top-down perspective and features real-time action as players explore a vast world made up of thousands of interconnected screens. Combat is immediate and accessible, focusing on melee encounters with enemies such as brigands and orcs, while progress also depends on exploration, puzzle-solving, and interaction with non-player characters via a menu-driven dialogue system.

video:video.video:title: Tir Na Nòg – Could You Ever Work Out Gargoyle’s Mythical C64 Adventure?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Gargoyle Games for the Commodore 64, Tir Na Nòg is a critically acclaimed arcade-adventure action-puzzle game inspired by Irish mythology, starring the legendary hero Cúchulainn. Players are transported to the mystical Land of Youth, where Cúchulainn must recover four fragments of the Seal of Calum to restore balance while evading the mysterious and dangerous sídhe enemies. The game world is vast and interconnected, featuring plains, forests, caverns, and hidden pathways that reward careful exploration and observation. Movement is built around a unique rotating-view system, requiring players to change the camera direction before travelling left or right, adding strategic depth to navigation. Progress depends on solving cryptic environmental puzzles and interpreting poetic clues, making inventory management and experimentation central to success. Instead of traditional deaths, defeat sends Cúchulainn to another location and strips him of carried items, encouraging thoughtful risk-taking and frequent use of the built-in save system.

video:video.video:title: To Be on Top – The C64 Game That Tried to Turn You Into a Pop Star
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Rainbow Arts for the Commodore 64, To Be on Top is an unusual music-themed action game that challenges players to create a chart-topping hit single. Players roam a busy street, dodging pedestrians, traffic, and roller skaters while visiting locations such as their home, disco, recording studio, and TV station in search of musical inspiration. Throughout the adventure, mini-games appear on television screens, allowing players to collect bass lines, melodies, accompaniments, and sequences. These elements are then combined using a synthesiser, along with one of sixteen drum patterns, to produce a finished demo track. Success in the charts unlocks a live television performance, where audience applause determines whether your song reaches number one. This adds a unique performance element rarely seen in 8-bit games. Visually, the game features colourful characters and lively urban environments that reflect its playful tone.

video:video.video:title: Toki – Ocean Brought the Fire-Spitting Arcade Ape to the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 for the Commodore 64, Toki is an arcade-style platformer developed by Taito and converted by Ocean Software. Players take control of Toki, a man transformed into a monkey by an evil sorcerer, as he battles through hostile worlds to rescue his girlfriend and reclaim his human form. The game focuses on fast, demanding platform action, with Toki firing powerful fireballs, dodging enemies, and navigating dangerous terrain filled with traps and vertical hazards. Despite the hardware limitations, the C64 version delivers a strong sense of momentum and challenge that reflects the spirit of the arcade original. Levels are packed with varied enemy types and large boss encounters that test timing and positioning. Controls are responsive, encouraging aggressive play while still punishing mistakes, keeping the action intense throughout. Audio is handled by Allister Brimble, whose energetic soundtrack complements the frantic gameplay and helps drive the pace forward.

video:video.video:title: Tooth Invaders – The Bizarre C64 Game That Taught You to Brush Your Teeth
video:video.video:description: Released in 1982 by Commodore International for the Commodore 64, Tooth Invaders is an educational action game created in collaboration with the American Dental Association and Camelot Marketing Group. Developed as part of National Dental Month, the game set out to teach good dental hygiene through fast-paced, arcade-style gameplay. Players take control of Plaqueman, tasked with cleaning a mouth containing eight teeth by removing plaque and stopping the notorious plaque germ D. K. Using a toothbrush, toothpaste, and dental floss, players must carefully navigate between teeth, clean surfaces thoroughly, and avoid direct contact with D. K. , which costs a life. Each tooth must be fully cleaned to prevent decay, and once completed it becomes immune to further plaque. Successfully cleaning a tooth also creates a brief opportunity to defeat D. K. for bonus points, adding a risk-versus-reward element to the gameplay.

video:video.video:title: Top Gun – Did Ocean’s C64 Game Match the Film?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Ocean Software, Top Gun is a licensed flight combat game for the Commodore 64 based on the hit 1986 film. Players step into the role of Maverick, piloting the iconic F-14 Tomcat through a series of high-pressure aerial combat missions inspired by the movie’s jet-fuelled action. Gameplay is split between fast-paced dogfighting and demanding aircraft carrier landing sequences. During combat missions, players engage enemy fighters using missiles, cannons, and defensive flares while carefully managing speed, altitude, and positioning. Success depends on timing and accuracy rather than brute force. The landing sequences add an extra layer of tension, requiring precise control to line up correctly and touch down safely on the carrier deck. These sections are deliberately challenging and serve as a test of skill between combat encounters. Presented using a distinctive 3D wireframe cockpit view, Top Gun delivers a strong sense of immersion for an 8-bit system.

video:video.video:title: Total Carnage – Smash TV’s Arcade Successor Unleashed on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1994 by International Computer Entertainment, Total Carnage brings all-out arcade mayhem to the Commodore Amiga as the spiritual successor to Smash TV. It delivers relentless top-down action with an unapologetically explosive tone. Set in the fictional war zone of Kookistan in 1999, you step into the boots of Captain Carnage or Major Mayhem, members of the Doomsday Squad sent to topple the deranged dictator General Akhboob. Each of the three stages throws swarms of enemies, environmental hazards, and screen-filling carnage at you, building toward a boss showdown. The twin-stick control scheme keeps movement and firing independent, making precision and positioning critical as the pace ramps up. Power-ups, screen-clearing bombs, and rescued prisoners add tactical choices to the constant pressure, while two-player co-op doubles the mayhem. On the Amiga, Total Carnage stands out for its bold visuals, smooth scrolling, and faithful arcade energy.

video:video.video:title: Total Recall – Did Ocean Turn Schwarzenegger’s Sci-Fi Hit Into a Good C64 Game?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Total Recall is an action-heavy platform game based on the hit science-fiction film starring Arnold Schwarzenegger. You play as Doug Quaid, a man caught in a web of shifting memories, corporate conspiracies, and deadly secrets that stretch all the way to Mars. The game blends multiple styles as you move through its stages, combining platforming, shooting, and light puzzle elements across varied locations. From hostile city streets to high-security interiors, progression depends on sharp reactions, careful movement, and dealing with enemies quickly before they overwhelm you. Despite the limitations of the hardware, the C64 version delivers a tense, atmospheric experience. Large character sprites, smooth scrolling, and moody screen design help capture the darker tone of the film, while Jonathan Dunn’s soundtrack adds a constant sense of urgency and futuristic grit.

video:video.video:title: Tour de France – Could You Survive Cycling’s Toughest Race on the C64?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Activision and developed by Novotrade Software, Tour de France is one of the earliest officially licensed cycling games to appear on the Commodore 64. It places you in the saddle for a gruelling race against the clock, recreating the endurance and rhythm of professional stage racing rather than head-to-head competition. The game’s defining feature is its unusual control system. Speed is built by rapidly moving the joystick left and right, while steering is handled by holding the fire button and adjusting direction. Gear changes play an important role too, forcing you to manage effort carefully as terrain and pace shift throughout each stage. Rather than racing visible opponents, Tour de France focuses entirely on time trials. Success depends on efficiency, stamina management, and maintaining a smooth rhythm, with overall victory decided by cumulative stage times rather than single-race wins.

video:video.video:title: Toy Bizarre – The Activision C64 Platformer Set in a Toy Factory Gone Mad
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Activision for the Commodore 64, Toy Bizarre is a platform-based arcade game set inside a chaotic toy factory brought to life after hours. Designed by Mark Turmell, the game casts players as a lone night watchman tasked with stopping malfunctioning toys before the factory descends into complete disorder. Gameplay centres on navigating multi-level platforms while managing factory systems in real time. Players must shut off valves to stop new toys being released, use pistons to deactivate roaming toys, and carefully time jumps to stun enemies temporarily. Each screen demands planning and awareness, as poorly managed valves can quickly overwhelm the factory floor. A unique time-based structure divides the game into hourly shifts, with difficulty steadily increasing as the night progresses. The balance between movement, enemy control, and system management gives Toy Bizarre a distinctive rhythm that rewards calm decision-making over reckless play.

video:video.video:title: Track & Field – The C64 Sports Game That Destroyed Joysticks Everywhere
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Konami, Track and Field brings the explosive energy of the 1983 arcade hit to the Commodore 64. You compete across a series of Olympic events, each demanding speed, timing, and nerves of steel to beat records and rivals alike. The game features six classic events: the 100m Dash, Long Jump, Javelin Throw, 110m Hurdles, Hammer Throw, and High Jump. Success comes from frantic button tapping to build momentum, followed by perfectly timed inputs to launch jumps and throws at just the right moment. The C64 version preserves the fast pace and competitive spirit of the arcade, with support for up to four players turning it into a tense party favourite. Clear visuals and responsive controls keep the focus firmly on skill and reflexes, making every fraction of a second count. Track & Field remains one of the most iconic sports games of the 8-bit era, remembered for wrecked joysticks, heated rivalries, and its pure test of physical timing and coordination.

video:video.video:title: Trains – The 1983 C64 Game That Turned Toy Railways Into Big Business
video:video.video:description: Trains (1983), developed by Interactive Picture Systems and published by Spinnaker Software, is a top-down management simulation where you run a steam locomotive hauling goods across shifting industrial landscapes. You transport resources such as oil and coal to factories and depots while balancing supply and demand, refuelling your engine, avoiding crashes, and managing payroll costs. Progress depends on uncovering hidden track segments, planning efficient routes, and keeping your operation profitable as each new level increases in complexity. For its time, the game delivers clear graphics, engaging sound effects with whistles and engine chugs, and surprisingly deep economic mechanics. While more modest than later transport simulators, Trains remains a smart and rewarding early example of strategy-based management on the Commodore 64.

video:video.video:title: Trashman – The C64 Game That Turned Collecting Bins Into an Arcade Challenge
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by New Generation Software and developed by Malcolm Evans, Trashman is an arcade-style action game that turns an everyday British job into a tense and memorable challenge. Set across suburban streets, players take on the role of a refuse collector racing against the clock to keep each road spotless. Each of the seven levels represents a street lined with houses, where bins must be collected and thrown into a constantly moving garbage truck. Efficiency is everything, as time is tight and mistakes are costly. Stepping onto the grass rapidly drains the bonus timer, while getting hit by passing cars results in an instant game over. Additional hazards such as dogs and cyclists add pressure, disrupting movement and forcing careful planning of each run. Success depends on precise timing, smart routes, and resisting the temptation to cut corners for speed.

video:video.video:title: The C64 Game That Sent a Troll Treasure Hunting | Trolls and Tribulations
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Jimmy Huey and published by Creative Software for the Commodore 64, Trolls and Tribulations is an inventive platformer that blends action, puzzles, and strategy into a distinctly unusual experience. Players take control of a lone troll exploring sewer-like mazes in search of hidden relics, while facing constant danger from hostile creatures and unforgiving layouts. Gameplay is split into two interconnected phases. First comes Cretin Elimination, where enemies must be neutralised using a water gun that turns them into eggs. These eggs must then be disposed of correctly, or they’ll hatch back into active threats. Once the area is cleared, the focus shifts to maze exploration, collecting treasures and keys while avoiding indestructible monsters that force careful route planning. Movement is deliberately grid-based, with the troll moving one tile at a time, giving the game a strong puzzle-like rhythm rather than traditional free-flowing platform action.

video:video.video:title: Turbo Out Run – New York to LA at Full Boost on the Commodore 64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989, Turbo Out Run is a high-speed arcade racer developed by Sega AM2 and expertly converted to the Commodore 64 by Probe Software. Acting as a sequel to Out Run, the game sends players on a coast-to-coast race from New York City to Los Angeles, battling a rival Porsche 959 while dodging traffic and police along the way. Gameplay builds on the original formula with the introduction of a turbo boost system, allowing brief bursts of extreme speed at critical moments. Across 16 stages, players can upgrade their Ferrari F40 every fourth level, choosing improvements such as engine power, turbo performance, and tyre grip to stay competitive as the difficulty ramps up. The Commodore 64 version is widely praised for its sense of speed and smooth scrolling, delivering an impressive arcade-style experience on 8-bit hardware.

video:video.video:title: Turrican – Manfred Trenz Packed 1,300+ Screens into the Commodore 64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by Rainbow Arts and developed by Manfred Trenz, Turrican is widely regarded as one of the most ambitious and technically impressive action games ever created for the Commodore 64. Designed as a run-and-gun platformer with a strong emphasis on exploration, it raised expectations for what the C64 could deliver late in its lifespan. Players control a lone warrior encased in a powerful assault suit, battling through five expansive worlds across 13 interconnected levels. The game blends fast-paced side-scrolling combat with open-ended level design, rewarding exploration with hidden areas, secret bonuses, and powerful upgrades. A defining feature is the rotating laser weapon, which can be aimed freely through 360 degrees, adding tactical depth to both combat and traversal. From a technical standpoint, Turrican is a standout achievement on the Commodore 64. Smooth multi-directional scrolling, detailed sprite animation, and large environments push the hardware to its limits.

video:video.video:title: Turrican II – 11 C64 Levels… Including THREE Full Shoot ’Em Up Stages
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Rainbow Arts and developed by Factor 5, Turrican II: The Final Fight is the explosive sequel to one of the Commodore 64’s most celebrated action games. Building on the foundations of the original, it delivers faster gameplay, larger levels, and a far more refined sense of scale and control. Players once again step into the role of Turrican, battling through hostile alien worlds in a mission to defeat the menacing Maschinenmensch. The game blends run-and-gun action with platforming and exploration, encouraging players to search for hidden paths, power-ups, and secret areas scattered throughout its sprawling environments. Combat is expanded with a wide range of weapons and abilities, including the iconic multi-directional firing and the powerful wheel form, allowing Turrican to roll through tight spaces and enemies at speed. The variety of movement and attack options gives the game a fluid, almost arcade-like feel rarely matched on the C64.

video:video.video:title: Tusker – The C64 Adventure That Wanted to Be Indiana Jones
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by System 3, Tusker is an action-adventure game for the Commodore 64 that blends exploration, combat and puzzle solving in a cinematic African expedition. Developed by Duncan Meech with music by SID composer Matt Gray, the game follows a young explorer attempting to finish his father’s final quest: locating the legendary Elephant Graveyard hidden deep within the African wilderness. Gameplay combines side-view exploration with item-based puzzles and survival mechanics. Players travel across deserts, villages and ancient ruins while collecting weapons such as knives, machetes, guns and slingshots. These tools are not only used to defeat enemies but also to interact with the environment and solve progression puzzles scattered across the game’s locations. A unique mechanic in Tusker is the survival system. Energy and water levels must be carefully managed as the harsh environments slowly drain your resources.

video:video.video:title: Uchi Mata – Brian Jacks Put Illegal Judo Moves into a C64 Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Martech Games for the Commodore 64, Uchi Mata is a distinctive judo-based fighting game promoted by British Olympic judoka Brian Jacks, who also acted as technical advisor. Rather than arcade brawling, the game aims to replicate the discipline and technique of competitive judo. Matches take place in a tournament setting where success depends on positioning, timing, and executing precise joystick combinations to perform throws and holds. The control system rewards planning and technique over fast reactions, making each bout feel tactical and deliberate rather than frantic. Uchi Mata features more than 400 frames of animation, resulting in fluid and convincing character movement. Players can attempt both legal and illegal judo techniques, with the powerful Uchi Mata throw capable of ending a match instantly. Risky moves come at a cost, however, as repeated fouls can lead to disqualification.

video:video.video:title: Ultima I – The C64 Fantasy RPG That Suddenly Becomes a Space Shooter
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Origin Systems for the Commodore 64, Ultima I: The First Age of Darkness is a landmark role-playing game that laid the foundations for the legendary Ultima series. Set in the fantasy world of Sosaria, players are tasked with defeating the evil wizard Mondain by travelling through time to destroy his Gem of Immortality and end his reign of darkness. Gameplay is divided into several interconnected systems, including an overhead world map for exploration, first-person dungeon crawling, and even space combat sequences. This ambitious structure gave players an unprecedented sense of freedom. Character creation allows players to distribute points across key attributes such as Strength, Agility, and Intelligence, while choosing from races including Human, Elf, Dwarf, and Bobbit. These choices directly affect combat and progression. The Commodore 64 version was rewritten in assembly language and represented a major upgrade over the original Apple II release.

video:video.video:title: Underwurlde – Could Anyone Actually Finish This C64 Adventure?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Ultimate Play the Game for the Commodore 64, Underwurlde is a side-scrolling platform adventure that expands the Sabreman universe in a bold new direction. Moving away from the overhead exploration of Sabre Wulf, the game places players deep beneath the surface in a vast, interconnected cave system viewed from the side. You control Sabreman as he descends through hostile chambers filled with creatures, traps, and deadly drops, with the ultimate goal of escaping the Underwurlde itself. Progress depends on exploration and discovery rather than linear level design, with multiple routes, hidden areas, and guarded exits that require specific items to overcome. Weapons such as the dagger, torch, and knife are essential tools, each used to defeat guardians blocking the way forward. Precision movement and careful timing are critical, as the game is unforgiving and mistakes can quickly undo hard-won progress.

video:video.video:title: Up’n Down – Sega Let You Jump a Dune Buggy ONTO Other Cars on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984, Up’n Down is an arcade-style racing and action game developed by Sega and published on the Commodore 64 by U. S. Gold. Players take control of a distinctive purple dune buggy racing along a vertically scrolling, pseudo-3D track packed with hills, jumps, intersections, and hazards. The goal is simple but demanding: collect ten coloured flags scattered across the course while avoiding crashes and enemy vehicles. Cars can be jumped over or landed on to destroy them for bonus points, while sharp reflexes and careful speed control are essential to survive the constantly changing terrain. What sets Up’n Down apart is its unusual blend of racing and arcade action. Lane switching at intersections, dramatic elevation changes, and aggressive enemy traffic keep the pace relentless, rewarding players who master timing, positioning, and momentum.

video:video.video:title: Up Up and Away – The C64 Game That Put You in a Hot-Air Balloon
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Starcade Software and developed by Gwyll Jones, Up Up and Away is a distinctive side-scrolling action game for the Commodore 64 that puts players in control of a hot air balloon drifting across a hazardous landscape. Its unusual theme and mechanics set it apart from more conventional arcade titles of the era. Gameplay revolves around careful balloon control as the screen scrolls relentlessly forward. Players must dodge clouds, trees, kites, birds, and even people hurling rocks from below, all while managing a limited fuel supply that drains whenever the balloon ascends. To stay aloft, players can drop sandbags to reduce weight—these also double as weapons, used to hit targets marked with a “P” for bonus points. Strategic planning is key, as landing at checkpoints allows players to refuel and restock sandbags before pressing on.

video:video.video:title: Uridium – Andrew Braybrook Made the C64 Move at Ridiculous Speed
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Hewson Consultants and developed by Andrew Braybrook of Graftgold, Uridium is a blisteringly fast horizontal shooter that redefined what the Commodore 64 could do. You pilot the agile Manta fighter across fifteen vast super-dreadnought carriers, each named after metallic elements, in a relentless fight for survival. Each carrier demands precision flying as you skim across its surface, destroying defences, dodging drones, and avoiding lethal barriers. Once the core is breached, you must land successfully to trigger the self-destruct sequence before making a clean escape, turning every stage into a nerve-wracking test of control and timing. Uridium is famous for its technical brilliance, using clever manipulation of character graphics to simulate pseudo-parallax scrolling. The result is a sense of speed, depth, and smooth motion that was astonishing on C64 hardware at the time.

video:video.video:title: Uuno Turhapuro Muuttaa Maalle – Finland’s First Gaming Hit Was Brutal | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Amersoft for the Commodore 64, Uuno Turhapuro Muuttaa Maalle is a side-scrolling action game based on Finland’s hugely popular comedy character Uuno Turhapuro, portrayed on film by Vesa-Matti Loiri. The game follows Uuno’s chaotic move from city life to the countryside, turning everyday rural mishaps into arcade-style challenges. Gameplay is split across three distinct stages, each with its own mechanics and pace. In the opening sequence, Uuno is dragged behind a car while gripping a plough, weaving around obstacles along a dirt road. This is followed by a barefoot water-skiing section set on a lake, where fast reactions are needed to avoid hazards. The final stage sees Uuno sprinting through a forest, dodging trees and obstacles at speed. The difficulty is unforgiving, demanding precise timing and sharp reflexes, which adds to the game’s reputation as a tough but memorable experience.

video:video.video:title: V: The Computer Game – Infiltrating the Visitors’ Mothership on C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Ocean Software and developed by Kaos, V: The Computer Game brings the tension of the popular sci-fi television series to the Commodore 64. Players take on the role of resistance fighter Donovan, infiltrating the alien mothership to sabotage its systems and strike a blow against the Visitors. Gameplay blends side-scrolling action with stealth and puzzle-solving. Players must carefully navigate the ship’s corridors, avoiding or disabling robotic guards while conserving limited ammunition and health. Progress depends on placing bombs at key locations and outsmarting the ship’s defences rather than relying on brute force. A central mechanic is the Communiputer, a handheld device used to interact with terminals, decode alien systems, and manipulate security features. This adds a thoughtful, methodical layer to the action, drawing comparisons with games like Impossible Mission in both structure and pacing.

video:video.video:title: Vendetta – System 3’s Overlooked C64 Isometric Action Classic
video:video.video:description: Released in 1990 by System 3 and developed by Stanley Schembri, Vendetta is an ambitious hybrid action-adventure for the Commodore 64, blending exploration, combat, and vehicle sequences into one gritty experience. In the game, you play as an ex-soldier whose brother and niece have been kidnapped by a terrorist/mafia organisation. Your mission is to track them down and rescue them across seven dangerous levels. Gameplay combines isometric “Last Ninja–style” exploration — featuring rooms, items, weapons, and light puzzle elements — with fast-paced driving and shoot-’em-up sections including car chases, helicopter attacks, and police roadblocks. The game features detailed backgrounds and a moody introduction sequence, with music composed by Matt Gray. While in-game animation and controls can feel clunky at times, the atmosphere and ambition remain strong. Despite its flaws, Vendetta stands out as one of the more daring late-era C64 titles.

video:video.video:title: Vigilante – Rescue Madonna from the Skinheads in This C64 Arcade Brawler
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Irem, Vigilante brings raw, street-level action to the Commodore 64 as a direct follow-up in spirit to Kung-Fu Master. You play a lone martial artist battling through the mean streets of New York with one goal in mind: rescue Maria from the Rogues gang. The action is immediate and uncompromising. You push through five stages packed with thugs attacking from both sides, mixing punches and kicks while managing spacing and timing to avoid being swarmed. Nunchaku add extra bite when you can grab them, and the infamous grab mechanic forces quick reactions to escape enemy holds. On the C64, Vigilante focuses on delivering the feel of the arcade rather than spectacle. The presentation is stripped back, but the core mechanics remain intact, keeping the emphasis firmly on reflexes, positioning, and endurance.

video:video.video:title: Visible Solar System – In 1982 the Commodore 64 Was Already Running a Planetarium
video:video.video:description: Released in 1982 by Commodore for the Commodore 64, Visible Solar System is an early educational software title designed to function as a digital planetarium. It allows users to explore the layout of the solar system and observe planets and their moons from different perspectives. The program presents a visual model of the solar system, featuring basic animation such as planetary rotation and orbital movement. Users can zoom in on major bodies including Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, gaining a closer look at their appearance and relative positions in space. Rather than focusing on traditional gameplay, Visible Solar System emphasises visual exploration and curiosity-driven learning. It does not include quizzes, missions, or detailed scientific explanations, instead encouraging users to observe and interact with the simulation at their own pace. While its graphics and presentation are simple by modern standards, they represented an impressive technical achievement for early home computers.

video:video.video:title: Walker – Two Players Could Control ONE Mech on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in 1993 by DMA Design and published by Psygnosis, Walker is a distinctive side-scrolling shooter that puts you in control of a towering bipedal war machine. Set across multiple eras of conflict, the game blends heavy firepower with a unique control system that feels unlike anything else on the Amiga. Movement is handled via joystick or keyboard, while aiming is controlled with the mouse, allowing you to independently target enemies above, below, and ahead of the Walker. This dual-control approach gives combat a deliberate, weighty feel as you crush infantry, tanks, helicopters, and fortifications beneath your mechanical legs. Each of the four levels is set in a different time period, from wartime Berlin to a dystopian near future and beyond, with parallax scrolling used to add depth and atmosphere to the environments. Managing heat buildup and shield energy becomes just as important as raw firepower as the screen fills with enemies.

video:video.video:title: Water Polo – Gremlin Put TWO-Player Water Polo on the C64… Because Why Not?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Gremlin Graphics for the Commodore 64, Water Polo delivers a detailed and thoughtful take on the aquatic team sport, standing apart from the more arcade-driven sports titles of its era. Rather than focusing on speed alone, the game places a strong emphasis on positioning, timing, and tactical play. Matches take place on a pseudo-3D pool viewed from above, with six players per team including a fully controllable goalkeeper. Control automatically switches to the player closest to the ball, plainly identified by a coloured cap, keeping the action flowing while encouraging quick decision-making. Gameplay rules closely mirror real water polo. Attacks must be made from one of five forward-facing directions to retain possession, while fouls, penalties, and temporary player ejections introduce a deeper strategic layer. With four timed quarters and a strict shot clock, players must balance disciplined defence with well-planned offensive movement.

video:video.video:title: Ween: The Prophecy – Did This Forgotten Amiga Adventure Deserve Better?
video:video.video:description: Released in 1992 for the Commodore Amiga, Ween: The Prophecy is a darkly whimsical fantasy adventure developed by Coktel Vision. You play as Ween, a young wizard racing against a strict three-day deadline to gather three magical grains of sand and stop the evil Kraal before the Great Eclipse consumes the world. Gameplay centres on classic inventory-driven puzzle solving, branching quest paths, and trial-and-error logic that constantly toys with your expectations. Progression often depends on experimentation and lateral thinking, with solutions that feel deliberately strange but consistent within the game’s own rules. Visually, the game stands out with a faux-sepia overworld contrasted by richly coloured interior scenes, giving it a distinctive storybook quality. The Amiga version features a reduced colour palette and simplified digitised animations, yet still manages to preserve the eerie, slightly unsettling atmosphere that defines the experience.

video:video.video:title: Weird Dreams – The Amiga Horror Game Trapped Inside a Man’s Nightmares
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Rainbird Software, Weird Dreams is a cinematic platformer that drags you deep into a nightmarish subconscious. You play as Steve, a young man undergoing brain surgery who becomes trapped inside a sequence of hostile dreams shaped by the sinister presence of Zelloripus, a corrupting force linked to his colleague Emily. Each dream world is visually striking and deeply unsettling, ranging from twisted fairgrounds to vast deserts filled with impossible creatures. Progression relies on careful movement, observation, and precise timing, with every screen presenting hazards that punish impatience and reward methodical play. The game’s imagery takes clear inspiration from surrealist art, creating scenes that feel deliberately uncomfortable and unpredictable. This atmosphere is reinforced by David Whittaker’s haunting Amiga soundtrack, which gives the game a constant sense of tension and unease. Packaged with a 64-page novella by Rupert Goodwins that expands the narrative, Weird Dreams stands out as one of the Amiga’s most distinctive and challenging experiences.

video:video.video:title: West Bank – 12 Doors… But Shoot the Wrong Person and You Lose a Life | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Gremlin Graphics for the Commodore 64, West Bank is an arcade-style shoot ’em up inspired by Sega’s Bank Panic. Set in the Old West, the game puts players in the role of a sharp-eyed sheriff tasked with defending a busy frontier bank from bandits, troublemakers, and hidden threats. Gameplay revolves around twelve doors lining the bank interior, each opening to reveal a character whose intentions must be judged instantly. Players must gun down outlaws who draw weapons, avoid shooting innocent customers, and stay alert for disguised dangers such as bombs concealed under hats. Quick reactions and accuracy are essential as the pace steadily increases. Between stages, the action shifts to tense duel sequences where players face off against three gunslingers in classic quickdraw showdowns. Timing is everything, adding variety and an extra layer of skill beyond the main bank defence gameplay.

video:video.video:title: Who Dares Wins II – The C64 Sequel Born After Legal Action Over Commando
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Alligata Software, Who Dares Wins II is a vertically scrolling, top-down action game for the Commodore 64 that refines the formula of its predecessor with sharper gameplay and more confident design. You take control of a lone soldier dropped behind enemy lines, tasked with liberating occupied townships one screen at a time. Each area scrolls in a flick-screen style, presenting enemy patrols, fortified positions, and comrades tied to trees who must be rescued before you can move on. You’re armed with an automatic rifle and a limited supply of grenades, making positioning, timing, and precision essential if you want to survive the mission. The game keeps things focused and direct, prioritising responsive controls and readable environments over visual excess. There’s no in-game music, just sparse sound effects that reinforce the tense, no-nonsense atmosphere of a solo combat operation.

video:video.video:title: Wings – Over 200 WWI Missions Told Through One Pilot’s Diary on the Amiga
video:video.video:description: Released in October 1990 by Cinemaware for the Commodore Amiga, Wings places players in the cockpit of an Allied fighter pilot during the First World War. Blending intense aerial combat with personal storytelling, the game delivers a powerful sense of life at the front, both in the air and on the page. Missions are split across three distinct styles. Dogfights are presented in a dramatic 3D chase view behind the pilot, capturing the tension of aerial duels against enemy aces. Bombing runs switch to a top-down perspective, tasking players with destroying strategic targets, while strafing missions use an isometric view focused on low-level ground attacks. Between missions, the pilot’s journal entries chronicle the passage of time from 1916 to 1918, adding emotional weight as victories, losses, and the toll of war unfold. This narrative layer transforms each mission into part of a larger story rather than isolated encounters.

video:video.video:title: Wings of Fury – The Amiga WWII Shooter That Launched You from an Aircraft Carrier
video:video.video:description: Originally developed by Steve Waldo and released by Brøderbund in 1987, Wings of Fury arrived on the Commodore Amiga in 1990 via Unlimited Software Inc. , bringing its World War II Pacific air combat to a new level of audiovisual polish. Players take on the role of a US Navy pilot flying the F6F Hellcat, launching from the USS Wasp to strike Japanese targets across a chain of hostile islands. Gameplay blends fast-paced arcade shooting with light simulation elements. Missions involve strafing ground installations, bombing bunkers, and torpedoing enemy ships, while carefully managing fuel, ammunition, and aircraft damage. Successful pilots must return safely to the carrier to refuel, rearm, and make repairs before heading back into combat. The Amiga version stands out for its smooth animation, detailed visuals by John Boechler, and an atmospheric soundtrack composed by Kris Hatlelid, all of which enhance the sense of scale and tension during each sortie.

video:video.video:title: Winter Games – Epyx Took the C64 from Ski Jumping to Bobsleigh
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by Epyx, Winter Games brings the spectacle and pressure of Olympic winter sports to the Commodore 64. As the third entry in the celebrated Games series, it builds on the rhythm-based action and competitive spirit that made its predecessors so popular. You compete across a selection of demanding winter events including ski jump, bobsled, speed skating, biathlon, figure skating, and freestyle aerials. Each discipline has its own control style and timing challenges, rewarding practice, precision, and nerve under pressure. Players can represent one of 18 countries and take part in individual events or full competitions, chasing high scores and medals. Presentation plays a big role, with an opening ceremony featuring flags and national anthems that adds atmosphere and a real sense of occasion. Praised for its smooth gameplay and strong visuals, Winter Games is remembered as one of the finest sports titles on the Commodore 64.

video:video.video:title: Wizard – Every C64 Level Gave You a Different Spell to Find the Key
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Progressive Peripherals and Software for the Commodore 64, Wizard is a single-screen action platformer developed by Sean A. Moore and Steve Luedders-Dieckbrader. Players take control of Wilfrid the Wizard, navigating compact levels packed with enemies, hazards, and carefully placed obstacles. Progress revolves around collecting keys that unlock magical abilities, turning spells into the core mechanic rather than simple power-ups. Fireballs, teleportation, and other spells must be used thoughtfully to defeat enemies and reach the exit, blending arcade action with light puzzle-solving. Each screen features its own layout and challenges, encouraging experimentation and planning rather than brute force. The game offers six difficulty levels and nine speed settings, letting players fine-tune the experience to their skill level and preferred pace. A standout feature is the built-in level editor, allowing players to design and share custom stages.

video:video.video:title: Wizard of Wor – Team Up with Your Mate… Then Shoot Him for Bonus Points on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1983 by CBS Electronics and developed by Dave Nutting Associates, Wizard of Wor is a top-down maze shooter that quickly became a standout title on the Commodore 64. Players control armoured “Worriors” battling through dungeon-style arenas filled with aggressive monsters and constant pressure. Gameplay focuses on clearing each maze by eliminating enemies such as Burwors, Garwors, and the fast-moving Thorwors, all with distinct movement patterns. Once a maze is cleared, the deadly Worluk appears, followed by the Wizard of Wor himself, taunting players with digitised speech. A radar system helps track invisible enemies, while special stages like The Arena and The Pit introduce additional twists. The game shines in cooperative two-player mode, where teamwork and positioning become just as important as shooting accuracy. The Commodore 64 version closely mirrors the arcade experience, with strong visuals, tense pacing, and optional Magic Voice Speech Module support that adds extra atmosphere.

video:video.video:title: Wizball – The C64 Shooter Where You Had to Paint the World Back In
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Ocean Software and developed by Sensible Software, Wizball is a horizontal-scrolling shoot ’em up that completely rethinks the genre. Designed by Chris Yates and Jon Hare, with a standout soundtrack by Martin Galway, it combines fast action with inventive mechanics and a bold visual identity. You control Wiz, a wizard transformed into a bouncing green ball, travelling through a drained, monochrome world. Defeated enemies release colour droplets, and by collecting and mixing primary colours you gradually restore the landscape, unlocking new areas and abilities as colour returns to the screen. The Commodore 64 version is especially celebrated for its fluid animation and imaginative level design. A unique control system lets you manage both Wiz and his feline companion, Catellite, adding tactical depth alongside the constant action. Galway’s music drives the pace and atmosphere throughout.

video:video.video:title: World Games – Bull Riding, Cliff Diving and Caber Tossing | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1986 by Epyx, World Games is part of the legendary Games series and shifts the focus from Olympic stadiums to traditional sports from around the globe. Each event is themed around a different country, giving the competition a distinctive international flavour. You compete across eight varied disciplines, including weightlifting, cliff diving, slalom skiing, log rolling, bull riding, caber toss, barrel jumping, and sumo wrestling. Every event demands its own mix of timing, rhythm, and control, keeping the gameplay fresh and unpredictable. Presentation plays a big role, with travelogue-style introductions and national anthems setting the scene before each contest. The game supports up to eight players, making it a brilliant multiplayer experience and a staple for competitive play sessions. Praised for its variety, polish, and replay value, World Games stands as one of Epyx’s strongest releases on the Commodore 64.

video:video.video:title: WWF WrestleMania – Hogan, Warrior or British Bulldog? The C64 Gave You Just Three
video:video.video:description: Released in 1991 by Twilight and published by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, WWF WrestleMania is the first officially licensed WWF wrestling game to appear on major European home computers. Players can choose from three wrestling superstars—Hulk Hogan, The Ultimate Warrior, or The British Bulldog—and battle through a roster of legendary opponents in pursuit of the WWF Championship. The lineup includes iconic villains and rivals such as Mr. Perfect, The Warlord, Ted DiBiase, The Mountie, and Sgt. Slaughter, each bringing their own challenge to the tournament. Matches focus on fast, accessible arcade-style action, featuring punches, kicks, dropkicks, clotheslines, and risky grapples performed through rapid joystick movement. Weapons add extra drama, allowing players to grab a ringside chair for devastating attacks when the opportunity arises. Each bout is fought under a strict five-minute time limit, with draws and count-outs counting as losses, keeping pressure high throughout the tournament.

video:video.video:title: X-Out – The C64 Shooter Where You Bought Your Submarine Before the Battle
video:video.video:description: Released in 1989 by Rainbow Arts and developed by Arc Developments, X-Out is a horizontally scrolling shoot ’em up that swaps deep space for the depths of the ocean. You pilot advanced submarines through alien-infested underwater environments, facing relentless enemy waves and screen-filling bosses. What truly sets X-Out apart is its shop system. Between missions, you spend earned credits on submarines, weapons, and upgrades, carefully balancing firepower, shields, and support craft. Success depends as much on smart preparation as it does on sharp reflexes once the action begins. The game pushes the Commodore 64 hard, delivering detailed underwater visuals, smooth scrolling, and dense enemy patterns. Chris Hülsbeck’s driving soundtrack adds urgency and atmosphere, perfectly matching the intensity of the on-screen mayhem. Famously tough and unapologetically demanding, X-Out rewards mastery and planning over brute force. Today, it’s regarded as one of the finest shooters on the C64, remembered for its originality, difficulty, and unmistakable Rainbow Arts style.

video:video.video:title: Xybots – Could the Amiga Handle Atari’s 3D Arcade Maze Shooter?
video:video.video:description: Originally released in arcades in 1987 by Atari Games and later ported to the Commodore Amiga in 1989 by Teque Software and published by Domark, Xybots blends sci-fi action with tactical maze navigation. Players take on the role of Major Rock Hardy or Captain Ace Gunn, elite operatives fighting through hostile complexes overrun by robotic enemies determined to wipe out humanity. Gameplay centres on navigating 3D maze environments while managing positioning, aiming, and movement with care. The split-screen presentation shows the player’s perspective alongside a tactical overview, encouraging awareness of enemy placement and level layout. Energy capsules can be collected to survive longer runs, while upgrades and hidden areas reward careful exploration rather than reckless rushing. The Amiga version captures the tense atmosphere of the arcade original, combining deliberate pacing with bursts of intense combat.

video:video.video:title: Yie Ar Kung-Fu – Martin Galway Put Jean-Michel Jarre into a C64 Fighting Game
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64 by Konami and published by Imagine Software, Yie Ar Kung-Fu is one of the earliest games to define the one-on-one fighting genre. You play as Oolong, a determined martial artist on a quest to become Grand Master by defeating a lineup of opponents, each with their own weapons, tactics, and personalities. The action takes place on a fixed-screen arena, focusing entirely on timing, positioning, and learning enemy patterns. Every opponent fights differently, forcing you to adapt your approach rather than rely on a single strategy. While the mechanics are simple, the challenge ramps up quickly, rewarding precision and patience. On the C64, the game delivers colourful sprites and distinct arena backdrops that help each fight feel unique. Character animations are clear and readable, keeping the focus on duels rather than spectacle.

video:video.video:title: Yogi Bear – The C64 Trip to Jellystone Park You May Have Forgotten
video:video.video:description: Released in 1987 by Piranha Software, Yogi Bear brings the famous Hanna-Barbera cartoon character to the Commodore 64 in a large-scale arcade adventure set across Jellystone Park. When Boo-Boo is captured by a hunter, it’s up to you to guide Yogi through the park and save his best friend before time runs out. Gameplay spans an impressive 198 interconnected screens filled with hazards, wildlife, rivers, and puzzles. You explore freely, collecting toffee apples that reveal clues to a hidden code needed to unlock Boo-Boo’s cage. Yogi can even disguise himself as a bush to sneak past enemies, adding a playful stealth element to the adventure. A calendar-based time limit adds pressure, forcing you to plan routes carefully and avoid wasted moves. The Commodore 64 version delivers smooth scrolling, expressive character sprites, and a presentation that captures the lighthearted spirit of the cartoon.

video:video.video:title: Zak McKracken – Aliens Were Making Everyone Stupid Through the Phone Lines on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Lucasfilm Games for the Commodore 64, Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders is a landmark graphic adventure and the second title to use the SCUMM engine after Maniac Mansion. It expanded the scope of adventure games with a globe-trotting narrative, deeper puzzle design, and a strong sense of humour. Players take control of Zak McKracken, a tabloid journalist who stumbles upon a bizarre alien conspiracy aimed at dulling human intelligence using mind-control devices. The story spans multiple real-world and off-world locations, including San Francisco, Egypt, Peru, and Mars, with players switching between characters to solve puzzles using shared logic but separate inventories. On the Commodore 64, the game uses a colourful pixel-art style within a 16-colour palette, paired with minimal sound effects that keep focus on exploration and problem-solving. While more limited than later versions, the C64 release retains the game’s wit, inventive puzzles, and memorable scenarios that reward experimentation and careful observation.

video:video.video:title: Zamzara – 15 Minutes to Escape Before the Alien Base Explodes on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988, Zamzara is a side-scrolling platform shooter developed by Jukka Tapanimäki and published by Hewson under their Rack-It budget label. Set inside a futuristic laboratory complex, players control a strange alien lifeform attempting to escape before a time bomb detonates, all under a relentless 15-minute countdown. The game blends precise platforming with tactical combat across 29 interconnected levels filled with hostile creatures, traps, and environmental hazards. Movement is a key part of survival, with the alien able to float by repeatedly tapping the jump button, allowing careful navigation through tight and dangerous spaces. Combat is built around a distinctive weapon system. Players select from lasers, missiles, and other tools, each with limited ammunition. Weapons must be charged before firing, forcing players to balance timing, positioning, and resource management during intense encounters. Zamzara stands out for its smooth scrolling visuals, detailed sprite work, and oppressive sci-fi atmosphere.

video:video.video:title: Zaxxon – Your Shadow Was Part of the Controls in this C64 classic
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Sega and ported to the Commodore 64 by Synapse Software, with European distribution by US Gold, Zaxxon brings one of the most innovative arcade shooters of the early 1980s to home computers. Players pilot a futuristic spacecraft on a dangerous assault through a heavily fortified enemy fortress. The game’s defining feature is its isometric perspective, which creates a pseudo-3D battlefield unlike most traditional vertical or horizontal shooters. Players must constantly manage altitude and positioning, weaving between walls, fuel tanks, gun turrets, and enemy fire while maintaining forward momentum. Progression depends on precise control, spatial awareness, and careful resource management. Fuel must be conserved, shots timed accurately, and key targets destroyed in order to reach the later stages and complete each mission successfully. Visually, the Commodore 64 version delivers atmospheric environments and strong depth illusion that closely reflect the arcade original.

video:video.video:title: Zeewolf – Was This the Amiga’s Best 3D Combat Game?
video:video.video:description: Released for the Commodore Amiga in 1994, Zeewolf is a 3D helicopter combat game created by Binary Asylum. Combining fast shoot-em-up action with tactical missions, hostage rescues and vehicle transportation, it became one of the Amiga’s most distinctive military action games. My first experience with Zeewolf came from the Amiga Format cover-disk demo. I couldn’t afford the full game at the time, and none of my mates had a dodgy copy I could put through X-Copy, so I played that demo to death. I knew every target, building and stretch of water, but revisiting the complete game revealed how little of Zeewolf I had actually seen. Across 32 missions, players pilot the heavily armed Zeewolf helicopter over islands, military bases and open water. Objectives include attacking enemy installations, rescuing prisoners, escorting aircraft and transporting friendly Buffalo tanks into battle.

video:video.video:title: Zenji – Activision’s C64 Puzzle Game That Made You Rebuild the Maze
video:video.video:description: Released in 1984 by Matthew Hubbard and published by Activision for the Commodore 64, Zenji is a distinctive puzzle-action game that blends fast reactions with spatial problem-solving. Players control a floating, Mandarin-style head navigating a maze of rotating pathways suspended in a surreal void. The objective is to rotate maze segments to maintain a continuous connection with a glowing central power source, gradually turning the entire maze green before time runs out. As levels progress, the layouts become increasingly complex, demanding careful planning alongside quick decision-making. Hazards such as roaming flames that fire deadly sparks add real-time pressure, forcing players to balance maze rotation with evasive movement. Staying connected to the source while avoiding danger is key, giving Zenji its unique rhythm and tension. Praised for its originality and elegant design, Zenji stands out as an early example of real-time puzzle gameplay done right.

video:video.video:title: Zone Trooper – Crash-Landed on an Alien World with One Way Home | C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1988 by Gamebusters for the Commodore 64, Zone Trooper is a side-scrolling sci-fi action adventure set on a hostile alien world. After crash-landing on the planet’s surface, players take control of a lone astronaut tasked with recovering vital plasma capsules needed to repair their stranded spacecraft. Gameplay blends exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving as you move across the planet’s surface and descend into underground complexes. A distinctive gravity mechanic influences movement and jumping, adding an extra layer of challenge to platforming sections and forcing careful positioning during exploration. Survival plays a key role, with players needing to manage limited air supply and energy levels while navigating dangerous environments and hostile encounters. Progress depends on methodical exploration and smart resource use rather than pure reflexes alone. While reception at the time was mixed, Zone Trooper stood out for its ambitious design and moody sci-fi atmosphere.

video:video.video:title: Zork Trilogy – No Graphics, No Hand-Holding and One Very Hungry Grue | C64
video:video.video:description: Originally released individually in 1983 by Infocom, the Zork series brought sophisticated interactive fiction to home computers, inviting you into the vast and dangerous Great Underground Empire through pure text and imagination. Zork I, Zork II, and Zork III each build on the same rich fantasy world, gradually expanding its scope, puzzles, and narrative ambition. Gameplay revolves around exploration, logic, and language. You type commands to move, examine objects, solve devious puzzles, and survive encounters with trolls, thieves, and wizards, all guided by Infocom’s famously advanced text parser. Success depends on careful observation, memory, and lateral thinking rather than reflexes. On the Commodore 64, the trilogy retains the full depth and complexity of the original releases, translating Infocom’s storytelling and puzzle design faithfully to the platform. Each entry refines the formula, with Zork III introducing more structured challenges and a stronger sense of purpose.

video:video.video:title: Zorro – Get the Barman Drunk… Then Use His Stomach as a Trampoline on the C64
video:video.video:description: Released in 1985 by U. S. Gold and developed by Datasoft, Zorro brings the legendary masked hero to the Commodore 64 in a stylish action-adventure inspired by classic swashbuckling cinema. Created by James Garon, the game reflects Datasoft’s distinctive approach to licensed titles, placing atmosphere and presentation front and centre. Set in an evocative vision of Old California, players guide Zorro through pueblo towns, underground caverns, dusty streets, and candle-lit catacombs. Progress is driven by exploration and environmental awareness rather than constant combat, with each location feeling like a carefully framed scene from a graphic novel. The game’s visual design is one of its strongest features, with large, expressive sprites and period-inspired architecture giving the world a strong sense of identity. This is reinforced by the soundtrack, including a memorable rendition of Cielito Lindo, which adds a distinctly Latin flavour to the experience.
